paragraph_text: There is a system to assess the use of TRACES in BIPs by means of supervision. At the LVUs level the system of verification does not sufficiently cover the use of TRACES, therefore it is not ensured that deficiencies are detected and corrective actions are implemented when required. 6 OVERALL CONCLUSIONS Poland has designated a competent authority for use of TRACES in relation to products of animal origin and live animals. Other competent authorities use TRACES for non-animal origin products for training purposes. In general staff at BIPs and LVUs are qualified and experienced in relation to TRACES activities and use TRACES correctly, with the exception of the controls of live animals at aba

There is a system of supervision developed within the import control sector, which includes verification of the correct use of TRACES. This includes both local supervision by the head of each BIP and central supervision via supervisory visits to each B IP by the Borders Office (4 BIPs are visited per year). However, this supervision mainly focuses on correcting individual mistakes done by BIP staff. Supervision did not identify the shortcomings described in this report (e.g. use of collective user accounts, control of re-entry horses, follow-up at controlled bodies and destruction plants).

The Border Office also carries out periodic reviews of TRACES from central level using 11 data warehouse and Clickview since December 2012 to monitor the confirmation of receipt and takes appropriate actions when receipt is not recorded as required in respect of consignments imported under Articles 8 and 15 of Directive 97/78/EC.

The regional coordinator stated that TRACES was used for management of economic operators at LVUs and statistical information. Requirements for the regional coordinators do not foresee the supervision duties on the use of TRACES for INTRA-CERTS and control of animal by-products issued and received by LVUs .

At LVUs there is no system of supervision or other activity to assess the correct use of TRACES, therefore shortcomings identified by this audit and described under findings have not been noticed. There is no routine or pro-active analysis/verification of data within TRACES. Records are checked only in response to problems identified by the competent authority of the Member State of destination.

label_heading: Conclusion on the resources for the performance
paragraph_text: The competent authority has suitably qualified and experienced staff, facilities and equipment relating to TRACES activities. Different users of TRACES received appropriate training enabling the correct use of TRACES. In some areas where instructions were not sufficiently detailed for both BIPs and LVUs, the relevant official controls are either not recorded or recorded incorrectly in TRACES. 5.3 USE OF TRACES Legal Requirements Decision 2004/292/EC, Commission Decision 2000/571/EC, Regulation (EC) No 136/2004, Regulation (EC) No 282/2004, Regulation (EC) No 599/2004, Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009 of the European Parliament and of the Council, Commission Decision 93/444/EC, Directive 97/78/EC

In one BIP visited where imported live animals were sent to approved bodies, the confirmation from the place of destination was not received and consignments were not followed-up by BIP staff contrary to the requirements of Annex I of Regulation (EC) No 282/2004. Staff were not aware of this requirement and the instructions do not contain information about it.

GVI provided a number of training courses, as required by Article 6 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, relating specifically to the use of TRACES or including it as a part of training themes. Staff also obtain on-the-job training and practice. The training courses were provided to regional services, LVUs and BIPs staff. Evaluation of the training material on control of animal by-products showed that training was sufficient and clear, however training was not effective because it had not improved the awareness of staff on the control of animal by-products at the place of destination and TRACES was not correctly used for those purposes.

Several consignments were sent to customs warehouses located in other Member States, but confirmation of arrival in TRACES was not received from the competent authorities at destination, what is not in line with the requirements of Article 2 of Decision 2000/571/EC. However, the BIP staff contacted the Polish customs authorities, who confirmed that consignments had arrived to the place of destination. The data in TRACES were never confirmed and there is no evidence that the consignment was controlled at the warehouse by the veterinary authorities of destination. The lack of feedback from destination is not notified by the BIP to the GVI, since instructions do not foresee follow-up of non- co

For consignments re-imported, sent for destruction, transiting and others which need to be followed-up, the BIP of entry follows-up those consignments by contacting the customs services in writing. Customs provide confirmation in writing that the consignments in question arrived to the place of destination. Therefore such consignments were regarded as followed- up although confirmation was not recorded in TRACES.

One BIP visited received consignments of live animals destined for approved bodies in accordance with the national legislation, after the GVI issued an import licence for certain animals. CVEDAs issued were entered into TRACES, but part 3 (Control) of the CVEDA was never completed by an official veterinarian responsible for supervision of the controlled destination contrary to requirement laid down in Part 3 of Annex 1 of Regulation (EC) No 282/2004. 5.3.6.1.2 At destination

LVUs controlling the economic operator at the place of destination do not ensure that the outcome of control on the arriving consignment is correctly recorded in TRACES (this recording is required by Annex III of Regulation (EC) No 136/2004 and Annex I of Regulation (EC) No 282/2004). This requires additional follow-up efforts from the BIPs staff. The low level of confirmation of receipt at the place of destination (e.g. re-imported, sent for destruction, approved bodies) in Traces indicates that LVUs have a low level of controls to follow-up consignments at the place of destination. 5.3.7 Animal welfare checks

In relation to exports of live animals to third countries transiting through other Member States, it was noted: · that they are accompanied only by the certificate to export to the third country (in Polish and in the third country's language). The relevant instruction "Exportation of live animals and animal products to third countries" does not require an INTRA-CERT to be issued. Certifying officers entered data related to the consignment into TRACES as soon as possible after the consignment had departed but this could take a few days and the animals may have left the EU by then. Therefore, the requirements of Article 2(1) of Decision 93/444/EEC which requires consignments of live animals to

In relation to consignments of live animals arriving from other Member States, it was noted that: · according to the competent authority, all incoming TRACES notifications are checked to verify that the details they contain are acceptable, however in order to implment Article 5(a) of Directive 90/425/EC on non-discriminatory checks, 5 percent of consignments of live animals are physically controlled at destination often in the case of suspicion. · official controls related to ante-mortem inspections or welfare controls at Control Posts are not routinely recorded in TRACES, contrary to the requirements of Article 3.1 of Decision 2004/292/EC. There are currently no national instructions that r

In relation to the movement of specific animal by-products, it was noted that: · The GVI stated that commercial documents were provided via the INTRA-CERT module of TRACES as required. Neither of the LVUs visited during the audit were responsible for controls on trade that would require issuing documents for the outward movement of such animal by-products to other Member States. · There is a national instruction on the requirements of Article 48.3 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009 and it was covered in training courses in recent years. However, the GVI did not have an overview to what extent it was being implemented (i.e. the requirement that incoming consignments of certain animal by-products

Instructions on use of DOCOMs does not contain information on the requirement of follow- up of consignments of animal by-products received from other Member States contrary to the requirements of Article 48(3) of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009.

TRACES is used for import-related activities. Inaccurate and/or incomplete data in TRACES is linked to shortcomings in the official controls (controls done by non- authorised staff, lack of testing of official samples or controls not implemented, specifically in transhipments), which undermines confidence in the official control system on the whole. 5.3 VERIFICATION AND REVIEW Legal requirements Article 8(3) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Findings

TRACES is not used for transhipped consignments. There are no controls on those movements contrary to the requirements of Article 11 of Council Directive 97/78/EC. The consignments could go on to a non-BIP EU port, where no checks would take place; or if they went to another EU BIP port, the port would not receive information about the transhipment via the TRACES inbox notifications as provided for in the General Guidance for consignments of live animals and animal products from third countries in transit or transhipment. 5.2.3 Veterinary checks

The port is a free zone and operates 24/7 with few exceptions. Imports of products of animal origin are allowed only during the presence of the official veterinarians, but transhipments can happen at any time. This means that those consignments could leave the port without TRACES documents intended for transhipment, which is not in line with Article 3 of the Commission Decision 292/2004/EC. 5 20. In the airport BIP, checking the arriving consignments and issuing and signing CVEDS in TRACES is normally done by auxiliary staff using a generic TRACES account. The implementation of veterinary checks by auxiliary staff is not in accordance with paragraph 2 of the Annex to Decision 2001/812/EC, Ar

Documentary and identity checks are recorded in TRACES. The audit team evaluated a sample of documents, and found a number of shortcomings, for example: at the airport several CVEDs indicated satisfactory documentary checks even though the data on the health certificate did not match with data declared on the first page of the CVED by the persons responsible for the load; the approval numbers of controlled destinations in the CVEDs were incorrect; many CVEDs are issued by auxiliary staff who sign using a generic password; consignments of live lobsters were certified with CVEDAs instead of the required CVEDPs. In the 2010 report a high number of errors in TRACES data were also reported.

Consignments sampled in 2013 and 2014 under the monitoring plans and subsequently released into free circulation appeared in TRACES as still pending results. The competent authorities confirmed that the tests have not been done yet. This means that in the case of a non-compliant result, it is too late to act ­ for example, no re-enforced check (REC) or Rapid Alert System for Food and Feed (RASFF) notification could be triggered. The significant delay of a year between sampling and testing was already highlighted in the 2010 report.
The results of the tests actually carried out were not entered in TRACES either. This is not in line with Annex III to Regulation (EC) No 136/2004. 5.2.4 INTRA module

label_heading: Conclusions on planning of the verification activities
paragraph_text: The competent authority is developing the activities for verification of effectiveness of the official import controls including objectives and indicators. The competent authority has not planned to implement such verification activities since 2012 leading to an absence of the evaluation of effectiveness and appropriateness of the official import controls and their compliance with EU legislation. 4 5.2 IMPLEMENTATION OF THE VERIFICATION ACTIVITIES Legal requirements Council Directive 91/496/EEC, Council Directive 97/78/EC, Directive 2002/99/EC, Commission Regulation (EC) No 136/2004, Commission Regulation (EC) No 282/2004, Commission Decision 2001/812/EC, Commission Decision 2004/292/EC. label_heading: Conclusions on implementation of the verification activities
paragraph_text: The verification activities were not implemented for the last two years, which means that the competent authority cannot ensure the effectiveness and appropriateness of the official import controls and their compliance with EU legislation. 5.3 IMPACT OF THE VERIFICATION PROCEDURES Legal requirements Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Findings

label_heading: Conclusions on the impact of the verification procedures
paragraph_text: The organisation of the verification activities foresees the use of the results of verification for planning and improving the official controls and also the future verification activities. However, in the area of the official import controls this has not been done for the last two years. Regarding verification activities conducted until 2012, improvements in the performance of the import controls were evident, however there were cases in which shortcomigns were not addressed meaning that the verification activities did not ensure the effectiveness and appropriateness of the official import controls and their compliance with EU legislation. 6 OVERALL CONCLUSIONS The competent authority is de

The certified system (finding 2) includes verification of effectiveness of the audit activities (which also include the central level supervision). After the ISO certification no verification according the new procedure (finding 2) has been followed on the official import controls.
No verification of effectiveness of the official import controls by following the new verification procedures was available at the time of the audit.

The competent authority has last audited in 2011, one of the BIPs' visited by the audit team. Both BIPs visited underwent their most recent supervision from the central level in 2010. Apart from these, the competent authority conducted a supervision on the approved warehouse under Article 12 of Directive 97/78/EC in 2010. All other BIPs last underwent a supervision either in 2010 or in 2012.

There is no head of the BIP in Budapest airport since 2011. No verification (central nor local) activities were followed on this BIP for this period of time. The competent authority issued a decision in March 2014 to have the former head of the BIP once per week to supervise the BIP activities.
No verification has been conducted on the activities of the official import controls sector at central level (LATSTD).

The head of the BIP Roszke stated that he conducts an informal supervision every two weeks on documentary checks, physical checks, sampling, facilities. Once per month he picks files of imported consignments and he assesses the correctness of the controls. He stated that he also checks TRACES on a weekly basis. The audit team noted that there is no written instruction for the supervision and the results of the supervison are not documented, which makes the statement not verifiable.

The head of the BIP Roszke conducts a monthly meeting with the inspectors in which among others, he stated that he is providing feedback on the errors he identifies in the official controls. The audit team assessed the notes and the agenda of three meetings selected by the head of the BIP and these had no information on deficiencies identified during supervision activities.

The BIPs provide reports of the official import controls they conduct on a monthly, quarterly and annual basis to the central level. These include figures of imports. Currently the competent authority does not use this information to verify the effectiveness of the official import controls

The internal audit referred to in finding 14, identified some shortcomings and recommended to have available all relevant documented procedures and to keep staff up-to-date on their tasks. However, the audit report indicated that no action plan was required. There was no follow-up on the recommendations and no corrective actions were implemented contrary to the requirement of Article 8(3)(b) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

The system in place to assess the use of TRACES in BIPs and LVUs does not ensure that deficiencies are detected and corrective actions are implemented when required. As a consequence, (i) information in the database does not always reflect accurately the controls implemented and (ii) the system is not used to detect shortcomings in the implementation of controls (e.g. no controls at destination of consignments requiring them) and those remain inadequate. 6 OVERALL CONCLUSIONS Responsibilities have been allocated to various levels of the organisation, providing adequate support for a correct use of TRACES. Although there is a provision for training and instructions, a number of shortcomings o

There was one "technical audit"/central supervision carried by NFCSO-DAHAW-LATSTD in March 2014 on ABP legislation which included an assessment of the correct use of TRACES. The report was not available at the time of the FVO audit but preliminary feedback was that no 1 In their response to the draft report, the competent authority noted that CEDs must be issued via the use of TRACES in all DPEs (BIPs) within Hungary as from 1 September 2013. 10 significant issues were detected related to the use of TRACES at the one ABP establishment visited during the audit.

There is a system of local supervision by managers at the two BIPs and two LVUs visited which includes an evaluation of the use of TRACES. There are no instructions to cover local supervision and no specific reports are created. The head of one BIP visited stated that the results of the supervision are discussed during monthly meetings with staff although this is largely undocumented/recorded. The managers at both LVUs stated that they share the relevant outcomes of their supervision activity with appropriate colleagues but that this is largely undocumented/recorded (one LVU started supervision in January 2014). There was no local supervision at one of the two BIPs visited between 2011 to th

None of the issues identified by the FVO (findings 18 to 21, 24, 26 to 31, 36 and 37) had been identified by the various forms of verification being implemented by the competent authority with the exception of the rate of confirmation of receipt at destination for channelled consignments. Conclusion on verification and review

label_heading: Conclusion on the use of TRACES
paragraph_text: Staff at BIPs and LVUs use TRACES correctly for routine activities. However, the receipt at destination of many consignments is not notified to BIPs or Member States of origin (e.g. slaughter animals, animal by-products), contrary to the legal requirements. This means that the traceability of such consignments is compromised and the arrival of the goods at the intended operator is not confirmed to origin. 5.3 VERIFICATION AND REVIEW Legal Requirements Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Findings

There is one customs warehouse in Hungary which is approved under Article 12(4) of Council Directive 97/78/EC which stores very small amounts of consignments of non-conforming goods. The last consignment entered into TRACES by the LVU responsible for this warehouse was in November 2012. The LVU has been granted Super LVUs (SLVU) status so that it can issue CVEDs for split consignments. The SLVU used such a collective account where the officials' names were not listed and therefore their names were not recorded individually when they issued CVEDs for consignments split at the warehouses (see finding 34).

Designation of authorities (e.g. regional animal health and public health authorities and BIPs) are well defined. BIPs and regional animal health authorities have proper access to TRACES and use it with regards to imports and intra-Union trade of live animals and animal by-products. However, not all regional public health authorities have access to TRACES, thus they can not exchange information with other Member States in relation to animals sent for slaughter and re-imports. 5.2 RESOURCES FOR THE PERFORMANCE OF THE CONTROLS Legal requirements Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, Regulation (EC) No 136/2004, Regulation (EC) No 669/2009, Commission Regulation (EC) No 1152/2009, Commission Implementin

The competent authorities have experienced staff with the exception of the regional public health authorities, who have not been using the system, do not have access to it and have not received training. Therefore, the minimum prerequisites for the use of TRACES by the regional public health authorities are not in place. 5.3 USE OF TRACES Legal requirements Decision 2004/292/EC, Commission Decision 2000/571/EC, Regulation (EC) No 136/2004, Regulation (EC) No 282/2004, Regulation (EC) No 599/2004, Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009 of the European Parliament and of the Council, Council Directive 97/78/EC and Council Directive 90/425/EEC. 5 Findings 5.3.1 Management of users and organisations 5.3.1.

label_heading: Conclusions on the verification and review
paragraph_text: There is a system of verifying that TRACES modules are used correctly by the BIPs. However, it does not detect and correct on time repeated errors due to focusing on the implementation of control procedures. Therefore it is not ensured that official controls are effective, deficiencies in TRACES are detected and corrective actions are implemented when required.

label_heading: Conclusions on the verification and review
paragraph_text: There is no system of verifying that TRACES modules used by regional animal health authorities are used correctly (control of DOCOMs, channelled consignments or consignments sent for destruction) and LVUs (control of INTRA-CERTs). Therefore, the deficiencies are not detected and corrected on time. A system to verify that the TRACES control module is used by regional public health competent authorities is not developed since they have no access to TRACES or only have recently received access. Therefore, Spain does not comply with the minimum requirements of the use of TRACES for the recording of controls in abattoirs and re- imported consignments of products of animal origin). 6 OVERALL CONCL

label_heading: Conclusions on the implementation of official controls
paragraph_text: There is a lack of available procedures in some cases (e.g. procedures for screening of manifests and/or Customs database, transhipments) and the competent authority has not taken into account all the relevant monitoring parameters in the preparation of the 5 monitoring plan. These reduce the effectiveness of the official import controls in preventing non-compliant consignments from entering the EU. 5.3 VERIFICATION ACTIVITIES Legal requirements Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 Findings

In the three BIPs visited there was no written procedure on how to use the available information (screening of manifests, monitoring of Customs database) to identify consignments that should be subject to veterinary inspection. 5.2.2 Veterinary checks Legal requirements Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, Council Directive 91/496/EEC, Council Directive 97/78/EC, Commission Regulation (EC) No 136/2004, Regulation (EC) No 282/2004, Commission Decision 94/360/EC, Commission Decision 97/794/EC, Commission Decision 2000/208/EC, Commission Decision 2000/25/EC and Commission Decision 2001/812/EC. Findings

The audit team noted that the competent authority relies on Customs to identify transhipped consignments where the BIP of entry is in Romania and direct them to the BIP. The audit team found two consignments destined for Romania which had been issued with transhipment CVEDs by BIPs in other Member States. Both consignments were incorrectly released for free circulation by Customs when they arrived in Romania as Customs did not know the difference between different types of CVEDs and BIPs in Romania were not involved in either case. The competent authority stated that the procedure for transhipments is currently in draft stage. The audit team noted that the relevant EU Commission guideline wa

label_heading: Conclusions on the implementation of official controls
paragraph_text: The system for import controls covers the consignments presented at the BIPs and the official controls are generally performed correctly. However, the competent authority does not use available information (Customs database, manifests) to ensure that all consignments subject to veterinary control are presented to the BIPs and there is partial enforcement of the requirement to notify the goods prior to arrival at the BIPs.

label_heading: Conclusions on the implementation of official controls
paragraph_text: There is a lack of available procedures in some cases (e.g. procedures for screening of manifests and/or Customs database, transhipments) and the competent authority has not taken into account all the relevant monitoring parameters in the preparation of the 5 monitoring plan. These reduce the effectiveness of the official import controls in preventing non-compliant consignments from entering the EU. 5.3 VERIFICATION ACTIVITIES Legal requirements Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 Findings

In two of the BIPs visited (port, airport), staff stated that they carry out cross-checks between data available on the Customs database and transport manifests in order to verify that no imports violate the requirements of Article 4 (1) of Directive 91/496/EEC and Article 3 of Directive 97/78/EC. This process includes screening 100% of manifests to identify consignments which may contain products of animal origin. The audit team randomly selected seven examples from the files to assess the system, as follows: A consignment of live birds originating from a third country and coming from another Member State was highlighted in the manifest hard copy by BIP staff. However, there was no evidence

Two of the BIPs (port, airport) visited had access to the Customs database. However staff were only using this access to follow-up veterinary consignments when there was a specific question (e.g. to check if the consignments in transit had left the country). There was no cross-check to verify whether all consignments that required veterinary inspection had been presented to the BIP.

The road BIP visited had no access to the Customs database. The competent authority stated that this was due to a lack of compatibility of the local IT system with the Customs database. According to the competent authority the issue had remained outstanding for approximately five months and at the time of the FVO audit no action had been planned to address it. The audit team noted that there are approximately 1,000 consignments that pass through this border point each month and the lack of screening of the available information to identify consignments subject to veterinary inspection, may lead to a situation in which such consignments enter the EU without undergoing veterinary checks.

In the three BIPs visited there was no written procedure on how to use the available information (screening of manifests, monitoring of Customs database) to identify consignments that should be subject to veterinary inspection. 5.2.2 Veterinary checks Legal requirements Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, Council Directive 91/496/EEC, Council Directive 97/78/EC, Commission Regulation (EC) No 136/2004, Regulation (EC) No 282/2004, Commission Decision 94/360/EC, Commission Decision 97/794/EC, Commission Decision 2000/208/EC, Commission Decision 2000/25/EC and Commission Decision 2001/812/EC. Findings

label_heading: Conclusions on the implementation of official controls
paragraph_text: The system for import controls covers the consignments presented at the BIPs and the official controls are generally performed correctly. However, the competent authority does not use available information (Customs database, manifests) to ensure that all consignments subject to veterinary control are presented to the BIPs and there is partial enforcement of the requirement to notify the goods prior to arrival at the BIPs.

In the airport BIP visited, several consignments were not pre-notified contrary to the requirement of Article 2(1) of Regulation (EC) No 136/2004. In the port BIP, a full assessment of pre-notification by the audit team was not possible as the individual import files created prior to August 2014 did not contain a part I of the CVED signed and dated by the person responsible for the load. Evidence of pre-notification was available in files created post August 2014. In the road BIP visited, pre-notification was in line with the legal requirements.

label_heading: Conclusion on the use of TRACES
paragraph_text: Most CVEDs, INTRA-certificates and DOCOMs are issued correctly in Romania. However, for many consignments which require confirmation of receipt at destination, TRACES is not used in compliance with the legal requirements for ensuring traceability, e.g. consignments arriving from other Member States (slaughter animals, animal by- products) and imports (reimports and channelled consignments). The impact of the shortcomings is limited as some controls are implemented but not recorded in TRACES. The system of randomly checking notifications related to arriving products does not ensure that the LVU is aware of all consignments which require follow-up. Feedback received from other Member States in

Figures from the TRACES database indicate that 24 consignments were channelled from EU BIPs to destinations in Romania during the 18 months prior to this audit. Receipt at destination was confirmed by completing box 41 of the CVED in 12 of these cases.
There were five re-imported consignments during the same period and three had been confirmed as received at destination via completed box 41. 5 5.2.7.2 At the point of introduction

There are three Control Posts approved in accordance with Council Regulation (EC) No 1255/97 in Romania. There are no instructions for recording official controls carried out at Control Posts in TRACES and officials do not record such controls in TRACES. 5.2.9 INTRA module

A national instruction on the implementation of the requirements of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009 requires that TRACES should be used to confirm receipt at destination of category 3 animal by-products arriving from other Member States. However, it does not include a similar requirement for Categories 1 and 2 animal by-products which are also included in Article 48(3) of Regulation EC (No) 1069/2009. According to the TRACES database, less than 20% of arriving consignments of processed animal protein and categories 1 and 2 in the DOCOM module were recorded in TRACES as being controlled at destination during 2013. It was not possible to confirm what percentage of consignments were actually contr
Many consignments rejected by BIPs and sent for destruction were not recorded in box 41 of the CVED in TRACES as being received at destination and there is no instruction on this. 5.2.10 DOCOM module

label_heading: Conclusions on the use of TRACES
paragraph_text: Finnish competent authorities are correctly using TRACES, with some specific exceptions (controls on consignments which require confirmation of receipt at destination are not always recorded in the system). This lack of information in the system undermines the communication between competent authorities in relation to the specific controls. 5.3 VERIFICATION AND REVIEW Legal requirements Regulation(EC) No 882/2004 Findings

There is a standard form for food chain information for bovines, sheep and goats. According to the instruction on the form the veterinary medicinal products to be declared are only those delivered parenterally or in feed. It is thus not clear whether other routes of administration (e.g. by pour-on, bolus or via drinking water) should be mentioned. The period for which the use of medicines should be declared was unspecified in the instructions and the audit team observed that this was interpreted in different ways by farmers. Annex II Section III point 3c of Regulation 853/2004, requires that food chain information includes data on the veterinary medicinal products or other treatments adminis

Although official staff interviewed by the audit team at the slaughterhouse and DVO/RVS visited were knowledgeable about targeting criteria, all samples (both for group A and group B substances) from slaughtered and live animals were taken randomly. Food chain information and carcase conformation were not considered in relation to the substance(s) the samples would be tested for, although the latter was clearly indicated in the sampling order. Overall there was no evidence that producers linked to non-compliant results had been targeted in subsequent years. Annex III (section 2) to Directive 96/23/EC stipulates that for group substances A samples must be targeted. The same Annex III indicate

Sampling containers, their sealing, and standardised sampling reports were in accordance with the requirements of section 2.6 and 2.7 of the Annex to Commission Decision 98/179/EC. Nevertheless, the audit team noted that for feed samples taken on farm the product was not adequately identified on the sampling forms (required by 8th indent of 9 section 2.7). There was no batch number of the feed or sampling spot on the farm (shed, silo, trough) indicated.

Storage and transport conditions have been specified in the sampling instruction in accordance with section 2.9 of the Annex to Decision 98/179/EC. However, the temperatures at which samples were stored in the fridge/freezer of the VS in the slaughterhouse visited were not controlled. In line with the sampling instruction, samples which would be transported the same day were stored in a refrigerator and samples which would be transported later in a freezer. The fridge did not have a temperature measuring device, for which reason it could not be verified whether the temperature specifications of the sampling instruction were met. The (un-calibrated) thermometer of the freezer showed a tempera

Approximately half of the non-compliances reported from the residue monitoring plan and other residue programmes in the period 2011 to 2013 were directly or potentially related to feed. In these cases the Department of Agriculture and the VMPS were often not informed by the VPHS. Consequently, the supplying feed mills were not investigated and feed samples of the original batch retained by the mills or farms were not analysed in order to establish whether contamination of the feed took place on the farm, in the feed mill or during transport. This should have been feasible if the sampling form had contained more detailed information (see also finding 46). In some cases follow-up samples were

Representatives of BMG informed the audit team that it was reluctant to register traders of ABP/DP who do not actually receive the products concerned (hereafter: paper traders) owing to difficulties in controlling their transactions. Only one such paper trader has currently been registered in accordance with Article 23 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/20091.

Similarly, the registration of carriers of ABP/DP has currently been postponed due to a number of questions regarding the applicable requirements and practical difficulties2. Although this approach is not in line with Article 23 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009, the competent authority expressed concerns that carriers of ABP/DP could use their registration to conceal the origin and/or destination of the products. According to data extracted from TRACES for 2013 by the audit team, approximately 1,570 commercial documents notifications were sent to Austria from several Member States and the arrival of around 53% of these consignments was confirmed, including consignments of several types of processed animal proteins arriving at a feed mill visited by the audit team. Evidence was seen that commercial documents generated in TRACES for products intended for use as OF/SI were checked on a regular basis. However, the arrival of approximately 430 consignments of Category 1 fat was not confirmed although this is required for such products according to Article 48(3) of Regulation (EC) No 1069/20094.

The system of official controls for the traceability of ABP/DP is negatively affected by an early stage of registration process of transporters of ABP/DP and by the unreliability of the relevant official lists of plants, establishments and operators involved in the chain of ABP/DP.

In France, official lists of approved and registered establishments are managed at regional level and are publicly available. Each region is responsible for updating their official lists on the basis of information provided by each relevant Département by using the national database of business operators (SIGAL). In 2012 an instruction was issued by DGAL highlighting the need to change the previous codification of establishments handling ABP/DP in order to bring it in line with the EU technical specifications for establishments and plants handling ABP. However, the audit team noted that a number of operators included in the SIGAL database did not appear in the official regional lists. This w

As regards registration of transporters and traders, a Ministerial Decree was issued in 2011 highlighting the obligation for these business operators to notify their activities to the departmental authorities and, in 2013, another instruction was issued to remind the local competent authorities to update the lists of establishment handling ABP/DP with registered transporters and traders. Moreover, according to representatives from DGAL, a meeting with various associations of business operators was held in 2011 where, among other things, this obligation was clarified. However, the audit team noted that in many cases, transporters and traders did not appear in the official regional lists or th

The system of official controls covers a number of operators dealing with ABP/DP, however its effectiveness is negatively affected by the following: a) traders and transporters which are not subject to official controls without a risk based justification and, b) organisation of official controls which only allows superficial checks that cannot ensure enough attention to the risk of diversion or misuse of ABP/DP. 6 5.3 TRACEABILITY OF ABP/DP: OFFICIAL CONTROLS ON RELEVANT REQUIREMENTS Legal requirements Article 41, 43 and 48 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009; Articles 17(1), 25 and 32 of Regulation (EU) No 142/2011; Article 7 of Regulation (EC) No 999/2001; Article 8 of Directive 97/78/EC. 5.3.

Official controls on ABP/DP are carried out in accordance with the national plan and using a standard checklist but, the fact that there is a very limited confirmation of arrival of consignments of ABP/DP traded from other Member States and that checks on traceability requirements are often carried out in a superficial manner or not at all, negatively affects the ability of the competent authorities to detect any diversion or misuse of ABP/DP (see conclusion 16). 5.4 INFORMATION ON THE CHAIN OF PAP TO BE USED IN AQUACULTURE FEED

As indicated in the National Inspection Programme, the frequency of inspections of business operators handling ABP/DP is risk-based. It is determined by applying a formula which, among other things, takes into account the theoretical risk of the plant (on the basis of the nature of the activities and the products handled), the volume of the product placed in the market and the performance of the business operator (determined by the inspector in charge of the official controls). The resulting frequency of inspections may vary from once per year to once every four years. In the Départements visited, the audit team noted that Category 3 processing plants were inspected generally every three yea

In the Départements visited, inspections were carried out at the planned frequencies and were largely in line with the frequency-criteria established by the National Inspection Programme. However, the audit team noted that the National Inspection Programme does 5 not include some registered business operators, namely transporters and traders handling ABP/DP, without any solid risk-based justifications being provided by the competent authorities and, as a result, these business operators are not subject to planned official controls (see also paragraph 20). This is not in line with requirements laid down by Article 3(3) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

A standard checklist is available for officials to carry out inspections in ABP plants. This checklist consists of a list of generic items applicable to all processing plants. In addition to that, a guide released in 2009 provides further details and legal clarifications. According to the competent authorities the checklist and the guide are going to be updated soon to take into account, among other things, the relevant changes in the legislation. The audit team noted that, although the current checklist (and the draft of the new one) is largely comprehensive, it contains only two-three generic items related to the traceability of ABP/DP. The competent authorities stated that for such consignments of fishmeal, which had been released for free circulation, no analysis was available. The audit team noted that the competent authorities did not know this deficiency because the operator had never been inspected (see paragraph 12). 7 5.3.2 Operator obligatio

In particular, no checks were carried out which could identify discrepancies between the amounts of materials received and dispatched (e.g. checks on the patterns and congruence of incoming and outgoing material) and only one or two commercial documents were reviewed per inspection. The only controls carried out are during a routine inspection (see section 5.2.3) when a number of consignments may be checked. As a result, the current level of notification of consignments of Category 1 and 2 ABP/DP and PAP, traded into or from France, is not in line with Article 48(3) of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009.

Although the restricted scale of production and use of PAP for the production of feed for aquaculture animals (which is mainly traded to other Member States) and the good own- control systems of business operators lower the risk of diversion or misuse of PAP containing proteins of ruminant origin, during inspections, officials generally pay limited attention to the measures implemented by the business operators, in particular in relation to the sourcing of ABP/PAP and their transport. This limits the capability of the competent authorities to ensure that PAP destined to aquaculture does not contain proteins of ruminant origin. 5.7 FOLLOW-UP OF RELEVANT RECOMMENDATIONS ON ABP MADE IN PREVIOUS

However, the audit team noted that official controls paid limited attention to ensure the actual implementation and effectiveness of the business operator's control systems (see paragraph 22) and transporters and traders of ABP/DP are not subject to planned official controls (see paragraph 10). In particular, the audit team noted that these checklists do not contain specific items on transport and were not regularly checked despite this being identified as a potentially important issue in the follow-up of non-compliances (see paragraph 51). The system for certificates of competence does provide for the required exam with a good emphasis of practical situations through its use of pictures in the assessment. BOs have used the good practice guides effectively, but both these and the exam are not adequately covering tasks in slaughterhouses which present particular risks for animal welfare such as slaughter without stunning. 5.2 PLANNING OF OFFICIAL CONTROLS Legal requirements Articles 3, 41 and 42 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Article 4(9) of Regulation (EC) No 854/2004. Findings

With the transfer of responsibility for animal welfare to the regions, from 1 January 2015 the regions' animal welfare departments are responsible for organising training and exams and awarding certificates of competence for the activities referred to in Article 7(2) of the Regulation, as envisaged by its Article 21.

Pending this change, national level training and exams were organised as follows: · There is a specific university-level course for AWOs. It was noted that all but one of the AWOs met by the audit team had attended this course. In the latter case there has to be an independent exam. For this an online exam programme has recently been created which can be accessed from a computer in the slaughterhouse. A CCA representative explained that the exam covers all activities as it was difficult to make this differentiation using the on line format used to develop the exam. Exam participants have to respond to pictures rather than plain written questions. On exam questions and topics set in Annex IV to the Regulation, it was noted that when an applicant worked in a slaughterhouse that practiced slaughter without stunning there were no precise questions/pictures regarding this practice, where both the practices and the monitoring of the risks for animal welfare are very different compared to

label_heading: Conclusions on planning of official controls
paragraph_text: The checklists for controls are well designed with a weighting factor reflecting the seriousness of non-compliance, however the data produced from the checks is not being adequately used to plan the subsequent controls on the basis of the business operators past records, or to analyse if the weighting factors for the various non- compliances were appropriate.

label_heading: Conclusions on planning of official controls
paragraph_text: Centrally, FASFC is not using data such as Foodnet as effectively as it could to ensure requirements are met and to better prioritise checks. In general, analysis of the results of previous checks has not been carried out. In particular, the results of prioritising checks on slaughter without stunning were not available. 6 5.3 OFFICIAL CONTROLS ON BUSINESS OPERATORS' OBLIGATIONS Legal requirements Articles 8, 9 and 10(2)(a) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Article 5(1)(c) of, and Section I of Annex I to, Regulation (EC) No 854/2004. Articles 6 and 17 of Regulation (EC) No 1099/2009. Findings

The results of the OVs' official controls were collated in the Foodnet database in such a way that they can be analysed. However, FAFSC has not yet used this data to evaluate and review the system of official checks to ensure that requirements are met and to better prioritise checks on such issues as broiler monitoring, problems reported from checklists and the effectiveness of enforcement in different provinces (see also sections 5.4, 5.5 and 5.6).

Every question on the OV electronic checklist is subject to a weighting factor reflecting the seriousness of non-compliance (see also sections 5.3 and 5.5). 5 · The weighting of the seriousness of non-compliance cases in the checklists triggers action when an individual case of non-compliance scores 10 or when more than 20 % of the items on the checklist are non-compliant. · For example, the lack of signs on lairage pens showing their capacity and the animals' time of arrival scores low in terms of the significance of the non-compliance as there were other ways that the CA checked overnight stays and overstocking.

The competent authorities have the necessary elements, including co-operation, supervision and documented procedures, to maintain and implement a mostly effective system of official controls as required by Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009. Official controls are planned and carried out at a relatively high frequency. Nevertheless, in some cases, in particular in transporters, traders and plants carrying out intermediate activities, these are carried out and recorded rather superficially, which results in non-compliances being overlooked. 5.2 OFFICIAL CONTROLS ON TRACEABILITY REQUIREMENTS ALONG THE CHAIN Legal requirements Articles 4(3), 21, 22, 41, 43, 45(1), 46, 48 and 53 of Regulation (EC) No 1

The audit team noted that in some cases, the time spent on individual inspections is reduced in order that the required number of inspections can be carried out, leading to some tasks being completed in a superficial manner or not being completed. For example, in one transporter and two traders visited, the inspection reports indicated less

In an intermediate plant visited dealing with former foodstuffs (different cuts and parts from slaughtered animals) the audit team noted that the operator was unable to demonstrate to which customers a certain batch of incoming ABP was distributed because apart from the archived commercial documents, no register of incoming and outgoing batches of ABP was kept. In the said plant, stock balance checks were almost impossible. The audit team compared the in-coming and the out-going quantities and found that in certain periods of the year the operator appeared to have more incoming material than could be stored on site. The operator explained that indeed that happens and in those cases they make

National rules foresee dedicated transport for food or ABP/DP. However, in a transporter visited, the audit team noted that it could not be demonstrated that these requirements were fulfilled and that fats considered as food or ABP were actually kept separately, especially during reloading (the operator could not provide any evidence where reloading took place). This increases the risk that ABP could be diverted to the food chain. These findings were overlooked by official controls. In addition, the audit team noted that the official controls in 7 this establishment were particularly short (less than one hour), which would make a thorough covering of all points on the check-list impossible.

According to a trader of fats visited, his company was the only client of a transport company for the transport of fats. The audit team noted that the number of cistern vehicles owned by the specific transport company and registered as ABP vehicles was very high in comparison to the quantities of fats transported for the trader. In light of the national requirement for dedicated ABP vehicles, no plausible explanation could be provided about the usage of all ABP cistern vehicles which appear to be idle all year round. The audit team noted that official controls did not investigate this issue. It was also noted that official controls were particularly short (between half an hour and an hour) t

In a trader visited, incoming loads of fish meal were accompanied by commercial documents which did not contain any information about the batch numbers of the product concerned. This was overlooked by the official controls.

In addition, some examples of good practices were observed, which would be beneficial to disseminate more widely. The audit team identified that official controls on ABP in slaughterhouses and cutting plants overlooked that certain slaughterhouses or cutting plants were in several cases issuing commercial documents which are used for food products, although the materials being dispatched were destined for an ABP plant and thus the intended use was ABP and not food. This issue was also identified by an RVI inspector during a supervisory official control over DVI inspectors (who overlooked this issue). The RVI has sent letters to the DVIs concerned requiring the proper use of commercial documents in accordance with Article 17 of Regulation (EU) No 142/2011.

However, the fact that those traders operating only in the domestic market are not subject to regular official controls, limits the ability of the competent authority to ensure that ABP/DP handled by them are channelled and used correctly. 5.2 OFFICIAL CONTROLS ON THE TRACEABILITY REQUIREMENTS ALONG THE CHAIN Legal requirements Articles 4(3), 21, 22, 41, 43, 45(1), 46, 48 and 53 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009; Article 7 of Regulation (EC) No 999/2001; Articles

VFB has drafted a new risk classification of ABP/DP operators applicable from 5 May 2014. The rating goes from very high risk operators (to be inspected four times per year) to very low risk operators (to be inspected only "as necessary"). In this context, VFB distinguishes between traders operating only in the domestic market (classified as very low risk) and traders operating in the EU market (re-classified as low risk). Carriers have been re- classified as low risk and have to be inspected once every three years. VFB and CVC officials stated that those traders classified as very low risk (i.e. to be inspected "as necessary") would only be inspected if a fraudulent activity is suspected or

Official controls largely ensure that a) operators comply with the relevant rules, and b) officials are able to follow the flow of ABP/DP through the chain if necessary. In addition, the audit team noted good practices by certain officials, who undertook initiatives to better take into account the risk of diversion or misuse of ABP/DP. Nevertheless, the otherwise robust system ensuring that ABP/DP are only used or disposed of in permitted ways is weakened by i) the fact that the said initiatives cannot be considered an integral part of the system for official controls, and ii) gaps in verifying the arrival of consignments of ABP/DP traded in from other Member States. 6 OVERALL CONCLUSIONS Ov

Officials from two CVC visited, declared that the notification of arrival of consignments of products referred to in Article 48(3) consisted only in opening the TRACES document received on-line to check that the the data it contained were correct (e.g. name, address and approval/registration number of the plant of destination). However, physical checks in the plant of destination only took place when the plant was subject to general inspection in accordance with the ABP/DP control plan. The audit team noted that, although the control part in TRACES had been completed for most of the consignments, the time elapsed between the arrival of consignments and the completion of the control part vari

Checks which take into account the risk that ABP/DP may be diverted or misused are not systematically done, as this is not included in VFB guidelines, instructions and check-lists for CVC inspectors. This is not in accordance with Article 3 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. However, the audit team visited two processing plants where the inspectors were performing, on their own initiative, specific checks (in the form of reconciliation of quantities) to ensure this diversion or misuse did not happen. This is considered good practice. 5.2.3 Actions in case of non-compliance

Adequate arrangements are in place to enable the organisation and planning of regular official controls to monitor and verify that most operators comply with the requirements relating to the traceability of ABP/DP. However, the fact that paper traders and carriers transporting ABP/DP by road are not subject to regular official controls as required, limits the ability of the competent authorities to ensure the traceability of ABP/DP handled by these operators. 5.2 OFFICIAL CONTROLS ON TRACEABILITY REQUIREMENTS ALONG THE CHAIN Legal requirements Articles 4(3), 21, 22, 41, 43, 45(1), 46, 48 and 53 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009; Article 7 of Regulation (EC) No 999/2001; Articles 17(1), 32 and

No systematic controls of transporters are in place and while random checks on transporters are carried out at the place of origin and at the place of destination of ABP/DP, these checks focus on the presence of commercial documents and the registration status of transporters. According to the SVA representatives, transporters are informed about their duties at registration. 5 a) The first road haulier visited involved in transport of Category 1 fat, had been informed by the regional veterinary inspectors of the relevant legal requirements at the time of his application for registration. The operator held a register of all commercial documents for the previous two years as this had been requ

According to SVA, paper traders of ABP/DP are not subject to regular official controls as required by article 45 to Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009, because they may be difficult to locate and, in some cases, they are shown on the commercial documents as receivers or dispatchers of derived products for reasons of commercial confidentiality, although the products are never held on their premises (in most cases there are no premises where ABP/DP could be kept). label_heading: Conclusions on implementation of the eradication measures
paragraph_text: The low vaccination coverage on positive holdings in the area of Trás-os-Montes, compromise the overall effectiveness of vaccination in this area. As a consequence the disease frequently occurs in non-immunised animals.

label_heading: Conclusions on implementation of the eradication measures
paragraph_text: Lack of reliable information on all locations where animals are kept on a permanent or temporary basis prevents full traceability of animals, as well as enforcement and verification of movement restrictions. As not all common pastures are registered, the enforcement of movement restrictions and verification of their effectiveness cannot be fully ensured. Although tracing of movements of animals to common pastures is part of an epidemiological investigation, this information is of limited value because not all new brucellosis outbreaks have been investigated. Failure to fully inforce the movement 14 restrictions and traceability favours the spread and persistence of infections in areas with h

The CCA has established information systems that support continuous monitoring and evaluation of implementation of the BMEP measures. Desk-top evaluations allow to monitor the indicators of the progress of implementation of the programme (such as number of animals sampled, tested, vaccinated, observation of deadlines). The absence of checks on-the-spot, to evaluate implementation of measures carried out by OPPs (such as sampling and vaccination) as well as lack of verification of implementation of measures such as movement restrictions and cleaning and disinfection on infected holding, preclude the CCA from evaluating the quality, completeness and effectiveness of the specific BMEP measures.
In the area of Trás-os-Montes, on a significant number of positive holdings where vaccination coverage was investigated, animals have not been vaccinated as required by Point 4.4.7 of the BMEP.

Movement restrictions are largely applied according to Point 4.4.9 of the BMEP. However, full control and enforcement of movement restrictions of animals from BMNF herds to common pastures is not implemented in areas where 90% of holdings are dependent on common pastures on a daily basis.

There is a lack of procedures to verify on-the-spot implementation of certain control and eradication measures (for example sampling, vaccination, cleaning and disinfection) in order to evaluate their quality, completeness and effectiveness as well as to ensure corrective actions when needed. Thus, the CA cannot demonstrate that activities and measures are implemented as described in the approved programme contrary to the requirement in Article 15.1(a) of Commission Implementing Decision 2013/722/EU.

label_heading: Conclusion on organisation and implementation of official controls
paragraph_text: The documented procedures and instructions in place are sufficient for BIP staff to perform the controls correctly and consistently once the consignments are notified. However, an internal procedure to ensure that consignments will be presented for veterinary checks is not in place, which increases the possibility of a consignment entering without veterinary checks. 5.2 BIP FACILITIES AND EQUIPMENT Legal requirements Articles 4, 10 and Annex II of Regulation (EC) 882/2004; Article 6(2)(a) and (b) of, and Annex A to Council Directive 91/496/EEC; Articles 3 and 4 of Commission Decision 97/794/EC; Regulation (EC) 1/2005. Findings

The facilities proposed cannot ensure that standards for animal welfare can be maintained for dogs, cats or ferrets, where there is a need for housing. The BIP facilities are adequate for receiving and checking consignments of insects. 6 OVERALL CONCLUSIONS The proposed BIP will be integrated into the existing national import control system. Allocation of tasks, responsibilities and duties, training and instructions will support the correct implementation of the official import controls. The absence of an agreement with Customs to ensure that goods will be presented for veterinary checks increases the possibility of a consignment entering without veterinary checks. At the time of the audit,

The inspection room is suitable for different species of animals. However, it is not equipped with the necessary tools that would allow staff to perform identity and physical checks (e.g. refrigerator for storing samples, equipment to restrain, equipment to check their identification i.e. microchip readers), contrary to the requirements laid down in Articles 3 and 4 of Decision 97/794/EC.

The existing isolation spaces (kennels) to detain a typical consignment of the species expected are located outside the BIP facilities, near the tarmac. The distance between the kennels and the runaway of the airport is insufficient to mitigate adequately the noise levels. The kennels are not suitable for puppies, small dogs, cats or ferrets: they do not provide lighting, ventilation and/or temperature control. Overall, the isolation facilities proposed cannot ensure that the environmental conditions are adequate to avoid distress to the animals, contrary to the requirements of Regulation (EC) 1/2005.

Contracts and procedures are in place, as required by points 8 and 10 of Annex A to Directive 91/496/EEC, as follows: for cleaning and disinfection of the facilities of the BIP, laboratories where the samples have to be sent, disposal of carcasses/dead animals, and additional veterinary surgeon services. There is no contract for pest control in the area where the kennels are located, outside the building (see finding 16).

The legal framework to enable the full implementation of the revised measures introduced by CID 2015/789/EU, and the approval of the revised AP, was not in place at the time of the audit. There is no timeline for its adoption by the MIPAAF, or implementation, although all of the measures in that CID were applicable from 21 May 2015.

The SA stated that a new Decree would need to be adopted, to establish the necessary legal framework for the application of CID 2015/789/EU. They stated that it is intended that the new Decree will contain additional requirements, beyond those in CID 2015/789/EU. A new AP will be issued following the adoption of the Decree. The SA was not able to provide a timeline for completion of the process. In the interim period though, the Decree of 26 September 2014 remains in force, i.e. the measures introduced by CID 2015/789/EU will not be implemented (with the exception of the revision to the demarcation of the area, detailed in paragraph 10 above).

However, there is limited direct engagement with stakeholders and the message that, in the absence of concerted control measures, the disease has, and will, continue to spread rapidly with the resultant significant loss of olive trees and other host plants, is often not conveyed effectively. This undermines the ability for an effective implementation of the necessary control measures for Xf. 5.4 LABORATORIES AND TESTING FOR XYLELLA FASTIDIOSA Findings The RPS use either their own laboratories or contract others to analyse plant and/or insect samples collected during their surveys, monitoring and import contr

The RPS Apulia informed the FVO audit team that there is continuous regional media coverage of Xf. The media in other regions and at national level deal with the outbreak periodically. The opinion of the RPS and scientific institutions gains limited or very limited coverage and it is usually presented in an unconvincing manner in response to the arguments of opponents to eradication measures. This in not in line with Art. 7 of CID 2015/789/EU.

label_heading: Conclusions on Planning and Prioritisation of Controls
paragraph_text: CBs do not necessarily require the operators to submit important compulsory information, such as on the precautionary measures, or do not adequately asses it. In addition, the number of staff available for certification and control tasks is very limited. As a result, the timing and preparation of the annual and additional visits are not always adequate, which strongly undermines the effectiveness of controls.

Both CBs doubled the number of operators under their control in recent years. This huge increase was not accompanied by a proportionate readjustment in their resources, including staff, to carry out control and certification tasks. The ratio of inspections per inspector/year is very high, especially in certain periods in the year. The majority of operators in Bulgaria are plant producers, which narrows the timeframe to execute the inspections. As a result, a significant percentage of inspections are not carried out at the most suitable time, which renders these controls ineffective. This is not in line with Article 5(2)(b)(i) and (ii) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. The audit team noted seve

paragraph_text: Risk analysis as carried out by CBs does not serve as a good basis to determine the nature and frequency of the visits to operators. Compulsory requirements such as quantities or past records are not adequately taken into account, not all operators are subject to risk assessment and not all subcontracted activities subject to the same level of controls.

CB2 does not carry out the same type of annual inspection to all operators. Subcontracted operators, which carry out important core activities such as production, are not subject to the same level of control from the CB as certified operators. The CB uses a different checklist and carries out only short inspections, with significant scope limitations, in comparison to those carried out on certified operators. The CB stated that they considered subcontracted operators less risky operators as they were under the internal control of the client to whom they sell their products. As an example, the CB manager evaluated the information on the operator and signalled points of attention for the inspector to focus on during the inspection. The annual inspection was planned after both the organic and conventional plots had been harvested. This rendered the inspection ineffective. Operators are not required to keep such records and consequently, most operators do not keep them, thus not providing evidence that the relevant requirements have been complied with. In addition, units where non-organic products are produced or kept are not necessarily subject to the minimum control requirements.

Both CBs have documented procedures to carry out controls. The main document used for the inspections is the report template, which also serves as a checklist for the inspectors. In particular, operators are neither yet obliged to notify their activity to the CAs, nor are included in a publicly available list and this might hamper the traceability of the organic products. label_heading: Conclusions on organisation of official controls
paragraph_text: The system of official controls is in place as described in the Country Profile for Spain. Within the scope of the audit, the official control plans are implemented as foreseen and official controls are carried out in accordance with documented procedures. Despite systems being in place, there are some shortcomings in their thoroughness and follow-up. Systems for training varied between ACs, with no training on the use of additives being provided in one etc. Some of the deficiencies identified could directly be contributed to insufficient training. 5.2.2 Implementation of official controls

In one AC, the FVO audit team noted that most inspection visits in one establishment visited were planned instead of being unannounced. The CA of the AC stated that visits in large-scale establishments are usually announced in advance. Provided the nature of the control permits and the inspector knows that the presence of a particular member of the business is advisable, visits to large-scale establishments may be arranged according to the CA, at the shortest notice possible.

label_heading: Conclusion on official controls on food processing chain
paragraph_text: The significant non-compliances in one establishment raises question as to the efficacy of the official controls in this particular case. Concerning the many non-compliances relating to the incoming goods, while none of them can be considered as critical, their range and frequency indicate that, notwithstanding the official system in place, controls are superficial and unable to detect any systemic non- compliances regarding traceability (particularly with regard to quantities) and labelling. label_heading: Conclusion on official controls on food processing chain
paragraph_text: The absence of official controls on the flow of product through establishments undermines the effectiveness of the overall system of traceability. 5.3. Miscellaneous 5.3.1. Mechanically Separated Meat

Specific checklists for controls on traceability and labelling are in use. However no checklists or sampling reports of meat products were available on the use of additives. The V&I checklist for traceability and labelling (effective from 15-02-2015) does not 4 contain detailed questions on internal traceability and quantitative traceability (mass balance). In-depth verification of traceability within establishments is rarely performed.
The CA did not have a special checklist or instructions for checking the use of additives. Evidence of official sampling was not available in the establishments visited.

The Dutch CA has clarified their position in a note to the DG Health & Food Safety dated 3 June 2015 concerning internal traceability, pointing out that neither Article 18 of Regulation (EC) No 178/2002 nor the Commission Guidance on the implementation of Regulation (EC) No 178/2002 European law imposes any obligations on FBOs to have an internal traceability system, and that, as a consequence, the NVWA cannot impose requirements in this regard. The only exception concerns the traceability of beef.

The requirement that FBOs must be able to demonstrate from whom products are received and to whom products are delivered is checked and enforced. However, if the mass balance (correlation of quantities received with output of final product, quantities in-storage and production losses) is not correct, or absent, no follow-up actions are taken and no sanctions can be imposed.

label_heading: Conclusion on official controls on food processing chain
paragraph_text: In one establishment the audit team identified the presence of eight bags of dried blood without identification. The provider of dried blood had a procedure to remove all labels (including identification marks, process codes, use-by-date, etc.) from product supplied. label_heading: Conclusion on official controls on food processing chain
paragraph_text: Use of additives: In one establishment, according to the recipe of one non-heat treated meat product, the content of nitrite to be used was above the legal limit set out in Regulation (EC) No 1333/2008. Specifications, on several additive pre-mixes seen, did not mention the content of the additives for which a maximum limit is established and consequently this does not allow calculation of the maximal amount to be used. Official controls do not include checks on the use of additives.

The Dutch CA considers that for the production of MSM ("type 4") with reference to point 4 Chapter III, Section IV of Annex II of Regulation (EC) No 853/2004, there is no time limit between deboning and production of MSM. The FBO producer of MSM visited restricts the use of the poultry carcasses to five days after slaughter because they produce only "type 4", but has no indication if the three days between slaughter and cutting had been respected in all cases. In addition, the use by date (three days) of the 11 deboned poultry carcasses fixed by a German supplier was ignored by this FBO and had expired. The CA undertook to follow-up this issue.

label_heading: Conclusions on the implementation of official controls
paragraph_text: In all the establishments visited, the FBOs stated that a traceability system was in place. However, the evaluation of these systems revealed a less positive picture concerning traceability in general and quantitative traceability in particular. In one cold store a robust system was in place. Two establishments were making good progress towards implementing a good system but the others still had significant progress to make. Two establishments had yet to start work on implementing a traceability system.

label_heading: Conclusions on organisation of official controls
paragraph_text: The CA controls in relation to food additives are not included in the five year plan of controls. However according to the CA, this topic may be covered during controls. A system of official controls is in place as described in the Country Profile for the Slovak Republic. Within the scope of the audit, the official control plans are implemented as foreseen and official controls are carried out in accordance with documented procedures. Nevertheless, in some establishments, particularly those which export products, official controls on internal traceability are effectively performed. The CCA confirmed that the checklist does not contain specific questions on the us

The CCA stated that this checklist will be reviewed. 5 20. The EFET issued guidelines for prioritisation of controls. In 2014, the EFET recommended controls be targeted on the use of horse meat and MSM and in 2015, for example, on traceability, general hygiene, use of additives and gluten free declarations.

paragraph_text: The controls at the entry and exit BIPs on transits of non-EU goods comply with the EU requirements and provide guarantees that only eligible goods are accepted into the EU and they always leave the territory. paragraph_text: The competent authority was unaware of the requirement to control EU goods re-entering from external transits, and controls are not done.
