label_heading: Conclusion on controls at the exit BIP
paragraph_text: The official controls of exit transit consignments are correctly implemented in the vast majority of cases ensuring that consignments leave the EU territory as required by EU legislation, except for the Rijeka BIP. The different, undocumented implementation of instructions on exit transit controls at this BIP level cannot ensure that the exiting consignments are checked to confirm that they have not been manipulated during transit. 10 5.3 OFFICIAL CONTROLS IMPLEMENTED ON SPECIFIC TRANSITS 5.3.1 Derogations for consignments from Bosnia and Herzegovina and destined to third countries. Legal requirements Article 8 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004; Regulation (EU) No 553/2013, Regulation (EU) No 5

In April 2014, the central competent authority in cooperation with Customs approved an instruction for exit checks made by Customs officials outside the working hours of BIPs. Following the newly approved instruction, the BIP staff perform the exit checks of transit consignments during the working hours of the BIPs. Customs are responsible for 9 the exit checks of transit consignments outside the working hours of the BIPs. The instruction is prepared following the requirements of Directive 97/78/EC and Decision 2000/208/EC.

In those cases where the transit checks are done by the BIP staff the seal check is done at the BIP facilities. Outside of working hours, the seal check is done by Customs officials at the Customs control post. In both cases these controls are done following the requirements of Decision 2001/812/EC. The port BIPs visited keep track of exiting transit consignments until they are unloaded into ships for dispatch outside the EU.

The audit team noted that none of the BIPs visited follow the above-mentioned work instruction: a. In the Ploce port, Customs authorities always send the exit transit consignments to the BIP for checks even if the BIP is not working. The consignment then waits until the BIP is open. b. In the Rijeka port, the exit transit checks are always performed by Customs even when the BIP is open. The local agreement to divert from the national instruction (finding 44) is not documented. Central Customs officials confirmed that Customs are obliged to check veterinary seals only in cases defined in the national instruction. This means there is no legal obligation for Customs to check the veterinary seal

label_heading: Conclusions on controls at the entry BIP
paragraph_text: The veterinary checks for transit consignments at the entry BIP are implemented ensuring that consignments in transit fulfil the necessary animal health guarantees. The fact that the NVWA accepts explanatory letters when discrepancies are found during documentary checks weakens the effectiveness of the documentary controls. 5.2.2 Controls at warehouses and ship suppliers 5.2.2.1 Approval and listing of the warehouses/ship suppliers and specially approved warehouses

The audit team noted that Customs officials perform the documentary checks using a database which contains up to date and relevant information on requirements for transit consignments. The models of transit/storage veterinary certificates uploaded in the above-mentioned database are correct and comply with the model established by EU legislation. However, the audit team noted that a number of these certificates additionally bear the footnotes referring to the draft document number provided during the Standing Committee on Plants, Animals, Food and Feed. This leads to discrepancies between the certificates accompanying the consignments and the model in the database. There is no documented pro

BIP staff stated that, when officials detect errors in the certificates, explanatory letters from the third country competent authority were routinely requested. The NVWA 4 confirmed that replacement certificates are rarely requested. Despite the absence of EU legislation on this matter, the Guidelines for Design, Production, Issuance and Use of Generic Official Certificates (CAC/GL 38-2001), issued by the Codex Alimentarius Commission, indicate that, for certain administrative corrections or if the certificates are lost or damaged, replacement certificates are foreseen. This is also reflected in the Guidance on transit. The BIP operational procedures do not indicate when explanatory letters

label_heading: Conclusions on controls at warehouses and ship suppliers
paragraph_text: There is a well-functioning system of official controls on consignments in transit upon entry or exit from warehouses and ship suppliers which ensures that if a consignment has been manipulated during transit or does not arrive at the warehouse, this will be detected. Consignments ready for dispatch are subject to official controls. The controls during the storage are limited and do not include reconciliation exercises, which may potentially compromise the overall system of official controls at the warehouses. 5.2.3 Controls at the exit border inspection post

label_heading: Conclusions on controls at the entry BIP
paragraph_text: The warehouse operators identify each box of the consignment stored in the warehouse with a label with the reference number of the arriving CVED, in accordance with the requirement of Article 1(5) of Decision 2000/571/EC. In addition, the information on the consignments stored in the warehouse is recorded in the operators' databases, in accordance with the requirements of Article 3(1) of the same Decision. Nevertheless, the audit team noted discrepancies in the traceability of consignments stored (see finding 36).

label_heading: Conclusions on controls at the entry BIP
paragraph_text: The audit team conducted traceability exercises both to trace back and trace forward a randomly selected consignment stored in the warehouse. The audit team noted the following: In one warehouse, the warehouse operator incorrectly recorded the country of origin of the product stored in the warehouse (i.e. the country of origin of the product was Canada, but it was recorded in the operator's database as Argentina). In the other warehouse, the records were correct but the boxes stored displayed labels with an incorrect CVED number.

label_heading: Conclusions on controls at the entry BIP
paragraph_text: The official staff responsible for the official controls at the warehouses perform weekly verification of the consignments stored in the warehouse concerned. The audit team noted that during these verification visits the information on the selected consignments 8 is obtained from the warehouse operators' databases and it is cross-checked with the number of boxes stored in the warehouse. Official staff do not compare the data of the operator with official data available (e.g. amounts entering and exiting the warehouse). Therefore, the verification activities are not appropriate to identify the deficiencies described in finding 36, contrary to the requirements of Article 4(2)(a) of Regulation

label_heading: Conclusion on the development of the monitoring plan
paragraph_text: Whilst there is a monitoring plan in place, the absence of a risk-based rationale for the design and content of the plan does not ensure that the plan covers all relevant commodities and the related risks. 5.1.2 Implementation of the monitoring plan

The Veterinary and Import Division and the Consumer and Safety Division of NVWA are responsible for the planning of the monitoring plan on imported food of animal origin. The NVWA described that both divisions meet after the drafting of the monitoring plan and agree on the implementation at the BIPs. The NVWA stated that for the preparation of the following year's monitoring plan it takes into account RASFF information, quantities of imports, requirements of Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005, general information on problematic products and advice of the Office for Risk Assessment within the NVWA. There is no evidence that non-compliances not recorded in RASFF (e.g. consignments rejected at the bo

The monitoring plan includes residues of veterinary medicines, contaminants and microbiological examination (mainly Salmonella). The NVWA could not demonstrate that its controls are risk-based and did not present any risk assessment or other rationale for the design of the plan (e.g. for testing Trichinella in horse meat, beta-agonists in chicken meat or for excluding from testing honey or egg products, for which the Netherlands is the main country of introduction into the EU). In the absence of any such assessment, the NVWA is not in position to ensure that official controls are carried out on a risk basis as required by Article 3 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 (see finding 1).

label_heading: Conclusion on actions in case of suspicion
paragraph_text: There is a system in place which could allow BIP staff to take samples in case of suspicion. However, in practice, cases of suspicion where samples are taken are limited only to consignments which are already subject to EU safeguard decisions. The absence of sample collection in regard to any consignment other than the ones subject to EU safeguard decision, together with the limited scope of the monitoring plan, undermines the effectiveness of the official control system. 5.3 RASFF Legal requirements Article 5 of Commission Regulation (EU) No 16/2011. label_heading: Conclusion on the development of the monitoring plan
paragraph_text: Basically in compliance with the legal requirements, there is a monitoring plan in place to be implemented at the BIPs. The plan is prepared on the basis of risk management in order to ensure that it covers all relevant commodities and the related risks. The plan has not been reviewed/amended since 2011, therefore does not take into account the results of previous monitoring or emerging risks. This means that its ability to detect hazardous goods may be compromised. 5.1.2 Implementation of the monitoring plan

The monitoring plan was last made available to the BIPs and to the authorised island entry points listed in Annex I to Decision 94/641/EC in 2011. Since then it has not been reviewed/amended. The competent authority stated that this was due to a lack of human resources. In this way, the results of previous years are not taken into consideration, contrary to the requirement of paragraph 1 of Annex II to Regulation No 136/2004.

The NVWA is an independent agency commissioned by the VWS and the MEA. It is under the administrative responsibility of the MEA but functions as an executive delivery body for both Ministries. label_heading: Conclusions on Organisation and Scope of Official Controls
paragraph_text: While official controls on primary producers of FNAO cover the risk of microbiological contamination of irrigation water, the remaining major microbiological risks identified by EFSA are not considered (with the exception of one region visited) in the planning of official controls. This circumstance, coupled with the fact that the design of official controls does not make specific provision for targeting the high priority crops identified by EFSA as particularly prone to microbiological contamination, weakens the effectiveness of official controls in this area. 5.2.4 Implementation of Official Controls over Food Business Operators Obligations Legal requirements Article 10(2)(b)(i), Article 1

The risk ranking set out in the EFSA scientific opinion was not taken into account in the framework of the above-mentioned exercise. This negatively affects the effectiveness of official controls as the major risks identified in EFSA scientific opinion do not contribute to the risk basis for those controls, contrary to Article 3.1(a) and 4.2(a) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. However, the CCA, regional CAs and local CAs informed the audit team that microbiological hazards will be considered in the risk based planning for 2016. The CAs are planning to evaluate the risk assessments by the end of this year in order to take into account the microbiological risks identified in scientific opinions

In addition, in September 2015 the regional authorities in Calabria started to develop a new procedure for the official control on primary production of FNAO with relevant checklists containing certain microbiological risks. In 2015, the authorities were responsible for controls on approximately 2400 farms producing FNAO and they carried out approximately 200 inspections at those FBOs. However, at the time of the audit, inspections did not consider any microbiological risks except for contamination of water used at primary producers. Moreover, at the time of the audit, microbiological risks (other than relating to water) identified by EFSA concerning FNAO were not included in the risk-based

label_heading: Conclusions on measures in cases of pesticide residue detections
paragraph_text: The national Guidelines will help harmonising investigation procedures across CBs. Files for pesticide residue detections in 2014 show the different approaches taken by CBs at the time. This demonstrates the need for further harmonisation through the new Guidance, in order to achieve consistent investigation procedures compliant with Regulation (EC) No 889/2008.

Both CBs visited had included in their Manual of Procedure a Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) for inspectors on the risk assessment for prioritising samples for pesticide residue analyses. There were also detailed sampling instructions. CB1 requires a laboratory sample of 500 g only, which is less than the 1-2 kg required for fresh fruits and vegetables in the national Regulations. The SOP of CB2 correctly implemented the national sampling provisions, but two laboratory files for samples of leaves indicated a weight of 32 and 107 grams, respectively, which is less than the 200 grams required for leaves in the national Regulations, and which may not be sufficient for a representative sample

A file for pesticide detection in 2014 was examined by the audit team at CB1. The producer had been informed of the decertification of her field based on a pesticide residue detection of 0.03 mg/kg of the pesticide pendimethalin. There was no evidence of consultation of the producer concerned, contrary to Article 91(2) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. Neither follow-up inspection nor re-sampling was performed. In 2014, a total of 146 samples of organic products had been taken and in two cases only there were pesticides detected. In a further eleven cases, the producer admitted the use of unauthorised pesticides without samples being taken. Conclusions on measures in cases of pesticide residue

The laboratories and an NRL have been adequately designated in line with Article 12 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. The Guidance does not explicitly specify which pesticides should be checked, and the sensitivity of methods as expressed by the Limits of Quantification (LOQs) to be applied by the laboratory. In Germany, organic samples taken by CBs are analysed in laboratories for pesticide residues. There is no legal obligation for CBs to notify these laboratories. paragraph_text: The official controls in place do not guarantee FBO compliance with all the general hygiene provisions laid down in Regulation (EC) No 852/2004 for primary production, in particular concerning water quality and cleaning and disinfection practices. label_heading: Conclusions on implementation of the eradication measures
paragraph_text: In addition, some practices which deviate from the approved Programme (such as movement restrictions applying only to positive animals, absence of testing of all eligible animals on positive holdings, absence of bacteriological testing on positive holdings, no investigation of abortions, application of EU non-compliant testing scheme to classify a holding as BMOF, no restrictions of use of pastures used by infected animals). These practices have an adverse effect on elimination of the infection and hamper achievement of the Programme objectives to the detriment of the overall cost- effectiveness of the Programme.

According to the Ministerial Decision Ref 4888/130873 as well as Official Decisions on measures to be implemented on infected holdings in the vaccination zone, verified by the audit team on the spot, restrictions on movements apply to positive animals only. This is not in line with the Point 4.4.9 of the BMEP nor with the Article 3(13)(a) of Council Decision 90/242/EC, where the prohibition of exit and introduction of animals (except movements for immediate slaughter) applies to the infected flock.

paragraph_text: In addition, some practices which deviate from the approved Programme (such as movement restrictions applying only to positive animals, absence of testing of all eligible animals on positive holdings, absence of bacteriological testing on positive holdings, no investigation of abortions, application of EU non-compliant testing scheme to classify a holding as BMOF, no restrictions of use of pastures used by infected animals). label_heading: Conclusions on implementation of the eradication measures
paragraph_text: The absence of measures as regards the use of milk from animals in an infected holding on the same or on another holding in the vaccination zone, prevent minimisation of possible risk of infection of humans or animals. This is in particular relevant for infected herds where vaccination coverage is low.

Milk from vaccinated animals on infected holdings is considered as milk from non- infected animals. According to the Article 16(7) of the Ministerial Decision Ref. 4888/130873, milk from non-infected animals from an infected holding has to be used according to the provisions of Annex III, Section IX, Chapter I, Paragraphs 3 to 5 of the Regulation (EC) No 853/2004. However, no Official Decisions reviewed by the audit team, imposed restrictions or requirements regarding the use of milk from animals from the infected holding on the same or other holdings. Also, Official Decisions reviewed, did not specify any restrictions as regards the use of milk from infected animals as mentioned in Point 4.

paragraph_text: The system in place for registration and approval of establishments including milk collection centres was in general well implemented. However, some shortcomings were noted in relation to keeping the approvals updated regarding the actual production activities. 5.1.5 Prioritisation of official controls Legal requirements Article 3 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 Findings

Official controls on milk processing establishments are well organised and are risk- based and documented. While reasonable levels of compliance were observed in two of the three establishments visited, some deficiencies were detected indicating that controls were not fully effective.

Official controls were not effective in identifying the evidence that samples submitted to the laboratories had been manipulated. 5.3 SAMPLING AND ANALYSIS OF RAW MILK (SOMATIC CELL COUNT AND TOTAL PLATE COUNT) 5.3.1 Control of raw milk upon collection Legal requirements Article 8 and Annex IV to Regulation (EC) No 854/2004. Findings

Samples submitted for laboratory analysis for SCC and TPC showed evidence of having been manipulated in order to obtain satisfactory results. Contributing factors are the lack of standard procedures for collection of samples by FBOs and the absence of official controls on sample collection. The integrity of samples as required by Article 11.7 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 has not been achieved.

All three establishments visited by the FVO audit team have developed procedures for raw milk checks as laid down in Regulation (EC) No 853/2004. The FBOs could document all their own checks carried out in relation to raw milk supply. Nevertheless the results provided were implausible (See paragraph 40 - 42) and official controls had not identified evidence that samples submitted to the laboratories had been manipulated. 5.2.2 Traceability, labelling and identification marking Legal requirements Article 18 of Regulation (EC) No 178/2002. Article 4(6) of Regulation (EC) No 854/2004. Article 5 and Annex II, Section I to Regulation (EC) No 853/2004. Article 4(6) of Regulation (EC) No 854/2004.

The laboratories visited could provide the results for all the samples delivered to them and these were evaluated by the FVO audit team. For the reasons mentioned below, the results were not credible. Only one laboratory provided credible results. While this had been identified in a number of laboratories, only one (NRL) had documented these anomalies. However, no follow-up action had been taken by the official services and official controls had not detected problems with the lack of credibility of analysis results.

The results of the tests carried out in different public or private laboratories differed very significantly, with some public laboratories identifying high or very high numbers of unsatisfactory results, while the private laboratories identified hardly any non- compliance even when performing a high number of analyses including in the same geographical areas. The range went from zero to 30% for TPC and SCC.

In a high proportion of cases raw milk samples taken by an official or the FBO at holding level had been manipulated. They had been diluted before being submitted for analysis: this was evident when the values for fat content and/or freezing point were taken into consideration. For example, many examples were seen where the fat content was lower than 1%. This was also the case for official samples taken in the framework of the process for the classification of holdings. As a consequence the results for TPC and SCC were deemed satisfactory whereas, in reality, they would have been unsatisfactory if they had not been diluted prior to analysis.

When subjected to statistical analysis, it was found that the results of samples collected by specific FBOs on different holdings were lower than or approaching the limits of repeatability of the methods (for example 6,6 % at a level 140 000 cells where the acceptable variation limit was 10 % when analysing the same samples twice). Usually, results showing 50% to 90% (depending of the level of TPC or SCC) of variation are expected with such microbiological reference methods. This was the case for one laboratory, in particular, where a high number of analyses had been carried out. In such cases, it cannot be excluded that the sampling supposed to come from different holdings came from one sin

The method in place for detecting inhibitors is not suitable for detecting certain categories of inhibitors which has the potential to allow non-compliant milk to enter the food chain. The number and range of laboratory ring test organised by the NRL is insufficient to provide assurance of adequate performance by laboratories.

All four laboratories visited during the FVO audit were accredited for the analysis carried out. Nevertheless one of the laboratories visited was accredited for the reference method (ISO 13336-1) but was using an automated variance of this reference method without any internal or external validation having been carried out.

The analytical performance of laboratories is assessed by inter-laboratories tests (Ring tests) organised by the NRL for Total Plate Count (TPC), Somatic Cell Count (SCC) and residues analysis for inhibitors. It is compulsory for the public laboratories to take part in these ring tests and all private laboratories are invited to participate. Most private laboratories do so and the four laboratories visited by the FVO audit team had participated on a regular basis or at least partially (one laboratory had not participated in 9 the ring test in relation to SCC). Ring tests are not performed sufficiently frequently to allow a reliable assessment of the performance of laboratories. In addition,

Concerning inhibitors, the Bulgarian standard method was used in all laboratories visited, but its application varied between laboratories, in particular, concerning the cut off (time or acidity range) between compliant and non-compliant results. More generally, it should be noted that this method is insufficient to detect certain categories of inhibitors. This was confirmed in an evaluation carried out by the NRL and this could 10 also explain the almost complete absence of the detection of inhibitors in official and own check samples. label_heading: Conclusions on the official control systems
paragraph_text: Business operators, establishments and plants along the chain are subject to risk-based official controls; however, the competent authorities have not yet put in place the necessary arrangements (notably, updated checklists/guidelines) to ensure that: a) the checks along the chain of the production and use of PAP for aquaculture purposes are carried out and recorded on a regular basis, and b) that the process for the authorisation of operators handling products of ruminant origin is followed in a consistent manner. Although no sampling plans to detect the presence of ruminant proteins in PAP and aquaculture feed containing such PAP were organised in 2013 and 2014, a plan has been developed f

Operators along the chain are mostly checked according to the planned frequencies and non-compliances are followed in a structured and systematic manner. However, the absence of evidence of checks on the relevant feed ban requirements (notably, when an authorisation is required) and a low attention paid to the risk of cross-contamination during transport, undermines the overall reliability of the official controls. This weakness is mitigated by largely comprehensive own-control systems put in in place by the operators. 8 6 OVERALL CONCLUSIONS There is a system of official controls in place which ensures all relevant operators, plants and establishments in the animal by-products / feed chain

The audit team visited two establishments, located in two different Regions, which required an authorisation because they were handling ruminant and non-ruminant materials, and noted the following: In one case the establishment is a processing plant producing blood products of porcine origin to be used for the manufacture of feed for aquaculture. It was noted that, although the establishment largely fulfilled the necessary conditions to obtain 4 an authorisation, there was no evidence available to demonstrate that these conditions had been actually checked during official controls (see paragraph 16). In the second case the establishment is a feed manufacturer (see paragraph 19). It was noted

Slaughterhouses/cutting plants, processing plants handling ABP destined to be used in the aquaculture feed and transporters of ABP and derived products are subject to inspections according to risk-based frequencies which are determined taking into account the recommended frequencies decided at central level and the specific risks identified at local level. In the feed sector, the PNAA valid from 2015 to 2017, highlights the need to inspect all feed business operators according to risk criteria and provides comprehensive explanations on, among other things, the risk factors to take into account. In both sectors (i.e. the ABP and the feed sector) guidelines and checklists to carry out official

The audit team visited a processing plant supplying PAP of poultry origin in big-bags or bulk for aquaculture feed. The operator had devised a largely comprehensive own-control system based on Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Point (HACCP) principles and regular samples from the final products are analysed to detect the presence of ruminant DNA (always resulted negative). However, the audit team noted that the risk of cross- contamination during the transport of incoming ABP was not considered in the hazard analysis and had not been included in the agreements with outsourced transporters even 6 though it is one of the conditions laid down in Section D of Chapter IV of Annex IV to Regulat

In the second processing plant visited the products placed on the market for aquaculture consist of whole dried blood and dried haemoglobin both of porcine origin, dispatched in big-bags or in bulk. The whole blood is processed in a dedicated production line physically separated from another line which processes blood of other species (including ruminants), whereas the haemoglobin is purchased, as such, stored in dedicated silos and dispatched. Although satisfactory arrangements were in place to avoid the risk of cross- contamination and these were verified by sampling final products, there was no evidence these had been checked during official controls, as the checklist used does not yet in

The audit team visited two transporters, located in two different Regions, one handling ABP and the other PAP, both of poultry origin, for aquaculture. Both of them had been authorised as transporters of ABP or derived products, according to a national rule and were subject to planned official controls (although in one of the three Regions visited the competent authorities declared that no checks of transporters were planned due to the lack of resources). According to the aforementioned national rule, the authorisation is granted by the local competent authority for each individual truck owned by the transporter and the transport of ABP/DP and feed in the same truck is prohibited. The audit

The audit team visited a trader of, among other things, PAP, and two feed manufacturers producing feed for aquaculture using PAP as raw material, one of which produced for both aquaculture and other farmed animals (including ruminants). All of them had largely comprehensive own-control systems and were subject to official controls (once or twice per year) according to the risk-based criteria set up by the central competent authority. However, the audit team noted that no evidence of the official checks on the relevant feed ban requirements, as required by Section F, Chapter V of Annex IV to Regulation (EC) No 999/2001, could be provided by the local competent authorities.

No standardised criteria have been developed in relation to suspended establishments with the result that establishments can remain suspended for an indefinite time. Some minor errors in the lists of establishment activities were noted. 5.1.5 Prioritisation of official controls

Three of the milk processing establishments visited exhibited structural and maintenance deficiencies which meant that they did not fulfil the approval requirements as laid down in Regulations (EC) No 852/2004 and (EC) No 853/2004.
The SINTESIS system provides a single list of approved establishments. In addition, it records the various approved activities of individual establishments1

In one Region an establishment was suspended two years ago on the Sistema INTEgrato per gli Scambi, le Importazioni e le Strutture (SINTESIS) list. The CA explained that this was a consequence of the earthquake which took place in Abruzzo in 2009 when damaged establishments were waiting for aid from the authorities to renovate their premises. During the period of suspension, the establishment was visited four times per year to confirm that no activity was taking place. The establishment was delisted on the day the FVO audit team requested to visit it.

In another Region, the CA stated that an establishment is delisted after six months suspension. 1 Paragraphs 21-24 inclusive have been re-ordered for clarity. 5 25. One establishment was on the list of heat treatment (liquid milk establishment). However, based on the information provided by the FBO, this establishment has never produced liquid milk.

A comprehensive system of official controls along the ABP/DP chain has been put in place and all relevant operators are subject to official controls which are carried out using comprehensive checklists which include requirements on the traceability of ABP/DP. Official controls on ABP/DP are carried out largely as planned and their effectiveness is verified through verification activities. These arrangements enable the competent authorities to provide guarantees that the risk of diversion/misuse of ABP/DP is adequately taken into account and these will be will further strengthened by a software application to be implemented soon. However, the level of official controls would be more risk-base

The audit team noted that although the current planning of official controls takes into account some risk criteria, not all of those required by Article 3 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 are included, namely, the records of compliance of operators and the reliability of operators' own checks. According to the competent authorities it is planned to develop a software application which will allow these additional factors to be taken into account. However, this is at a very early stage of development and it is not known when the system will be operational.

paragraph_text: In the three BIPs visited, consignments in transit are checked as required but in Frankfurt/Main BIP staff have no access to the information from the relevant databases which would enable them to verify that consignments are always presented for the controls. Veterinary checks generally ensure that only eligible consignments are accepted for transit.

label_heading: Conclusions on Epitrix sp. surveillance strategy and results
paragraph_text: A detailed surveillance protocol and good inspection guidelines have been elaborated in Spain for the detection and identification of PFB. However, the percentage of ware and seed potato producing areas inspected and sampled in annual official surveys varies widely between the ACs and is, in many cases, significantly lower than required in the National Contingency Plan and is insufficient to reliably identify or rule out the actual presence of PFB.

label_heading: Conclusions on Epitrix sp. surveillance strategy and results
paragraph_text: The suspected occurrence of PFBs triggered increased surveying activities in both recently affected ACs. However, the implemented intensity of surveillance does not provide sufficient information about the actual distribution of the harmful organism in these ACs. 5.3 CONTROL MEASURES WHERE THE PRESENCE OF EPITRIX SP. IS CONFIRMED 5.3.1 Demarcation of Epitrix sp. infestation Legal requirements Article 5 of Decision 2012/270/EU. Annex II Section 1 of Decision 2012/270/EU. Findings

Data in Tables 2 and 3 indicate that for the vast majority of the ACs, there was practically the same overall level of implementation of the surveillance in 2013 and 2014. However, there was a significant increase in the area inspected and the number of inspections carried out in Galicia in 2014. In addition to potatoes, 40 ha of tomato crops were also inspected in 2013 and 20 ha in 2014. The average inspected area of the total ware potato production in 2013 represented 4.8 % and in 2014 3.8 %, which is in accordance with the required 3 % in the National Contingency Plan. However, there was very significant variance between the ACs from 0.5 % to 100 % of fields inspected. In Andalucía the pr

Another way of evaluating the inspection data is looking at the number of fields inspected compared with the total production area which gives an indication of the 8 inspection density. As shown in the last column of Tables 2 and 3 above, the average inspection density in Spain was 96 ha and 48 ha of potato production per inspection in 2013 and 2014 respectively and varies very much between the ACs. In Andalucía there were 311 ha of potatoes per one inspection in 2013 and 339 ha in 2014 which is significantly below the national density average. It indicates that large but few potato plots were inspected there and consequently a very low density of inspection. The inspection density in Asturi

Seed production in Spain is concentrated in three ACs, namely in Castilla y Leon with the largest share of production of around 68 %, followed by Basque Country and Navarra. In 2013 and 2014 on average some 30 % plots of seed potatoes were surveyed for PFB with some 1,300 visual inspections of seed potato fields per year. However, in the largest seed producing, AC Castilla y Leon, there were only 56 visual inspections carried out and 7 plots inspected each year covering an area of 12 ha in in 2013 and 13 ha in 2014. Furthermore, in the same AC there were no lot inspections carried out in 2014, although in total 515 lot inspections were carried for domestic seed produced in Spain. The intensi

Taking into account the high proportion of inspected fields found infested in Asturias and Andalucía, the high proportion of unregistered producers of potatoes, the lack of systematic surveys of other cultivated host plants and vegetable hobby growers, the intensity of survey is not considered sufficient to determine the actual distribution and spread of the pest. Furthermore there is a very low intensity of surveys for PFB carried out in some other key potato producing ACs in Spain which does not provide sufficient information of the presence of the organism. This is not in line with Article 4 of Commission Decision 2012/270/EU. Conclusions on Epitrix sp. surveillance strategy and results

The establishment of demarcated areas in Asturias and Andalucía were notified immediately in line with EU requirements. However, due to uncertainty regarding the actual spread of PFB, the establishment of infested zones and buffer zones was not carried out taking into consideration the sound scientific principles required by Decision 2012/270/EU. In particular, geographically close demarcated areas were not merged. This is not in line with Decision 2012/270/EU, Annex II, Section 1, points 2 and 3.

The representative of Asturias also stated that they establish a demarcated area and designate an infested zone and a buffer zone around each infested plot according to the minimum required by Decision 2012/270/EU of a 100 m width from the infested plot. The geographically close demarcated areas were merged. However, where the 100 m radius intersects plots, the entire plot is not added to the demarcated area, which is not in line with Decision 2012/270/EU, Annex II, Section 1, point 1.

label_heading: finding of PFB in Andalucía on 28 May 2015 and MAGRAMA notified the
paragraph_text: When delimiting the size of the buffer zone, the minimum required by Decision 2012/270/EU was always applied in Andalucía and Asturias. There was a very high proportion of inspected fields found infested in Asturias (some 50 %) with a high level of infestation, fragmented cultivation of host plants and presence of host weeds. Due to the recency of the outbreaks in Andalucía and insufficient intensity of surveillance, there was uncertainty about the actual spread of the pest. Thus the plant health services in both ACs did not take into consideration other elements for delimitation, such as, the presence of other cultivated or wild PFB hosts in the area and the capacity of the pest to spread n

Official control measures put in place in demarcated areas were generally in line with Decision 2012/270/EU, however, confirmation of the outbreak did not trigger intensive monitoring or additional investigation in the demarcated area or its vicinity. Not all necessary measures were put in place like prohibition of planting of host plants and alternative measures are not equally effective to achieve eradication. This is not in line with Article 5 of Decision 2012/270/EU and the requirements for official measures to be taken within demarcated areas as laid down in Section 2 of Annex II to the same Decision.

Control measures in place for commercial scale movement of potato tubers outside demarcated areas are adequate, however, surveillance is not carried out for non- commercial movement of potatoes. 6 OVERALL CONCLUSIONS The potato flea beetle has spread further in Galicia and to Asturias, possibly due to natural spread. Therefore the implemented control measures seem to be able only to slow down but not prevent further spread in these two (neighbouring) Autonomous Communities (AC) and eradication of the pest there is now very unlikely. Authorities in Andalucía have made significant efforts to prevent further spread and the initial control measures are broadly in line with the minimum requiremen

The FVO team visited five demarcated areas in Andalucía and met plant health inspectors, owners of the infested fields and of fields in the buffer zone and noted that: All the fields visited were tilled and without any potato debris left and clean of weeds, including along the field's borders. Owners of the infested fields and of the fields in the buffer zone confirmed the receipt of the official demarcation notice and were aware of the harmful organism and imposed control measures. They intended to plant other crops in the next growing season. Professional farmers have their own technical staff responsible for the management of the crop production and protection. They confirmed regular and

The representative of Galicia stated that five warehouses in the demarcated areas comply with the requirements for the marketing of potatoes outside demarcated area, including the management of waste. Potatoes are inspected in the warehouses after washing. In Asturias all infested plots identified by the regional authorities so far were intended for own-consumption or at most for local market and surveillance of the movement of potato tubers out of the demarcated areas was not carried out. Thus, the control activities in Asturias do not ensure that all potatoes produced in the demarcated areas comply with the requirements for movement laid down in Annex I to Decision 2012/270/EU.

National control programmes for implementing the requirements laid down in relevant EU legislation have been established. However, discrepancies exist between Slovakian SNCPs and EU requirements as regards sampling at the initiative of the FBO in the rearing phase in breeding and laying hen populations.

The audit team noted that some discrepancies exist between the SNCP for breeding and laying hen flocks and relevant EU legislation, in particular sampling at the initiative of the FBO is not mandatory in the rearing phase. This is not in line with Annex II, Part B, Point 1 of Regulation (EC) No 2160/2003. The CA explained that since 2014 this sampling is no longer a FBO's obligation for financial reason. For more details see paragraph 75 and 91.

label_heading: Conclusions on the organisation and implementation of official controls
paragraph_text: Some procedures and contracts were still under preparation at the time of the audit and were therefore not possible to evaluate. Some procedures were missing altogether and others were insufficient, e.g. procedures for cleaning, disinfection, pest control and sampling of the imported animals. Such gaps could affect the implementation of official controls if they are not resolved before the BIP is approved.

A sampling procedure to ensure risk-based testing of imported animals through the Airport Bucharest Henri Coand in accordance with Part III of Annex II to Decision 97/794/EC had not been developed at the time of the audit although the staff was aware about these requirements. This is not in line with Article 8(1) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

The eight RCPPQCs are tasked with the coordination of the DREVs in their jurisdiction. The RCPPQCs draw up the annual programme of regular on-site inspections jointly with the competent DREVs. However the audit team was informed that such activities had not yet been implemented at the time of the audit (see paragraph 17). Conclusions on Competent Authorities

The national legislation requires that in relation to PGI wines, at least 20% of applications for certifications have to be sampled and analysed as well as at least 20% of the total production quantity of the PGI wine in the relevant regional unit. Given that there is no coordination being undertaken by the RCPPQCs, the audit team could not determine whether or not these requirements were met. In the particular DREVs visited, the inspectors met stated that these requirements had not yet been met.

Although the majority of inspectors met were knowledgeable on oenology, at the time of the observed inspections, there were no obvious guidelines or checklists used by the inspectors. Subsequently, the CCA stated that guidelines and checklists were provided by an implementing circular to the DREVs which were provided to the audit team. There was however no further explanation provided to the audit team as to why these guidance documents were not used by the inspectors observed. During two site visits the audit team requested traceability exercises to be performed. Although these were undertaken satisfactorily, the information of the producer, both in electronic and paper format, were fragmen

The RCPPQCs visited had not implement a risk based approach to controls and neither was there any coordination of the DREVs in place. In addition, any communication between DREVs was informal and undertaken on an ad hoc basis. Controls on the Market: (visit to supermarket)

label_heading: Conclusions on national measures and sampling design
paragraph_text: The competent authority has documented procedures in place to support the implementation of most of the provisions laid down in the legislation. However, delays in the inception of the sampling plan, shortcomings in the proportional allocation of samples and in the selection of the epidemiological units to be sampled, undermine the representativeness of the samples taken. 5.2.2 OFFICIAL LABORATORIES Legal requirements Article 10 of Directive 2003/99/EC; Article 4 and Annex Part A.5 of Decision 2013/652/EU. Article 33 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Findings

In 2014 and 2016 the number of caecal samples to be taken from turkey slaughterhouses was not calculated correctly. This is because for this calculation, the only turkey slaughterhouse in the country was treated as a broiler slaughterhouse. As a result, the number of samples allocated for turkey ceca was significantly lower than the one necessary to obtain the required isolates. This does not meet the requirements of point 2.2 of the Annex to Decision 2013/652/EU.

label_heading: Conclusions on national measures and sampling design
paragraph_text: The competent authority has documented procedures in place to support the implementation of most of the provisions laid down in the legislation. However, delays in the inception of the sampling plan, shortcomings in the proportional allocation of samples and in the selection of the epidemiological units to be sampled, undermine the representativeness of the samples taken. 5.2.2 OFFICIAL LABORATORIES Legal requirements Article 10 of Directive 2003/99/EC; Article 4 and Annex Part A.5 of Decision 2013/652/EU. Article 33 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Findings

Contrary to the requirements set out in part A of the Annex to Decision 2013/652/EU, the AMR monitoring programme did not ensure that samples were distributed over each month of the year. Instead, monthly sampling took place from March to December in 2014 and from May to December in 2015 and 2016. The competent authority informed the audit team that the monitoring plan was issued only when the Grant Decision, which details the EU funds that would become available for co-financing of the plan, was published. NSVFSA stated that they will consider the possibility to have bi-annual financial plans to avoid this issue reoccurring.

The annual Service Notices state that sampling days should be limited from Monday to Wednesday to ensure that the laboratory starts processing the samples within 48 hours of collection. In the slaughterhouses visited, officials took most of the samples on Mondays. This cannot be considered random and therefore is not in line with point 2.3 of Decision 2013/652/EU.

The Service Notices state that repeated epidemiological units cannot be sampled. Nevertheless, the epidemiological unit definition given therein is not fully in line with Decision 2013/652/EU. As a consequence, in two of the three slaughterhouses visited, the audit team noticed a few examples of repeated epidemiological units sampled. This is not in line with point 2.3.1 of Part A of the Annex to Decision 2013/652/EU.

According to the explanation provided by NSVFSA on this issue, the decision to select these counties was mainly based on the consumption of fresh meat therein. However, 6 the competent authorities did not present any consumption data to show that the actual county selection ensured representativeness. Moreover, the audit team noted that the population in the selected counties was far below the 80% required by EFSA guidance document 2014 representing 54% and 49% for 2015 and 2016, respectively. Therefore, it cannot be concluded that as required by Article 2.2 and point 1 of part A of the Annex to Decision 2013/652/EU, the isolates obtained were representative.

The competent authorities responsible for the monitoring of AMR in food producing animals and food are clearly designated, well-structured and organised, and have the necessary powers and resources, which is a prerequisite for the adequate implementation of the harmonised monitoring of AMR. The lack of powers of the designated laboratory staff for accessing slaughterhouses and perform sampling has an impact on fulfilling the Decision requirements regarding the poultry population to be covered by the sampling design. 5.2 ORGANISATION OF THE MONITORING SYSTEM 5.2.1 NATIONAL MEASURES AND SAMPLING DESIGN 5.2.1.1 National measures

During the audit, the audit team confirmed that under the Spanish legal framework the competent authorities have adequate powers to take the necessary samples for AMR monitoring. However, the personnel from the designated laboratory are not considered part of the competent authority and therefore can only access slaughterhouses if the operators voluntarily agree to grant this access. In 2014, staff from this laboratory were not allowed to enter a significant number of broiler slaughterhouses initially included in the work plan. In one particular case, this problem was overcome through the intervention of MAGRAMA, which resulted in the operator of the largest turkey slaughterhouse in the coun

Regarding the broiler slaughterhouses the following was noted by the audit team: In 2014 the broiler slaughterhouses included in the sampling plan, contrary to point 2.3.1 of Part A of the Annex to Decision 2013/652/EU, processed only 40% of the domestic production while for 2016 the figure improved and has reached 54% (see point 6). The figures on slaughter production used for the sample allocation corresponded to two years before the sampling year and not to the previous year as recommended in EFSA 2014 guidance document. These data were obtained from an industry publication that does not include all the national slaughterhouses. As a consequence, in the case of slaughtered broilers the de

The documented procedures and instructions in place could ensure adequate implementation of most of the provisions laid down in the legislation. However, there are deficiencies in the design and implementation of the sampling plan that call into question the representativeness of sampling. These concern notably the information available to exclude the sampling of repeated epidemiological units, the amount of samples taken for C. jejuni in relation to the prevalence, the exclusion of some months of the year, the type of samples taken at retail and, notably, the sample allocation to slaughterhouses and retail, These issues could lead to the gathering of AMR monitoring data not fully comparable

In 2014, the minimum required 170 Campylobacter jejuni isolates were not achieved for broilers and turkeys. Only 80 and 37 isolates were tested for AST and reported to EFSA for these populations respectively. According to the data provided by the competent authority in Spain C. coli is more prevalent than C. jejuni. The competent authority stated that for this reason they have difficulties to achieve the minimum required 170 isolates for the latter, especially in the turkey population. However, the amount of caecal samples to be taken for both populations of broilers and turkeys in the 2016 sampling plan (500 each), has been unchanged from 2014 despite the minimum number of isolates not bein

The requirement set out in point 2.3.1 of Part A of the Annex to Decision 2013/652/EU that caecal samples collected at slaughterhouses shall be distributed evenly over each month of the year was not adhered to in 2014, 2015 and 2016. The designated laboratory stated that this was due to delays in the public tender approval and to the fact that submission of the AST results to MAGRAMA has to take place by December. In 2014 caecal samples were gathered from May to November while in 2015 sampling took place from March to October and in 2016 it started in April.

AECOSAN has designed the collection of samples at retail outlets distributing the samples to be taken proportionally in the 13 provinces (NUTS-3 areas) more populated representing 60% of the total population. This approach to ensure the representativeness of sampling at this level is detailed in EFSA 2014 guidance document, where it is highlighted that NUTS-3 areas selected should cover at least 80% of the population (see section on Closing Meeting). In Catalonia, the authorities allocate the requested number of samples proportionally to the population to the three administrative areas of the province of Barcelona, which is the only Catalan province included in the sampling plan. In Murcia t

The overall bovine slaughter data were used for the sampling design of caeca from bovine under one year of age. As a consequence, the sampling allocations were not proportional to the slaughter of eligible animals as required by point 2.3.1 of Part A of the Annex to Decision 2013/652/EU and detailed in EFSA 2014 guidance document.

The audit team also noted that the difference between own-check and official sampling was not very clear to the staff responsible for implementing the SNCPs.

In this regard the VFSD informed the audit team that prior to 2015 all samples taken in the framework of the SNCPs were considered as official samples. However, since 2015 a distinction has been made by the CA between own-check and official sampling in national rules and the SNCPs because the relevant EU legislation stipulates that poultry populations should be sampled at the initiative of the FBO and as part of official controls. The CA explained to the audit team that due to the fact that these changes have taken place recently, the staff is still encountering difficulties in differentiating between the sampling for own-checks and the sampling for official controls and it therefore may hap

The audit team noted in all the farms visited that official sampling had not been carried out in 2015 and that one official sample taken in 2016 was analysed in a designated laboratory instead of being tested in the NRL as required by the SNCP.

The audit team was provided by the CA with the data of official sampling performed in 2015. According to this data the frequency for official sampling was not in line with EU requirements (six official samples were tested while there were 64 holdings with more than 1,000 birds). The audit team noted in one of the laying hen farms visited that no 17 official samples had been taken in 2015. The CA explained that this fact was due to the mistake made in the 2015 annual planning (see paragraph No 65).

In the majority of cases reviewed by the audit team, the protocol used in official sampling was not in line with point 2.2.2 of Annex to Regulation (EU) No 517/2011 (e.g. in a caged laying hen farm two faecal samples were taken instead of the required three faecal samples and in a free range farm two faeces samples were taken instead of three pairs of boot swaps). In practical terms, the protocol for own-checks was used instead of the official one in both type of production due to the confusion between own- check and official sampling (see paragraphs Nos 68 and 69).

label_heading: Conclusions on Organisation and Scope of Official Controls
paragraph_text: A control system of primary producers covering the verification of microbiological risks was in place, however, the controls only started in 2016 and were not planned taking into account the risks posed by pathogens that may contaminate FNAO.
By the time of the audit there were no direct imports from third countries of seeds for sprouting in Romania. Conclusions on Implementation of Official Controls over FBO Obligations

For 2016, controls are planned for producers of fruits and vegetables that also have storage and/or processing activities of FNAO and are registered as such. These FBOs will be visited once in 2016. A risk-based control system, taking into account the EFSA scientific opinions on the public health risk posed by pathogens that may contaminate FNAO, is not in place. This is not in accordance with Article 3.1(a) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. For 2017 a risk-based control system is planned to be developed.
None of the three FBOs were ever inspected before the audit concerning the risks of microbiological contamination of FNAO, as identified by EFSA, only their storehouses had previously been inspected.

The CA informed the audit team that, considering the size of the operation and the information provided, the FBO is in compliance with EU Regulations for sprouts.

For virus analysis in soft fruit, the method used does not follow the applicable international rules. It can prevent official controls from reliably detecting viral pathogen in official samples while these pathogens are considered relevant hazards by the CAs. 5.2.7 Procedures for Performance and Reporting of Control Activities Legal Requirements Article 8, and Article 9 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 Findings

The laboratory runs molecular methods to detect norovirus and hepatite A virus in food using some principles of EN ISO/TS 15216-2:2013 and reports results. These methods do not fall within the laboratory's scope of accreditation.

The main principle of virological analysis of soft berries lies in the virus concentration from 25g of berries. The most reliable method is the Polyethyleneglycol Precipitation. This method is part of ISO 15216-1 and 15216-2 and has been successfully tested in an inter-laboratory trial. Other methods for virus concentration are so far not as efficient and this has been shown in the Norovirus outbreak 2012 in Germany. The results are published and available as open access (Mäde, D.; and collaborators. Detection and Typing of Norovirus from Frozen Strawberries Involved in a Large-Scale Gastroenteritis Outbreak in Germany. Food and Environmental Virology. Volume 5 (2013), Issue 3, pp 162-168).

paragraph_text: CBs are accredited and approved in accordance with national and EU rules. CBs are subject to effective annual supervision by the CA which includes office and witness audits as well as direct inspections at operators selected based on relevant risks. Both CBs have well developed and comprehensive documented procedures in place providing good guidance to inspectors to achieve a high level of consistency and effectiveness of controls at operators. Comprehensive information is generally available to the inspectors in advance of the controls allowing them to prepare well and to acquire a good understanding of the situation on the spot. However, other aspects such as planning and preparation of inspections and control measures to be applied by CBs were not verified in this supervision. The lack of adequate verification of the internal procedures used by CBs for the controls is not in line with Article 92c(1) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. The audit team identified several shortcomings in the office audits carried out to both CBs (e.g. inadequate selection of operators for additional

However, the CCA only evaluates the topic covered by the supervision, and the overall performance of the inspectors is not evaluated. This is not in line with Article 27(9)(b) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007. As a result, the supervision by the CCA did not identify the systematic shortcomings observed by the Commission audit team during the inspections witnessed. (see findings 54 and 55). 7 21. When non-compliances are found during supervision, they are reported to the CBs and deadlines are set for the CBs to implement corrective action. The audit team reviewed the supervision reports for the witness inspections carried out in September 2015. It was also informed about the results of the supe

However, the report on the result of the supervision carried out in early September 2015 was submitted to CB1 only on 20 April 2016. As a consequence, both CBs had not yet implemented corrective actions to address the shortcomings identified by the supervision. Some of the shortcomings described in the CCA reports were again observed during the inspections observed by the audit team. Laboratories for pesticide residue analysis in organic products have been designated. However, the lack of clear instructions from the CA for designated laboratories with regard to the methodology and implementation of laboratory analysis results in weaknesses in the implementation of routine pesticide residues analyses and may reduce the reliability of analytical results.

In Finland, three laboratories are designated to perform pesticide residue analysis in organic products. In order to be designated, laboratories have to be accredited for pesticide residue analysis under ISO/IEC 17025, as required by Article 12 (2) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Another criterion, taken into account by EVIRA for designation of laboratories, is the number of analytes sought. However, the scope of accreditation is not a criterion for designation. In addition, there are no clear instructions for designated laboratories with regard to methodology and implementation of laboratory analysis in order to detect and quantify substances not authorised for organic production, as requir

In the first laboratory, a quality management system for routine pesticide residue analyses is in place. However, the audit team observed some weaknesses, including the following: 9 for standards, standard solutions and working solutions, records were available, but inconsistent labelling of standard solutions does not allow for a proper traceability; testing and replacement of standard solutions is performed by only a single injection and application of deviation criteria for comparison of old and new standards could not be demonstrated; requirements for identification and confirmations, i.e. application of acceptable deviations in retention time and ion ratio could not be demonstrated, whi

The overall performance of the second laboratory is generally good. Some weaknesses were identified in the implementation of routine pesticide residue analyses, such as: sample homogenization performed at room temperature, in-house validation data for some of the commodity groups was incomplete and traceability for calculation of analytical results could not be demonstrated comprehensively clear.

The lack of clear official criteria on sampling procedures for products other than those of plant and animal origin covered by Royal Decree No 290/2003 poses a risk that the interpretation of laboratory results is affected by a sampling procedure which is not representative for its purpose.

The lack of clear official CA criteria for the scope of analyses to be carried out (in particular, as to gas and liquid chromatographic techniques) impacts negatively on the control system: as gas chromatography is used as the only laboratory detection technique in many cases, the data on pesticide detections is likely to represent an underestimation of the true presence of pesticide residues in organic produce. 5.3 LABORATORY PERFORMANCE Legal Requirements Article 5 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 on delegation of specific tasks related to official controls; Article 12 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 on official laboratories; Article 33 of the Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 on national reference

Weaknesses exist in the system to issue equine identification documents. These do not contain all the required information and are frequently issued with no regard to the lifetime treatment of horses with veterinary medicinal products or the animals' age. Together with incomplete FCI, this results in ineligible animals entering the food chain. Additionally, late identification results in an unknown number of horses not being tested for EIA in accordance with national surveillance programme requirements.

ANZ confirmed it is not currently possible to print a replacement identification document from database. Consequently, equidae not identified by 12 months of age are issued a standard identification document with no associated restrictions.

Equidae which are issued a duplicate or replacement identification document are not excluded from the food chain contrary to the requirements of Articles 29(2)(c) and 32(2)(c) of Regulation 2015/262. Identification verification (Transponder)

The audit team reviewed two veterinary health certificates (from the previous week) for movement of horses from traders to the slaughterhouse visited, covering 20 and 11 animals respectively. 15 animals in the first, and six in the second, had consecutive transponder numbers. Seven consecutive numbers were checked on ANZ database and all of them had corresponding identification documents issued 1-2 days before slaughter of which two were issued to horses greater than 2 years old. CA agreed that horses with consecutive numbers had been identified at traders holding and had moved there from holding of birth with no identification.

The audit team reviewed 10 passports returned from equidae slaughtered in March 2016 from the slaughterhouse visited. Three were duplicate passports and two were "original" passports (issued for the first time). The ages of the animals ranged from 1 to 15 years old. In eight of the ten, the outline diagram had not been completed and no photograph or print depicting the animals was available.

The audit team checked data held on ANZ database relating to five horses from a holding approved under Commission Decision 2010/346/EU (and visited by audit team). In the week prior to visit, one horse had been identified and issued with a passport for 6 the first time at 5 years of age. A second horse was re-identified and issued a duplicate passport.

The CA is actively involved in measures that improve the welfare of cattle on dairy farms. Official controls provide satisfactory assurances of compliance with animal welfare requirements for cattle in dairy farms. Awareness levels on national legislation prohibiting tail docking are not high and, despite some preventive measures, there is an apparently low but continuing level of the banned practice of mutilation (tail-docking) of dairy cows.

paragraph_text: Improving trends are perceived in the majority of welfare indicators, particularly those which are being promoted by several actors from the industry. Actions for the management of mastitis, through the control of somatic cell count in milk, are strongest since most actors are addressing this issue. Actions addressing tail-docking are weakest, as they are being addressed by only one actor other than the CA. 15 6 OVERALL CONCLUSIONS The measures in place generally ensure that cattle on dairy farms are not caused unnecessary pain, suffering or injury. The Irish national strategy for dairy farming actively involves the CA and all other actors in managing animal welfare on dairy farms including

National legislation on animal welfare is found under the Animal Health and Welfare Act of 2013 which prohibits persons from doing, or failing to do, anything or causing or permitting anything to be done to an animal that causes unnecessary pain, distress or suffering. Both farms visited by the audit team had been inspected recently without any non- compliances being reported. One farm had less than 50 cattle in total (dairy cows, calves and heifers), kept tethered when indoors but grazing at pasture at the time of the visit, and produced milk exclusively for direct sale. The other had over 1000 dairy cows kept in loose housing conditions: In the smaller farm the cattle stalls were too short for the length of the animals present but, although both the AV and the County veterinarian agreed with this assessment, neither the County veterinarian nor the AV had reported it as a non- compliance nor required in writing any actions to rectify the problems (which i

Official controls on animal welfare of dairy cattle are performed on a regular basis, based on risk-assessment (see also paragraphs 16 and 17): by County veterinarians on the welfare of calves, in the case of farms with more than six calves; by AVs for all other types of cattle, so all of both dairy and beef cattle of all ages. 8 Or ad-hoc, by County veterinarians: to follow up on reported non-compliances by the AVs who are not empowered to impose sanctions. Due to that, if sanctions are envisaged, any non-compliance with animal welfare requirements reported by an AV must be confirmed by a County veterinarian; or as a consequence of complaints.

County veterinarians informed the audit team that the ad-hoc control focuses in principle on confirming the presence of the reported non-compliance, or the cause of the complaint. A full animal welfare control (which would use the instruction and checklists for County veterinarians that has the complete requirements for cattle instead of only those from Directives 98/58/EC and 2008/119/EC) may be done during these ad-hoc visits but usually only if additional non-compliances are noticed during the visit.

The number of animal welfare non-compliances in dairy farms reported by the AVs and County veterinarians is low: out of 2006 controls in 2013 and 1487 controls in 2013 in cattle farms (dairy and beef cattle) there were respectively 51 (2.5%) and 30 (2%) animal welfare non-compliances reported. Additionally, in the two Counties visited there were almost no complaints related to animal welfare issues in dairy farms within the last three years. The current system of directly linking each on/off notification prevents keepers from making notifications in certain situations where the connected buyer or seller has not completed their part in the notification process. It is very difficult for the competent authority to detect if the buyer fails to submit a notification on behalf of the buyer and the seller.

The fact that 100% of on/off paper notifications (over 150,000 in 2015) include the same date of signature for both the buyer and the seller may indicate that in some instances keepers insert an incorrect date on the notification which affects perceived compliance levels and merits further investigation by the competent authority. For electronic notifications, the date of notification by the buyer is also recorded by the database as the date of notification of the seller.

Various events such as births, deaths and movements must be notified by the keeper to database within specific deadlines, e.g. movements between holdings of bovines, ovines/caprines and porcines have to be notified within 7 days according to national legislation which implements the requirements of Article 7(1) of Regulation (EC) No 1760/2000 of the European Parliament and of the Council. All national deadlines for notifications either comply or go beyond EU requirements.

In both of the above options, the database will only accept movement when both the seller and the buyer complete the notification. The competent authority stated that the decision to link the notification from the seller and the buyer in one common notification to the database had improved overall compliance, and in particular data coherence. However, the current notification system has potentially negative impact on data completeness in FACR as described in findings 6 and 7.

For paper notifications, if a buyer fails to notify the database then the seller, through no fault of their own, has also failed to meet their legal obligation to notify. As indicated in finding 55, over 50% of movements are notified via paper. The only way to detect if the buyer fails to report the movement is through official controls on site, by matching movement documents with the database entries or when the seller becomes aware that the database has not been updated and they contact the competent authority. For electronic notifications, the buyer is prevented from making the notification for the on- movement if the seller fails to notify the off-movement.

In 2015, there were 845 movements of bovines where the destination holding did not notify the arrival (floating animals). This figure is based only on electronic notifications because there is no systematic way to know if a buyer does not notify a movement and no figure is available for the number of movements for which the buyer did not notify via hard copy.
The database does not flag "floating" animals if the buyer does not confirm receipt by a certain period or trigger any follow-up action by the competent authority.

The template paper notification form includes the date of movement, a date of signature for the seller and a date of signature for the buyer. The date of signature is accepted as the date of notification and is used to calculate compliance with legal deadlines. According to the competent authority, buyers and sellers always insert the same date of signature on the paper notification form. Therefore, the same date of notification for on and off-movements is always recorded in the database. For electronic notifications, the date when the buyer notifies the on-movement is used as the date of notification for both the on and the off-movement. 6 10.
