Target figures for on-the-spot controls comply with EU requirements but the selection process for holdings is not based on the criteria in relevant EU legislation. A new risk analysis currently being developed will form an important part of rectifying this situation and better target holdings with higher risks of being non-compliant.

Article(2)(3) of Regulation (EC) No 1082/2003 and Article 3 of Regulation (EC) No 1505/2006 require that the selection of holdings to be inspected by the competent authority shall be made on the basis of risk analysis. The two articles go on to specify the criteria that the risk analysis shall take into account. The competent authority stated 8 that although there had been a risk analysis in the database for several years to select holding for inspection that it could not be used by DVFA's because it did not provide appropriate data/results. Therefore, a new one was being developed which should be available in the near future.

The audit team visited two DVFAs and discussed how holdings were selected for on- the-spot inspections. Discussions focused on 2015 as an example year because the new risk analysis was discussed at national training in April 2016 and was subsequently implemented which meant that two systems were applied during 2016. In DVFA 1, staff were aware of the new methodological instruction but the annual plan for IRS inspections was based on the annual plan for Cross Compliance (CC) controls, i.e. in May 2015, the 12 holdings selected to be visited for CC checks were also selected for IRS controls. Subsequently, another 15 holdings were inspected for IRS controls during 2015 based on a number of crit

Although some criteria used for the selection of holding to be visited for CC controls may be the same as those for selecting holdings for IRS controls, they are not all the same, e.g. disease history and therefore the 3% holding selected may not represent the highest risk based on purely IRS criteria. Also CC controls are only carried out on holdings which receive subsidies and therefore not all holdings are included. The CA stated that CC controls are generally notified in advance (up to 48 hours) to the keeper. This presents difficulties for complying with Article 4 of Regulation (EC) No 1082/2003 which states that in general on-the-spot checks shall be unannounced.

The competent authority has not increased the minimum rate of checks in subsequent years where a significant degree of non-compliance existed as required by relevant EU legislation which could lead to an improvement in accuracy of the database.

The SVFA confirmed they had not considered increasing the minimum rate of checks in subsequent years where a significant degree of non-compliance existed (see finding 16) as required by Article 2(2) of Regulation (EC) No 1082/2003 and Article 2 of Regulation (EC) No 1505/2006.

The movement of live sheep to "temporary holdings" which are not registered on the central database and which are not subject to the normal legal requirements or official controls results in significant numbers of sheep moving outside the official control system and lost traceability.

National legislation allows sheep less than 12 months of age to move to "temporary holdings" where they should be slaughtered within 7 days of the move. A generic code in the database captures all off-movements to "temporary holdings", of which there were 4,044 in 2015. However, the "temporary holdings" are not registered on the national database as required by Article 7 of Council Regulation (EC) No 21/2004 and do not have to comply with the normal legal obligations of a holding. EU legislation does not include the concept of "temporary holdings". All slaughters associated with these movements should be notified to the DVFA's but DVFA staff confirmed that this does not always happen and the
There were non-compliances related to information recorded in the holding registers for sheep which can affect identification/traceability of animals.

The audit team visited three farms (bovine, ovine and porcine) and examined the IRS on each, including reports from the last on-the-spot official controls. In general, the level of compliance was high and the reports from the last official controls on each holding indicated that a comparative examination between individual identifications on animals, holding registers and the national database was carried out during the visit. No non- compliances were detected on any of the three holdings during those controls. But the audit team noted that the national template for the sheep holding register does not 11 include the following information required in point B of the Annex of Regulation 21/2004

label_heading: Conclusions on Organisation of Official Controls
paragraph_text: Official controls on both marketing and use of PPPs are performed in accordance with written instruction, in a uniform manner, which ensures consistency and operation of PPP wholesalers and professional users to the same standards. However, the complications for ASTA staff to take enforcement measures under Article 54 (2) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 in the case of irregularities identified at pesticide distributors, small scale growers and landscapers could compromise the effectiveness of official controls. 5.3. IMPLEMENTATION OF OFFICIAL CONTROLS 5.3.1. Controls on the Marketing of Plant Protection Products Legal Requirements Article 28 of Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009 on the authorisatio

For official controls on the use of PPPs, a system is in place for decision making on compliance with national and EU legal requirements, including enforcement measures and sanctions. However, this is not the case for official controls on the marketing of PPPs and for professional users with no extensive use of PPPs (landscapers and small scale growers), where there is a risk that non-compliances are not remedied by infringing operators, as no corrective measures are recommended to non-compliant operators and due to the absence of verification by any of the CAs. The complications with regard to imposition of penalties is one further complication. As a result of all these, the effectiveness o

In addition to the responsibilities stated under paragraph 7, ASTA is the CA in charge of decision making with regard to compliance or non-compliance of pesticide wholesalers, as part of official controls on the marketing of PPPs. ASTA staff are also responsible for carrying out of ad-hoc inspections at small scale growers and landscapers (see paragraphs 36 and 74 below). ASTA stated, however, that their staff do not have the status of "judicial police officers" ("officier de police judiciaire" (OPJ)). In order for ASTA staff to take any of the measures under Article 54 (2) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, they have to be accompanied by police officers. Once the Regulation, listed under parag

ASTA staff do not have the OPJ status allowing them to take enforcement measures (see paragraph 8 above), unless accompanied by police officers. However, there are provisions in the PPPA, allowing the Minister of Agriculture to take a number of administrative measures, which correspond to some of these, laid down in Article 54 (2) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. According to information provided during the audit, in the case of irregularities identified and reported by ADA, ASTA staff could only recommend non- compliant operators as to what corrective measures to take in order to remedy the situation. There are no other follow-up actions by any of the CAs in order to verify that adequate act

According to information provided by ASTA, at the time of the audit, national legal provisions and rules regarding penalties applicable to infringements of Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009 and Directive 128/2009/EC were laid down in the PPPA. For the same reasons, as listed above (see paragraphs 8 and 70), ASTA staff are not allowed to impose penalties. At the time of the audit, imposition of penalties, as well as any further measures in the case of serious infringements, were the responsibility of the Court of Justice. Once the Regulation, listed under paragraph 2, has been adopted, ASTA staff will have the powers to enforce the imposition of the penalties referred to in the final bullet points

At grower level, in the case of ad-hoc inspections by ASTA, the situation with regard to enforcement measures is similar to that described under paragraph 70 above. The reason is the same; ASTA staff do not have the OPJ status to apply any of the measures under Article 54 (2) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, or to impose sanctions. label_heading: Conclusions on measures in the demarcated areas
paragraph_text: No surveys were carried out in 2015 in the BZs in PACA. In Corsica the intensity of the surveys in the BZs is lower than that required by Article 6(7) of Decision 2015/789/EU. As a result there is no comprehensive information available about the infection status of the BZs.

label_heading: Conclusions on measures in the demarcated areas
paragraph_text: The sampling and testing practice within a radius of 100m around the infected plants is not in line with the provisions of Article 6(3) of Decision 2015/789/EU. Therefore, the real extent of the spread of infection is not known in each outbreak site.

The audit team noted that due to sampling and laboratory capacity problems, especially immediately after the first outbreaks, it was not possible to sample and analyse all the specified plants in the 100m area around the IZ. Instead, the area of 15m around each IZ was prioritised. In this area the specified plants were sampled and tested in line with provisions of the Decision.

In PACA the majority of the outbreaks were discovered in the last months of 2015 or in 2016, therefore no surveys had been carried out in the BZs at the time of the audit, which is not in line with the provisions of the Decision. In Corsica, due to the numerous recent outbreaks, the CA stated that it was not in a position to carry out surveys in line with the provisions of the Decision (i.e. visual inspections and sampling of plants with 18 symptoms based on a 100m x 100m grid). At the time of the audit, the entire BZ area was 380,100 ha; therefore the same number of visual inspections would be required annually to fulfil the requirements of the Decision.

The audit team was informed that visual inspections were and will be carried out in the BZs based on a grid split into 1km x 1km squares. The CAs noted that the proper implementation of the plan could be hindered by the inaccessibility of some areas. 5.3.4 Tracing back and forward of infection sources

label_heading: Conclusions on measures in the demarcated areas
paragraph_text: The measures taken in the DAs show the commitment of the French CAs to eradicating Xf, in order to protect major crops and environmentally and economically important areas. Specific efforts were made to implement appropriate measures. The demarcation of the affected areas, the eradication of infected plants and hosts (known at the time of detection) in the 100m radius and the trace back and forward of the infections was carried out in line with the provisions of Decision 2015/789/EU. However, as outbreak sites where eradication activity had been completed were not revisited after new hosts were identified, there is a risk that infected plants remain in those areas.

In the case of the first three outbreaks in Corsica it was assumed that the infection was caused by Xf subsp. pauca, therefore in the 100m area around the IZ, hosts plants of that subspecies and all symptomatic plants of other species were removed. Later, based on the assumption that Pm was the prominent source of infection, each plant of this species was removed. The audit team noted that due to capacity problems, Corsica SRAL could not return to all the outbreak sites where removal had been completed, to check for the presence and order the removal of plants of newly identified host species. For all outbreaks in PACA, immediate removal of host plants (known to be hosts at the time that the

The audit team visited nurseries in the DAs in Corsica and PACA, to whom derogation B had been granted and noted: They keep records on entries and sales. In the case of private clients the name, address and telephone number is recorded; Plants are treated with pesticides at least once a month; They are inspected by the SRAL regularly; In the nursery in Corsica, host plants (Lavandula sp.) were present, although this species was not considered as a host plant at the time of the demarcation. label_heading: Conclusions on measures in the demarcated areas
paragraph_text: Nurseries located in DAs are allowed to move non-host specified plants outside their DA without fulfilling all requirements of Article 9(2) of Decision 2015/789/EU. It creates a potentially high risk as the plants spend time in the nursery, surrounded by potentially infected plants without any protection against transmission by vectors.

DGAL stated that it interprets the provisions of Article 9 of Decision 2015/789/EU as providing the possibility to grant three different types of derogations to nurseries in the DAs. SRAL authorises the movement of host and specified plants within and outside of the DAs according to the scheme outlined in paragraphs 72-75 below. In general, the applicable derogation depends on the type of plants and the length of time they spend in the DA. Derogation A is applied to nurseries who deal with marketing of plants which are in pots or containers and the premises are not considered as growing fields (i.e. plants are not multiplied and kept on solid surface). It is granted for non-host specified pl

Derogation A is granted if the nursery Carries out an inventory on the stocks; Carries out permanent insecticide treatment of the plants against insect vectors; Keeps a record on sales and keeps a register of observations any disease symptoms; Receives prior authorisation of the stocks from SRAL; Subscribes for the BSV and follows training on Xf organised by an expert body.

Derogation B is granted if the nursery Keeps a record on entries (date, supplier, quantities) per plant species; Carries out permanent insecticide treatment of the plants against insect vectors and keeps a record of the treatments; 20 Keeps a record on sales (date, client, quantities) per plant species and keeps a register of observations of any disease symptoms; Subscribes for the BSV and follows training on Xf organised by an expert body.

The audit team noted that derogations A and B are not in line with provisions of Decision 2015/789/EU. However, DGAL stated that based on the French language version of the Decision, it interprets that the movement ban of Article 9 refers to plants which have been cultivated in the DAs and does not include those that are kept on premises for wholesale and retail purposes only. The CA considers that the measures, linked to derogation A and B provide the necessary guarantees of not distributing the pest through sales of planting material. The CA has also emphasised that the approach was developed based on the need to allow trade of planting material without pronounced risk while taking efforts

The audit team visited nurseries in the DAs in Corsica and PACA, to whom derogation B had been granted and noted: They keep records on entries and sales. In the case of private clients the name, address and telephone number is recorded; Plants are treated with pesticides at least once a month; They are inspected by the SRAL regularly; In the nursery in Corsica, host plants (Lavandula sp.) were present, although this species was not considered as a host plant at the time of the demarcation. SRAL informed the audit team that the lot was put on hold and sampled, and that destruction was planned in the case of positive results; 5.3.6 Other measures to prevent the spread of Xf

In 2015 France carried out a comprehensive and risk based Xf national survey as required by EU legislation. The surveys outside the DAs in Corsica took into consideration the new risk elements identified as a result of the outbreaks. In PACA, as the outbreaks were detected recently, there was no time for comprehensive surveys outside the DAs. In both regions, the limited accessibility of private properties, scrublands or other natural sites compromise the surveys. The lack of movement controls of specified plants beyond the controls related to the implementation of the plant passport system outside the DAs does not increase the risk of spread substantially as there is limited trade of plants

Outside the DAs, surveys in the two regions targeted nurseries and public places, where there were reports about the presence of Pm plants or symptomatic plants. The audit team was informed that in both regions, there are numerous private properties where Pm and other host plants are present. Accessing these properties for surveillance purposes is very difficult. In Corsica many private properties are second homes of residents in continental France and the owners are not present for much of the year. Therefore in many cases it is difficult to obtain the consent of the owner/tenant for the survey.

In some areas, especially in Corsica, Pm has become part of the wild flora and is commonly found in scrublands (in French - maqui). The audit team was informed that there are signs that some of these wild plants exhibit symptoms of Xf. However, the majority of these plants are located in sites that are difficult to access in order to take samples and practically inaccessible for the implementation of eradication measures, if necessary. SRAL Corsica surveyed some scrublands with a drone and confirmed the presence of symptomatic Pm plants. SRAL intends to contact the National Botanical Conservatory of Corsica, who are involved in flora mapping of wild areas, in order to collect information abo

The audit team was informed that visual inspections were and will be carried out in the BZs based on a grid split into 1km x 1km squares. The CAs noted that the proper implementation of the plan could be hindered by the inaccessibility of some areas. 5.3.4 Tracing back and forward of infection sources

The surveys were carried out at times not being the most appropriate for certain specified plants or even inappropriate for some other specified plants. Therefore the effectiveness of the visual inspections as a means of identifying symptomatic plants and suspected cases of infection were compromised. The impact of this could be mitigated to some extent by the 2016 sampling and testing regime, which goes beyond EU requirements.

Although EU and Italian legislation established the current BZ in May 2016 (see chapter 5.1.2) the full scale 2016 surveys started there only in August after the Prosecutor's ban was revoked (see chapter 4.2) and the necessary financial and human resources were put into place including the training of the surveillance staff.. The work was being carried out by ARIF, based on a 100m x 100m grid approach, as required by the EU legislation. It was decided to start the work at the northern border of the BZ and to move progressively southward in order to first detect any infection situated farthest from the IZ (see figure II).

After recruiting and training the necessary personnel, the survey started on 29 August 2016 and full capacity was reached in September, involving 172 ARIF agents working in 86 teams. ARIF agents have the status of public agents and Ministerial Decree 2014/2005 gives them the right to enter private property. Each team has an average capacity of 20 squares per day enabling ARIF to check around 1,500 squares and collect 2,000-2,500 samples daily. A complex and sophisticated IT system supports the activity.

The visual inspection and the sampling are carried out following a very detailed guideline. ARIF regularly controls the quality of the work of its agents. The guideline lists the main elements of the methodology as follows: The survey team shall identify the physical borders of each grid square with the help of orthophotos, high resolution satellite images and by using GPS coordinates. The system ensures that there is no overlap of the inspected squares and that no gaps are left uninspected in the territory; The entire area of the square shall be scouted and checked visually. The host and specified plants shall be identified with particular attention to visible symptoms. As the first symptom

The audit team observed a survey carried out by an ARIF team and noted that: The agents were experienced and had good knowledge about the legislation and about the host and specified plants; ARIF organises the sampling properly; the activity of the teams and the logistics of the samples are fully coordinated; The IT system used ensures the proper identification of the squares and the host and specified plants present. The electronic report, which is prepared according to a template, contains all information necessary for the authorities and for other statistical and analytical purposes; The agents carried out the visual checks and the sampling fully in line with the provisions of the guideli

From September 2016 onwards, ARIF started its activity also in the "20km zone". First they checked some high risk spots while the systematic survey with the method described in chapter 5.2.2 started in October after the work in the BZ was largely completed. At the time of the audit, in the "20km zone" 11.6% of the area had been checked and sampled. The work started at the border of the BZ and was to continue at the rate of 1,500 squares a day until completed. RPS expects the completion of the work in January 2017 (see table III). For the same reasons as set out in relation to the BZ (see paragraph 36), the audit team considers that the timing of the survey was inappropriate or not the most a

label_heading: Conclusions on specific surveys and information campaigns
paragraph_text: The surveys for Japanese beetle in Italy are organised appropriately, however, they are unevenly distributed between both affected regions and the implemented intensity does not provide sufficient information about the actual distribution of the pest.

Visual inspections were concentrated in the areas not infested by Japanese beetle, i.e. the buffer zone, and were carried out between mid June and mid August 2016. The three km buffer zone is subdivided in three concentric bands of one km in width within which a 1000 m square matrix grid is used and the sites for inspection were as equally distributed as possible. This density of survey points is significantly lower than that required in EU legislation in other outbreaks, e.g. for buffer zone surveillance for Xylella fastidiosa (100 x 100 m), however, the RPSs performs more dense visual inspections in the area closer to the infested zone. The sites contained preferred host plants on which th

In 2016 the RPS in Lombardy carried out 1 825 visual inspections and the RPS in Piedmont 430. With the recent update of the demarcated area in the summer 2016, the area of the buffer zone was extended and is very large. As mentioned above, a 1 000 m x 1 000 m survey grid is not very dense for a secure delimitation of the infestation and the number of inspections indicates that Piedmont in 2016 was far from achieving even that coverage. Thus the authorities might not obtain sufficient information on the current distribution of the pest and may not delimit the outbreak adequately. This is not in line with the requirements of Article 16(1) of Directive 2000/29/EC that all necessary measures mus

However, given the relative low level presence of the host, particularly in Piedmont and Lombardy, where outbreaks have occurred, the variation in susceptibility, as well as the issue of latency with respect to delayed symptom expression, the current level of monitoring intensity of timber producing trees is inadequate to reliably delimit for the presence of Thousand canker disease.

Similarly, in Veneto, despite a higher presence of host trees, predominantly plantations of J. nigra, and based on the same issues with respect to susceptibility and latency, the current level of monitoring intensity there is also inadequate to reliably delimit the disease.

Insufficient monitoring is carried out for mono-cultures of J. regia in commercial walnut fruit production in all of the regions, and for which no contingency plan exists. Such absences pose particular potential challenges with respect to disease management and further control should Thousand canker disease enter the fruit production industry.

Despite a high degree of homogeneity with respect to the monitoring approach and overall surveillance strategy, the level of monitoring intensity varies between regions but, in each case, is considered insufficient to reliably delimit the presence of Thousand canker disease and provide for the protective measures required by Article 16(2) of Directive 2000/29/EC (see paragraphs 40 to 52). Veneto

Veneto manages a total of 50 strategically positioned monitoring sites across its region. Identified from the public nursery database (of Veneto Agricultura) and the regional register (see also paragraph 33), the sites are also selected, as much as is practically possible, to a defined geometrical grid.
Trees at all 50 sites are subject to visual inspection. Thirty of the sites are complemented with a pheromone trap. Sites are inspected on a monthly basis.

In addition, the RPS stated that one trap is positioned in one plantation which is also subjected to monitoring. No Thousand canker disease has been observed there to date. Furthermore, both producers and an industry association met during the audit stated they have never witnessed Thousand canker disease, nor the vector, in their plantations. Piedmont

Piedmont has a total of 15 strategic monitoring sites across its region. Of the four pheromone trap deployments, two are located at each of the notified outbreak sites. Eleven other sites are subject to visual monitoring only. Sites, as well as traps, are inspected on a monthly basis.

From their observations, Piedmont stated that no Thousand canker disease has been observed on varieties of J. regia for walnut fruit production. Therefore, the commercial walnut fruit plantations to the South east and south west of the region have not been included in their monitoring regime.

Lombardy monitors 10 strategically selected sites with pheromone traps within its region each year. Each site typically comprises up to 20 trees. Each site is visited on a monthly basis during which the traps and trees are checked for the vector and 12 Thousand canker disease, respectively. This regime, in place since 2014, was preceded by a less stringent preliminary monitoring approach in 2013 following notification of the first outbreak case in Veneto. The location of some of the monitoring sites are changed each year.

In addition to selected sites for visual inspections, Friuli Venezia Giulia originally deployed 21 pheromone traps in 2016 (on loan from the University of Padua), 16 of which are currently operational as five were removed for operational reasons. Deployment is partially random, but some are strategically positioned close to road and railway lines, the others in small young commercial timber plantations of typically 0.5 to 1 Ha. Sites are visited once per month.

As commercial walnut fruit plantations of J. regia are limited in Friuli Venezia Giulia they are not included in the RPS monitoring regime. 5.2.5 Commercial availability of Thousand canker disease pheromone

label_heading: Conclusion on situation of Trioza erytreae
paragraph_text: The outbreaks of T. erytreae have been notified to the European Commission and other Member States, but after a significant delay. That is not in line with Article 16(1) of Directive 2000/29/EC nor Article 2 of Decision 2014/917/EU; it also hinders the response of other Member States, in particular in adapting their official controls as necessary.

The notifications provided the information required by Decision 2014/917/EU, however the long delay, between confirmation of the presence of the pest and its notification to the Commission and other Member States in both cases, is not in line with Article 2 of Decision 2014/917/EU, which provides for a maximum of eight working days for the provision of at least a preliminary notification. 5.2.2 Surveys for Trioza erytreae and Ca. Liberibacter spp

label_heading: Conclusion on control measures for Trioza erytreae
paragraph_text: However, the application of authorised plant protection products, which is the only measure aimed at inhibiting the further natural spread of the pest, is not carried out systematically, particular in those areas bordering the remaining free areas of the AC of Galicia. The further spread of T. erytreae is therefore inevitable. It cannot therefore be concluded that all necessary measures have been taken to inhibit the spread of the pest, at least in those areas, as required by Article 16(1) of Directive 2000/29/EC. 5.4 CONTINGENCY PLAN FOR CANDIDATUS LIBERIBACTER SPP Legal requirements There are no EU requirements for contingency plans for harmful organisms Article 16(1) to Directive 2000/29/

The audit team observed the application of a pesticide treatment to a recently identified infested tree, on the boundary of the infested zone close to Santiago de Compestela, within the area targeted by the official pesticide treatment programme. It was noted that the treatments were applied by specially trained staff from TRAGSA using appropriate equipment. The active ingredient applied was chlorpyriphos, which was chosen primarily on the basis of cost.

label_heading: Conclusion on control measures for Tecia solanivora
paragraph_text: The objective of the control measures for T. solanivora in both Galicia and Asturias, is its eradication, however the measures, as applied, are unlikely to achieve this.

The control measures taken following a finding of T. solanivora focus on infected tubers or the field or store in which the trap on which the moths were caught was placed, which is not necessarily their source. This means that the measures are unlikely to result in the eradication of the pest from the infected area, however they should at least inhibit its spread in line with Article 16(1) of Directive 2000/29/EC. 5.6.2 Control measures for Tecia solanivora in Asturias

paragraph_text: The delayed elaboration of the national Xf contingency plan may impact negatively on the implementation of the necessary measures in the case of possible future outbreaks. 5.2 NOTIFICATION OF THE OUTBREAK, ESTABLISHMENT OF THE DEMARCATED AREA Legal requirements Article 2 (1) of Commission Implementing Decision 2014/917/EU. Article 4 of Commission Implementing Decision 2015/789/EU. Findings 5.2.1 Notification of the outbreak

At federal level, preparatory steps have been made under the leadership of the JKI for developing a contingency plan for Xf. A working group was set up with participation of diagnostic and plant health control experts from Bavaria, Thuringia, Brandenburg, Baden-Württemberg, North Rhine-Westphalia and Lower Saxony.

The intention of the CAs is to elaborate a national contingency plan with annexes, dealing with the specific conditions of each Land. The first draft has already been prepared and it concentrates on the provisions for establishing the DA. The future steps 4 include the elaboration of the details of the plan, consultation with professional organisations and discussing this with the CAs of the Länder to obtain their agreement for publication and implementation.

The audit team noted that: Some elements of the existing contingency plans in Saxony and Thuringia are in line with some provisions of Article 3a of Decision 2015/789/EU. However, the plans cannot be considered as meeting the requirements of the Decision; It is unlikely that the national contingency plan will be finalised by 31 December 2016, the deadline set by Article 3a of Decision 2015/789/EU. 5.1.4 Communication and cooperation within the plant health services and with other authorities involved in controls

label_heading: Conclusions on surveys for the detection of Xylella fastidiosa
paragraph_text: The presence of Xf in the BZ was monitored with a methodology, in line with EU provisions and the most risky sites were prioritised. However, as the entire territory of the BZ was not checked, the absence of Xf has not yet been fully verified. 5.4 ERADICATION MEASURES Legal requirements Article 6 of Commission Implementing Decision 2015/789/EU. ISPM 9, ISPM 14 and ISPM 31 as referred to by Article 6 (3) and (10) of the Decision. Findings 5.4.1 Trace back and forward of possible infection

The LPPS of Saxony and Thuringia carried out surveys in the BZ, based on a grid split into 100 x 100 m squares, as required by Article 6(7) of Decision 2015/789/EU. At the time of the audit, Saxony had inspected 1,394, while Thuringia 2,535 squares, 9% and 16% of the squares in the BZ in their territory, respectively.

The 2016 surveys stopped in mid-October, because the appearance of autumn leaf colours made the recognition of symptomatic plants impossible. The audit team noted that due to the staff shortage and the available time the CAs were not able to complete the surveillance according to the provisions of the EU Decision.

label_heading: Conclusions on the movement control of specified plants
paragraph_text: The implementation of movement restrictions relies mainly on public awareness. Little actual control of the sale/movement of specified plants takes place and the level of guarantee foreseen in the Decision 2015/789/EU may not be achieved. 6 OVERALL CONCLUSIONS With comprehensive assistance of the federal CAs, Saxony and Thuringia implemented appropriate measures with the aim to eradicate Xf following a confirmed finding in May 2016. Human and financial resources were mobilised to address the outbreak. A robust information campaign channels all necessary information to the relevant producers and traders and to the general public. An adequate laboratory regime was established for testing Xf wi

The audit team noted during visits in nurseries and garden centres in the BZ that the operators: All have stocks of specified plants and market them all year around; Grow or keep the specified plants in open field or in non-vector-proof establishments; Do not carry out vector controls, the applied chemicals target the main pests of the plants, but not the xylem feeding vectors; Usually do not have detailed inventories of the specified plant stocks, their origin and time of arrival; Do not register their customers, however they stated that they are usually from the area and are informed about the movement restrictions; Are fully aware of the details of the EU legislation, including the list o

The audit team also noted that: LPPS inspectors of Saxony and Thuringia carry out some controls on the movement of specified plants in the nurseries and garden centres in the BZ; The customers of the nurseries and garden centres are not checked and no road controls are carried out; The implementation of movement restrictions relies mainly of the extensive public awareness measures (see chapter 5.5.1 and 5.1.5). The audit team therefore considers that the official controls cannot ensure that plants which have been grown for at least a part of their life in the DA are not moved out of that area. label_heading: Conclusions on organisational aspects of controls
paragraph_text: There is a clear organisation of the controls related to PWN and there is a good cooperation and communication between the entities involved. However, in Galicia, this organisation did not ensure the timely and appropriate implementation of surveys, testing of samples and control measures in the demarcated area of As Neves.

label_heading: Conclusions on organisational aspects of controls
paragraph_text: The current Action plan for the demarcated area of As Neves is not fully in line with Decision 2012/535/EU as it limits the intensive survey to the surroundings of the new finding although such an intensive survey was still required around the initial outbreak. 5.2 ANNUAL SURVEYS OF THE TERRITORY OUTSIDE DEMARCATED AREAS Legal requirements Article 2 of Decision 2012/535/EU 7 Findings

Control measures have been taken to address the new detection of PWN based on the assumption that this is a new outbreak linked to a new incursion from Portugal. However, this is not based on evidence and the extension of the outbreak of 2010 cannot be excluded. This risk is not addressed by control measures taken so far.

The delays in felling and removing the infested symptomatic tree and the absence of preventative measures resulted in a risk of further spread of PWN. These risks would have been significantly less if control measures had been implemented in accordance with Point 7 of Annex I to Decision 2012/535/EU. The inadequate implementation of the clear-cut following the finding of PWN further adds to this risk. 5.4 CONTROL MEASURES IN THE DEMARCATED AREA Legal requirements Article 6 of Decision 2012/535/EU Points 6 to 10 of Annex I to Decision 2012/535/EU Findings 5.4.1 Annual surveys in the demarcated areas

However, despite of the fact that the demarcated area had been in place since the end of 2010, the regional service had not set up a system ensuring the timely implementation of PWN control measures as required in Decision 2012/535/EU, the Regional legislation and the Action plan for the demarcated area. In particular, In 2016, the resources allocated to the surveys, identification of dead trees or trees in decline and sampling activities were insufficient for the work to be completed in the whole demarcated area at the frequency and within the required deadlines; (see also section 5.4.1) In 2015 and 2016, the work of felling and removal of identified dead or declining trees in the demarcate

The audit team noted that the sample taken from the symptomatic tree in Salvaterra do Mino on 18 February 2016 was confirmed to be infested with PWN by the regional laboratory on 2 May 2016 i.e. 2,5 months after the sample was taken. Although the symptomatic tree was in a demarcated area where there was a requirement to fell and remove identified dead or declining trees before the 1 April, the tree was not felled until the diagnostic was confirmed. Although the confirmation by the National Laboratory is a prerequisite for taking official measures, the handing of the infested wood sample by the Regional laboratory was not done so as to minimise the delays in getting the results confirmed: the

The audit team noted that the surveys of trees in the 20 km zone along the border with Portugal and the demarcated area are performed by the same two people from Tragsatec. The map above shows that the work is conducted starting from the border with Portugal and progressing Northward in accordance with the regional service's assessment of the highest risk for PWN infestation. The results of the intensive surveys conducted in this 20 km zone along Portugal since 2010 have demonstrated that PWN is not present outside the existing demarcated area of As Neves. This is confirmed by the preliminary results of the surveys conducted in 2016. Conclusions on annual surveys of the territory outside dem

The audit team noted that Tragsatec staff involved in these felling and sampling activities did not check for the presence of signs of vectors' activity either in the infested tree or in the dead or declining trees and branches surrounding it. There was no assessment of the risk of further spread from this site before the felling and removal of the susceptible trees. Based on the interviews held by the audit teams, staff involved in these activities and in their supervision had a limited knowledge of the biology of the vector and ways of spreading PWN and could not explain the signs of vector activity.

The audit team noted that there was no investigation of the possible origin of the PWN infestation. The regional service considered that this new finding was a new incursion from Portugal, either by dispersal flight of the vector or human assisted dispersal. However, they had not identified any particular risk in the surroundings or any evidence for two such incursions at short distance despite intensive surveys showing that the 20 km zone along the border with Portugal is free from PWN (see section 5.2). The audit team noted that while there was no evidence of a new incursion from Portugal, the following facts points towards an extension of the outbreak detected in 2010: The two infested tr

The action plan dated May 2016 further specifies the different zones comprising the Buffer Zone and control measures to be implemented in each of these: Zone A: clear-cut zone of 100 m radius around the new infested tree; Zone B: a 100 m to 3 km zone around the new infested tree where intensified surveys of susceptible trees and vectors are conducted; Zone C: the remaining part of the buffer zone also referred to as 3-20 km zone.

The audit team noted that the order delegating the work of felling and removing trees to Tragsa was signed mid-July i.e. at the end of the period given to private owners to organise their sales of wood. Consequently the clear-cut zone was implemented from end-July to September, which is after most of the vectors would already have emerged from trees and branches. These measures were therefore implemented too late to be effective in preventing PWN spread and are therefore not in line with point 2 of Annex I to Decision 2012/535/EU.

According to the regional service, 1,282 susceptible trees were felled in the clear-cut zone. A total of 17 samples were taken from symptomatic trees which were sampled. Only one sample was taken from asymptomatic trees without this being justified based on the risk of spread of PWN which is not in line with point 2 of Annex I. This requires that a number of asymptomatic trees be sampled selected based on the risk of spreading of PWN. All samples tested negative for PWN.

The audit team visited the infested site and the clear-cut zone and noted that the stump of the infested tree was marked with a red ring and was located in an uneven and rocky terrain on a steep slope. The representative of the regional service who had supervised the work stated that after the felling and removal of trees, the branches and cutting remains had been crushed on-site by a tractor and that the result had been judged satisfactory given the characteristics of the area. The audit team noted that on such terrain the method implemented could not be effective and indeed spotted the presence of some branches big enough to contain pupae of the vector. This is not in line with point 2 of

The competent authority reported that at the time of the audit, the survey was completed in zone B while work was still on-going in zone C, as shown in table 1. The audit team noted that the level of samples taken from asymptomatic trees in zone B in 2016 is not consistent with requirements laid down in point 4(a) of Annex I. The regional service confirmed that the asymptomatic trees sampled were those present at the grid points surveyed (see also 5.3.3). At the time of the DG SANTE audit, protocols had been signed between FASFC and each of the Regions under which FASFC will perform animal welfare controls at slaughterhouses and on farms. Regions remain directly responsible for follow-up of non-compliance and any necessary enforcement action arising from the results of the controls carried out by FASFC. A representative of the regional internal audit service of the Flanders Region was also present. In the case of Flanders, the internal audit representative confirmed that his service was aware of the need to plan audits in relation to animal welfare controls to meet the requirements of Article 4(6) of Regulation (EC) No. 882/2004 and that while the planning for 2016 did not include its topic, audits were expected to take place in 2018. AFSVSPP does at present not have a system in place for independent scrutiny.
IRSAFHF is in the early stages of planning for independent scrutiny.

HIRS has a quality system in place that gives limited assurances to the management on the audit processes' achievement of the objectives of Article 4(6) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. 5.2.3 Auditor competence 5.2.3.1 Legal requirements Articles 2(6) and 4(6) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 do not lay down specific requirements regarding the competence of auditors. Article 6 of the same Regulation requires that staff performing official controls "receive, for their area of competence, appropriate training enabling them to undertake their duties competently" and "keep up-to-date in their area of competence and receive regular additional training as necessary" Section 6.6 of the Annex of Commis
AFSVSPP had at the time of the audit not made plans for independent scrutiny.
IRSAFHF has not engaged in independent scrutiny so far. One external audit is planned for 2018, but at the time of this audit, no terms of reference for this external audit had been determined.

HIRS is subject to an external evaluation every year, as part of its ISO accreditation. These external evaluations focus on compliance with ISO standards and cover a much wider scope than their official controls which fall under Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. The external evaluator gives an opinion on the independence of the audit body/auditors in the context of the Quality Management system, but does not demonstrate that Article 4(6) of Regulation (EC) 882/2004 has been taken into consideration. However, as the evaluation reports identify areas for improvement and best practices, they can provide for some aspects of independent scrutiny. Conclusions

The range of official controls that must be covered by audit programmes has been adequately identified and considered by two of the three audit bodies. IRSAFHF does not include relevant activities at central level.
AFSVSPP has a system in place for development and approval of audit programmes. However, all areas cannot with current arrangements be covered in a reasonable timeframe.

AFSVSPP establishes its programme based on specific food and feed risks. There are documented procedures for development and approval of audit programmes. A risk assessment with risk analysis and its impact, considering "effectiveness" and "sensitivity", has been done with participation of the Director of Food Safety, Veterinary and Plant Health Inspection; the Heads of Professional Divisions and the Heads of Regions. The participants did their assessments on their own and separately for each area/topic. The total results were compiled and the areas/topics with highest scores were prioritised for audits. The Director General approves the plan and can propose areas to include. Recommendations
In AFSVSPP the impact of the audits is undermined by the failure to address recommendations in a systematic and timely fashion.

AFSVSPP indicated that certain audits (e.g. border inspection posts) lead to recommendations which are focused on the inspection level and follow-up is easier than when audits identify certain policy measures which need to be improved. When recommendations address policy level issues it is sometimes less clear who should take responsibility to develop an action plan.

For DGCCRF, independent scrutiny of the current audit processes has not yet been carried out. This is contrary to the requirements of Article 4(6) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. 5.2.3 Auditor competence 5.2.3.1 Legal requirements Articles 2(6) and 4(6) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 do not lay down specific requirements regarding the competence of auditors. For DGCCRF, even if some potential mechanisms exist (the Ministerial Audit Committee) that could be suitable to undertake independent scrutiny of the audit processes, these mechanisms are not being used for this purpose at present.
At the time of the DG SANTE audit, no decisions had been taken as to when and how independent scrutiny of the DGCCRF internal audit processes would be achieved. Conclusions

A system for training of officials and for keeping their competence up-to-date is in place and the knowledge of the officials met was in general satisfactory, with the exception of HACCP-based programmes. 5.1.9 Enforcement measures Legal requirements Article 54 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Findings

Official controls do not sufficiently verify the implementation of HACCP-based procedures by the FBOs, thus possibly overlooking incompletely designed and implemented HACCP-based procedures. 5.2.3 Microbiological criteria for foodstuffs Legal requirements Article 4 of Regulation (EC) No 854/2004 and Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005. Findings

The audit team noted that the officials met during the visits in the dairy processing establishments had a limited knowledge with regard to evaluation of FBOs' HACCP- based procedures (see paragraph No 60); The CCA stated that no specific training on HACCP-based procedures has been provided so far. Conclusions on training

The documented official controls seen by the audit team showed that, in some cases, non-conformities such as non-updated procedures, absence of action thresholds for certain microbiological criteria to be set by the FBO, corrective actions not reflected in the real activity of the establishment (e.g. acceptance of raw milk exceeding the limits for TPC/SCC and notification to the CA, potable water treatment, etc.), were not properly identified and evaluated by the CA.

The evaluation of FBOs' HACCP-based systems is included in the inspection checklist for processing establishments. However, the checklist includes a generic reference to the existence of HACCP-based systems and to their evaluation. No instructions on how to evaluate HACCP-based programmes had been provided to official staff at the time of the audit. The audit team noted that some of the official staff interviewed had a limited knowledge in the matter. Conclusions on HACCP based systems

While all competent authorities have taken steps to ensure independent scrutiny: in two competent authorities the arrangements had only very recently been put in place; in another two competent authorities the arrangements were insufficient to achieve the objectives of the process either because the whole audit process was not included in the scrutiny or because the arrangements for such scrutiny did not involve individuals with sufficient relevant experience in the field of audits conducted in accordance with Article 4(6) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

In DAFM, the audit charters of both VIAU and IAU state that independent scrutiny shall be carried out by the Audit Monitoring Group. In practice, this group is one person: both VIAU and IAU have for a number of years used an external expert to scrutinise and provide feedback on their audit programmes, in particular to ensure that appropriate risks were considered. This same individual is a co-signatory of their audit charters.
While this process adds value to the audit programmes, it does not consider other aspects of the audit process and no particular feedback on these aspects has been received.

SFPA has recognised that some adjustments will be necessary to enable the committee to discharge this newer responsibility: The current audit committee membership was set up before the inclusion of audits conducted in accordance with Article 4(6) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 in its remit. As a result its membership was established with a focus on financial auditing and internal controls. The SFPA representative met by the DG SANTE audit team stated the reinforcement of the committee with additional external members with specific expertise relevant to the internal audit of fisheries control and food safety of fishery products was under discussion; The terms of reference for the committee in

The charter states that its scrutiny should have a particular focus on ensuring that the audit process "is capable of producing objective results and meeting its obligations under Regulation (EC) No 882/2004". At the time of this DG SANTE audit, the terms of reference for the independent scrutiny had been drafted, based on the NAS Network document on Independence and Independent Scrutiny. A suitable individual to carry out independent scrutiny had just been identified and it was intended to finalise the terms of reference with this person over the following weeks.

label_heading: Conclusions on legislation and implementing measures
paragraph_text: National legislation and guidelines necessary to implement EU requirements relevant for the sector audited have been issued and, from a preliminary analysis, they are in line with EU legislation with the exception of the national measures applied to FBOs who 4 process their own milk at farm level. These latter measures are not in line with Article 5 of Regulation (EC) No 853/2004 as they provide for placing products on the national market with the application of an identification mark which does not comply with the requirements of Annex II, Section I of Regulation (EC) No 853/2004.

Ordinance on special conditions for approval of certain establishments dealing with food of animal origin (OJ 100/15) sets out the requirements for FBOs processing their own milk on the holding and selling their dairy products on farm, markets, exhibitions, restaurants and retailers in the country. The Ordinance establishes that the products must be marked with a round identification mark bearing the same approval number (see paragraph 39): this is not in line with the requirements of Annex II, Section I of Regulation (EC) No 853/2004, prescribing an identification marking of foodstuffs of animal origin, when manufactured in the EU by an approved establishment, of oval shape. Conclusions on

The Ordinance on special conditions for approval of certain establishments dealing with food of animal origin covers specific requirements to be complied with by facilities processing milk at the farm of origin for direct supply of dairy products, marked with a special identification mark, to final consumers at the place of production and at markets and exhibitions in the whole country. These requirements are related to layout, equipment, operation and hygiene and provide that dedicated spaces must be arranged for equipment destined for collection/storage of raw milk and for by-products not intended for human consumption, rooms must also be dedicated for milk processing and for maturing of d

label_heading: Conclusions on registration/approval of food business establishments
paragraph_text: There is a system in place for the registration and approval of establishments that allows the CAs to keep them under official controls. However, the system in place does not require the approval of all MCCs, contrary to the requirements of Article 4 of Regulation (EC) No 853/2004.

label_heading: Conclusion on controls on HACCP-based systems
paragraph_text: The control system in place includes official controls for verification of FBO compliance with HACCP-based procedures. However its effectiveness is compromised as controllers are not able to identify some non-compliances in the design and implementation of the HACCP-based procedures and therefore cannot verify that FBOs identify the risks associated to their production, via CCPs, have them 19 under control and take appropriate corrective actions when necessary. 5.4.6 Microbiological criteria for foodstuffs Legal requirements Article 4 of Regulation (EC) No 854/2004 and Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005. Findings

A training system aimed at ensuring that official staff is able to carry-out its tasks adequately is in place. However, based on the findings noted during the audit, it does not seem to be effective. 5.1.8 Enforcement measures Legal requirements Article 54 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Findings

Despite the above and the fact that training sessions relevant to the scope of this mission are organised by the CCA, the level of knowledge of official control staff was in certain cases inadequate, notably in relation to the approval of establishments, pasteurisation and traceability, especially so in two of the four counties visited.

Controls on food of non-animal origin, under the responsibility of DGCCRF, are performed in temporary storage facilities where hygiene conditions are only verified after the goods arrive. This arrangement does not ensure that goods are handled hygienically.

DGAL uses BIP facilities for the controls under their responsibility (products of animal origin and feed). For the controls on food of non-animal origin, identity and physical checks are implemented in interim storage facilities operating under Customs supervision. The importers propose on a case-by-case basis the storage facility, chosen amongst any operator (not necessarily food or feed operator) functioning in the area2. The competent authority underlined that this practice is not a use of the derogation provided under Article 19 of Regulation (EC) 669/2009. They also stated that they are satisfied with the guarantees provided by the current arrangements.

The system described in the previous paragraph does not ensure that the facilities used for identity and physical checks are hygienically adequate to store food. The registration as food operators of these interim storages is not a pre-requisite, so operators are not necessarily subject to the obligations laid down in Regulation (EC) No 852/2004. Verification of the hygiene conditions is done when the officials go on-the-spot to implement the import controls. This arrangement does not ensure that products are always handled hygienically (which is required by Article 16(3) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004). 5.1.3 Fees

In compliance with the EU legal requirements, staff are appropriately qualified to perform their job, and instructions are available. The communication between and within the competent authorities functions well, which contributes to the effectiveness of the controls.

If the premises have a food storage activity, they are registered in the food sector and subject as such to hygiene rules. paragraph_text: There is an adequate system allowing the implementation of identity and physical checks and ensuring that the consignments are not released before satisfactory laboratory test results are received. However, in Thessaloniki port DPE the conditions under which the checks are carried out do not comply with the general hygiene requirements.

label_heading: Conclusions on the implementation of identity and physical checks
paragraph_text: The required sampling frequency is not always respected in DPEs and BIPs. The current sampling practices (i.e. not testing for all analytes subject to enhanced control measures) 15 do not ensure the compliance with requirements of EU legislation regarding sampling scope. 5.3.4 Decision on the consignments Legal requirements Articles 18, 19, 20 and 21 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 Articles 4(4), 5(1) and Annex III to Directive 97/78/EC Articles 8(2) and 13 of Regulation (EC) No 669/2009 Articles 9, 11 and 12 of Regulation (EU) No 884/2014 Article 8 of Regulation (EU) No 885/2014 Article 8 of Regulation (EU) No 2015/175 Article 12 of Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) No 2016/6 Findings

The AHD drafted the monitoring plan including sampling instructions with the support of experts from the DHSFAO in 2011. However, this plan does not cover the implementation of the requirements of Article 3(1) of Commission Decision 2010/381/EC. The audit team noted that the competent authority did not set up any plans in order to ensure that official samples are taken from at least 10 % of consignments of aquaculture products imported from India presented at BIPs1. Therefore, Pireas BIP did not implement required sampling for this type of consignment (see finding 34).

The audit team noted that the central competent authority did not provide instructions on principles to be applied in relation to random sampling of consignments of hazelnuts from Turkey in order to implement the requirements of Regulation (EC) No 884/2014 to ensure the balanced frequency of identity and physical checks upon import to different DPEs in Greece2.

The audit team noted that aquaculture products imported from India and intended for human consumption were not sampled contrary to the requirements of Article 3(1) of Decision 2010/381/EC. Peplos BIP and Kipi Evrou DPEs use a courier service to transport samples. The samples are packaged into an additional box before transportation to the laboratory. At Thessaloniki port DPE, the sample is handed to the handling agent who gives it to a courier service to take it to the laboratory. This practice does not exclude the possibility of the sample being tampered with therefore it does not guarantee the legal and analy

The audit team noted that staff of BIPs and DPEs visited (except Peplos BIP and Kipi Evrou DPE) have a procedure in place to verify that the consignment leaves the territory of Greece, requesting the person responsible for the load to submit the bill of lading or other documentary proof. At Peplos BIP and Kipi Evrou DPE, the detained consignments are located in the vicinity of the official facilities, and in case of rejection, 16 are returned to the country of origin. The staff at Peplos BIP and Kipi Evrou DPE could not provide the documented evidence that rejected consignments have left the territory respecting the 60 day deadline contrary to the requirements of Article 21(2) of Regulation

At the Thessaloniki port BIP the competent authority has taken corrective actions to rectify deficiencies in the facilities reported in 2015: the changing room and ceiling in the unloading room for products for non-human consumption have been put in place, and the walls have a hygienic slope finish. The audit team noted that the BIP staff do not follow the hygiene requirements to steer the flow of personnel (risk of cross- contamination) in the area for products for human consumption.

label_heading: Conclusions on the training, supervision and audits
paragraph_text: In the list there are two private food and feed business operator facilities approved as DPEs. They are located in the port territory and they accept to store consignments for identity and physical checks, including laboratory analyses from other FBOs. At the same time they are approved as DPIs as well. However, documentary checks for these consignments are carried out at local FCOs instead of DPEs.

Where a rejected consignment of products of non-animal origin is re-dispatched, the operator is not requested to submit any evidence that the consignment left Denmark for an approved destination. label_heading: Conclusions on the general requirements regarding the control system
paragraph_text: The current facilities at the DPEs/DPIs visited are not appropriate to undertake the necessary checks and to handle food of non-animal origin hygienically, leading to a risk of contamination or spoilage.

In the three DPEs/DPIs for food of non-animal origin visited, the audit team noted non-compliances concerning the structure of the facilities that negatively impact on the hygienic handling and storage of the consignments, contrary to requirements of Article 4 of Commission Regulation (EC) No 669/2009, Article 8 of Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) No 884/2014 and Article 16(3) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

In the DPE/DPI Genova, the DGISAN informed the audit team that they have accepted plans for new DPE/DPI facilities. The current facilities are of a non- permanent nature (a marquee located in a customs warehouse) and are not appropriate to undertake the necessary checks and to handle the food hygienically. It is foreseen that the new facilities will be in place by March 2017.

In the DPE/DPI Ravenna, the competent authorities gave a very short deadline to the operators of the DPE/DPI to rectify the non-compliances identified during official controls in order to ensure that the facilities have the basic structures for the hygienic handling and storage of the consignments. The competent authorities responsible for the monitoring of AMR are clearly designated, adequately organised and have the necessary powers for the implementation of the harmonised monitoring of AMR. As a consequence, the available Salmonella isolates were not tested and/or reported (see points 22 and 25) in order to achieve the minimum number required. 1 http://ec.europa.eu/food/audits-analysis/country_profiles/details.cfm?co_id=NL 3 Conclusions on the competent authority

In 2014, the competent authority did not report any Salmonella isolates obtained at farm level for the three categories requested by Decision 2013/652/EU (broilers, laying hens and turkeys), despite their availability. The competent authority stated that some of the reported isolates may have originated from samples taken in the context of the SNCP but the flow of information does not allow distinguishing them from isolates from other origins.

Data on the isolates provided by the RIVM do not include information regarding the sampling programme/context, which does not allow the NRL for AMR to ensure that an adequate selection of isolates is subject to AST. As a consequence, all the reported Salmonella isolates were identified as obtained from caeca at slaughterhouses while their origin was unknown.

The RIVM is responsible for the selection of isolates that are submitted to the NRL for AMR for AST. However, the RIVM only gathers a small amount of isolates obtained under the SNCP. This is not in accordance with the technical requirements of point 2.3.2 of Part A of the Annex to Decision 2013/652/EU as, if available, Salmonella isolates obtained in the framework of the national control programmes shall be collected to achieve the minimum number required.

label_heading: Conclusions on assessment and reporting of AMR
paragraph_text: The annual report includes all the mandatory information for each individual isolate reported under harmonised monitoring, and a significant amount of information reported on a voluntary basis which exceeds the current mandatory monitoring under EU legislation. There are though some weaknesses in the completeness and quality of information provided for some isolates and the lack of overall description of the implementation of AMR monitoring that have an influence on the harmonised reporting of AMR data. 13 6 GOOD PRACTICES AND DEVELOPING AREAS Findings

The veterinary and imports division of the NVWA is responsible for reporting AMR data under Decision 2013/652/EU to EFSA. The verification of the reported data, prior to their uploading, is minimal. As a consequence, the omission of some compulsory reporting areas, such as Salmonella isolates at farm level and in the context of Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005, was not noticed.
In the case of the Salmonella isolates reported in 2014 and 2015 the sampling stage and the matrix was reported incorrectly.

Also incorrect isolation dates were reported for the ESBL-producing E. coli isolates tested in 2015 by the NRL for AMR where different isolation dates were reported for the first and second panel testing of the same isolate.
The ESBL-producing E. coli identified in 2015 from bovine and pig meat retail samples were not reported. The competent authority stated that this was due to a mistake.
The competent authority could not exclude that isolates from repeated epidemiological units were reported, which is requested by point 2.3 Part A of the Annex to Decision 2013/652/EU.
The collection form used for reporting the `generic description of the implementation of the AMR monitoring' was not submitted to EFSA. Conclusions on assessment and reporting of AMR

Variability in the comprehensiveness of registration of both producers and pack houses exists between the various RCAs visited/consulted. Registration is particularly incomplete in two ACs where considerable surface areas of ware potatoes are grown but the growers are not registered or known to the relevant RCAs. This undermines fundamentally the overall effectiveness and reliability of surveillance efforts and ultimately any control measures in place.

All RCAs consulted use the CAP register as a basis for their respective official records of professional potato producers. Typically this is further supplemented with industry information on an on-going basis. However, the team noted that in certain ACs registration is incomplete.

All RCAs acknowledged difficulties in dealing with the generic issue of small private growers. As there are no legal requirements, small non-professional growers are not registered, and normally produce for private consumption within the immediate locality of production. RCA inspections are largely conducted at random or guided by local knowledge. 5.2.2 Surveillance strategy

label_heading: Conclusions on control measures for Epitrix sp.
paragraph_text: Whilst some largely administrative issues with respect to plant passports were identified with respect to the movement of potatoes from the DA in Galicia, gaps in the registration and export of infested potatoes from unregistered premises and/or traders from Andalucía result in a high risk of international dissemination from infested, uncontrolled lots.

In Galicia, there is a concrete strategy for the containment of the pest in place, with respect to movement and traceability of potatoes from the DA to other autonomous communities in Spain via certain pack houses. However, the audit team also noted that one packer was using conventional commercial potato labels in place of replacement plant passports, whilst for another pack house there was a lapse in registration due to change in ownership. The use of commercial potato labels in place of replacement plant passports appeared to be a generic approach by this RCA which did not consider it a non-conformity.

However, the sampling approach retains a very high level of focus on crop surfaces, with insufficient attention given to other hosts and/or weeds in neighbouring fields and/or boundaries (hedgerows), which present a natural reservoir of potato flea beetles and function as sources of re-infestation. 5.3 CONTROL MEASURES WHERE THE PRESENCE OF EPITRIX SP. IS CONFIRMED 5.3.1 Demarcation of Epitrix sp. infestation Legal requirements Article 5 of Decision 2012/270/EU. Annex II Section 1 of Decision 2012/270/EU. Article 16.2 of Directive 2000/29/EC. Findings
However, with respect to other hosts, very little practical guidance is provided in the NCP.

In all RCAs visited, sampling was largely focused on the surface crop. Less systematic and comprehensive attention was paid to borders and hedgerows, or other areas in the immediate vicinity or adjoining potato fields under survey, populated by other host plants, such as weeds. This is not fully in line with Article 4(1) of Decision 2012/270/EU. Such areas, when included, were typically subject to visual inspection only.

No entomological nets were employed in any of the RCAs visited as part of Epitrix surveys. Similarly, insect traps, where used, were deployed in low numbers. 12 Conclusions on Epitrix sp. surveillance strategy and results

However, irrespective of the legal approach, monitoring around and in the vicinity of fields remains unsatisfactory, in particular with respect to other hosts and weed hosts (see also paragraphs 41 and 42).

label_heading: Conclusions on the development of the programme of audits
paragraph_text: The process for the audit programme development is not well-documented or transparent and it does not follow risk-based prioritisation, which means that it does not result in programmes that could achieve an appropriate risk-based coverage of relevant official control activities. The development of the audit programme is further constrained by the lack of stable and sufficient resources without which the continuity in the provision of audit services cannot be ensured. 5.2.5 Implementation of the audit process 5.2.5.1 Legal requirements Article 2(6) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 states that "Audit" "means a systematic and independent examination to determine whether activities and related re

The audit activities have consisted of one pilot project per year since 2014 and each project covers a specific area of the official controls. Plant health, the residue control programme for food of animal origin, and the Salmonella control programme are the three projects that have been carried out so far. In 2017, an audit project on the control of fertilisers will be carried out. The competent authority has prepared a multi-annual audit programme for the period 2015-2018 that includes areas based on the choices made by the Directors of Evira in the context of the pilot phase of the audit function. The purpose was to have audits in sectors that could be used for modelling and further devel

The audit system has not defined the audit universe and as regards the audit programme development, the process is not well-documented and transparent, and it does not include risk-based prioritisation.

The audit team noted that the extended scope and time-consuming nature of the audit programme and its execution combined with the limitations in the availability of human resources, makes it unfeasible to cover all relevant areas of official controls in a five- year period. However, in some notable cases, consignments were accepted without the required health guarantees, which could lead to the import of live animals, food and feed which does not comply with the EU health requirements, potentially causing a risk to public and animal health. 5.4 THE USE OF TRADE CONTROL AND EXPERT SYSTEM Legal requirements Article 3(2) of Commission Decision 2004/292/EC Findings

Whilst the health guarantees were included for three of the consignments (with requirements comparable to those in the model certificate), the welfare requirements were not included in the competent authority's own template. b) The central competent authority instructed the BIP staff to all

While current arrangements give some assurance about the performance of the IIAS and can add value, they do not fully address the requirement for independent scrutiny in that the MF assessment does not consider objectives of Article 4(6) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 and the MF cannot give an independent assessment of the suitability of its own audit procedures. 5.2.3 Auditor competence 5.2.3.1 Legal requirements Articles 2(6) and 4(6) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 do not lay down specific requirements regarding the competence of auditors. Article 6 of the same Regulation requires that staff performing official controls "receive, for their area of competence, appropriate training enabling

Examination of the reports of these assessments showed that they did give useful input regarding compliance with MF requirements and international internal auditing standards. While the assessment does not explicitly consider the objectives of Article 4(6) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 or the guidance laid down in Commission Decision 2006/677/EC, the template used addresses many points of relevance for the implementation of audits required by Article 4(6) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, including issues such as: Purpose, powers and responsibility of the audit service; Independence and objectivity; Competence/professional expertise and continuing training; Quality assurance of internal audit

The DG SANTE audit team consider that MF cannot give an independent assessment of the suitability or effectiveness of the common audit procedures which IIAS are required to implement, since these procedures are developed and defined by MF itself.

It was noted that the external quality check reports contain a disclaimer stating that they cannot be considered to constitute an external assessment as envisaged under the International Standards for the Professional Practice of Internal Auditing 1312. 12 33. The IIAS-MA representative indicated that an external independent scrutiny would be very welcome, but difficult to arrange due to the cost.

All three CCAs have developed and implemented processes for establishing annual and multiannual audit programmes. These processes are not adequately documented thus the CCAs cannot demonstrate that all relevant areas have been considered, an adequate coverage in a reasonable timeframe has been achieved and that audit programmes result from a risk-based prioritisation.

The audit team noted that, when developing the audit programme, SVA has not properly defined all relevant audit areas (the audit areas are not sufficiently detailed e.g. animal health is determined as an audit area although this could be further broken down to different animal species, activities, diseases etc.) and the audit programme development process is not well-documented as regards risk-based prioritisation (it is not evident whether all relevant areas were considered and on which basis decision on selection of audit topics was made).

The audit areas in CAFIA audit system are expanded since 2011, and the annual audit programme indicates an addition of new audit topics. The topics include microbiological sampling, traceability, genetically modified organisms in food, risk-based planning of official controls etc. The audit team noted that there is no evidence on how new topics are determined and there is no overview of the areas that need to be considered in the audit programme. In addition, there is no evidence that the development of the audit programme has considered all relevant areas, and it is not evident how this results in risk based prioritisation and effective coverage of all areas in a reasonable timeframe.

The audit team noted that CISTA has not adequately defined the areas that need to be covered by the audit activities. In addition although the planned arrangements refer to risk based planning of audit programmes, CISTA could not demonstrate that audit programmes resulted from a risk-based prioritisation.

paragraph_text: The approach to risk-based planning is inadequately documented and defined. paragraph_text: In general, the documentary checks are performed correctly in order to ensure compliance with the requirements of the legislation.
