label_heading: Conclusions on surveillance, controls on domestic pigs
paragraph_text: Although with regional variations, the active surveillance programme for domestic pigs provides substantial guarantees that the CSF virus is not circulating in commercial holdings. The system gives more limited guarantees for holdings with low biosecurity, where shortcomings in holding registration and records undermine the ability to fully assess the CSF epidemiological situation but the sharp drop in the number of backyard holdings following comprehensive verification by the competent authority mitigates the significance of this weakness.

The active surveillance system for wild boars has significantly improved since the authorities issued guidelines on the targeted sampling of wild boars for the CSF surveillance programme in 2013. The programme, as implemented, has adequate sensitivity for confirming absence of CSF virus circulation in wild boars. The significant under-performances in some regions lead to uncertainty regarding the disease status of these zones, especially for peripheral regions, where a vaccination programme has been implemented until recently. There are no procedures in place to confirm or rule out the presence of the disease when a wild boar is tested seropositive.

Based on the data provided by the competent authority, they surpassed the total target set for industrial and type A holdings where animals had to be clinically examined, but not all regions achieved the targets set for them. In 2015, authorised veterinarians had to inspect 100% and official veterinarians 10% of backyard farms; in 2016, the surveillance scheme changed to 10% and 5% respectively.

In Corsica, eradication measures, fully in line with provisions of the Decision were implemented only in the case of the first outbreaks, identified in 2015. The audit team noted: The number of outbreaks is very high; 237 were identified until February 2016 and a further 104 in the period February 2016 ­ March 2017; The number of host species, found positive increased rapidly and at the time of the audit there were 36; A part of the IZs are located in areas with difficult access where the removal of any plant is sometimes very difficult; A considerable part of the IZs cover natural land or abandoned agricultural land, where, after the removal of the hosts, no agricultural activity is expecte

The following plants present in the IZ are removed and destroyed: Until May 2016: plants which were tested positive or showing symptoms and all the Polygala myrtifolia plants, regardless of their health; Since May 2016 in addition all plants of the species, which tested positive, are also eradicated.

The audit team was informed by the CA that although numerous new host species were identified in Corsica in 2016, only about 25% of the IZs, established in 2015 and about 75 % of the IZs established in 2016 were revisited. The DPPP has not issued comprehensive national inspection guidelines for import controls. The DPPP stated that, since inspectors were highly qualified and well trained, there was no need to provide detailed guidance documents, and that, moreover, the specific details of the implementation of import controls was left to the discretion of the regional and local services. The DPPP have issued translations of relevant ISPMs, notably ISPM 23 and 31, which inspectors are instructed to follow. In addition, some specific guidance documents have been issued by the DPPP, which deal with controls of Egyptian potatoes, collecting and dispatching samples for laboratory analysis and record keeping.

The audit team noted that many of the tasks and procedures involved with import controls are not covered by the guidelines prepared by the DPPP, for example, no 5 specific guidance is available on the procedure to follow when carrying out documentary, identity or plant health checks, or the process to follow in the case of non- compliance.

At Thessaloniki seaport, the RCPPQC had prepared a local guidance document on import procedures, the DPPP stated that it had not been approved centrally. Evira informed the audit team that it does not consider surveillance of national production through sampling and testing necessary, because the Customs' checks on incoming food ingredients (used by domestic producers) is considered to provide sufficient safeguards since GMOs are not commercially grown in Finland. According to Evira no food items containing GMOs are produced in Finland and consequently as the customs already checks the imported potential GM ingredients, there is little need to check potential cross contamination again at the national production level. Annual tests carried out up to 2013 did not, according to Evira, give any non-compliant test results. However, due to the subs

Evira classifies feed business operators into risk categories. The classification determines the frequency of inspection. Production of medicated feed, use of animal proteins and production volume are the main factors determining the risk category. As regards GMOs, Evira has chosen to almost exclusively sample and test (for authorised and non-EU-authorised GMOs) feed that is not labelled as containing GMOs (not supposed to contain authorised GMOs above a 0.9% level). However, there is no evidence that feed containing authorised GMO above 0.9% (and labelled as such) is less 7 likely to contain non-EU-authorised GMOs supporting its exclusion from sampling and testing.

The CAs have access to a broad scope of accredited analytical capability for GM events, which underpins the effectiveness of the control system. label_heading: Conclusions on national measures and sampling design
paragraph_text: The documented procedures and instructions in place could ensure adequate implementation of most of the provisions laid down in the legislation. The competent authorities have over time improved the design and implementation of the sampling plan addressing some issues that weakened this plan in the past. However, the gathering of AMR monitoring data in Italy is still not fully comparable with those obtained by other Member States. This is because further strengthening of the procedures is necessary, notably to verify that the minimum required slaughtered population is covered by the sampling and that an even distribution of sampling takes place during all months of the year.

The audit team noted that in 2016 over 90% of sampling was completed for all categories. The achievement of the targets set in the sampling plan improved from 2014 when only 83% and 66% of the planned caecal samples were achieved for broilers and turkeys respectively. Regarding 2015, the competent authorities achieved over 95% for all categories except for bovines under 1 year of age where only 74% was achieved.

The central competent authority has introduced in the 2017 AMR monitoring plan a new supervisory element that consists of the obligation for the regional authorities to submit the regional sampling plans for review to central level. Nevertheless, the audit team noted that the instruction does not specify the different elements to be included in the information provided in order to verify effectively compliance with certain elements of 2 In their response to the draft report the competent authority provided information on actions taken after the audit to address this issue. In the two regions visited, samples were generally taken on a Monday and Tuesday and on a few occasions on a Wednesday. This approach reduced the randomisation of the sampling days. The audit team noted that the NRL for AMR accepted samples until Friday which implies, with the sample delivery service available, that sampling could be routinely randomised from Monday to Thursday to fulfil the requirements of point 2.3 of Part A of the Annex to Decision 2013/652/EU and the EFSA guidance document 2014 9.

In the bovine slaughterhouse visited, samples were taken randomly selecting the day, with the constraints described above, and the animals to be sampled using an IT programme. In the poultry slaughterhouse visited, on the selected sampling dates most of the available lots were sampled in order to fulfil the required number of samples. In the pig slaughterhouse the sampling days and the carcasses to be sampled were selected by the sampling officer for reasons of convenience, which is not fully random 9.

This shortcoming undermines the assurances necessary for the protection of animals during transport.

There is therefore the risk that travelling times are exceeded once past the EU border.

Nevertheless, shortcomings and/or inconsistencies were noted in some of the establishments visited. These ranged from a lack of inspection visits and/or reports for approvals for which such inspection was required, to an incomplete list of relevant documentation which would have demonstrated that all of the approval steps had been performed. label_heading: Conclusion on the planning and implementation of inspections
paragraph_text: The competent authorities have a risk-based control plan in place covering feed additives, their ingredients and traceability, but their failure to consistently adhere to 7 planned arrangements and select establishments for inspections on the basis of established risk criteria weakens the efficiency of the control system.

The audit team noted that the number of planned routine controls had not been reached for at least the previous three years. As explained by the competent authority, this was due to human resource constraints, structural changes, the processing of available data, and outstanding inspection cases from previous years. Consequently the stated risk- based frequency of inspections is not being met. Furthermore, official controls that are performed at feed establishments no longer follow the planned risk-based criteria.

In the case of comprehensive inspections, the frequency is set once every three years but solely applying to the higher two categories of producing FeBOs and all feed additive producers, and only the higher category of non-producing FeBOs. As with routine controls, examples were seen of comprehensive inspection frequencies not being met. This is not in line with the requirements laid down by Article 3 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

label_heading: Conclusion on the planning and implementation of inspections
paragraph_text: The appropriate level of competency and knowledge were shown by all relevant competent authorities. Official controls targeted the relevant areas of feed business operators' obligations such as the implementations of HACCP based procedures, own control programmes including traceability, labelling and sampling. However, official controls did not verify that feed business operators met their obligation as regards the retention of samples. This weakens the effectives of the system of official feed controls. 5.2.2 Sampling 5.2.2.1 PLANNING OF OFFICIAL SAMPLING

label_heading: Conclusion on the planning and implementation of sampling
paragraph_text: Planning of official sampling is risk-based and the implementation, for the most part, is adequate, being carried out by staff with the requisite competence and expertise. Notwithstanding this, inadequate homogenisation of sampled materials and the absence of a suitable sampling tool for large volumes collectively undermine the effectiveness of the sampling programme and the legal and analytical validity of some of the official samples taken. 5.2.3 Actions taken on non-compliances

label_heading: Conclusion on the planning and implementation of inspections
paragraph_text: The audit team presented the BAES inspectors with various sampling scenarios and in all instances, they were able to quickly analyse the situation, and upon consulting the legislation, present the correct sampling procedural plan. Nevertheless, a systemic shortcoming was noted, in that the preparation of final samples from the aggregate sample was performed by simple manual mixing. This practice cannot ensure the appropriate homogenisation as required by part 9(4) of Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 152/2009.

label_heading: Conclusion on the planning and implementation of inspections
paragraph_text: The sampling equipment observed, whilst appropriate for sampling in certain conditions, did not allow sampling throughout the sampled portion when the product is stored in large bags or in bulk form. This is not in line with the requirements laid down by part 4 and 5 of Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 152/2009.

label_heading: Conclusion on actions taken on non-compliances
paragraph_text: Whilst there is a well-structured system for the identification and categorisation of non- compliances and initial communication to FeBOs requesting corrective action, its effectiveness is undermined by either an absence of monitoring or a much delayed follow-up of such non-compliances. BAES is unaware as to the level of resolution of non-compliances and is unaware of those unresolved non-compliances which would warrant an escalation of official enforcement. 10 5.2.4 Establishments producing/trading non-authorised (in the EU) feed additives but are exporting or re-exporting them from the EU to a third country

paragraph_text: The audit team saw several examples of such warning letters for minor and major non- compliances. The FeBOs visited were able to demonstrate that, following their internal analyses and investigations, corrective actions had been taken.

paragraph_text: With regard to the BAES' monitoring, follow-up and escalation of enforcement of unaddressed non-compliances, the audit team observed that in the case of the three major non-compliances presented as examples, in two of these, four weeks were given to the FeBOs to take appropriate action, with the follow up inspection only taking place around one and a half years after the original inspection visit. In the third case from the latter months of 2016, no date for corrective action had been given nor had follow-up yet taken place. paragraph_text: In the case of minor non-compliances, for which a time-scale for corrective action is, as defined in the BAES procedures, not given to FeBOs, there is no reporting mechanism, either by the FeBOs or the BAES inspectors, on corrective actions (if any) being taken. The degree to which sectors are covered varies according to the planning of the sectoral offices and the RPHSs and efforts are made to prioritise according to risk; While the coverage of audits is intense, in common with the situation seen by DG Health and Food Safety in a number of other Member States, there is a gap 3 In their comments on the draft report the Veterinary and Prevention Service of the Region of Lombardy stated that they will formalize, in the next planning documents, the criteria on which to define the priorities for sector audit activit

In relation to the ICQRF, audit programming is based on covering the full range of official control activities of each Territorial Office within a five-year cycle rather than on a risk-basis. In common with the situation for MH (and in a number of other Member States), there is a gap in coverage of the planning and programming activities carried out at the central level.
The activities of the sectoral offices in relation to planning and development of programmes of official controls are not covered.

The internal procedure requires an annual programme be drawn up based on available documentation and new alerts. All Territorial Offices must be audited at least once every five years. On-site audits include all relevant official control activities and specific sectors are not targeted. The activities of the central office responsible for planning and development of programmes of official controls are not covered. No annual audit programme was provided to the DG SANTE audit team.

label_heading: Conclusion on the planning and implementation of inspections
paragraph_text: In the Land where the official samples are taken by technicians, in three of five interviews held, the samplers did not correctly identify the minimum number of incremental samples to be taken due to their erroneous identification of the sampled portion, which resulted in fewer incremental samples than required by part 5 of Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 152/2009. In addition, the alternative method of sampling applied was not fully described and documented in the sampling protocol as required by part 5 of Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 152/2009. This is not in line with the requirements laid down by Article 11(1) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

paragraph_text: Official controls on imports of live animals and feed and food of both animal and non- animal origin were, for the most part, carried out properly by the competent authority with minor shortcomings noted in relation to the implementation of documentary checks. label_heading: Conclusions on implementation of official controls on imported goods
paragraph_text: The implementation of the import controls on live animals and feed and food of both animal and non-animal origin was generally in line with EU legislation, though there were shortcomings in the implementation of documentary checks on some consignments of live animals and products of animal origin, weakening assurances that only compliant consignments are imported into the EU via the BIPs in question.

The controls on live animals were, based on the documentation checked by the audit team, in general well-implemented with a few exceptions: the Combined Nomenclature - CN code mentioned in part I of some common veterinary entry documents for animals (CVEDAs) did not cover all fish species, crustaceans, molluscs or corals; the catch area of wild fish was not mentioned on some other health certificates examined by the audit team. These omissions had not been noticed by the BIP staff. The audit team noted that in 2017 some registered equidae had entered Austria from Serbia as temporary admissions. Some of the animals had been converted into permanent imports contrary to the declaration in part

The audit team noticed the following shortcomings related to the documentary checks of products of animal origin: a) A consignment of raw hides from a non-approved establishment was allowed for further processing. This is not in line with point 2(c) of Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 136/2004. 8 c) A consignment of a blood preparation was exported from Austria to a third country without an export certificate. The consignment was re-imported without the original export certificate containing

A number of CVEDPs examined by the audit team had been accepted even though there were discrepancies in the content of the health certificate e.g. chilled instead of frozen meat, carcasses versus packed meat. There is a system in place for channelling of products according to Article 8 of Directive 97/78/EC. Confirmation of arrival at the establishments of destination is received via e-mail and thereafter registered in 9 TRACES by BIP staff. The audit team identified some shortcomings regarding the channelling of products, in particular related to the awareness of the approval of the physical place of destination within Austria or in another Member State.

In one processing plant visited in 2018 (up until the end of August), 467 consignments of PAP containing ruminant protein were sent to third countries (the total number of export consignments containing ruminant PAP from Belgium in that period was 2100). In 2018, the point of exit was different on the transport documents and TRACES documents in around 30 cases (e.g. transport document Antwerp and Rotterdam, TRACES only Antwerp). The representative of the BIP mentioned in the TRACES document confirmed that these consignments had never arrived at the point of exit. The consequence is that seal checks had not been carried out at the BIP declared in 3 In its response to the draft report the comp

The lack of a control mechanism in PAP processing plants to verify that confirmation of the identity (seal) controls at the point of exit had been received through TRACES and the improper implementation of sampling requirements on imported PAP undermine the effectiveness of official controls on export and import of PAP. 13 6 OVERALL CONCLUSIONS As regards implementation of official controls requirements regarding the hygiene, traceability and the trade of PAP in Belgium, the overall picture is mixed. On the plus side, the system of official controls is underpinned by comprehensive establishment listing, well-managed cooperation and communication within and between the different Federal and R

The FASFC has prepared guidance on sampling requirements for imported PAP. Samples for microbiology have to be taken from the first 6 consecutive bulk consignments of PAP from each third country. The audit team identified that in some cases only 20% of the imported PAP consignments in bulk had been sampled without any evidence that analyses on the first 6 consignments had been carried out as required by point 2, Section 2 of Annex XIV to Regulation (EU) No 142/2011.4

However, the lists of plants in the chain of production and use of non-ruminant PAP for the aquaculture sector are not sufficiently accurate. This weakness hampers the competent authority's overview and has resource implications for officials who have to investigate each case when a decision on the presence of ruminant protein in a given consignment of PAP has to be taken. Moreover, certain inaccuracies identified in the approval and registration of some ABP plants and operators partly undermine the overall effectiveness of official controls. 8 5.2 IMPLEMENTATION OF OFFICIAL CONTROLS Legal requirements Articles 4(3), 21, 22, 41, 43, 45(1), 46, 48 and 53 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009 Articl

The audit team noted some inaccuracies in the official lists of plants along the chain of production of non-ruminant PAP to be used in the aquaculture sector, as follows: a. The list of food plants contained a very limited number of plants and in one case a plant approved for cutting bovine, ovine and caprine meat was wrongly listed in such list. b. The list of ABP processing plants did not contain several plants which were included in another official list containing ABP processing plants eligible to export non-ruminant PAP (see finding 16). c. The competent authorities confirmed that the above-mentioned lists could not be considered realistic, although in July 2017 the DGAHVM and DGFHFSN r

As a consequence of the previous finding (No 15), whenever an export/trade certificate of non-ruminant PAP has to be issued, or an ABP operator wants to have confidence that his suppliers are eligible for the production of non-ruminant PAP, it is necessary to contact the authority in charge of controls on the supplier and request an official declaration. The Ministry of Health keeps a list of operators, mainly processing plants, 6 which are eligible for the export of non-ruminant PAP, but this list does not cover all types of establishments covered in Section A, Chapter V of Annex IV to Regulation (EC) No 999/2001 (see also finding 35). 5.1.3 Planning of official controls Legal requirements

The competent authority was unable to meet its planned targets for official controls in the ABP sector in 2016 and 2017 due to a spike in unscheduled approval visits and the limited time available to inspectors to carry out official controls. This indicates a weakness in the official control system given the resources available are insufficient to carry out the number of planned inspections and there is no built-in contingency to be able to absorb ad-hoc requests such as new establishment approvals. As official controls on registered operators will also have to be factored in from 2018 on, the implementation rate of inspections will almost certainly decrease further, weakening the system ove

The implementation rate of the scheduled inspections of approved ABP operators was 62% in 2016 and 58% in 2017 (174 out of 298 scheduled controls was actually carried out). The competent authority explained this low implementation rate by the fact that there had been an increase in the request for approval of composting plants and biogas producers, due to a national programme in this sector, and therefore, 215 approval visits had to be carried out in 2017. As these approval visits have to be prioritised and are time-consuming, scheduled official controls often have to be postponed to the following year. As inspections of registered operators will have to be considered in the future planning,

Routine official controls still need to be strengthened as they did not detect a number of shortcomings, in particular with regards to the issuing of commercial documents. Inaccuracies and information gaps in commercial documents used for domestic trade weaken the competent authority's ability to verify the traceability of certain ABP and PAP and to verify whether they are used in accordance with their intended purpose. The implementation of official controls in relation to hygiene requirements was in general satisfactory.

The audit team visited a storage plant which stored PAP on behalf of two processing plants. The establishment had been approved for the storage of PAP in big bags in 2016 and has never been inspected since. The audit team noted that the establishment has not been well maintained and at the time of the visit did not comply with legal requirements laid down in Section 1 of Chapter III, Annex IX to Regulation (EU) No 142/2011 anymore. The operator declared that they are currently planning a comprehensive refurbishment of the storage premises. Moreover, in addition to the storage of PAP in big bags for which it was approved, the establishment is storing also a liquid product (poultry fat) in tan

In general, checks on commercial documents accompanying consignments of derived products were regularly carried out during inspections and these checks were recorded in the relevant points of the checklist. The officials met were largely familiar with relevant requirements; however, some of them mentioned difficulties in assessing commercial documents as they were not familiar with the model for intra-EU trade. In France, for national trade, there is no specific form required, but any document is accepted which includes the relevant information, in line with point (4a), Chapter III, Annex VIII to Regulation (EU) No 142/2011. In all premises visited during the audit, the audit team checked a

The OF/SI manufacturer visited traded an amount of around 800 tonnes (3% of his production) in 2018 to other Member States, including consignments consisting of 100% PAP and/or MBM mix. Contrary to Article 48(3) of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009, TRACES notifications relating to intra-EU trade were not made for these products. The competent authority stated that such notification is not required by the relevant internal instruction (see finding 21). The operator had not issued commercial documents for these consignments either, which had not been spotted during official controls. During an official control in 2017, the inspector had identified non-compliances as regards the accompanying commer

The audit team identified several shortcomings relating to TRACES notifications of intra-EU trade of PAP and OF/SI. For OF/SI, the competent authority had omitted to include a requirement for the operator to issue a TRACES notification, thereby undermining the traceability of the consignments. The percentage of PAP consignments arriving to France from other Member States which are notified back to the competent authorities in the Member State of origin is still wholly inadequate (approximately 4%), impacting on the fulfilment of traceability requirements in intra-EU trade.

In 2017, DGAL prepared two service notes (590 and 790) on the requirements of the national and intra-EU trade of ABPs and derived products, including PAP and MBM. The audit team reviewed the notes and determined that there is a detailed description of how the French competent authority has to notify the competent authority of origin via the Trade Control and Expert System (TRACES) about the arrival of the consignments as required by Article 48 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009. In particular, note 590 is very detailed and includes also a comprehensive annex with a list of specific cases. However, OF/SI containing PAP and/or MBM are not listed as requiring notification. 8 This is not in line wi

The audit team noted that, although training and instructions had been provided (see findings 5, 7, 21), in the vast majority of cases arrivals of consignments of PAP were not confirmed by the French competent authorities to the competent authorities of the Member States of origin by means of TRACES, contrary to Article 48(3) of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009. In 2017, according to figures of the competent authorities, arrival of only 7.37% of such consignments was confirmed, and in 2018, 4.45%.

The audit team identified several shortcomings relating to TRACES notifications of intra-EU trade of PAP and OF/SI. For OF/SI, the competent authority had omitted to include a requirement for the operator to issue a TRACES notification, thereby undermining the traceability of the consignments. The percentage of PAP consignments arriving to France from other Member States which are notified back to the competent authorities in the Member State of origin is still wholly inadequate (approximately 4%), impacting on the fulfilment of traceability requirements in intra-EU trade.

The reduction of seal checks of consignments of PAP containing ruminant protein exiting the EU from 100% of all consignments to just 3% chosen on a random basis is not implemented in accordance with the procedure developed for this purpose. The BIPs do not receive documents confirming the exit for all consignments which have been notified to them, the target of 3% seal checks of consignments is not being met and the competent authority is not consistently reacting to failures of the operators to confirm the arrival of the consignments at the port and their ultimate departure from the EU. Taken together with the fact that not all BIPs have access to the tracking 16 application that would enab

When, following the amendment of Regulation (EC) No 999/2001, exports of consignments of PAP derived from ruminants started in July 2017, the BIPs in France implemented the instruction communicated by SIVEP (see finding 22). In the BIP visited, the procedure for export checks established by the BIP included a verification of the arrival of the consignment in the port via an extract of the tracking application "AP+" including the seal number, which the operator has to provide as the BIP only has limited access to this application. In addition, a second extract from the application is required when the container has been loaded and the ship has left the port, which usually is sent seven days a

In this way, the BIP visited by the audit team verified the exit of all 24 consignments of PAP containing ruminant protein in 2017 and 43 in 2018 notified to them via TRACES, until the exit of consignments via this port stopped in February 2018. Since the SIVEP procedure TI 240 was issued only in March 2018 (see finding 23), no seal check was ever carried out at this BIP.

According to the evidence provided by the competent authority, in another BIP, through which the majority of consignments were exported from France, the information that the consignment actually left the EU was received in relation to around 99% of consignments in 2017 and around 94% in 2018 up to the time of the audit (for 2018: 1049 out of 1139 valid commercial documents). Around 70 consignments were still under verification at the time of the audit, as the departure of these containers had not yet been confirmed via the extract of the tracking application. Evidence was received after the audit that these 70 consignments had exited the EU. In some cases, the operators had created the comme

In another BIP however, no verification of whether the containers had exited, either following the procedure TI 240 (see finding 23) or their own procedure, was ever carried out; containers were neither tracked nor a seal check performed. This was the case for 270 consignments which were notified by operators via commercial documents in TRACES in 2017 and 653 consignments in 2018 up to the time of the audit. This is not in line with point 1(c), Section E, Chapter V, Annex IV of Regulation (EC) No 999/2001. Following the audit, the BIP confirmed the exit of the 653 consignments in 2018 by providing extracts of the tracking application "AP+". The audit team verified a random sample of these co

All processing plants visited exported PAP to non-EU countries via the last mentioned port as the exiting point. The audit team noted that in several cases different points of exit were selected in the corresponding box in TRACES (the BIP, but also the port as designated point of entry for phytosanitary controls). Neither the operator, nor the competent authority could provide evidence that the seals of these export consignments had been checked at any BIP, contrary to the requirements of point 1(c), Section E, Chapter V, Annex IV of Regulation (EC) No 999/2001. At one operator, the audit team noted when reviewing a random sample of commercial documents for exported PAP consignments that for

Operators producing insects or insect PAP for animal feed are subject to official controls which, inter alia, provide a basis for their registration, approval and listing. In one of the two plants visited by the audit team, there was sufficient evidence to support the approval. This was not the case for the second plant where approval had prematurely been granted without relevant EU requirements being fulfilled, indicating that the approval process is not consistently applied by the competent authority. 5.3 IMPLEMENTATION OF OFFICIAL CONTROLS ON THE PRODUCTION, PLACING ON THE MARKET AND TRADE OF INSECT PAP AND INSECTS AS FEED Findings

On the basis of the information provided by the operator of the second plant, although the main final product was dried larvae of Black Soldier Fly, the intention was to place on the market insect PAP. The audit team noted that the full approval had been granted recently (July 2018) without the testing of the final product over a period of 30 production days being completed, as this period only started on 1 November 2018. This decision is not in line with the provisions laid down by Article 44 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009 and the specific provisions laid down in Point G, Chapter III of Annex IV to Regulation (EU) No 142/2011. label_heading: Conclusions on implementation of residue monitoring
paragraph_text: Whilst sampling in 2017 was implemented as planned, the inordinate delay in laboratory testing of samples taken in 2017 has substantially weakened the effectiveness of the residue monitoring plan for that year. Even if those samples are eventually analysed, there is a possibility that time-dependent analyte instability will invalidate the results (i.e. samples which were truly non-compliant at the time of sampling will test as false-compliant) and, in the event that non-compliant results would be found, the delay between sampling and analysis will militate against identification of the cause of the residue and effective follow-up investigations. 5.1.3. Other residue monitoring programmes Leg

Recommendation 2 of the 2011 report requested the competent authority to ensure that the length of time between sampling and laboratory results would be sufficiently short to allow for effective follow-up in case of non-compliant results 16. In 2017 the tendering procedure to contract an external laboratory failed and, as a result, half of the samples taken in 2017 had not been analysed at the time of the audit, remaining in the freezers of the NVL waiting for new arrangements to be put in place with subcontracting laboratories. paragraph_text: Notwithstanding certain shortcomings noted for not including all animals sent for direct slaughter to Italy from other Member States in the calculation of samples to be taken, not subjecting equidae sent from other Member States for direct slaughter to residue monitoring and sampling of farmed and wild game, the timely and largely comprehensive planning contributes to the effectiveness of controls on residues. 5.1.3. This is not in line with point 2.3.3.1 of Commission Decision 98/179/EC which requires considering the species when selecting targeted samples from animal carcasses at primary processing establishments. 80% of samples from wild boar to be tested for heavy metals were planned to be taken in one region, while wild boar is also plentiful in other regions. The competent authority can largely have confidence in the laboratory performance and the reliability of analytical results as all laboratories are accredited, methods are generally appropriately validated and staff well-trained. However, a few factors weaken the system, such as the long sample analysis turnaround times, the non- adequate validation for a few rare matrices/species combinations and the fact that the NRL for residues of veterinary medicinal products does not completely meet its NRL obligations and has deficiencies in its quality assurance procedures. 5.2. Veterinary medicinal products 5.2.1. Competent authorities

The national residue monitoring plan stipulates that the sample analysis turnaround time is 10 working days for Group A substances and 30 working days for Group B substances . The audit team noted that these turnaround times count from the moment the sample arrives at the laboratory which analyses the sample. In many cases IZS laboratories (IZSs) sent samples to another IZS laboratory for analysis (see also findings 32 and 45), which leads to the fact that the turnaround times from sampling to finalising the laboratory report are longer than 10 or 30 days.

The audit team was provided with sample analysis turnaround time statistics. These showed that 80% of all samples analysed by the IZS laboratory were processed within the required turnaround time. However, 49% of the samples to be analysed for beta-lactam antimicrobials exceeded the 30 day turnaround time and were analysed within 70 days, and one sample within 165 days. Samples sent by the visited IZS to other IZS laboratories exceeded the 30 day deadline for 81.4% of all samples and 4.2% of samples had a turnaround time of 91 to 218 days. The long processing times may affect the analytes' stability and sample integrity (in particular for beta-lactam antimicrobials), which is not in line wit

The competent authority can largely have confidence in the laboratory performance and the reliability of analytical results as all laboratories are accredited, methods are generally appropriately validated and staff well-trained. However, a few factors weaken the system, such as the long sample analysis turnaround times, the non- adequate validation for a few rare matrices/species combinations and the fact that the NRL for residues of veterinary medicinal products does not completely meet its NRL obligations and has deficiencies in its quality assurance procedures. 5.2. Veterinary medicinal products 5.2.1. Competent authorities

The Italian laboratory network comprises five NRLs and 10 regional laboratories. Four NRLs belong to the National Health Institute (ISS) (residues of veterinary medicinal products, mycotoxins, heavy metals and pesticides) and one NRL (dioxins/Polychlorinated Biphenyls (PCBs)) plus the 10 regional laboratories belong to the Experimental Animal Health Research Institute (IZS). All the laboratories are accredited to ISO 17025 by the Italian accreditation body Accredia.

The NRL has created and maintains a database which includes the information on, inter alia, CC-alphas and CC-betas of the methods applied by the IZSs. The information provided in the database is periodically evaluated and discussed within the IZS laboratory network, which was demonstrated in the form of minutes from two recent annual workshops between the NRL and the IZSs.

The competent authority can largely have confidence in the laboratory performance and the reliability of analytical results as all laboratories are accredited, methods are generally appropriately validated and staff well-trained. However, a few factors weaken the system, such as the long sample analysis turnaround times, the non- adequate validation for a few rare matrices/species combinations and the fact that the NRL for residues of veterinary medicinal products does not completely meet its NRL obligations and has deficiencies in its quality assurance procedures. 5.2. Veterinary medicinal products 5.2.1. Competent authorities

The audit team observed the standard operating procedure for the validation of methods and found that it was in line with the relevant provisions of Commission 8 Decision 2002/657/EC. Staff of the NRL stated that a software-based validation protocol will in future be applied for all method validations. The envisaged validation protocol is based on the approach outlined in part 3.1.3 of the Annex I to Decision 2002/657/EC.

The audit team examined the validation files and reports for the analysis of chloramphenicol in muscles and found that the validation plan was adequate and included all relevant provisions laid down by Decision 2002/657/EC. The validation process was adequately presented in the validation report. However, quality assurance documentation for routine samples was not available, which is not in line with the requirements laid down in Article 5 of Decision 2002/657/EC.

label_heading: Conclusions on Implementation of Official Controls over BOs and FBOs
paragraph_text: During official controls inspectors are able to verify the presence of DoC and, to a certain extent, to assess the completeness of those declarations. Limited controls were made on the completeness of supporting documentation for the DoC, which would lead to inadequate or incomplete risk assessments/DoCs being overlooked. Thus, non- compliant products might go undetected and correct application of the relevant legislation would not be enforced.

label_heading: Conclusions on Implementation of Official Controls over BOs and FBOs
paragraph_text: The effectiveness of the controls in place is hampered by the fact that inspectors are not suitably trained or experienced to evaluate compliance of FCM legislation, including a thorough analysis of the DoC and supporting documentation. Expertise available at central level is rarely sought3. 3 In their response to the draft report the CCA noted that concerning two DRAPs visited, whenever doubts are raised, an official request for support is sent to the Directorate-General for Food and Veterinary Matters - Department for Nutrition and Food. Different situations may result from the fact that the level of knowledge differentiation among the technicians carrying out the checks is still such that

At the first FCM manufacturer (producer of PET bottles) the inspectors verified the DoC of the ready-to-use bottle, asked questions regarding the raw materials used, identified an issue with regard to surface/volume ratio and also requested to see the supporting documents. The inspectors confirmed that they were not able to go further on what is already stated in the DoC since more expertise is needed. 13 68. The second FCM manufacturer (PET bottles blower) was inspected for the first time in relation to FCM. DoCs concerning raw materials and final products were requested and evaluated by the inspectors. However no further supporting documentation was requested and the inspectors did not ask

At the third manufacturer, the inspectors carried out a verification check in relation to FCM (see paragraph 31). The inspectors examined additional documents provided and decided for which areas action was still required by the BO. They stated that they do not have the expertise to evaluate the completeness of the DoC and the supporting documentation. They informed the audit team that they can only evaluate what the BO provides to them. If a substance is not mentioned in the DoC they do not have the expertise to find out if such a substance is not present in the formula or is not mentioned for whatever reason.

The audit team observed that inspectors rely mainly on what the BOs provide to them during the inspections concerning manufacturing procedures and risk analysis including the presence of non-intentionally added substances (NIAS). The inspectors have limited expertise to evaluate the formula for a product or to identify if information concerning certain substances is missing. There was no documentary evidence that they systematically requested organoleptic test results from BOs.

The audit team noted that official controls on plastics, in most cases, do not include sufficient checks on the supporting documentation for statements in the DoC (final product). In particular, the following were missing: An assessment of the supporting documentation relating to the completeness of laboratory results in matters of SML or organoleptic tests; An assessment of NIAS ­ e.g. impurities, reaction products and decomposition that can occur during the processing of a granulate into the final product; A verification of the BO's risk assessment required under Article 19 of Regulation (EU) No 10/2011.

At one DRAP visited the audit team noted that the evaluation of DoCs covers the formal aspects. The inspectors stated that they do not have the expertise to evaluate the formula of the product and thus they are not able to determine if a substance is not present in a product or if the DoC is incomplete. In a particular case, and although the DoC was forwarded to the NRL and DGAV for their opinion on whether to carry out sampling, neither provided feedback advising DRAP's inspectors that the specific DoC was incomplete (substance missing), since they also rely completely on the information provided by the BO.

The CCA informed the audit team that the risk assessments carried out by FCM manufacturers and/or processors, for substances referred to in Article 19 of Regulation 14 (EU) No 10/2011 had to date not been requested and therefore not evaluated by the inspectors since that requires specific knowledge and expertise and support from central level. However, such a support was not available (and it had never been sought) at the time of the audit.

Hazard Analysis Critical Control Points (HACCP) plans are evaluated by the inspectors also in relation to the chemical hazards associated with FCM used. However, concerning FCM, the inspectors during the documentary checks relied on the information provided by the FBO rather than checking whether chemical risks associated with FCM foreseeable use are adequately identified and managed by the FBO2. 2 In their response to the draft report the CCA noted that relevant questions of this topic can be raised during the visit to the facilities. 15 82. Regarding FCM controls at FBO level the audit team was presented with an example on how ASAE controls are carried out in relation to FCM. The procedure

Regarding this specific case the audit team requested that the inspectors sought an expert opinion. Based on the information they collected on-the-spot a draft expert opinion was prepared by central level identifying certain non-compliances related to the articles/ FCM selected. Some non-compliances not related to the DoCs had not be identified by the inspectors during their control but were mentioned in the expert opinion. The expert opinion drafted contained information on what the inspectors should additionally request of the FCM retailer to be able to conclude whether the article/FCM in question complied with the legal requirements.

ASAE informed the audit team that FCM controls were not a priority at the time of the audit and therefore advice/guidance from central level was rarely sought. It was explained that in 2016, and although a few non-compliances were identified related to the DoC, the possibility of requesting an expert opinion was not availed of.

This was not identified by the inspectors during the import control.

label_heading: Conclusions on relevant national legislation and guidelines
paragraph_text: The legal provisions in place designate and empower CAs at central and provincial level for the implementation of official controls on microbiological risks in the whole production chain, including primary production. 5.2 ORGANISATION AND IMPLEMENTATION OF OFFICIAL CONTROLS 5.2.1 Designation of competent authorities and resources for official controls Legal requirements Article 4(1) Regulation (EC) No 852/2004 Designation of competent authorities

There are central and regional CAs designated by national legislation regarding official controls on microbiological risks at all stages of production. However, the central and regional CAs did not act to implement such controls before and during harvest, contrary to the requirements of Article 4(1) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Therefore, a considerable part of the FNAO production is not covered by the official control system.
The CA stated that they can apply penalties to operators as imposed by the LMSVG, but this is restricted to food after harvest. Conclusions on implementation of official controls over FBO obligations

The main national legislation in the context of this audit is the Food Safety and Consumer Protection Act (LMSVG), Federal Law Gazette of the Republic of Austria (BGBI) I No. 13/2006.3 This act covers the EU food law and Hygiene Package. The scope of the Law is described in paragraph 1(1) and comprises the requirements for food, water for human consumption, utensils and cosmetic products and the associated responsibility of the FBO. It applies to all stages of production, processing and distribution. It does not apply to primary production for private domestic use or to the domestic processing, handling or storage of food, commodities and cosmetic products for domestic private consumption. P

Several BMASGK guidelines are in place, in particular regarding: health requirements for persons handling food after harvest; staff training handling food after harvest; fruit processing at farms after harvest.
The Chamber of Agriculture of Austria has published guidelines on hygiene and own controls for direct suppliers after harvest. Conclusions on relevant national legislation and guidelines

The audit team visited five growers in two different Provinces. All growers had packing facilities and were direct sellers or distributing to retailers. In all visited premises, inspectors stated that they only carry out inspections if the primary production is linked to direct sales or the distribution to retail chains.

The inspections took place at the facilities where produce was received, cleaned, packed and stored. The inspectors followed the four modules of the checklist "producer" which cover facilities and equipment, produce and handling, hygiene and training and documentary checks.

During the audit visit, some inspectors asked questions regarding the use of field toilets during harvest and the protection of crops against pets and wild animals. The inspectors declared that this would not be part of their routine controls.

Staff performing official controls are trained on food safety in general, but there is no training regarding the reduction of microbiological risks and sampling for microbiological testing at primary production level and at sprouting premises. which is not in line with Article 6 and Annex II of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. 5.2.2 Registration / approval of food establishments Legal requirements Article 6 of Regulation (EC) No 852/2004, Article 2 of Regulation (EU) No 210/2013 and Article 31 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 Findings Registration of primary food producers 6 18. The registration procedure for food establishments has changed since the 2013 audit. In 2013 only direct suppliers were

The audit team noted that the sampling procedure is very general and does not instruct the inspectors to foresee specific measures to ensure that the sample is not contaminated during sampling (e.g. no provision to use sterile tools and bags for loose produce). The inspectors did not receive specific training for sampling.

The inspectors met in the establishments informed the audit team that no specific training has been provided to them regarding the detailed legal requirements for the production of sprouts and seeds for sprouting. A few inspectors participated at BTSF training for FNAO. The knowledge gathered there, however, has not been shared between the inspectors.

label_heading: Conclusions on organisation and scope of official controls
paragraph_text: There is no official control system in place covering microbiological risks before and during harvest. The system in place for controls of primary production after harvest is not risked-based. This is not in compliance with the provisions of Article 3(1) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

The audit team noted that the sampling procedure is very general and does not instruct the inspectors to foresee specific measures to ensure that the sample is not contaminated during sampling (e.g. no provision to use sterile tools and bags for loose produce). The inspectors did not receive specific training for sampling.

Official controls at farm level concerning microbiological contamination at primary production of FNAO were not defined in the planning process in any Province of Austria. The method for risk ranking set out in EFSA's scientific opinion (see above Section 4 Background) was not taken into account. BMASGK stated that the EFSA document will be used as base for a future risk assessment.

There is a system of risk categorisation included in ALIAS. It comprises of 10 steps, from 0 (lowest) to 9. FNAO primary producers with the exception of sprouting establishments are categorised in step 0 "other". The CAs should carry out controls every ten years. The frequency can be changed according to the specific situation at an establishment and the outcome of the official controls. The microbiological risk of the different FNAO products, e.g. ready-to-eat or soft berries is not taken into account for this risk categorisation and no routine control system is in place.

A sampling plan is developed each year by the BMASGK in co-operation with AGES. In addition to the risk-based plans, targeted national or provincial priority actions are carried out each year. Samples can be taken in the case of suspicion. The plan includes the scope of possible tests for each group of foodstuffs but does not specify for which parameters the sample shall be tested.

The CA has documented procedures, instructions and checklists to enable the CA to perform official controls at primary production level of FNAO after harvest. Regarding sprout-producing establishments the procedures, instructions and checklists are too general to achieve an adequate level of controls which is not in line with Article 8 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. 5.2.8 Follow-up of former audits of DG Health and Food Safety The table below summarizes the follow-up to the relevant recommendations made in report DG SANTE 2013/6663-MR Final No Previous Assessment 1. Ensure that all staff performing official Not addressed. controls receive appropriate training enabling them to undertake thei

Procedure VA-K 020A describes the planning preparation and execution of controls. It refers to the relevant paragraphs of the LMSVG. It does not contain provisions for primary production before or during harvest.

The checklist CL-K020A is annexed to the procedure. It is divided in chapters and modules which cover the different stages from production until distribution. The modules for the official controls start at the FBO controls on incoming goods (see paragraph 8).

Inspectors used the same general check-list as for FNAO. The checklist gives no guidance concerning specific sprouting issues. The inspectors checked the documentation of the FBO, including results of sprouts analyses, water analyses, cleaning and disinfection. The facilities visited complied with good hygiene standards in general; some minor shortcomings were detected by the inspectors and noted in the inspection report.

In both establishments, raw material was tested before use and monthly samples were analysed during production. However, regarding the testing requirements of sprouted seeds, the audit team observed that both operators did not follow the procedures as described in Annex 1 Chapter 3, point 3.3 of Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005. The CAs accepted these sampling procedures but did not follow the rules for granting derogations as set out in the same Regulation. The operators and the CA presented to the audit team some communication with AGES on this topic, but there was no formal decision taken. One establishment did not let analyse for Salmonella spp. as required by the Regulation.

At the second sprouting establishment the audit team noted that the batch identification number on the health certificate of a third country consignment of mung-beans did not correspond with the number printed on the labels fixed to the bags of the consignment. 10 Moreover, the checks on incoming goods did not comprise the check of batch numbers. One consignment of mung-beans did not bear identification marks or labels. These non- compliances were not spotted by the operator or the CA.

label_heading: Conclusions on Registration / Approval of Food Establishments
paragraph_text: There is a system in place for approval of sprouting establishments aimed at ensuring that applicant FBOs meet the relevant requirements, but this system does not ensure that non-compliances have been rectified before the approval is granted. 5.2.3 Organisation and Scope of Official Controls Legal requirements Article 17 of Regulation (EC) No 178/2002 and Articles 3 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 Findings Primary producers and sprouting business

There is an official control system in place along the FNAO production chain. The implementation at primary production, however, shows a number of gaps, notably related to provision of training and specific instructions (i.e. what are relevant non- compliances regarding the hygiene of staff, safe handling of food and suitable facilities). Therefore, significant non-compliances were not detected. Thus, non- compliant products might be undetected and the correct application of the relevant legislation might not be enforced.

Regarding the sprouting businesses the inspectors did not verify effectively compliance of import certificates because they were not familiar with the certification and traceability requirements established in Regulations (EU) Nos 208/2013 and 211/2013. Furthermore, inspectors did not verify that the own checks contained the analyses of sprouts for Listeria monocytogenes and STEC. Thus, the implementation of official controls on sprout producers is not sufficiently effective in verifying and, as appropriate, enforcing applicable hygiene rules.

The CA did grant informally derogations for the pre-testing of seeds of sprouting without any conditions which is not in line with the rules and criteria laid down in Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005 for seeds for sprouting. Thus, non-compliant products might be placed on the market and could pose a health risk for the consumers. 5.2.5 Official Sampling Procedures Legal requirements Article 11 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 and Annex I, Chapter 1 of Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005 Findings

There are 17 staff on central level and around 70 inspectors in charge of official controls for primary production. Around 30 are dedicated to food safety controls. They have at least a bachelor degree with additional training for food safety issues. Inspectors had received training on microbiological risks at primary production stage in 2017. However, some staff showed a lack of knowledge regarding basic food hygiene requirements in FNAO and legal obligations for sprouting businesses (see chapter 5.2.4).

paragraph_text: The audit team observed three different inspections at producers/processors of PDO/PGI/TSG agricultural products and foodstuffs. In each case the inspectors reviewed the key elements of the relevant Product Specifications. Official samples are taken according to the VMVT sampling plan and analysed by NMVRVI. The inspectors met were generally competent and satisfactorily performed a traceability check. However, they did not always check every element of the Product Specifications. In addition, some elements of the controls were superficial. Examples include restricting the documentary checks to very recent production batches rather than reviewing documents from a range of batches since the la

It became clear to the audit team, that none of the key players were fully aware that this non-compliant situation existed until the time of the audit. This is not in line with

This situation highlighted a lack of coordination between the key players involved (see

(see further details under this chapter, point (c) Labelling ­ correct use of Union symbol and presentation of the protected name). The ensuing discussion between the CB, CA, the producer and the audit team illustrated the challenge associated with labelling and the different interpretations that exists. One of the inspections observed was the first official control of a particular PGI which constituted the verification of the Product Specification prior to placing the product on the market. In fact the labelling did not fully comply with the minimum requirements of the legislation, and in particular Article 12(3) of Regulation (EU) No 1151/2014. 1 In their response to the draft report the CA noted that issues relating to the exact geographical location had been

Official controls at producers/processors of PDO/PGI/TSG agricultural products and foodstuffs are undertaken on a regular basis by following documented procedures and they are overall effective. However it cannot be ensured that all of the relevant elements of the product specification are checked by the CBs for all products

The audit team noted that not all the elements necessary to verify compliance with the product specifications were contained in the checklists, and therefore were inadequately checked, even if records were available at the operators´ premises. For example, the control plans for PDOs of animal origin did not cover verification that the feed came from within the same geographical area (which is also a requirement established in Article 1 of Regulation (EU) No 664/2014). The CA stated that so far it has been satisfied with the statements made by operators that such feed is sourced from the geographical area specified in the product specification.

The CB records also demonstrated that the planning was followed. All users of the registered names were inspected at least once a year and other stages of the production, including producers supplying the products, were also subject to inspection in the period of three years foreseen in the control plans. However, as described in the previous paragraph, as the origin of feed is not verified, no separate inspections are planned to feed mills supplying to the producer to cross-check the invoices and delivery notes provided. paragraph_text: There is a system in place for the official controls of FIAs, including import, marketing and their use that is overall fit for purpose, and includes appropriate action in case of non-compliance. However, not all requirements of the EU legislation on FIAs are presently included in the controls and therefore not subject to verification and enforcement, as appropriate. 6 OVERALL CONCLUSIONS The system of official food controls related to production, trade and use of Food Improvement Agents currently in place can largely verify effectively that their use is in line with the applicable EU legislation. This system was found to be implemented as foreseen, in practice. Control personnel are support

Both competent authorities avail at central level of dedicated staff which provide support to inspection units, while the staff in these units and which perform the official controls, are knowledgeable. The two competent authorities combined cover food improvement agents in all

The current control system in place does not compel control staff to check, during inspections at FBOs whether the use of FIAs in foodstuffs fully complies with the relevant EU legislation. The pool of inspectors that should carry out second line inspections, is not in place yet7.

label_heading: Conclusions on official controls of FBOs providing or using FIAs
paragraph_text: There is a system in place for the official controls of FIAs, including import, marketing and their use that is overall fit for purpose, and includes appropriate action in case of non-compliance. However, checks of compliance with the FIAs legislation are only carried out now and then since 2016, at the initiative of individual inspectors. Therefore the production, marketing and use of FIAs are not systematically subject to verification and enforcement where necessary, as regards the FIAs legislation. 8 6 OVERALL CONCLUSIONS The system of official food controls related to production, trade and use of FIAs currently in place can verify effectively that their use is in line with the applicable

label_heading: Conclusions on official controls on the production of RTE foods
paragraph_text: Each CA has put in place a system of risk based official controls over production of RTE foods, supported by procedures and covering relevant aspects of the legislation. Most establishments producing RTE products are placed in the "high risk" category, reflected in a higher frequency of controls which is largely achieved by the CAs, except SFPA.

All CAs reported a shortage of resources over recent years, which according to the CAs and the internal audit reports seen led to not achieving the target for planned controls and occasionally to reducing the official samples for process hygiene criteria (limited staff at laboratory level as well). All CAs reported progress in hiring new staff after the ban on recruitment of public servants in Ireland was lifted. Currently, most CAs achieve targets above 90% of the planned controls with efforts being made to ensure a swift handover and training of new staff.

In contrast, certain difficulties in this respect are still encountered in SFPA. Figures emanating from the new quantification system (see paragraph 20) indicate that SFPA achieved 71% of the overall planned official controls, and 60% of the controls in high risk RTE food producing FBOs. The figures indicate that the two regions with the 7 highest number of FBOs have the lowest rate of implementation of controls (43% and 57%).

The same quantification system highlights that the FBOs producing high risk RTE fishery products have amongst the lowest rates of implementation of SFPA controls (between 29% and 39%) compared to other types of FBOs in the regions with the highest number of FBOs. The highest rate of implementation of controls concerned FBOs producing low risk non-RTE foods, which was explained by the lower number of scheduled controls. In most cases, FBOs had been subject to controls at a minimum of once per year in 2017, with only a small number of RTE food producing establishments receiving no official controls in 2017

The SFPA resource challenge had been identified by FSAI in a 2016 audit and work has been done to quantify it through the new quantification system, resulting in the data provided in paragraphs 10 and 11, but the corrective action is outstanding. SFPA attributed this to a lack of staff, difficulties in recruiting also due to budgetary constraints as well as the fact that SFPA is undergoing a management reorganisation.

The controls are largely implemented by the CAs as planned, with the risk based frequency, mainly without prior warning. However, in the case of SFPA, while the planned frequency of controls in establishments producing high risk RTE fishery products is three times per year, the implemented frequency in 2017 was approximately once per year - the same as for establishments producing low risk RTE - in the regions with the highest numbers of FBOs.

The similar level of implemented controls for all types of FBOs in these two regions, despite having been assigned different inspection frequencies on the basis of identified risks, together with the limited attention given to new approvals in another region (see also paragraph 30) suggest that SPFA, in the face of dealing with limited resource and with multiple tasks may have to look again at the prioritisation process to ensure resource for higher risk facilities within and between regions. 4.4.1.2 Procedures for official controls

SFPA highlighted that the joint controls between SFPA official controls staff support the identification of shortcomings and gave an example of one region where 80% of the inspections are joint inspections. However, in one of the regions with the highest number of FBOs, 1% of the inspections were explained by the CA to be joint inspections. The CA highlighted a constant increase in the number of fishery establishments in the busy regions.

No official control officer was assigned to one of the fishery establishments visited by the audit team. No official controls had been carried out in this establishment in the past year, although three were planned. Several non-compliances were noted on the day of the audit team visit, including some long standing ones.

While the official control staff met were experienced and in general trained and knowledgeable for their field of work within the scope of this audit, some individual points for guidance/support or training were identified during the audit (see paragraph 15), mainly in relation to: a. approval of establishments and keeping it under review (see paragraphs 30, 47 and 82c). b. the focus and depth of the controls in fishery establishments, establishments where non-compliances were found at official testing, as well for assessing the flexibility options implemented by FBOs (see paragraphs 43, 45, 46, 47, 50, 51, 54 and 76). c. sampling and testing requirements (see paragraphs 53 to 59 and 82 f).

label_heading: Conclusions on official controls on the production of RTE foods
paragraph_text: The official controls over FBOs compliance with the EU food hygiene requirements are largely satisfactory, in particular in large establishments subject to DAFM controls. The unsatisfactory elements concern mainly the controls over FBOs compliance with Regulation (EC) No 852/2004 (a.in particular for the use of flexibility options and avoidance of cross-contamination in small establishments (LA and Dairy Certification), establishments with multiple activities (HSE) and establishments subject to SFPA control; b. for the use of food additives and flavourings, including smoke flavourings in their production), as well the controls over FBOs sampling and testing methods.

Some CAs aim to cover compliance with all legal requirements within two to three years (with two visits per year), while others aim to achieve the same in one year with a range between two to twelve visits per year, depending on the CA. The depth and thoroughness of the controls vary between CAs. The DAFM checklists for HACCP tend to focus on the main activity and due to the infrequency of the marginal activities the related controls focussed on the main production in the small dairy establishments visited. Marginal activities are subject to official sampling and the food safety management system that manages all activities is subject to audit (see also paragraph 47e).

label_heading: Conclusions on official controls on the production of RTE foods
paragraph_text: The official controls over FBOs compliance with the EU food hygiene requirements are largely satisfactory, in particular in large establishments subject to DAFM controls. The unsatisfactory elements concern mainly the controls over FBOs compliance with Regulation (EC) No 852/2004 (a.in particular for the use of flexibility options and avoidance of cross-contamination in small establishments (LA and Dairy Certification), establishments with multiple activities (HSE) and establishments subject to SFPA control; b. for the use of food additives and flavourings, including smoke flavourings in their production), as well the controls over FBOs sampling and testing methods.

In some of the establishments visited (producing fishery, dairy and meat products able to support the growth of Listeria), CAs accepted that FBOs do not carry out sampling for the detection of Listeria in the processing area and equipment during processing, but only after cleaning and disinfection, to assess its efficiency. This does not take into account the EURL Guidance on sampling the food processing area and equipment for the detection of Listeria monocytogenes which recommends sampling during processing. Sampling only after cleaning and disinfection makes the detection of the pathogen difficult and can lead to a false sense of security.

paragraph_text: The contingency plan is outdated and thus it does not reflect the current structure and competences of both central and local veterinary services. This precludes better identification of rules and responsibilities of all services in delivery of the on-the-spot operations. As stated in the 2015 Commission report, it also resulted in the absence of 8 involvement of most major stakeholders during epidemic situation.

The Commission audit report DG(SANTE)/2015-7508 MR Final states several deficiencies related to the contingency plan, e.g. it does not contain: all relevant provisions to ensure the legal powers necessary for its implementation, detailed information on staff involved in control measures, their skills and their responsibilities, a register of staff that may be called upon nor a clear procedure for emergency staffing to deal with an animal disease crisis. These deficiencies have not yet been addressed.
