label_heading: Conclusions on monitoring and sampling scheme
paragraph_text: The fact that during the 2016 Salmonella outbreak some serotyping test results were issued with delays of up to 3 weeks, indicates that the system in place did not satisfactorily deal with high demand on its capacities in crisis times, in particular to assure timely testing. The measures implemented still prevented additional risk to consumers, nevertheless, without the serotyping result, the competent authorities could have faced legal difficulties in imposing the necessary marketing restrictions.

During the 2016 outbreak this laboratory needed additional days (up to 3 weeks) from the detection of Salmonella to provide the results on serotyping. This was caused by different factors including the very high number of additional samples to be serotyped at this crisis period and to exhausting the stock of reagents. In both laying hen holdings visited affected by the 2016 outbreak and with samples tested at this laboratory, the measures restricting marketing of eggs from these holdings as class A eggs (for direct human consumption) had been implemented at the time of Salmonella detection (without waiting for serotyping) therefore preventing additional risk for consumers. 5.2.3 SNCP for bre

label_heading: Conclusions on welfare of the animals arriving at the port
paragraph_text: The fact that the authorities do not request journey logs for most consignments, as these start mostly in Spain, prevents them from ensuring that journeys are realistic and have been planned in line with the requirements, in particular to avoid unnecessary waiting times at the port and the identification of a person or entity responsible for the sea leg of the journey.

The large majority of consignments arriving at the port are accompanied by a national movement document instead of a journey log (see also finding 18). This movement document is not nationally harmonised. In the different versions seen by the audit team, the declaration of fitness for transport was always signed by either the transporter or the farmer at the place of departure.

For the few trucks that arrived after long road journeys, the official checks do not detect the absence of a transporter for the sea journey on the journey log (which should have been indicated in box 6.4 of Section 1). Copies of tachographs are not collected, as required by Article 21(2) of the Regulation, to verify journey times from the place of departure to the port.

The competent authorities follow the instructions of the national protocol and do not request journey logs for animals travelling short road journeys before reaching the port. This is not in line with the Zuchtvieh judgement4, which indicates that these should also be considered as long journeys since it takes more than 8 hours to reach the destination in the non-EU country. In 2015 the Spanish authorities asked the Commission in writing about this issue and they proposed means of addressing it (see also finding 22); they have received no reply to date.

label_heading: Conclusions on welfare of the animals arriving at the port
paragraph_text: The new documented procedures could ensure ­ when fully implemented ­ that in general, animals are spared unnecessary suffering during the journey.

label_heading: Conclusions on welfare of the animals arriving at the port
paragraph_text: The lack of appropriate facilities at ports for checking the animals in the trucks and of no permanent veterinary presence during loading of the livestock vessels, combined with the absence of an official veterinarian at the place of departure to certify fitness for transport5 create a risk of unfit animals being transported. The system is further weakened by the lack of registers at the ports about the animals' fitness for transport.

label_heading: Conclusions on welfare of animals during sea transport
paragraph_text: The official veterinarians seen carrying out pre-loading inspections of livestock vessels were competent in this task and this provides a good level of assurance that livestock vessels inspected in this way are suitable to prevent unnecessary animal welfare problems notwithstanding the poor quality of records kept. However, the poor conditions on a livestock vessel which was allowed to load at one of the Spanish ports earlier in 2018 indicates that some pre-loading inspections are insufficient and do not ensure that essential systems for animal welfare are in place. 6 OVERALL CONCLUSIONS The competent authority has recently updated its procedures which, if properly implemented, should ensure

The national protocol also includes sections indicating legal requirements and additional instructions. They both go into more detail than that the Regulation for both the approval of livestock vessels and their inspection prior to loading. It also includes relevant checklists. The pre-loading inspection checklist (Annex 5D) is incomplete, e.g. it does not include checks that the equipment listed in Chapter IV of Annex I of the Regulation is in good working order.

The competent authority indicated that the above-mentioned national protocol has not yet been fully implemented. Namely, the central competent authority has not yet verified how the measures prescribed in the protocol translate into practice, and how they are being applied. Article 4(2)(a) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 requires the competent authority to ensure the effectiveness and appropriateness of official controls. 5.2 TRANSPORT CONDITIONS ON ARRIVAL AT THE PORT Findings

During the audit, the competent authorities at the two ports exporting animals could not provide annual data on the number of animals for which they had refused loading due to the animals being unfit or having arrived dead at the ports.

The national protocol procedures are in general sufficient for inspections to livestock vessels, but have not yet been fully implemented. These procedures include many of the criteria contained in the Network Document on livestock vessels agreed by the National Contact Points' network, and were well-known by the personnel met by the audit team.

The competent authority provided the information in the table below. This shows the total number and outcome of livestock vessel inspections at the time of loading (Article 20 of the Regulation) between January 2015 and June 2018. The type of deficiencies detected included: non-operational drinkers, presence of rust, lack of identified "hospital/isolation pens", dirty or poorly maintained feeders, no first-aid kits/supplies for the animals, lack of alarms at the wheelhouse for the systems for ventilation, light and water production, and lack of stunning equipment. The competent authority informed the audit team that all deficiencies could be corrected prior to loading and there was no need t

During the audit, the officials described and demonstrated pre-loading animal welfare controls of livestock vessels carried out at the port visited. They were correct and well- performed. Regarding documentation: Records indicate that controls are carried out on ventilation (Point 2 Section 1 Chapter IV Annex I of the Regulation), cleaning and disinfection, watering equipment (Point 4 Section 1 Chapter IV Annex I of the Regulation) and ramps; Records also indicate that calculation is made to evaluate the stocking density (Chapter VII Annex I of the Regulation) and the amount of water and feed necessary for the animals (Section 2 Chapter IV Annex I of the Regulation); There are no records ind

The available documentation of those controls in the port which was not visited was very poor, indicating only that a control according to Article 20 of the Regulation had been carried out but without giving details on what had been checked.

label_heading: Conclusions on welfare of the animals arriving at the port
paragraph_text: The absence of facilities to unload the animals at the port might lead to welfare problems, particularly if a delay occurs with the loading of the animals. Although this is 5 In their response to the draft report the Competent Authority noted that at the place of departure there is an official veterinarian who issues health attestations, although these do not always include an attestation of fitness for transport. 8 mitigated by provisions in the contingency plans, the feasibility and suitability of the arrangements have not been fully verified by the relevant authorities. 5.5 WELFARE OF ANIMALS DURING SEA TRANSPORT Legal requirements Article 3, 7(2), 19 and 20 of the Regulation. Findings

Both ports lack appropriate facilities to rest, feed and water the animals outside the means of transport. This would not allow the authorities to fulfil the requirements in Annex I, Chapter III, Point 1.2(a) of the Regulation in the case, for instance, where unloading and loading of the animals from each truck requires more than four hours. The competent authorities require organisers to plan the arrival of trucks at the port in a way that avoids unnecessary waiting.

In one port there are no plans to add such facilities. In the other, there is a project to build a facility, with an estimated capacity for 600 cattle and a covered area with a capacity to park 40 trucks in the shade. The authorities will discuss this project for its approval in November 2018. 5.4 DELAYS AT THE BORDER Findings

The competent authorities require organisers to submit contingency plans for each shipment, which must include providing for a situation where the loading of animals is not authorised. At the port visited, the operator, as part of its contingency plan, has an agreement with a holding, located 60 km from the port, to use it for unloading the animals in case of need. According to the operator, the holding has capacity for 5600 cattle or 15000 sheep. The competent authorities have not visited this holding to confirm whether it would be feasible to use it at short notice, and its suitability.
The other port has not identified nearby facilities in which to unload the animals in case of need. Conclusions on welfare of the animals arriving at the port

label_heading: Conclusions on welfare of the animals arriving at the port
paragraph_text: The official controls at the port are insufficient to minimise the risk of welfare problems for the animals involved in the journey. These are the result of under resourcing, insufficient planning (e.g. no sufficient time for vessel inspection), absence of detailed instructions and verification to trigger improvement.

label_heading: Conclusion on welfare of animals during sea transport
paragraph_text: The port veterinarians do not have the sufficient technical knowledge to perform a proper inspection of the livestock vessel and thus they do not assess effectively all the necessary elements. This, together with the short time allocated for the inspections, the absence of an approved classification society to verify the strength calculations of pen rails and decks indicates that the Croatian system to approve livestock vessels for transport in the EU and for inspecting them subsequently before each loading is insufficient to guarantee that animal welfare requirements are respected.

The procedures did not indicate that there needs to be a transporter for the sea journey who is established, or in the case that the applicant is established in a non-EU country, represented in the Member State (Article 10(1) of the Regulation). As a result port inspectors did not detect the absence of an authorised transporter responsible for the journey by sea (which should be in box 6.4 of section 1 of the journey logs). In practice, the port veterinarians make all requests regarding fulfilling the legal requirements for the export of animals to a forwarding agent, or the captain of the livestock vessel, although the competent authority has not defined if either of these actors have any l

The written procedures did not include instructions to take into account the judgement of the European Court of Justice in case C-424/13: Zuchtvieh3 (hereafter "the Zuchtvieh ruling") when checking journey logs; i.e. the organiser of the journey has to submit a journey log which is realistic and compliant with the Regulation up to the destination, including the stages of the journey which take place outside the EU.

The officials did not receive sufficient information in advance of the arrival of a livestock vessel, thus they had to assess everything (e.g. stocking density plan and feed plan for the sea journey) once the vessel was in the port.

The authorities have procedures for approval of the livestock vessels. Although these procedures include the network document translated to Croatian language, this has not been adapted to create suitable procedures and instructions to officials at the port. The instructions for staff to perform the vessel approval are not sufficient, which is not in line with Article 8(1) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

The audit team noted that on 31 July 2018 the port veterinarians completed in one hour the preloading inspection of a large vessel used to carry over 3000 bovine animals (see also paragraph 23). For that vessel, it was unrealistic to complete a preloading inspection in just one hour.

The port veterinarians checked 78 loadings in 2017 and 40 loadings in the first semester of 2018. The reports of inspections did not indicate any deficiencies for vessels in the port in the last three years.

The veterinary inspector did not check the water production records or the working order of the drainage pump, alarms of the ventilation, fresh water and lighting systems5. This is not in line with Article 20(1)(c) of the Regulation. The procedures indicated the legal requirements for ventilation and alarms but did not indicate how to check these. The inspectors admitted that they were not competent to assess some of the "non-veterinary" requirements of the Regulation, such as the number of air exchanges required to provide sufficient ventilation.

The procedure indicates also the need for assessing the amount of feed, but not how to do it, conclude, record and report. The veterinarians generally relied on the agent's statement 5 In their response to the draft report the Competent Authority noted that " Inspection of the ventilation, alarm system, fresh water system and lighting system is carried out by the engineer of Ministry of Transport and infrastructure, Port authority-Pula at least 2 times a year, and when approving the ship jointly in cooperation with veterinary inspectors. After these checks, the veterinary inspector checks the functionality of all systems before loading, but does not perform detailed technical checks" 8 for t

The inspectors confirmed to the audit team that they assess ventilation subjectively, based on their experience, and did not verify the air changes per hour required by Annex I Chapter IV, Section 1 point 2(a) of the Regulation.

label_heading: Conclusions on welfare of the animals arriving at the port
paragraph_text: The official controls at the port are insufficient to minimise the risk of welfare problems for the animals involved in the journey. These are the result of under resourcing, insufficient planning (e.g. no sufficient time for vessel inspection), absence of detailed instructions and verification to trigger improvement.

label_heading: Conclusions on welfare of the animals arriving at the port
paragraph_text: As the authorities have not established a verification procedure over the official controls at the port, they are unable to detect and correct the existing weaknesses in their checks; 4 In their response to the draft report the Competent Authority noted that "During the incident a decision was made to load the animals on the ship, as the competent authority considered that returning the animals by road transport to the place of origin would cause additional animal suffering due to the weather conditions". 7 non-conformities persist undetected and thus are not communicated to the authorities of the Member States of departure. All this hinders continuous improvement to ensure the welfare of an

There were no reports on checks performed before November 2017. From November 2017 to May 2018 10 consignments were the subject of reports to the Member States of origin: one without one hour rest in the journey log, four that did not provide temperature records, three animals unfit for transport (two mastitis and one sick animal euthanised), one dead animal with no water in the vehicle and one with unsuitable dividers in the vehicle.

The audit team reviewed documentation of consignments arriving from five other Member States. None of them indicated who the sea transporter was. The audit team noted that: 5 In all journey logs seen, only organisers from one Member State had indicated the transfer of animals to a livestock vessel in box 6.1 of section 1. The logs from all other countries indicated the journeys ended at the port. However, in some journey logs the organisers indicated the name of the livestock vessel ­ so they had considered the journey out of the EU. But they failed to indicate the name and number of the authorised transporter responsible for this stage of the journey in box 6.4 of section 1 of the journey l

During four days, 101 trucks from five Member States arrived at the port during a heatwave to load cattle in a vessel that departed in August 2018. For those 101 trucks, veterinary inspectors detected that: in 26% of the trucks, animals had been exposed during the journeys to temperatures above 35oC; 6 16% of the truck drivers did not provided temperature records of the vehicles and 7% did not provided the journey logs; the journey planning, which is responsibility of the organisers, did not avoid the arrival of vehicles at the same time; daytime temperatures were well over 30oC, and thus the loading of vehicles at departure should not have been carried out if authorities there had checked t

In that incident, the port veterinarians and representatives from the central authority did not have a clear course of action to follow to deal with the animals already in the port and those on their way4. After this incident the Croatian authorities notified three Member States by e-mail and for the other two Member States issued section V of the journey logs. Only one Member State replied to the Croatian contact point.

The central authority indicated that they did not impose sanctions in relation to this incident. In their opinion, the detected infringements were caused by the lack of proper planning in the countries of departure of the consignments. They indicated they have a procedure that allows any vehicle to be detained until the fine is paid.

After this incident the Croatian authorities requested better coordination, scheduling and communication to all interested parties (shipping agent, port operator and main road transporter). During the closing meeting of this audit, the central authority stated that they will improve the related procedures.

The authorities provided a document with the financial penalties for infringements to the Regulation. These range from HRK 10,000 (EUR 1,347) to HRK 100,000 (EUR 13,476). The average daily rental of a livestock vessel is EUR 25,000. The central authority indicated during the closing meeting that they plan to have new rules for sanctions next year. label_heading: Conclusions on welfare of the animals arriving at the port
paragraph_text: The current arrangements do not guarantee the welfare of the animals if there is a delay in loading a vessel. Neither the organisers, nor transporters, nor the authorities had contingency plans for this eventuality.

At the port, there was a single veterinary official in charge of many tasks, some of which occurred simultaneously, e.g inspection of the ship, control of documents from arriving trucks, assessment of fitness of animals. As result, not all tasks were completed properly and with the necessary attention.

The capacity of the assembly centre is not sufficient to accommodate all the animals loaded onto certain livestock vessels. In most cases, this is not a problem as the authorities co-ordinate the arrival of the trucks to the port and there are no major delays in transferring animals from road vehicles to the vessels. However, this can constitute a major problem in a case where the authorities refuse the loading of a big vessel. The authorities did not have arrangements to unload, accommodate, feed and water the animals in such cases and safeguard their welfare. This is not in line with Article 22(2) and Article 23 of the Regulation. 5.4 DELAYS AT THE BORDER

Procedures do not indicate that it is responsibility of the organisers to ensure that the time of arrival at the port should not coincide with the arrival of other vehicles in order to minimise the waiting time inside the port. This issue had to be raised with the organisers concerned, as required by Article 5(3)(a) of the Regulation, are legally responsible for coordinating the different parts of the journey.

label_heading: Conclusion on welfare of animals during sea transport
paragraph_text: The port veterinarians do not have the sufficient technical knowledge to perform a proper inspection of the livestock vessel and thus they do not assess effectively all the necessary elements. This, together with the short time allocated for the inspections, the absence of an approved classification society to verify the strength calculations of pen rails and decks indicates that the Croatian system to approve livestock vessels for transport in the EU and for inspecting them subsequently before each loading is insufficient to guarantee that animal welfare requirements are respected.

The veterinary inspector did not check the water production records or the working order of the drainage pump, alarms of the ventilation, fresh water and lighting systems5. This is not in line with Article 20(1)(c) of the Regulation. The procedures indicated the legal requirements for ventilation and alarms but did not indicate how to check these. The inspectors admitted that they were not competent to assess some of the "non-veterinary" requirements of the Regulation, such as the number of air exchanges required to provide sufficient ventilation.

The procedure indicates also the need for assessing the amount of feed, but not how to do it, conclude, record and report. The veterinarians generally relied on the agent's statement 5 In their response to the draft report the Competent Authority noted that " Inspection of the ventilation, alarm system, fresh water system and lighting system is carried out by the engineer of Ministry of Transport and infrastructure, Port authority-Pula at least 2 times a year, and when approving the ship jointly in cooperation with veterinary inspectors. After these checks, the veterinary inspector checks the functionality of all systems before loading, but does not perform detailed technical checks" 8 for t
The competent authorities indicated they only get information on completion of sea journeys if vessels return to the port and if they request information on incidences in the last five journeys.

The inspectors confirmed to the audit team that they assess ventilation subjectively, based on their experience, and did not verify the air changes per hour required by Annex I Chapter IV, Section 1 point 2(a) of the Regulation.

label_heading: Conclusion on welfare of animals during sea transport
paragraph_text: The failure to identify any natural or legal person as the authorised transporter for the journey by sea is further risk for animal welfare. However, this is also the failure of the authorities of the other Member States who approved journey logs which did not indicate an authorised transporter for the sea journey. 6 OVERALL CONCLUSIONS The system in place is insufficient to minimise the risks that can negatively affect the welfare of the animals that arrive at the port and that are transported further by sea. The Croatian system to approve livestock vessels for transport in the EU and for inspecting them before each loading does not minimise the risk of adverse welfare conditions for the an

The procedures did not indicate that there needs to be a transporter for the sea journey who is established, or in the case that the applicant is established in a non-EU country, represented in the Member State (Article 10(1) of the Regulation). As a result port inspectors did not detect the absence of an authorised transporter responsible for the journey by sea (which should be in box 6.4 of section 1 of the journey logs). In practice, the port veterinarians make all requests regarding fulfilling the legal requirements for the export of animals to a forwarding agent, or the captain of the livestock vessel, although the competent authority has not defined if either of these actors have any l

Poland has detailed documented procedures for official controls on animal welfare at all stages of transport and on animal health certification, even though with a few shortcomings. Some instructions for those procedures are also not sufficiently clear and thus differently understood by the different districts resulting in a non-harmonised approach in carrying out official controls.

Although the central competent authority indicated that the journey plan must be until the final place of destination in the non-EU country and that this has been always their interpretation, this was not clear to all DVOs and therefore there is a risk that travelling times are sometimes exceeded once past the EU border.

There is a system in place to assess planned and actual resting and travelling times before and after the journey. Assurances given by this system are nevertheless weakened by the failure to ensure that all journey plans cover the full journey until the final place of destination in the non-EU country and by the lack of evidence that the prescribed retrospective checks have been carried out.

Some points in the animal welfare instructions are unclear, such as: The instruction to check that journeys are planned until "final place of destination". Two of the districts visited were correctly evaluating journey plans until the final place of destination in the non-EU country. In the other district visited journey plans to non-EU countries did not include the non-EU leg of the journey and the exit point but were still incorrectly stamped as satisfactory by that district; When supervising transporters, the instructions indicate "compare SNS data with completed journey logs". Organisers notify the DVO well in advance of the intention to transport animals over long distances. This notification: Indicates the date and place of departure, the place of destination, the number of animals to be transported, the transporter and the vehicle number plate; Does not include a properly completed signed copy of Section 1 of the journey log, contrary to the requirements of Point 3(b)(ii) of Annex II of Regulation (EC) No 1/2005. The OVs therefore cannot check in advance if the planned journey is realistic and complies with the requirements of Regulation (EC) No 1/2005, in particular with travelling and resting times.

Certificates of approval of vehicles for long distance journeys do not distinguish between adult and unweaned animals. As a result unweaned animals may not have access to liquid and be if necessary fed during long distance journeys. This shortcoming may negatively impact journeys starting from another Member State, if in that Member State the suitability of the vehicles is not also systematically verified at the moment of loading. 5.3 RESTING Legal requirements Articles 14, 15, 19, 25 and 26 and Chapter V, Annex I of Regulation (EC) No 1/2005. Articles 1 and 2 of Commission Decision 2013/188/EU. Findings

Certificates of approval of vehicles for long journeys do not distinguish between adult and unweaned animals, contrary to Chapter IV Annex III of Regulation (EC) No 1/2005. This implies that unweaned animals may be transported on vehicles that are inadequate for this category of animals with the biggest risk being the inability to access liquids due to unsuitable drinking devices (Point 2.2 of Chapter VI, Annex I of Regulation (EC) No 1/2005).

The regions' ineffective verification of the reports submitted on the number of checks during transport can undermine the validity of the data collected and negatively affect the analysis of data that the GVI is required to perform. 5.4 UNEXPECTED DELAYS AT THE BORDER Legal requirements Article 11 of Regulation (EC) No 1/2005. Articles 3, 4, and 5 of Directive 96/93/EC. Findings

Regarding retrospective checks to verify the travelling and resting times to provide water, feed and rest to the animals (Articles 15(1) and 15(4) of Regulation (EC) No 1/2005): According to the animal welfare instructions each DVO has to carry out retrospective checks on 20% of journeys departing from and arriving at the district. Returned journey logs were available for all exports examined by the audit team. The audit team saw evidence of retrospective checks carried out on those journeys for which notifications of non-compliances had been received. However, there was no evidence of retrospective checks done on returned journey logs for which there was no notification of non-compliance. O

However, if the organisers provide incorrect accompanying age documentation and that documentation is forwarded without any official remark there is the risk of animals being detained in a stationary truck at the EU borders.

Calves were being transported from one of the districts visited to a non-EU country (other than Turkey). There are therefore inadequate assurances that the needs of animals can be met if blocked at the border on board Polish vehicles and that these animals are not caused unnecessary suffering. 6 OVERALL CONCLUSIONS The system in place has produced good results with live animal exports to non-EU countries operating with a tiny number of non-compliances. However, Poland did no exports to Turkey which is the EU land border with more frequent live

These include: names and phone numbers of persons responsible for taking decisions, description of strategies for the change of means of transport, procedures to be followed in the event of unexpected stops and in case assistance is needed to care for the animals. label_heading: Conclusions on welfare of the animals arriving at the port
paragraph_text: Port inspectors carry out official controls in accordance with Article 21(1)(a),(b) and (c) of the Regulation, and the results of these checks confirm that the majority of animals arrive at the port in good condition, and where necessary, the port inspectors take action to ensure that any unnecessary suffering is dealt with. However, procedures do not indicate that port inspectors should enter all relevant data in Traces after the checks and although port inspectors do enter certain data in Traces they have under-reported the numbers of animals deemed unfit for transport. As a result useful information is not readily available to the authorities in the Member State of departure.

label_heading: Conclusions on welfare of the animals arriving at the port
paragraph_text: Port inspectors had not detected systematic deficiencies in journey logs and although procedures indicate the relevant legal requirements, they do not instruct inspectors to check critical points such as the planning for a transfer onto a livestock vessel and an identifiable authorised transporter for the journey by sea. The central competent authority was not aware of these deficiencies as it had not supervised the work of inspectors to ensure the quality of controls carried out at exit points. As a result, the competent authorities had not ensured the effectiveness and appropriateness of official controls, contrary to Article 4(2)(a) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, and these deficiencies h

Therefore, the competent authority has not ensured adequate inspections of livestock vessels, as required by the Regulation, and has been repeatedly recommended in previous DG Health and Food Safety audit reports.

The port inspectors do, nevertheless, enter data in Traces according to Article 3(2) of Decision 2004/292/EC for each consignment of animals using the reporting model provided in Commission Regulation (EC) No 599/2004. label_heading: Conclusions on welfare of the animals arriving at the port
paragraph_text: The authorities deal with situations such as their refusal to allow the loading of a livestock vessel on a case by case basis; however, there is a risk that animal welfare may not be safeguarded if there is a delay in a sailing and the capacity of the control post is exceeded as the authorities have not determined any options for the arrangements they are required to make in such situations. 5.5 WELFARE OF ANIMALS DURING SEA TRANSPORT Legal requirements Articles 3, 7(2), 19 and 20 of the Regulation. Findings

The capacity of the control post is not sufficient to accommodate all the animals loaded onto certain livestock vessels. Co-ordination of the arrival of animals has taken place so that this has not been a problem; i.e. there have been no major delays in transferring animals from road vehicles to livestock vessels. However, the authorities had no arrangements to care for animals where they refused the loading of a livestock vessel and where the number of animals exceeded the capacity of control post. Article 22(2) of the Regulation requires the competent authority to ensure that appropriate arrangements are made to care for animals, and if necessary to unload, accommodate, feed and water them

The audit team also noted that the transporter responsible for the road transport did not have a contingency plan to put into operation in the event that the authorities refused the loading of animals onto

The central authority has given repeated commitments, first given in 2009, that a system was being devised which included sufficient competence for inspection of livestock vessels. label_heading: Conclusions on registration and approval of food business operators
paragraph_text: The comprehensive approval procedure supports official control staff in their work and several elements of it are implemented satisfactorily. Nevertheless, staff's lack of correct understanding of certain provisions thereof as well as the less strict national rules do not ensure that compliance with the EU legislation is routinely achieved. 4.4 OFFICIAL CONTROLS OF FBOS PRODUCING RTE FOODS 4.4.1 Organisation and implementation of Official Controls Legal requirements Article 17 of Regulation (EC) No 178/2002, Articles 3, 4(2)c, 8, 9, 10, 11 and 12 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, Article 5 of Regulation (EC) No 852/2004, Article 4 of Regulation (EC) No 854/2004, Articles 1 and 5 of Regulation

label_heading: Conclusions on official controls on the production of RTE foods
paragraph_text: The differences in the development of the control systems for the different sectors suggest a missed opportunity for sharing good practices and exploiting synergies within and between DGCCRF and DGAL with a view to providing comparable support for staff carrying out controls in establishments with similar risks, further strengthening the control systems and their consistencies as well as ensuring a uniform control approach towards all FBOs. 4.4.3 Challenges encountered by the CA in the organisation and performance of controls over the production of RTE foods

Both administrations have systems to ensure officials have access to training, amongst other, on relevant RTE topics. a. DGAL training includes food technology, inspection of food safety management systems, HACCP based procedures, microbiological criteria, alerts and outbreaks management and auditing. In this regard the audit team noted that while the training for most of the above technical topics was delivered to a large number of officials, this was not the case for audit training, although national control procedures require local CAs to carry out audits or to use auditing techniques routinely in their controls in RTE producing establishments. b. DGCCRF training includes Hygiene Package

Both DGAL and DGCCRF staff have access to the "Better Training for Safer Food" (BTSF) initiative and the "resource persons" met participated in BTSF sessions. The official control staff met was in general experienced and knowledgeable for their work. Some support/training needs were identified during the audit, mainly in relation to: a. CAs' assessments and audits of good hygiene practices and HACCP, grading of non-compliances and enforcement and follow-up action (see paragraphs 11, 58-62 and 88 - 93). b. approval of establishments and keeping it under review (see paragraphs 25 to 28) linked mainly to the staff understanding of the rules. c. CA's controls over sampling and testing procedures

This suggests that the official control staff is not adequately kept up-to date in their area of competence as required by Article 6(b) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 for the areas highlighted above. The audit team did not note any problems related to facilities and equipment for the performance of official controls.

DGAL's had recently updated the approval procedures. The general inspection handbook instructs inspectors to check that the activities carried out by the establishment correspond to those covered by the approval. The FBOs visited by the audit team were in most cases approved for the activities they carried out. However, the audit team noted in four of the six approved establishments visited instances on non-compliance with the provisions of Article 31(2) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 and/or the national procedures explained by the CCA as local staff's apparent lack of awareness of the rules.

label_heading: Conclusions on registration and approval of food business operators
paragraph_text: Both CAs have procedures in place for registration of RTE producing establishments and in the case of DGAL also for approval. However, the registration system does not favour the correct identification of production activities, including ready-to-eat, for all types of establishments. This has an impact in the DGCCRF's ability to organise the related risk based official controls.

label_heading: Conclusions on official controls on the production of RTE foods
paragraph_text: Each CA has put in place a system of routine risk based official controls over production of RTE foods, supported by comprehensive procedures and covering relevant aspects of the legislation. The procedures for organisation of controls are currently under review for further fine-tuning the risk determination for the RTE sector. While some of the national provisions and procedures provide clarification for aspects that go beyond the EU requirements, other are less strict and if applied as such may potentially provide a lower level of safety than the EU requirements, in particular as regards Listeria, Coagulase-positive Staphylococci and controls for parasites in fishery products.

All FBOs are required to register with the Business Formalities Centres to enable the company to be created and be assigned a SIREN (business) number and a SIRET6 number. The FBO declares the main activity performed in accordance with the French Administrative Nomenclature (NAF) codes drawn up by the National Institute of Statistics and Economic Studies (INSEE). The Business Formalities Centres are obliged 6 In their comments to the draft report, the CAs noted that a SIRET number is assigned to any primary or secondary establishment within the meaning of Article R123-40 of the Commercial Code, i.e. `any permanent establishment, distinct from the registered office or principal establishment a

The lack of clarification on what constitutes RTE which takes account of national consumption habits and FBOs' approaches as well as the lack of guidance for the composite products RTE sector do not support the related official controls and uniformity thereof. 4.2 COMPETENT AUTHORITY Legal requirements Articles 4 and 6 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Findings
An array of sector specific support mechanisms and access to several technical training, aid the CAs in their controls on production of RTE food, but to lesser extent for composite products.

label_heading: Conclusions on official controls on the production of RTE foods
paragraph_text: The controls on Hygiene Package requirements in establishments producing food of animal origin are well developed. This was noted to a lesser extent for establishments producing composite products in particular in the case of DGCCRF, with an unknown percentage of registered establishments not subject to such controls on a scheduled basis.

label_heading: Conclusions on official controls on the production of RTE foods
paragraph_text: The controls cover satisfactorily a range of aspects of the Hygiene Package, with some areas for improvement in relation to FBO's measures for prevention of cross- contamination and sampling and testing procedures. The CAs' ability for detection of the 23 non-compliances and assessment of the impact thereof is sometimes hindered by the current system for targeting controls and the limited use of systematic reviews.

The CAs' ability for detection of the 23 non-compliances and assessment of the impact thereof is sometimes hindered by the current system for targeting controls and the limited use of systematic reviews.

The official controls over FBOs compliance with the microbiological sampling and testing requirements of Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005 are limited. CAs are not 17 required to verify FBOs' sampling methods. In the case of alerts, CAs verify the testing method indicated in the laboratory test results. Nonetheless, official control decisions are taken on the basis of FBOs' test results. The CCA clarified that CAs have the option of taking official samples from time to time to provide clarification to the inspector, guide his/her work and determine the measures taken following the inspection.

label_heading: Conclusions on official controls on the production of RTE foods
paragraph_text: The effectiveness of the control and enforcement system is also weakened by the fact that some long-standing deficiencies detected and classified by the CAs as medium or major ones are not adequately followed­up and enforced by the CAs to ensure the FBOs swiftly remedy the situation.

The procedures also establish deadlines for finalising the controls, reporting and following-up of non-compliances. Within the current establishment rating system, these deadlines do not support swift FBO action to address non-compliances when such non 7 In their comments to draft report, the CCA noted that the threshold of 1 000 cfu/g was set instead of 10 000 cfu/g for the other products to be consumed cooked, in order to take into account the risk of minced or thinly sliced products being insufficiently cooked through. label_heading: Conclusions on official controls on the production of RTE foods
paragraph_text: Official sampling and testing of RTE food is in place. Official laboratories are accredited and subject to NRL coordination. The organisation of the official sampling for RTE food of animal origin prepacked by the producers, with a view to testing for Listeria, suggests a discriminatory approach focusing more on RTE food produced in other countries, including other MS.

Between 2013 and 2017 DGAL took 2167 RTE samples. From 2013 to 2016 the sampled matrixes only included unpasteurised dairy products and sausages while in 19 2017 sliced pig meat products were targeted. During this period the testing focussed on Salmonella and Listeria testing (STEC in 2014). Sampling of RTE for microbiological criteria does not take place every year at production level. The non-compliance rates identified range from zero in 2017 for Listeria in sliced meat products to 2.25% in 2016 for Listeria in unpasteurised dairy.

There is a training system in place aimed to ensure that official staff carry out their tasks adequately,and as regards the new rules introduced in the cow milk sector, it appears effective. However, the system in place does not take into account that new tasks can be assigned to official staff within the rotation system in place and therefore there are no guarantees that they will undertake these new duties competently. 5.3 REGISTRATION AND APPROVAL OF FOOD BUSINESS ESTABLISHMENTS Legal requirements Article 6 of Regulation (EC) No 852/2004, Article 4 of Regulation (EC) No 853/2004, Article 3 of Regulation (EC) No 854/2004 and Article 31 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Findings

Concerning the rotation of the staff, exceptions and some flexibility are allowed in specific circumstances (e.g. remote areas, availability of personnel). It is up to the RFSD to decide when and if the rotation should take place: in one region staff rotates every six months and in another one every year. The CA of the latter region explained that the frequency of rotation of staff working in slaughterhouses involved in exports is lower as the knowledge required for this sector and the language skills are very important.

A training system aimed to ensure that official staff is able to carry out their tasks properly is in place. However, the audit team noted that the system does not take into account if training is needed for those officials rotating and dealing with new tasks they are not familiar with.

All competent authorities have audit services in place to implement the audit programmes and these significantly vary in terms of planning process and availability of auditors. While DAC (SVFA) provides, in principle, assurance that audits will be continued as planned, this cannot be ensured by ODKAS (PHA) which is struggling with a decrease in the number of auditors and increase of audits and, in 2018, SSCIA (CCTIA) that has neither the audit programme in place nor the resources to execute it.

Until recently (the end of 2017) SSCIA carried out audits completed by two auditors of which one was a permanent employee of SSCIA and another worked on a contractual basis. From 2018 these auditors are no longer available and audit activities are suspended.

CCTIA covers four fields of official controls falling under Regulating (EC) No 882/2004. The SSCIA representative stated that audit planning requires regular audits in 20 each of the areas once a year, therefore for selection of audit areas a risk-based approach does not apply. Until the end of 2017 SSCIA managed to meet the target of four audits per year. At the time of this audit the 2018 audit programme was not in place as SSCIA has lost two auditors (see finding 23).

According to the SSCIA representative prior to 2016 no arrangements for monitoring and review of the audit process were in place. The Methodological instruction No 1/2017 put in place some provisions for these activities but they have not been implemented. Moreover, in 2017 the audit team was so small (two auditors only) that all improvements/changes could be implemented immediately therefore, there were not recorded. SSCIA has not initiated further work on monitoring and review procedures since the future format of the audit process has not been decided yet.

All competent authorities have put in place arrangements for independent scrutiny as required by Article 4(6) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. However, both the Committee and the Forum lack a fully-independent person (or body) with audit expertise. This limits the abilities of the existing arrangements to assess the suitability of the audit process and to ensure that it can contribute to improving the performance of the audit activities. As a consequence, in their current format, the arrangements in place cannot assess whether internal audit systems are achieving their objectives. 5.2.3 Auditor competence 5.2.3.1 Legal requirements Articles 2(6) and 4(6) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 do not

The DG SANTE audit team examined the records from the Commission meetings and noted that none of them contained evidence that: a) the Commission checked whether the audit processes achieved their objectives, and/or b) how and to what extent the Commission contributed to the continuous improvement of the SVFA and/or the CCTIA audit process. SVFA and CCTIA were unable to present such evidence. Moreover, the summary information presented by the SVFA and the CCTIA representatives to the Commission reflected on the outcome of audits and performance statistics (number of 12 audits carried out vs. audits planned) but did not present an insight into other steps of the audit process, for instance pla
The DG SANTE audit team noted that the Commission members have sufficient authority but insufficient expertise to assess the audit process and contribute to its improvement.

The DG SANTE assessed the records and noted that: Evaluation of the implementation of the audits on official controls was limited to checks on performance statistics (number of audits carried out vs. audits planned). The review focused on the outcome of the audits (audit findings and conclusions) rather than the audit process itself. As a result the Forum suggested adjustments for issues identified during audits on official controls and did not propose any improvements to the audit process. The Forum did not conclude if, or to what extent, audits achieved their objectives. The Forum concluded that audits were carried out in accordance with the audit procedure. The DG SANTE audit team noted that of twelve members of the Forum: at least one person was involved in development of the audit procedures, nine persons represented RPHAs ­ from an audit point of view they were auditees, and except the one person involved in development of audit procedures, the other Forum members had no expertise in audit. 13 Conclusions

All competent authorities have arrangements in place for developing audit programmes and these reflect responsibilities and areas of official controls laid down in the Slovak MANCP. Nevertheless, competent authorities have a variety of approaches for risk- based prioritisation of areas for audit, and these are neither supported by clear methodologies nor systematically documented. As a consequence, currently, none of the authorities could demonstrate that their programmes were risk-based or achieved an appropriate coverage of relevant official control activities.

The DAC representative stated that, although it is planned, there is currently no methodology in place demonstrating how the risk criteria are applied through the risk universe to result in the audit programme. For establish the coverage DAC uses a combination of geographical distribution and topics audited in each of the DVFA. Within three years, each of the DVFAs must be audited at least once. Within one series of audits in selected area, individual audits must be carried out at least in two and preferably in three DVFAs. The Head of DAC selects areas and topics for the audits on the basis of a history of non-compliance in official controls, results of DG SANTE audits and available human r

CCTIA covers four fields of official controls falling under Regulating (EC) No 882/2004. The SSCIA representative stated that audit planning requires regular audits in 20 each of the areas once a year, therefore for selection of audit areas a risk-based approach does not apply. Until the end of 2017 SSCIA managed to meet the target of four audits per year. At the time of this audit the 2018 audit programme was not in place as SSCIA has lost two auditors (see finding 23).

The PHA audit programme reflects the Slovak MANCP and covers all areas of official controls by RPHAs. ODKAS develops the programme on a yearly basis and presents it to the Advisory Forum for modifications and approval. The ODKAS representative stated that the audit programme is based on a geographical distribution of RPHAs and it does not cover the central level of PHA.

The PHA audit programme does not focus on specific areas or risks but rather follows the number and type of claims registered by ODKAS from a given region or a topic. Following the decision of the Advisory Forum (February 2018), beginning from 2018 the programme will cover all 36 RPHAs within a period of five years and focus on more specific areas; e.g. claims on deteriorating food quality triggered more targeted audits on food and food traceability.

The ODKAS representative stated that currently no methodology for risk-based selection of areas for audit is in place and the Head of ODKAS follows the procedure requiring him to propose areas and topics for audits. These are selected following the occurrence of claims notified to PHA, the number of notification of infectious diseases, e.g. hepatitis, or particular interest in some specific areas, e.g. production of baby food. Moreover, the Advisory Forum has the right to add areas and topics for audits which deems necessary.

The DG SANTE audit team interviewed the DAC representatives and examined some audit files and noted the following: Procedures for preparing, approving and distributing audit reports, and arrangements to review audit conclusions and ensure the monitoring of corrective and preventive actions are in place. The consistency between auditors at the level of generating audit findings (including identification of evidence of compliance and noncompliance) and their proper recording in audit reports in accordance to the newly introduced procedures following the 2017 Directive is ensured by the Head of DAC who participates in at least the first audit of the series and conducts regular consultations wit

Responsibility for auditing of official controls has been clearly allocated and all competent authorities carrying out official controls have put internal audit arrangements in place with the exception of the VS, which have temporarily suspended their audit system. Therefore, VS has currently no internal audit system in place as required by Article 4(6) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. 5.2 AUDIT ARRANGEMENTS 5.2.1 Independence 5.2.1.1 Legal requirements Article 2(6) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 defines "audit" as "a systematic and independent examination to determine whether activities and related results comply with planned arrangements and whether these arrangements are implemented effect

The VS established an internal audit system in 2007. In mid-2016 a decision was taken to reorganise the internal audit arrangements and to suspend the internal audit system until new arrangements could be put in place. Therefore, no audits were carried out between mid-2016 and 2017 and no audits are planned for 2018. 3 3 In their response to the draft report the VS provided information on the reasons for the suspension of their audit system. 7 Conclusions

In the context of passive surveillance in domestic pigs, the audit team saw examples where laboratories not accredited for RT-PCR forwarded samples to a laboratory which was accredited. In some instances, the arrangements in place resulted in the samples being held for a number of days (at appropriate temperature) in the initial laboratory before they were despatched.
In one county visited, the time between sample submission from found dead wild boar and reporting of RT-PCR results exceeded 9 days. Conclusions on laboratories

The many backyard holdings (~ 535,000 containing just under half the domestic pig population) and Type A holdings, with rudimentary biosecurity, represent the most likely route for the introduction of disease to the domestic pig population.

The risk of spread of disease is much greater from Type A holdings as they breed pigs and can have commercial activity (sale of live pigs). 5.3 SURVEILLANCE IN DOMESTIC PIGS Legal requirements Council Directive 2001/89/EC; Commission Decision 2013/722/EU. Findings

In the Type A and backyard holding visited by audit team, biosecurity was rudimentary and there was no availability of disinfection facilities at the entrance to holding as required by Article 6 of Implementing Decision 2013/764/EU. 5 Conclusions on Biosecurity in pig holdings

label_heading: Conclusions on surveillance in domestic pigs
paragraph_text: The fact that there was no suspicion on CSF reported in the country in the past two years indicates lack of awareness of both pig keepers and veterinarians towards this disease. This weakens the field surveillance and thus the capacity to detect early the introduction of the virus.

In one county visited, the competent authority had recently investigated a pig herd where clinical signs included an increased number of abortions, dullness and discolouration of ears. In a second county, a circumscription veterinarian submitted samples from five backyard holdings in the same locality, at the same time, with no indication on submission forms there may be a common disease problem or that the samples should be processed as a priority. Neither event was treated as a suspicion of CSF.

paragraph_text: The system now also includes enforcement of additional declaration requirements for phytosanitary certificates, for which there is a comprehensive guidance document to assist inspectors. However, the omission in the guidance, although quite minor, means that some EU requirements are not enforced in the Netherlands, and not implemented by the many exporting countries which use this document as guidance.

This document is published in English on the NVWA website7. The audit team identified a minor shortcoming with this guidance document, in that it omits the requirement for certain additional declarations, that the area or place of production established as free must be stated in the declaration. However, Decree No 15-580 of 30 April 2015 of the Préfet is not in line with Article 19 of the Decision as it implements additional protection measures and trade restrictions which are not justified by the existing plant health risk.

In Corsica, Decree No 15-580 of 30 April 2015 of the Préfet (as amended), allowing import of specified plants from non-EU countries and entry from EU territory outside the DAs to Corsica only by professionals and only following a detailed request, is still in force. label_heading: Conclusions on eradication measures in the DAs in the PACA region
paragraph_text: The 2018 annual monitoring in the BZs was partly in line with provisions of Article 6(7) of the Decision as certain parts of of the BZs were not checked and the applied system of two observation points does not ensure that specified plants present in each grid are visually inspected. Therefore symptomatic plants could be overlooked and not sampled. Consequently the monitoring cannot fully confirm the status of Xf in those areas.

In the PACA region, in the period April-October 2018, FREDON carried out monitoring in the circles of 5km radius around the established IZs according to the DGAL work instructions (see blue circles in Figure IV). In line with provisions of Article 6(7) of the Decision a grid split into 100m x 100m squares within a zone of a width of 1 km surrounding the IZs and a grid split into 1km x 1km squares within the 1-5 km part of the BZs was applied. However, no surveillance was carried out beyond 5km radius in the remaining territory of the 44 municipalities, declared as BZ (see chapter 5.3.1). Therefore the presence of Xf was not checked in some parts of the BZs, which is not in line with Article

The audit team was informed that the monitoring protocol requires the pre-definition of two observation points in each grid square from which the presence of symptomatic specified plants needs to be checked visually. Each identified symptomatic specified plant must be sampled for laboratory tests.

The audit team observed a monitoring, carried out by FREDON in a BZ, and noted that the agents: Carried out the grid-based monitoring in line with DGAL work instructions; Were well trained and experienced and possessed all necessary equipment for the visual surveys and sampling; Selected two observation points in each square then located those points with the help of maps, aerial photos and a GPS device; Carried out a 360o visual check from each observation point, checked the vicinity for the presence of specified plants with visible or suspicious symptoms and took samples only from symptomatic plants; The exact GPS position of each sampled plant was recorded and the plants were labelled. Consequently symptomatic specified plants could be overlooked and not sampled. This is not in line with Article 6(7) of the Decision; In the BZs laboratory samples are taken only from the symptomatic plants, while Article 6(7) of the Decision also requires sampling of asymptomatic plants in the vicinity of the sym

label_heading: Conclusions on eradication measures in the DAs in the PACA region
paragraph_text: In the IZs established for Xf subspecies multiplex there were delays in the removal of certain host plants in the 100m radius around positive tested plants and France does not consider to remove a range of other host plants in the same areas as a priority. In addition in the IZ for Xf subspecies pauca the physical protection of olive trees was discontinued. Therefore provisions of Article 6(2) of the Decision were not entirely implemented. label_heading: Conclusions on movement controls of specified plants
paragraph_text: The authorisation of movement of vine bud-wood produced in Corsica for thermotherapy in mainland France is not in line with provisions of Article 9 of the Decision.

label_heading: Conclusions on movement controls of specified plants
paragraph_text: The frequency of official controls in the nurseries together with the limited information about the final destination of the plants do not ensure that specified plants, which have been grown for at least part of their life in a DA, do not move out of those areas. In particular in the DAs of the PACA region there is a risk that specified plants leave the DA which could contribute to the spread of Xf.

There are many nurseries in the DAs, especially in the Department Alpes-Maritimes. FREDON agents are responsible for controlling the movement of specified plants within and out of the DAs. The audit team was informed that the nurseries are inspected generally twice annually during the vegetation period. One of the visits is the annual 21 plant passport control. Besides the producer and trader nurseries, inspections are carried out at the markets of national interest (MIN), at florists and at hyper- and supermarkets dealing with plants.

label_heading: Conclusions on movement controls of specified plants
paragraph_text: Although road signs provide certain indication about the Xf risk, they cannot inform the public effectively about the delimitation of the DAs.

In 2018 the SRAL of the PACA region placed signs at some petrol stations of a retail chain located inside the DAs. The signs provide information about Xf and the associated plant health risk in a visually attractive form. The audit team noted that the signs are not placed at the border of the DA. Although the format attracts attention, it is difficult for the bypassing drivers and passengers to read the entire text. The CAs consider that the current signs provide information for a broader range of recipients and can be better protected from vandalism than any sign erected at the border of the DA.

Recommendation No 3 of the 2017 audit report requested France to ensure that road signs are set up, indicating the borders of the DAs as required by Article 6(8) of the Decision. As the signs are not placed at the borders of the DAs, they do not indicate the limits of those areas; therefore the recommendation is partially addressed. 5.6.4 Road controls, controls at seaports, airports 5.6.4.1 In the PACA region

paragraph_text: However, only limited awareness raising efforts regarding ring rot and brown rot have been made by the regional competent authorities to inform potato producers. These do not cover adequately the registration requirements when moving or trading potatoes. Despite the legal obligation for their registration with the NPA, registration of producers is not enforced. A large number of producers remain unregistered, and hence, they are not subject to supervision or systematic controls.

paragraph_text: As there is lack of communication functionality between the databases of the NPA and the APIA, compliance with phytosanitary registration requirements cannot be verified against the APIA database. This reduces the capacity of the NPA to have a proper overview and control of the current ring rot situation. During the recent potato crop production periods, the NPA and its regional county offices had not organised information campaigns, conferences or any other events on potato bacteria. Extension and/or consultation services to producers or other operators of the potato production and marketing sectors are provided occasionally at the beginning of the potato surveillance period or after ring rot outbreaks.

Non-registered growers usually state that they do not grow potatoes for commercial purposes but only for their own needs or limited local circulation (family consumption or animal feed). According to the data provided, in 2017 there were 49,125 small scale and 5,547 larger scale (more than one ha) producers who were receiving subsidies from 7 the APIA but were not registered with the NPA. This is not in line with the national requirement for registration with the NPA of potato producers with more than 0.5 ha and Article 6.6 of Directive 2000/29/EC.

The audit team came across cases of small scale non-professional producers growing potatoes on more than 0.5 ha who, despite being registered with APIA, stated that they were not aware of the obligatory registration with the NPA or that, in any case, they could not afford the registration fees imposed by the NPA.

Data from the National Statistics Service of Romania indicate that during 2017 ca. 133,600 ha were cultivated with ware potatoes. However, despite a collaboration agreement between the NPA and APIA, there is no consistent access by the NPA to the database of APIA. The producers with ware potato areas totaling more than 0.5 ha who do not comply with the requirement of registration in the phytosanitary database are not known by the NPA. Overall, producers registered with the NPA correspond only to ca. 9.5% of the total ware potato producing area; the majority (ca. 70%) of the area of ware potatoes is grown by operators who are not registered either with the NPA or APIA. paragraph_text: The current practice of performing confirmatory sampling when the FBO requests it for breeding and laying hen flocks without good reason to suspect false positives is not in line with the requirement for it to be done only in exceptional cases such as those. This can have negative impacts when Salmonella is present but not detected with the confirmatory test, resulting in a continued contamination and mistakenly reporting lower Salmonella prevalence. Those negative impacts are only partially reduced by the lower number of tests, in the last two years, which were initially positive but became negative after confirmatory testing.

The audit team noted that all salmonella positive results in laying and breeding hen flocks that it analysed (all from official sampling) in which the FBO had placed a 5 written objection with a request for confirmatory sampling that confirmatory sampling was never denied. paragraph_text: There are official controls at pig holdings and they are effective. label_heading: Conclusion on the planning and implementation of inspections
paragraph_text: The system of planning of inspections is based on appropriate risk-related factors and thus ensures that the official controls are carried out regularly, on a risk-basis and with appropriate frequency. Verification of the correctness of labelling is adequate to ensure that labelling requirements have been met by the operators. The effectiveness of the inspections is however weakened by several elements including the giving of prior notice to establishments prior the inspections, deficient assessment of operators' HACCP-plans, and incomplete verification of the appropriateness of the operators' retained samples. 5.2.2 Sampling 5.2.2.1 PLANNING OF OFFICIAL SAMPLING

The audit team noted that in the vast majority of the cases observed, a warning had been given to the FeBOs (2-14 days in advance) on the visits by the authorities (both from the DGAL and the DGCCRF side). Both authorities confirmed this practice and explained that prior notification was given to ensure the availability of the necessary staff and access to relevant documentation. The audit team pointed out that while such an approach can be justified in rare cases (remote locations, irregular working hours, etc.), providing the FeBOs with prior notice is not in line with the requirements laid down by Article 3(2) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

The audit team noted that the operators' quality assurance systems seen rarely contained unambiguous provisions on ensuring that the raw materials and ingredients are sourced from registered or approved FeBOs. This contradicts the requirements laid down by Article 5(6) of Regulation (EC) No 183/2005. This was neither spotted by the inspectors met during the audit nor had been identified in any of the previous inspection reports.

The audit team noted that the CVO has developed detailed guidance on the assessment of homogeneity of compound feed. The purpose of the document is to determine rules for assessing homogeneity of compound feed based on the degree of mixing of the key ingredient(s). While most of the inspectors met demonstrated good knowledge of verification of establishments' controls on this aspect, the audit team encountered instances when the inspectors did not possess adequate knowledge on the assessment criteria for homogeneity. Consequently, the inspectors could not adequately verify that the requirements laid down in part 3(b) of the section "Facilities and equipment" of Annex II to Regulation (EC) No

The audit team noted that there was no dedicated guidance on the assessment of carry- over. At all operators visited, where the risk for carry-over was relevant, the inspectors interviewed were struggling with the assessment of the operators' control for the carry- over, specifically of coccidiostats to non-target feed. For example, two operators used markers which were irrelevant to assess carry-over of coccidiostats ­ this was not spotted by the inspectors interviewed. As a result, the inspectors could not adequately verify that the requirements laid down in part 2(b) of the section "Facilities and equipment" of Annex II to Regulation (EC) No 183/2005 were respected by the FeBOs.

The audit team noted that many inspectors interviewed experienced difficulties in verifying that establishments' controls on scales and metering devices (in form of a check of documented and traceable procedures for testing/calibration and its completeness/adequacy) were appropriate. Thus, the requirements laid down by part 3(a) of the section "Facilities and equipment" of Annex II to Regulation (EC) No 183/2005 could not be properly verified by the inspectors. 6 5.2.1.3 TRACEABILITY

label_heading: Conclusion on the planning and implementation of official sampling
paragraph_text: The system in place for planning of official sampling is effective and risk-based. However, the effectiveness of this element of official controls is weakened by the competent authorities' failure to adhere to planned arrangements and by the fact that the representativeness of sampling, and thus samples' legal and analytical validity, is not ensured for substances with a non-uniform distribution.

paragraph_text: The interpretation of the analytical results does not take into account all required parameters thus weakening the legal validity of the decisions made by the competent authority on compliance. 5.2.3 Actions taken on non-compliances

A systemic shortcoming was noted by the audit team in terms of the preparation of final samples from the aggregate samples for control of substances where non-uniform distribution of the analyte/substance is presumed. The inspectors would normally use simple manual mixing to ensure appropriate homogenisation rather than special equipment (e.g., mechanical or automatic dividers) which is required by part 9(4) of Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 152/2009. For substances with a non-uniform distribution, simple manual mixing alone cannot ensure complete homogenisation of the aggregate sample. While official controls on the identification and registration of bovine animals are carried out as planned and identified shortcomings are subsequently followed up, these controls have, to date, not identified some non-compliances related to the identification of bovine animals and notification of births of calves at holdings.

A lack of effective action by the competent authority to enforce the operators' obligations to notify all events at holdings has contributed to a situation where the information in the national database for registration and identification of bovine animals is unreliable. In addition, due to limitations in the database's functionality, information that would be relevant for the planning and implementation of official controls on BSE and ABP cannot be easily extracted. Overall, these deficiencies cumulatively undermine the reliability of the BSE monitoring programme. 5.3 BSE MONITORING SYSTEM, LABORATORY NETWORK AND TESTING ARRANGEMENT

Despite the above, the audit team noted in the holdings visited ­ which had been subject to official controls - that the records of these controls did not show that the following issues (which were seen by the audit team during the audit) had been identified: a. In two out of four holdings visited, operators had not: (i) recorded in holding registers, (ii) notified, and (iii) identified newborn calves; (for example, in one holding visited, 17 cows had 17 calves in the last 12 months, none of which had been registered). 6 b. In two out of four holdings visited, animals that had died on farm (fallen stock) and/or were emergency slaughtered had not been recorded as such in the holding register

For example: a. Contrary to Article 4a of Regulation (EC) No 1760/2000 which requires identification of bovine animals within a maximum of 20 days from the birth of the animal and in any event before the animal leaves the holding on which it was born, in one of the holdings visited, six bovine animals out of 43 kept had no ear tags, and approximately 50% of those remaining ones had only one tag; b. In particular, in one of the slaughterhouses visited, bovine animals presented for slaughter were accompanied by passports that had been issued (for the first time) on the day prior to slaughter or on the day of slaughter. These animals were aged between 18 and 24 months. 7 22. The audit team analysed the data on the location and the number of bovine passports issued in comparison with the location and the number of registered new-born calves born in the country and noted a lack of correlation between the figures. According to the data from VetIS, in the period from 2014 to 2018, the population of bovine animals has steadily increased from approximately 721,000 to 765,000. However, the audit team noted that there was a large cohort of bovine animals missing from the database. For example in 2018, the difference between the number of animals born and traded (into Bulgaria) and the number of animals slaughtered, dead, traded and exported (out of Bulgaria), resulted in a surplus of approximately 34,000 animals, without a known (confirmed) history (3). This represents approximately 4.5% of the bovine population in the country.

The owners of bovine holdings visited stated that their main activity is production of milk, and their cows calve every year. The audit team noted that except for two regions where the numbers of new-born calves registered in VetIS were plausible, in the remaining 26 regions registered calves represented from 17% to 30% of the expected number.

In one of the holdings visited, the owner stated that there were 17 calves born within the last 12 months ­ all were sold aged one to two weeks old. In another holding visited, the animal keeper confirmed that his cows calved annually and that he retained a few heifer calves for rebuilding the herd. The audit team cross-checked the situation on that holding with the VetIS data and noted that: a. The calf retained in the herd had no ear tags and was not identified by any other means. b. For 17 cows, ranging in age from 14 to 19 years old, only one to three calves per cow had been notified in VetIS during the entire cows' lives; the owner retained the notified calves in the herd, and during th

The BFSA has granted access to VetIS to officials from the central and regional level, official veterinarians in slaughterhouses and to registered veterinarians. One person at central level (VetIS administrator) has access to all the information, whilst other users are only allowed to see information limited to an individual animal or a holding. These users have limited possibilities to correct or edit data in the event they see a non-conformity. Slaughterhouse operators, those collecting and disposing of fallen stock and animal (3) Data by BFSA (VetIS) and from TRACES. 8 keepers, have no access to VetIS.
