In light of the above, VetIS does not meet the requirements of Article 5 of Regulation (EC) No 1760/2000 as it neither reflects the actual population of bovine animals in Bulgaria nor does it facilitate the supply of the required items of information set out in Article 14 of Council Directive 64/432/EEC.

The quality and quantity of samples, once collected, are able to ensure sufficient material for BSE testing. However, the method of identifying samples does not guarantee to trace back to the sampled animal in the event of a positive result.

Despite the fact that the NRL-TSE and regional BSE laboratories are accredited to EN ISO/IEC 17025, use the approved test kits listed in the Regulation (EC) No 999/2001 and have performed satisfactorily in proficiency tests for BSE, both the competent authority and the NRL-TSE have consistently failed to ensure the availability of a sufficient number of diagnostic tests to analyse all the samples taken. This has resulted in an unsatisfactory situation where large numbers of samples from high-risk sub- 16 populations have either not been analysed or their analyses had been delayed for months, further weakening the reliability of the BSE monitoring results.

The audit team noted that the information provided by the competent authorities on monitoring in this sub-population is incomplete. There are significant discrepancies between the number of bovine animals from the sub-population of emergency slaughtered animals and found sick at ante mortem inspection reported by FCD and AHFCD (see Appendix, Tables 6 and 7). Data presented by FCD, AHFCD and those sourced from the BSE testing laboratories differ and cannot be reconciled (see Appendix, Tables 8 to 10, and Tables 16 to 18).

Due to the limited availability of testing kits, BFSA decided that samples collected from fallen bovine animals were of a low priority and delayed their testing. This resulted in a situation where samples from a group, which would ordinarily be considered as being a high risk (of BSE), were kept for several months before being tested (see findings 55 and 56).

The NRL-TSE is responsible for ensuring that there is a sufficient availability of BSE diagnostic tests for itself and for the regional BSE laboratories. The audit team noted that the arrangement for acquiring tests did not work effectively in 2018 as the regional laboratories and the NRL-TSE did not have sufficient tests available. This resulted in over 18,000 collected BSE samples (and an additional 11,000 for Scrapie) not being analysed. Due to this shortage of testing kits since August 2018, the samples from the sub- populations of bovine animals slaughtered at holdings as healthy, in emergency and dead were categorised as low priority and collected, but not tested. With respect to the arrangements for BSE testing, the audit team noted that the NRL-TSE did not overcome difficulties in ensuring availability of sufficient BSE test kits in 2019 and the backlog of untested samples is growing. At the time of this audit, there were 6,500 samples awaiting BSE testing (and 5,500 for Scrapie).

While the information from labels (date of slaughter, the 15 slaughterhouse number and the slaughter number of the animal or the ear tag number) could ensure traceability to the bovine animal sampled, the sole consecutive sequential number could not; especially if more samples with the same number were delivered for examination. The samples are not taken from all animals that should be tested in the relevant sub- population. A significant proportion of eligible healthy bovine animals, mainly slaughtered outside slaughterhouses, which should have been tested for BSE, have not been sampled. Likewise, sampling of eligible animals emergency slaughtered or found sick at ante mortem inspection is limited to very few regions, whereas the majority of such animals have not been notified or sampled. In comparison with other Member States and even with the competent authority's own estimates, the number of fallen bovine animals sampled remains extremely low.

The CAs have not demonstrated that they have put in place actions that would effectively address recommendation 4 of audit report DG(SANCO)2011-8944. This additionally undermines Bulgaria's request for a relaxation of the frequency of testing for BSE.

The implementation of the actions to address recommendation 6 of audit report DG(SANCO)2011-8944 has not been effective. Collection of SRM produced as a result of on-farm slaughtering of bovine animals in backyard holdings continues to be inexistent.

label_heading: Conclusions on the bovine identification and registration system
paragraph_text: While SNIRA is operational and available to all relevant users, the data available therein is incomplete for backyard holdings (retaining over 90% of the bovine population) in relation to the sub-populations relevant for the BSE monitoring and as such does not support the BSE monitoring and eradication system.

label_heading: Conclusions on the bovine identification and registration system
paragraph_text: Official controls on identification and registration of bovine animals (inventory checks) are carried out as planned and are able to detect non-compliances, which are subsequently recorded in SNIRA. However, the lack of regular follow-up of these non-compliances weakens the effectiveness of official controls and in turn does not result in any improvement of the reliability of the national database, in particular, with respect to the absence of recorded movements of animals and of notification of newborn calves. 10 34. There is an increasing trend in the number of notified dead animals, indicating growing awareness of this obligation amongst the bovine animal owners; nonetheless, the mortalit

In the commercial holdings visited, the audit team noted the following: a. The majority of adult bovine animals had two ear tags, some had one ear tag and, in one holding, only one animal was without both ear tags. This animal, however, had an electronic collar allowing linking of the animal with the holding register. Moreover, the holding operator had already in his possession ear tag duplicates also for this cow. b. With respect to young calves, in one of the holdings, all the young calves had ear tags while in another at least 10 (out of approximately 200 bovine animals) had not. The operator stated that the calves would be tagged soon (new ear tags were available at the holding) and demo

The CSVFSDs have contracts with authorised veterinarians who carry out controls on animal identification and holdings registration. On a monthly basis, each CSVFSD verifies the reports of these controls submitted by the authorised veterinarians. The verification concerns at least 10% of the holdings submitted to the identification actions. The audit team noted that: a. The controls by authorised veterinarians take place regularly, every year and cover at least 3% of holdings in the counties. b. The controls on animal identification and holding registration by authorised veterinarians have a form of an inventory check, cross-checking all animals present in a holding (including bovines) with t

A proportion of bovine animals slaughtered as healthy and eligible for BSE testing remains not tested; these are mostly animals slaughtered at backyard holdings. Consequently, the data available cannot reliably demonstrate that testing in this sub- population has been effectively implemented.

Overall, the system of collection and disposal of ABP, including of the fallen bovine animals from backyard holdings, has deteriorated since the previous audit. Therefore, recommendation 2 of audit report DG(SANCO)/2011-8941 remains unaddressed. 6 OVERALL CONCLUSIONS With regard to Romania's application for review of its BSE monitoring programme it is concluded that, despite some positive trends observed, there are yet no grounds to allow for received 180 days of transitional period to comply with the requirements. 24 the frequency of testing to be relaxed. Exit controls by BIP officials regarding transit consignments leaving the EU through the road BIPs Evzoni and Peplos are carried out outside normal working hours by BIP officials. Whilst this is not in line with EU requirements, Customs confirmation of exits was available. 5.3 PROCEDURES IN PLACE TO VERIFY THAT OFFICIAL CONTROLS ON IMPORTS OF ANIMALS AND GOODS ARE EFFECTIVE AND APPROPRIATE

It is common for the transits between BIPs Evzoni and Peplos and vice versa that the exits take place after working hours when there are no BIP officials available. In this case, the exits controls are done by the Customs officials. This finding was also mentioned in point 24 of the audit report DG(SANTE)2015-7437. This results in a situation where the exit of most consignments transiting between the BIPs Evzoni and Peplos and vice versa cannot be declared in TRACES as, in line with Article 11 (2)(e) of Council Directive 97/78/EEC, only BIP officials are allowed to do this. The audit team verified files of several consignments of animal origin which entered or exited the EU through the BIPs

Evidence was available that TRACES was in general used in line with Article 3 of Commission Decision 2004/292/EC and without undue delay by BIP officials with the exception of the two road BIPs visited, where the exit of transit consignments leaving the EU outside the working hours are not confirmed by BIP staff in TRACES. However Customs confirmation of the exit was available (see finding 26).

The BIP and DPE facilities visited were fit for purpose except the facilities for import controls of registered equidae and ungulates at the road BIP Evzoni which were unsuitable for these species and the facilities for import of goods of animal and non- animal origin at the road BIPs Evzoni, Peplos and the DPE Kipi Evrou. The facilities of BIP Peplos and DPE Kipi Evrou are located on the wrong side of the road i.e. in the direction of Turkey, causing logistical problems and potentially hampering the implementation of official controls. 13 6 OVERALL CONCLUSIONS The Greek authorities have established a well-functioning control system for imports of animals and goods of animal and non-animal o

The facilities for animals (categories U and E), however, have serious shortcomings, which might impair the health status of the animals placed into the facilities. The installations do not comply with the requirements of Annex A to Directive 91/496/EEC. The facilities are not pest-proof (evidence of bird and wasps nests), floors are worn-out, and floors and walls are not easy to clean and disinfect. Some of the drinking facilities are rusty and not well-maintained. Conclusions on suitability of facilities

The BIP and DPE facilities visited were fit for purpose except the facilities for import controls of registered equidae and ungulates at the road BIP Evzoni which were unsuitable for these species and the facilities for import of goods of animal and non- animal origin at the road BIPs Evzoni, Peplos and the DPE Kipi Evrou. The facilities of BIP Peplos and DPE Kipi Evrou are located on the wrong side of the road i.e. in the direction of Turkey, causing logistical problems and potentially hampering the implementation of official controls. 13 6 OVERALL CONCLUSIONS The Greek authorities have established a well-functioning control system for imports of animals and goods of animal and non-animal o

Regarding the layout and location of the BIP facilities, the shortcoming identified during the previous audits (ref. DG/(SANTE)2016-8867 and DG/(SANTE)2015-7439) remains. The BIP facilities are located on the wrong side of the road i.e. in the direction of Turkey, causing logistical problems.
The MRDF has requested a technical study to identify possible solutions to improve the situation. However, no short-term solutions are in sight. 5.4.2 BIP Evzoni

The facilities for products of animal origin for human consumption are adequate except for the broken cooling equipment of the freezer storage room for products destined for human consumption, which is not in line with Article 4 of Decision 2001/812/EC. During the audit the competent authorities took action to secure the budget to repair the freezing equipment.

The ambient storage facilities for products of animal origin destined for non-human consumption are not in line with the requirement laid down in Article 4 and the Annex to Decision 2001/812/EC as pests such as birds and insects had access to the facilities and there was no adequate artificial lighting.

The facilities for controls of goods of animal origin destined for non-human consumption are shared with the DPE Kipi Evrou for controls of goods of non-animal origin. Consequently, the same shortcoming regarding the lay-out and location of the BIP applies to the DPE facilities.
The MRDF has requested a technical study to identify possible solutions to improve the situation. However, no short-term solutions are in sight. 5.4.2 BIP Evzoni

label_heading: Conclusions on suitability of facilities and equipment
paragraph_text: All facilities visited with the exception of the BIP facilities at Venezia Port, did not meet the operational hygiene standards resulting from either lack of maintenance and/or inappropriate cleansing and disinfection. Whilst some facilities are being reconstructed to comply with Regulations (EU) 2017/625 and (EU) 2019/1014 there is, however, no plan to upgrade the substandard facilities and equipment at Civitavecchia Port BIP.

label_heading: Conclusions on suitability of facilities and equipment
paragraph_text: In relation to import controls on food of non-animal origin, DGISAN has not made available to the public a list of points of entry with suitable designated DPE/DPI facilities. The list of DPEs only erroneously refers to local offices of DGISAN and the published list has not been updated since 2016. DGISAN does not ensure that documentary checks are done at the DPE and that physical checks, including sampling, are carried out at the DPE/DPIs. 6 OVERALL CONCLUSIONS The responsibilities of the competent authorities for the official import controls are clearly defined. The Italian authorities have established a comprehensive framework for official controls on imported animals and goods, supporte

label_heading: Conclusions on implementation of official controls on imported goods
paragraph_text: USMAF-SASN do not check the originals of certificates or other relevant documents and therefore are not in a position to ascertain their authenticity. Furthermore, the way in which the system for documentary checks on consignments of food of non-animal origin subject to special import conditions has been set up at the designated point of entry in Venice Port (checks are being carried out at local office level instead of at the entry point at the border) is contrary to EU requirements.

The controls on food of non-animal origin subject to special import conditions were not implemented in line with EU rules in several cases below.

At Venice port, documentary checks on food of non-animal origin subject to special import conditions took place at the local USMAF-SASN office instead of in the port of (2) In its response to the draft report the competent authority noted that the BIP staff of Civitavecchia carry out the identity checks of the containerised frozen and chilled goods and collect the packages selected for physical checks at the BCP facilities. 12 entry where physical facilities are in place (see related finding point 82). This arrangement is not in line with the requirements laid down in Article 8(1)(a) of Regulation (EC) No 669/2009, Article 9(2) of Regulation (EU) No 884/2014 and Article 8(1) of Regulation (E

USMAF-SASN staff carry out documentary controls based on copies of original certificates and/or laboratory test results. This hinders the verification of the authenticity of the health certificates, declarations and the laboratory results due to the reliance on copies. This procedure is not in line with the requirements laid down in Articles 4, 5 and 9(2) of Regulation (EU) No 884/2014 and Articles 4, 5 and 8(1) of Regulation (EU) 2015/175.

In addition, in one port visited, DPE/DPI staff could not provide copies of the certificates and laboratory test results for one out of three consignments of peanuts from Egypt and one consignment of guar gum from India verified in order to demonstrate that the requirements laid down in Articles 4 and 5 of Regulations (EU) No 884/2014 and (EU) 2015/175 respectively were met.

The official samples, taken by DPE/DPI staff are sent to the designated laboratories for analyses. The consignments were detained awaiting results. The results of the laboratory tests were available in all cases verified, but in one case there was no link between the sampling and the consignment due to absence of the lot/batch number. 5.2.5 Decision on consignment and its follow-up

In case consignments are selected for official sampling, the consignments are forwarded to the inspection facilities for food of non-animal origin, which are located in the port of entry. In Venice port, physical checks and sampling takes also place in customs warehouses, which are not designated by DGISAN as DPIs. Carrying out physical checks at these warehouses is not in line with Article 9(2) of Regulation EC) No 669/2009, Article 8(1)(b) of Regulation (EU) No 884/2014 and Article 8(2) of Regulation (EU) 2015/175.

label_heading: Conclusions on implementation of official controls on imported goods
paragraph_text: The guarantees in response to recommendation 1 of a previous audit report in relation to entering required data into TRACES by the local veterinary units, confirming the arrival of consignments at destination have not been effectively implemented.

Regarding records of supplies of goods from the customs warehouse to cross border means of sea transport checked by the audit team, the certificate referred to in Article 1(3) of Decision 2000/571/EC (the model certificate being laid down in the Annex thereto) was issued by the BIP staff. However, the audit team noted that in a few cases, operators had not provided the BIP staff with the completed certificate confirming the delivery of goods on board the vessel within the deadline of 30 days, which is not in line with Article 2 of that Decision.

The BIP staff issued a similar document for delivery of goods from the warehouse to NATO/US army bases, and validated thereafter the CVEDs in TRACES. The proportion of cases where confirmation of arrival at NATO/US army bases within the deadline of 30 days varies significantly between bases, ranging from 99,6% to as little as 13.4 % confirmed. DGSAF stated that further action is still needed to ensure that this legal obligation is satisfied in all cases. 5.2.4 Documentary, identity and physical checks 5.2.4.1 Checks on animals

The audit team carried out a desk review of 50 consignments of animal origin which were allowed entry and must be channelled to their destination in line with the requirements of Articles 8(4), 12(1) or 15(1) of Directive 97/78/EC. DGSAF and BIP staff provided evidence that the local veterinary units had been informed of the dispatch and had reported the arrival of such consignments at destination. However, local veterinary units did not enter in TRACES the completion of part III of the CVEDs in 16 of the cases, but used instead other means to report the arrival e.g. by email. This is not in line with the requirements laid down in article 3(2) of Decision 2004/292/EC. 13 Furthermore, audit r

However, inaccuracies identified in the list of operators eligible to supply ABP and produce PAP to be used for aquaculture weakens the reliability of the feed ban measures in this area. 5.2 IMPLEMENTATION OF OFFICIAL CONTROLS Legal requirements Articles 4(3), 21, 22, 41, 43, 45(1), 46, 48 and 53 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009 Articles 8, 17(1), 20, 21, 31, 32 and Annexes IV, VIII, IX, X, XV and XVI to Commission Regulation (EU) No 142/2011 Article 7 and Annex IV to Regulation (EC) No 999/2001 Article 3 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 Findings

Listing of food establishments authorised to deliver raw materials for production of non- ruminant PAP and ABP, and feed operators authorised to produce feed materials and compound feed with PAP for aquaculture animals, is a federal responsibility. Each Land has to communicate the list of these establishments to the federal level. These lists are available on the BMEL website. The audit team identified that in Bavaria several food establishment (slaughterhouses, cutting plants) slaughtering and/or cutting bovine and porcine animals were listed. The competent authorities stated that some of these establishments had not provided evidence of having an effective system in place to prevent cross-

The processing plant visited delivered poultry PAP for feed production for aquaculture animals. This processing plant was not listed on the BMEL website contrary to the requirements of point 1(d), Section A, Chapter V, of Annex IV to Regulation (EC) No 999/2001 While this processing plant was subject to regular official controls, the competent authority has not detected this non-compliance.

Official inspections on operators' HACCP systems are carried out adequately, however problems identified regarding official validation of processing method 7 and official sampling weaken the effectiveness of these controls.

Three processing plants visited were using processing method 7, which had been authorised by the competent authority. In one processing plant during the 30 days validation period microbiological samples were taken (Salmonella, Enterobacteriaceae, Clostridium perfringens) directly after the treatment. This is not in line with the legal requirements for the testing of Salmonella and Enterobacteriaceae in PAP. The problem was identified by the competent authority and the sampling was repeated for Salmonella and Enterobacteriaceae two weeks later. During the repeated sampling the operator increased the minimum temperature in the drier and reduced the speed of the conveyor screw which may increas

In another processing plant visited using method 7, during the 30 days validation period samples were taken for microbiological controls (Salmonella, Enterobacteriaceae and Clostridium perfringens). However, for control of Salmonella and Enterobacteriaceae only one sample of each were taken contrary the requirements of point G 1(c) (ii) of Chapter III of Annex IV to Regulation (EU) No 142/2011. The competent authority did not note this problem and approved the validation of the processing method. In the third processing plant visited using method 7 the validation documents were comprehensive and complete as required by the legislation. 2 In its response to the draft report the competent auth

Official inspections on operators' HACCP systems are carried out adequately, however problems identified regarding official validation of processing method 7 and official sampling weaken the effectiveness of these controls.

In two processing plants visited located in Lower-Saxony, official microbiological samples were taken for control of Salmonella and Enterobacteriaceae from PAP. However, in several cases the number of samples sent for laboratory tests was lower than that required by Chapter I, Annex X to Regulation (EU) No 142/2011.

In all processing plants visited, regular microbiological samples were taken by operators for microbiological control of produced PAP. In one plant, samples were always taken from the production line not from the storage of final product; in another plant, only 1-1 samples were taken from each production batch for control of Salmonella and Enterobacteriaceae. While these plants were subject to official inspections, the local inspectors had not identified that such sampling is not in line with the requirements of Chapter I, Annex X, of Regulation (EU) No 142/2011.

Inadequate checks on the implementation of requirements concerning confirmation of TRACES notifications of intra-EU trade of PAP and OF/SI negatively affect the reliability of the flow of information on the intra-EU trade of such products.

A number of guides are available to support the use of TRACES: - The FLI has prepared a guidance document with the most important questions and answers relating to the use of TRACES and a general instruction on the use of the DOCOM (commercial document) part of TRACES in case of trade in Category 1, 2 and 3 ABP and derived products. - In Bavaria, chapter 13.2 of the ABP manual gives detailed instructions on the use of TRACES in case of intra-EU trade of PAP including the obligatory notification back to the place of origin. Chapter 14.3 gives detailed instructions on the use of TRACES in case of export of PAP containing ruminant protein. There is no instruction on the requirement for TRACES n

The audit team noted that, although guidance/instructions (see finding 22) were established to this effect by the competent authorities, arrivals of consignments of PAP were not systematically confirmed by the German competent authorities to the competent authorities of the Member State of origin by means of TRACES, contrary to Article 48(3) of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009. In 2017 and in 2018, around 23% and 30%, respectively, of such arrivals were not notified back.

Inadequate checks on the implementation of requirements concerning confirmation of TRACES notifications of intra-EU trade of PAP and OF/SI negatively affect the reliability of the flow of information on the intra-EU trade of such products.

The federal competent authority confirmed that intra-EU trade of consignments OF/SI containing PAP and/or MBM must be notified in TRACES, based on Article 48(3) of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009. In one Land visited, the competent authority stated that this requirement was not clear for them and they started to implement it only recently. In 2018, the majority of consignments of OF/SI containing PAP traded to other Member States were notified in TRACES. 5.2.3 Exports and imports of PAP

Considering the high number of missing confirmations on the arrival of consignments containing ruminant PAP from points of exit in Germany and in other Member States and the lack of control mechanisms in PAP processing plants to verify that the confirmation of the seal check at the point of exit had been received through TRACES, the German competent authorities could not always ensure that the channelling 14 procedure for export of PAP containing ruminant protein is adequately implemented. 6 OVERALL CONCLUSIONS The structure of the official control system and the planning of official controls along the chain of production and trade of PAP provides a good basis for implementation of official

The audit team visited a paper trader (see finding 10). The trader started its business in 2008 and it was registered based on Article 23 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009 in December 2016. In 2018, the arrival to the BIP of approximately 10% of the export consignments containing PAP with ruminant protein traded by the operator was not confirmed in TRACES and no information was available on the seal check, contrary to the requirements of Section E, Chapter V, Annex IV to Regulation (EC) No 999/2001. Local official controls had not detected this problem during the last official inspection in January 2019. The audit team reviewed the documentation provided by the operator (invoice, bill of loadi

The audit team identified several systematic shortcomings relating to TRACES notifications of consignments containing ruminant PAP intended for export from Germany to third countries and to the official controls in this regard: 11 Contrary to the requirements of fourth sentence of point 1(c) of Section E, Chapter V, of Annex IV to Regulation (EC) No 999/2001, the arrival of significant numbers of consignments intended for export at the point of exit notified in TRACES was not confirmed by the relevant BIP in Germany. In cases where the consignments were intended for export via another Member State and the authorities of the exit point did not confirm the arrival of these consignments at thei

In 2018, 14 Category 3 export consignments were notified in TRACES as Category 1 and Category 2 products. The competent authority had identified these mistakes although the TRACES notifications were only corrected during the audit.

Inadequate implementation of EU requirements concerning transmission of information to the competent authority of the Member State of origin or destination via TRACES relating to intra-EU trade of PAP undermines the reliability of information on the intra- EU trade of such products.

The audit team noted that, contrary to the requirements of Article 48 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009, the NVWA does not systematically confirm the arrival of consignment of PAP to competent authorities of the Member State of origin by means of TRACES. The system of checks in place is based on random selection of certain consignments in TRACES and a cross-check of these data on the spot. Only 10% of required confirmations took place in recent years. The frequency of confirmation to the place of origin did however increase to 20% in 2019 (see also finding 20).

Inadequate implementation of EU requirements concerning transmission of information to the competent authority of the Member State of origin or destination via TRACES relating to intra-EU trade of PAP undermines the reliability of information on the intra- EU trade of such products.

The competent authority stated that trade of consignments of OF/SI containing PAP and/or MBM is not notified in TRACES. This is not in line with Article 48(3) of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009. 5.2.3 Exports and imports of PAP

The lack of an adequate control mechanism in place to verify at the point of exit that all consignments of ruminant PAP exported from the Netherlands and other EU Member States have actually left the EU territory undermines the effectiveness of official controls in place. 6 OVERALL CONCLUSIONS As regards implementation of official controls requirements regarding the hygiene, traceability and the trade of PAP in the Netherlands, the overall picture is mixed. On the positive side, the system of official controls is underpinned by comprehensive establishment listing, well-managed cooperation and communication within the competent authority, and comprehensive instructions and guidance for inspec

Checks on exports of consignments of ruminant PAP via the port of Rotterdam are is carried out in accordance with the internal instructions of the NVWA. The competent authority stated that there are two types of official controls on exported consignments from the Netherlands, namely administrative and physical controls. Administrative checks on consignments with the origin in the Netherlands are carried out in the processing plants, including check of data in TRACES. Following the pre-notification via e-mail the local inspectors can carry out a random check of the containers at the point of exit. However, the audit team noted that the pre-notification via e-mail from the operator to the comp

Physical controls (seal checks) are carried out at an inspection centre of the BIP Rotterdam approved for import of liquid fats, oils and fish oils at Maastank B.V. No seal checks are carried out on consignments with origin in other Member States (Belgium, United Kingdom). This is not in line with point 1 of section E of Chapter V of Annex IV to Regulation (EC) No 999/2001. As regards consignments from Ireland, the competent authority stated that these consignments are only being transhipped in the port of Rotterdam.

The NVWA inspectors who do not have access to TRACES carry out seal checks on a certain proportion of consignments intended for export. There is no procedure in place to require that the competent authority responsible for the exit point (border inspection 10 post) informs via TRACES the competent authorities of the processing plants about the arrival of the consignment at the exit point and such notifications are not made by the inspectors. This is not in line with point (c) of section E of Chapter 5 of Annex IV to Regulation (EC) No 999/2001.

However, problems identified regarding operators' validation of method 7 in the 11 processing plants and the official assessments thereof, undermine confidence in the reliability of the results of official controls on this aspect of PAP production.

Three processing plants visited during the audit use processing method 7, which had been authorised by the competent authority. In one processing plant, during the 30 day validation period microbiological samples had been taken (Salmonella, Enterobacteriaceae, Clostridium perfringens) by the operator. The audit team noted that the sampling frequency and laboratory results were in compliance with EU legislation.

In another processing plant visited, the validation report provided by the operator to the competent authority at the time of validation did not contain all of the processing 8 parameters required by point G 2, Chapter III, of Annex IV to Regulation (EU) 142/2011. The competent authority had not noticed this shortcoming.

The process for granting approval ensures that insect PAP placed on the market complies with microbiological safety criteria, but was insufficiently robust as regards the assessment of the validation of the processing method and of the HACCP-based procedures; this however did not affect the safety of the product.

The audit team noted that two of the operators visited had received approval for using processing method 7 in a continuous system, however: a. One operator, despite being approved for processing in a continuous system, had carried out validation for the processing method in a batch system with single loads of material ranging from 80 to 120 kg while the targeted operational capacity of the system was up to two tonnes per hour. This way of processing was neither reflected in the operators HACCP-based procedures nor in the approval document issued by the authority; b. Neither of the two operators explained in the validation file the way they measured the feeding rate to demonstrate the minimum

Whilst an arrangement for listing and maintaining the list of approved ABP operators is in place, it is not publicly available and is not updated promptly. This limits the possibility of the public, authorities from other Member States and other operators to verify if a given operator placing its products on the market is approved or not. 5.3 IMPLEMENTATION OF OFFICIAL CONTROLS ON THE PRODUCTION, PLACING ON THE MARKET AND TRADE OF INSECT PAP AND INSECTS AS FEED

The DGAL website contains the link to the lists of ABP-approved and registered establishments and personnel responsible for official controls have access to these lists. The audit team noted that the link restricts external access and therefore, neither the public nor operators can access the lists. Moreover, the list for Category 3 ABP processing plants (relevant for this audit) held by the authority was outdated (October 2018) and, as a consequence, did not contain information on one of the two approved operators visited. This is not in line with Article 47 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009 requiring that Member States shall keep up-to-date lists of approved or registered establishments, pla

paragraph_text: The residue monitoring plan is generally implemented in accordance with planned arrangements. The inspectors met stated that the choice of the farms to be sampled was mainly based on the farm profile and the size and even information on the use of veterinary medicinal products available via VetStat could be consulted. In many cases, the inspectors stated that the samples on the farms would be taken randomly thus underestimating the importance of targeted sampling, which is not in line with the requirements laid down in points 2.1 and 2.3.2.1 of the Annex to Decision 98/179/EC). The audit team noted that the same establishments (e.g. farms and slaughterhouses) had been sampled for several substance groups on the same day, in some cases even for the same substances. In some cases, this was because the number of samples to be taken was higher than the number of establishments to be sampled. However, in other cases, although the number of samples was limited and much smaller that the number of establishments to sample, several samples were taken from the same establishment. This contradicts the DVFA's own sampling procedure and is not in line with the sampling strategy and targeting criteria laid down in point 2.1, 2.2, 2.3.2 and 2.3.3 of the Annex to Decision 98/179/E

Other residue monitoring programmes Legal Requirements Articles 9 and 11 of Directive 96/23/EC; Articles 8 and 10 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Findings

Although instructions and documents seen by the audit team unambiguously require official samples to be sealed, the audit team observed a number of cases where no official sealing had been performed, or performed in a way not ensuring the custody chain and such samples (e.g. from small slaughterhouses) had been kept/transported by a third party service provider. Moreover, during reception of the samples by the laboratories no sufficient control of the seals was carried out and non-sealed samples were accepted and processed. Thus, the requirements laid down in point 2.6 of the Annex to Decision 98/179/EC are not met7. This shortcoming was also observed during the 2010 audit.

paragraph_text: The follow-up of non-compliant test results largely meets EU requirements but its effectiveness is reduced by delays in communicating the results after testing, and sometimes incomplete investigation (in cases where feed could be the origin).

Veterinary medicinal products 5.3.1. Competent authorities

paragraph_text: The standard of record-keeping of treatments on farms was not in line with EU requirements, with the potential consequence of an increased risk of placing on the market animal products within the withdrawal periods. In the event that such violations would occur, the incompleteness of the records hampers the effectiveness of any follow-up investigations.

label_heading: Conclusions on official controls of FBOs providing or using FIA
paragraph_text: Official controls at FIA users' level are lacking in completeness and depth resulting in an insufficient verification of the compliance with FIA legislation. The absence of specific guidance or instructions creates inconsistencies in the approach followed by the inspectors (i.e. omission to ask for the recipe of the product being examined in relation to FIA used, define the product category and examine the specifications of all the raw materials used in the production of a that product). Adding to that, the limited hands-on experience of the inspectors leads to the oversight of certain issues regarding FIA during such controls. 16 78. Adequate enforcement measures are in place and used when

There is no common checklist or guidance at national level to control FBOs regarding FIA use, hence the local authorities using different approaches for these controls (documents to be requested, aspects to be covered, controlling FIA either during inspection or audit). In one of the Regions visited, the local authorities prepared a detailed checklist which acts as guidance for those controls. In the other Region, officials are advised to use a checklist prepared for the controls of FIA in approved establishments handling food of animal origin, also in controls at registered establishments. The depth of the controls also depends on the expertise and knowledge of the individual inspectors. Di

Regarding the FIA users, local authorities in the first Region visited explained that they have recently prepared a pilot checklist which will allow them to cover the aspects not covered to date. The audit team noted that, since this is a relatively new development, inspectors do not follow a structured approach, and sometimes rely solely on the information provided by the FBOs. Some of the elements that the inspectors omitted to examine were: the specifications of raw materials for possible presence of FIA, the recipe of the product examined (which should be the starting point of such controls), the identification of the correct food category; in addition, no requests were made for addition

With regard to FIA users, as indicated at regional level, there is no specific checklist for registered establishments. The approach followed by the inspectors during controls of FIA users was, in the majority of the cases, not consistent (as to what, when and how to 10 check) and not well structured. Some of the inspections were detailed and complete (checking specific requirement for labelling, knowledge of Aluminium-lakes requirements for colours) whereas in others certain elements were not addressed.

Some of the omissions observed by the audit team were: absence of checks of the specifications of the different ingredients to see if some additives could be present, and which of these additives could have a technological function in the final product; failure to note that the specifications regarding purity criteria were incomplete; and conduct of calculations using the weight of the intermediate product (dough) and not of the final product, as appropriate. Nevertheless, when asked by the audit team, in all cases the inspectors were able to re-evaluate or seek for more information for those aspects.

In the second Region visited the audit team was informed that inspectors cover the topic of FIA at FIA users' level during audits. Only in one case the inspectors confirmed that they would start using the dedicated checklist for approved establishments, also for registered establishments as recommended by the regional authority.

The Animal Health and Welfare Division (AHWD) of the VS is responsible for aquaculture farms (animal health issues).

The audit team noted that: The checklists for aquaculture farms are restricted to animal health issues to the exclusion of public health issues. The vessel checklist in use (form for the unloading of fishery products) focusses on the general hygiene and organoleptic characteristics of fishery products at the time of unloading and onward transport. It does not make reference to the detailed vessel requirements laid down in Section VII, Chapter 1 of Annex III to Regulation (EC) No 853/2004. This procedure is used by the officials when determining the frequency of inspections. In practice, official controls are carried out twice/year but sometimes more frequently, if the risk assessment requires this. Larger vessels (i.e. more than 12 meters in length and fishing for more than eight hours) are now inspected annually (previously up to four times per year) and there is a proposal (not yet adopted) to inspect RVs once every four years. Any horse entering the country as part of intra-community trade is covered by a health certificate and is registered in TRACES. It must be registered in the CBC within 30 days and in any case before any change in keeper. Where no health certificate can be submitted to the CBC at the time of the registration request or where the health certificate is non-compliant, an approved veterinarian must perform a clinical examination of the animal and a blood sample is taken to test for the absence of specific diseases, such as Infectious anemia at the keeper's expense. label_heading: Conclusions on organisation of official controls
paragraph_text: Official controls are planned on the basis of the risk categorisation of FBOs, which does not give the necessary weight to the key elements supporting the categorisation. As a consequence, the frequency of controls and follow-up of previously detected non- conformities may be not appropriate.

Risk classification is determined by DGAL by the application of a formula which comprises the outcome of the last inspection and the volume, type and target of production; the reliability of the FBOs, in performing their own-checks and informing the CAs of any real or potential risk, is not weighted appropriately in this formula. label_heading: Conclusions on official controls on the production of RTE foods
paragraph_text: Both CAs have put in place a system of routine risk-based official controls over production of RTE foods, supported by procedures and a comprehensive network of accredited laboratories under national coordination. Inspections, official sampling and in the Cataluña also audits cover relevant aspects of the legislation. The procedures for organisation of controls are currently under review in Navarra for further fine-tuning the risk determination for the RTE sector, for deciding the frequency for controls over FBOs HACCP based procedures, currently limited, and specific sector requirements and for starting to implement audits of FBOs' procedures and practices.

label_heading: Conclusions on official controls on the production of RTE foods
paragraph_text: The controls cover satisfactorily a range of aspects of the "Hygiene Package", although there is scope for improvement in the controls over FBO's measures for prevention of cross-contamination and verification within the HACCP-based procedures, including the requirements of Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005 and of the EURL guidelines. The CAs' ability to detect relevant non-compliances and require adequate corrective actions is hindered by the fact that the control focus does not or not necessarily target (all) the areas relevant for food safety, whether by design or at the time of their implementation, and by some gaps in the knowledge of control staff.

The CAs met reported certain human resources challenges over recent years, which in some cases - together with organisational changes, information technology (IT) systems changes and resources allocation - were highlighted by the CAs met as the cause for reduced implementation of certain controls (e.g. on FBOs HACCP based procedures in Navarra, and supervisory controls in both regions visited).

However, some recommendations dating from 2015 such as putting in place audits of FBOs and an internal (CA) verification/supervisory system had not been closed to date. This is not in line with Article 4, Paragraph 6 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. The ACCA took some actions to address them, though limited for the RTE sector. The CA cited IT - and staffing issues (see paragraph 14), but indicated that these recommendations would be addressed this year.

In Navarra, the risk-based criteria are used for establishing the frequency for general hygiene controls for new FBOs and new activities. For other cases, the frequency is every five years. The risk- based criteria are not used for establishing the frequency of controls over FBOs own controls including HACCP- based procedures, nor for controls on specific sector requirements (e.g. raw milk criteria). In Cataluña, the frequency of all types of controls is established on a risk basis.

In Navarra, CAs are required to carry out controls over FBOs HACCP-based procedures at approval, for expansion of activity, and in the case of alerts. Individual inspectors decide when to carry out controls on specific sector requirements. In the dairy establishment visited in Navarra the last control for specific requirements was carried out in 2014. In the same establishment, the last control related to FBOs HACCP- based procedures took place at the time of approval (in 2007) despite expansion works and changes in production.

The CA prioritisation of the controls for an FBO with multiple-activities and more establishments with the same approval (in Cataluña) did not allow an adequate focus on the risk areas. Consequently, the high-risk area visited by the audit team was not subject to recent controls. This prevented the CA from detecting several non-compliances noted during the audit team's visit, some of them long-standing. 4.4.1.2 Procedures for official controls

Each CA has procedures and instructions for staff performing official controls that apply to RTE food production. To the extent assessed by the audit team, these procedures are facilitating the official controls and are in general known and used by the staff met during this audit. The inspectors met considered them as supportive to their work. The procedures cover inspections and sampling, and in Cataluña also audits. Navarra does not have procedures for audits of FBOs' practices and procedures as required by Article 4, Paragraph 3 of Regulation (EC) No 854/2004.

In Navarra the procedures are under review to ensure that a frequency for certain controls (e.g. on routine controls for FBOs HACCP based procedures and on sector 13 specific requirements) and for the use of related checklists is defined. Certain aspects (e.g. some provisions of Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005, the use of identification marks) that are mandatory for official controls, were not included in the checklists. This led to a lack of related controls. The regional CA undertook to include them during the revision of the checklists.

The CAs produce reports on the official controls carried out. In line with Article 9 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, these reports include a description of the purpose of official controls, the methods applied, the results obtained and action to be taken by the FBO concerned. The FBOs receive a copy of the report. The audit team noted, in some of the reports in both AC, limited evidence that all aspects included in the scope of the control were covered, as required in the ACCAs control procedures. 4.4.1.3 Scope/coverage of official controls

Official controls are performed in Programmes that are grouped together in blocks. The following Programmes, particularly relevant for the scope of this audit, and the related implementation data provided by the CCA are summarised below: a. Programme 1 - general control of food establishments - include hygiene inspections. The MANCP data indicate that this Programme is applied yearly in all ACs and that the ACCAs implemented approximately 85% of the 435 809 scheduled controls under this Programme for the country in 2017 and detected non-compliances in 26 % of these controls. b. In establishments (excluding retail) in the meat, dairy, fishery and composite products/prepared dishes sectors - i

Challenges were identified in particular in relation to aspects of training, efficient cooperation and coordination in practice, and the verification of effectiveness of controls. These challenges, together with delays in effectively addressing audit findings, may and sometimes do impact on the controls over the production of RTE foods. 4.3 REGISTRATION/APPROVAL OF FBOS Legal requirements Article 6 of Regulation (EC) No 852/2004, Article 4 of Regulation (EC) No 853/2004, Article 3 of Regulation (EC) No 854/2004 and Article 31 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. 9 Findings

While an overall good number of inspectors receive yearly relevant training, there are differences between the AC in the array of training topics offered to their staff, and in the percentage of inspectors participating to training. Limited training was offered for controls over microbiological criteria in some AC.

The official control staff met was in general trained and knowledgeable for some parts of their work within the scope of this audit. The audit team identified training needs, mainly in relation to: a. the approval of establishments in Cataluña (see paragraphs 31-35). A new training session on this topic was ongoing at the time of the audit; 7 b. the focus and depth of the controls, and the assessment of the flexibility options and HACCP-based procedures implemented by FBOs, including compliance with Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005 in both AC visited (see paragraphs 53-62, 66, 88.e, f and g); c. the evaluation of the gravity of certain non-compliances in both AC and taking the required actions i

The findings above suggest that while a wide range of training is offered to staff, the systems in place for identifying and addressing training needs do not adequately capture the individual needs that arise, in particular considering the wide area of official controls over production of RTE food, in order to ensure that staff is kept up-to date in their area of competence as required by Article 6 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

The procedure for adding new approved activities in Cataluña emphasised that the official controls should not verify FBOs HACCP based procedures, but focus on infrastructure. The ACCA explained that this approach was intended for particular situations. However, its wording led to some confusion amongst control staff on the requirements in the case reviewed by the audit team. The ACCA swiftly modified this procedure during the audit and provided examples of reports of approval visits demonstrating that the approval visits check FBOs' compliance with all relevant requirements of the applicable legislation.

These reports indicated delays of days or months for the approval visits in five out of eight cases (e.g. nine months conditional approval; five months between the first and second approval visit). The district team carrying out controls in the newly approved 10 establishment visited during the audit considered that six months between the first and second approval visit complies with the rules in place. These examples are contrary to the provisions of Article 31, paragraph 2(d) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, and of the regional procedures.

In the case of a recent approval assessed by the audit team, the district CA evaluated FBOs HACCP-based procedure solely during the visit for full approval contrary to the regional procedures. The duration of the full approval visit did not allow a thorough check of FBOs HACCP-based procedures. Consequently, the inspector had not evaluated certain elements thereof, like its validation and verification, as required by the regional procedures.

The CA acknowledged that the extent to which FBO's own procedures are evaluated depends on the background of the inspectors, and some aspects may be overlooked. The inspectors met had not received training in relation to the approval of establishments. A new training session on this topic was ongoing at the time of the audit.

The audit team noted during another visit that more establishments of the same group, located over a few km radius, with public roads between them, have the same approval number. The CCA clarified this is not in line with the legislation. The ACCA indicated this as a particular case due to historical reasons and that work was ongoing to address it. The ACCA started an investigation during the audit to confirm that this was not the case with other establishments in the AC.

The inspectors were in general able to detect non-compliances during the visits carried out as part of the current audit, in particular as regards the general hygiene requirements. While several aspects were adequately covered by the official controls, some aspects were missed and/or not addressed: a. In three establishments (two dairies and a fishery) CA challenges concerning the implementation of flexibility measures led to acceptance of cross-flows in the absence of adequate mitigating measures, as well as to under-detection of some unhygienic practices (e.g. in relation to unpacking, cleaning during production) with potential for cross contamination; b. In one of these establishments (in

The CAs met required the FBOs to take corrective action once they understood the potential impact on the safety of the product and provided the audit team with official control reports of swift follow-up controls. In an establishment producing RTE fishery involved in several alerts in another AC, not visited by the audit team, the official control report immediately prior to the alert suggested a fully compliant FBO. The control reports related to the alerts indicate several non-compliances including structural, hygiene, temperature controls and shelf-life studies. The ACCA reported to have replaced the inspector in the meantime (see paragraph 80).

The approach to controls over FBOs HACCP-based procedures differs between the ACCAs. In Navarra, these controls are comprehensive at the time of approval (except for validation and verification of HACCP based procedures), but they are limited afterwards (see paragraphs 49 and 51d). In Cataluña these controls are part of the routine controls carried out within the risk-based frequency, but limited as regards certain elements of FBOs' HACCP-based procedures. In particular: 15 a. in a multi-activity establishment, FBOs' practical implementation of the critical control point cooking validation and the reprocessing activity had not been part of CA controls for one of the production lines consider

The official controls over FBOs' compliance with Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005 are part of Programmes 1 and 2. In Cataluña, these controls are part of the routine risk-based controls. In Navarra, these controls check if the FBOs implement the sampling plans described in their HACCP based procedures (evaluated before starting operation). Nonetheless, FBOs further changed the procedures after approval, as noted in the establishments visited, and the CA did not evaluate if the changes ensure continued compliance with the above Regulation.

In the cases assessed by the audit team, the CAs checked whether FBOs implement their sampling and testing plans for food safety criteria. In one case, the CA accepted the limit of 100cfu/g Listeria monocytogenes at the end of production for RTE sushi with a shelf- life of five days, in the absence of adequate FBO demonstration that this value would not be exceeded throughout the shelf-life of the product. This is not in line with Chapter 1, Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005. The CA acknowledged challenges with the controls over FBOs' compliance with this Regulation and the lack of related training.

As regards process hygiene criteria, the controls had not been satisfactory in one of the three cases evaluated by the audit team. The CA considered the process hygiene criteria in Chapter 2, Annex II of Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005 as a FBO's choice and did not require the FBO to include in their procedures the compliance limits for these criteria and the action to be taken in case of non-compliance, as required by Article 7 of Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005.

The controls as regards the number of sampling units were in most cases satisfactory. In the relatively recently approved establishment visited, the CA accepted the FBO's reduction of sampling units from five to one in the absence of historical documentation proving effective HACCP-based procedures, contrary to the requirements of Article 5.3 of Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005. FBOs' testing methods had not been subject to official controls in the cases assessed. This is not required by the procedures in Navarra.

FBOs' shelf-life studies for RTE food able to support the growth of Listeria are required to be verified by the CAs routinely in Cataluña, but not in Navarra. The cases assessed by the audit team, both in Cataluña and in Comunidad Valenciana, revealed that in 16 general the CA asks for FBO shelf-life studies for Listeria monocytogenes or checks them thoroughly at the time of alerts, but not beforehand or routinely otherwise.

The provisions of the EURL Guidance on sampling the food processing area and equipment for the detection of Listeria monocytogenes and of the EURL Technical Guidance Document for conducting shelf-life studies on Listeria monocytogenes in RTE foods were in general not known, and not taken into account by CAs met which had not dealt with Listeria alerts.

Consequently, CA accepted that FBOs sampling only after cleaning and disinfection, which makes the detection of the pathogen difficult leading to a false sense of security. In one case where the CA evaluated the FBOs studies as satisfactory, the studies did not demonstrate that the food safety criteria applicable throughout the shelf-life of the products can be met under reasonably foreseeable conditions of distribution, storage and use as required by Article 3 of Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005. Also, the CA did not detect the lack of shelf-life studies for some product classes. In other cases, the CA accepted shelf-life studies based solely on organoleptic properties.

The national measures in place support both FBOs in addressing the microbiological hazards and control the production process of RTE foods, as well as CAs in performing the related official controls. Advice for consumers aiming to prevent food borne outbreaks is also available. There is scope for reviewing the regional measures to support a harmonised and correct implementation by the dairy industry of the measures for verifying the effectiveness of pasteurisation and related official controls.

paragraph_text: In those cases where the potential risk associated with non-compliances considered as "minor" is not adequately assessed, this impacts on both the necessary requests for corrective action, as well as on the timeliness of their implementation. The action in case of non-compliance differs between the regions visited and the action in relation to the products is in general limited to instances of confirmed non-compliant official test results. 5 In their comments to the draft report the CA noted that under the procedures corrective measures must always be taken in case of non-compliance, whether minor, serious or very serious. The actions taken in the cases of alerts related to RTE food assessed by the audit team showed a mixed picture. In Navarra, the CA carried out a swift visit on-the-spot and had verified and documented, in subsequent visits, a rapid tracing back, recall and destruction of the merchandise. Contrary to the national procedure for alerts, an official control to ascertain that the measures put in place by the FBO adequately address the cause(s) and prevent its(their) reoccurrence, does not take place. The new information received resulted in the CA questioning the FBO's food safety management system, called for more thorough official controls and CA requests for adequate shelf-life studies. Nonetheless, the CA had accepted that the FBO uses Salmonella-positive ingredients, in the absence of an indication of the level of contamination, provided 15 samples of the final products were negative. According to the FBO demonstration made available to the CA, the respective production process ensures one log reduction.

The ACCA stated the approach taken by the district CA in managing the RASFF alert above is not the routine one. In addition, following the audit team's visit, the CA requested the FBO to review their HACCP based procedures and to demonstrate that the processing is eliminating the hazard in question as required by Article 7 of Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005.

The action taken by the CA in Comunidad Valenciana in relation to several alerts concerning the same establishment producing RTE fishery products revealed also difficulties in ensuring that the contaminated foods are traced and recalled in a timely fashion, and that the actions put in place by the FBOs prevent recurrence. a. Some of the CA on-the-spot visits took place with one and two weeks delay that could not be justified. label_heading: Conclusions on official controls on the production of RTE foods
paragraph_text: The controls cover satisfactorily a range of aspects of the "Hygiene Package", although there is scope for improvement in the controls over FBO's measures for prevention of cross-contamination and verification within the HACCP-based procedures, including the requirements of Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005 and of the EURL guidelines. The CAs' ability to detect relevant non-compliances and require adequate corrective actions is hindered by the fact that the control focus does not or not necessarily target (all) the areas relevant for food safety, whether by design or at the time of their implementation, and by some gaps in the knowledge of control staff.

The provisions of the EURL Guidance on sampling the food processing area and equipment for the detection of Listeria monocytogenes and of the EURL Technical Guidance Document for conducting shelf-life studies on Listeria monocytogenes in RTE foods were in general not known, and not taken into account by CAs met which had not dealt with Listeria alerts.

Consequently, CA accepted that FBOs sampling only after cleaning and disinfection, which makes the detection of the pathogen difficult leading to a false sense of security. In one case where the CA evaluated the FBOs studies as satisfactory, the studies did not demonstrate that the food safety criteria applicable throughout the shelf-life of the products can be met under reasonably foreseeable conditions of distribution, storage and use as required by Article 3 of Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005. Also, the CA did not detect the lack of shelf-life studies for some product classes. In other cases, the CA accepted shelf-life studies based solely on organoleptic properties.

The CAs of the AC Valencia decided to check the possible presence of Xf with a grid- based survey beyond the borders of the DA of 5 km radius, established in 2017. The 10km area surrounding the borders of the BZ was divided into 1km x 1km grid. In 2018, the majority of the squares were visually inspected and the symptomatic plants were sampled. This surveillance resulted in 18 positives, each of those was found close to the border of the BZ established after the 2017 surveys.

Although numerous host plants were removed in the IZs established in 2017, due to the partial and delayed removal of the positives and the host plants in their 100m vicinity, the conditions remained favourable for the spread of the disease within and from the DA. paragraph_text: Both RPSs carry out intensive surveillance for the detection of new outbreaks of A. bungii on Prunus plants. However, the exclusion of Prunus cerasifera cv. pissardii from the systematic inspections is based mainly on observations and not on justified scientific evidence.

Despite a legal requirement and an intensive awareness campaign since 2015, only a limited number of non-commercial holdings are registered which makes it difficult for the authorities to detect promptly the disease and to control its spread. The proactive measures taken by the authorities to depopulate backyard holdings in high-risk areas are likely to significantly reduce the risk of disease introduction and spread. However, there is uncertainty about how this limitation of the risk will be maintained when the defined period for the non-population expires, and about how the authorities will monitor these holdings in particular when they are going to restock.

Private registered veterinarians are complicit in maintaining the unregistered pig population as they do not actively support the registration of non-commercial holdings but rather continue to provide service to unregistered holdings.

Despite the recent efforts to reduce the number of non-commercial holdings and to bring them into compliance with biosecurity requirements, it is very likely that there still exits a considerable number of unregistered backyard holdings in the country. The absence of reliable data on the location and movement of pigs within the non-commercial sector means that it is often not possible to trace animals that could have carried ASF virus to or from outbreak holdings. It also means that it is difficult for the veterinary authorities to enforce the prohibition to dispatch live pigs originating from the areas included in the Part III territory in the case of non-commercial holdings. label_heading: Conclusions on monitoring and sampling scheme
paragraph_text: The FBO monitoring and sampling schemes are implemented in line with the approved SNCPs. The central level has tools to monitor and continuously review the progress of the programmes, including official actions. However, some RVAs did not fully respect the planned official sampling frequency in the last two years, in particular for laying hens and broilers.

However for official samples the data and results since 2016 show that not all holdings with more than 1,000 birds were sampled and tested for Salmonella (see tables under Point 5 in Annex 2) contrary to the requirement in point 2.1 of the Annex to Regulation (EC) No 517/2011. According to the SVA analysis, in 2017 only 56 out of 71 eligible holdings were officially sampled. This issue was discussed in one RVA visited where in 2017 no official sample was taken, and in 2018 only some eligible holdings were officially sampled; in that period the RVA diverted available resources to other more urgent issues.

The audit team reviewed results since 2016 (see tables under Point 6 in Annex 2) and in general the number of holdings officially sampled and tested for Salmonella reached the targets in the SNCP. However, in 2018 in two of the 14 regions the RVA had not reached that target (sample 10% of broiler holdings); in one region only two holdings were tested instead of five; in another region instead of two none were officially sampled. The CCA was aware of this deficiency, but since the overall number of planned official samples for the whole country had already been achieved it instructed the RVA not to take the samples.

Since 2016, confirmatory sampling was carried out in 15 of 21 laying flocks that had FBO samples with results positive for Salmonella. Only two confirmatory samples returned positive for relevant Salmonella serotypes with the remaining 13 reported as negative. The impact on Salmonella prevalence rate in laying hens is that if the FBO positive results had been included (instead of discarded after the confirmatory sampling 8 returned negative for 13 out of 15 flocks) in 2016 the prevalence rate in Czech Republic would go above the 2% EU target.

For confirmatory sampling the CA is required (point 2.2 of the Annex to Regulation (EC) No 517/2011) to carry out further checks namely by laboratory tests or documentary checks to ensure that the results are not affected by the use of antimicrobials. The RVAs did not take additional samples of birds for antimicrobial residues or bacterial growth inhibitors in any of the confirmatory samplings reviewed. Instead in all cases they relied on the results of documentary checks on the holdings - verification of treatment records - that showed no antimicrobial treatment of birds. Although EU legislation allows using documentary checks the use and results from laboratory tests can significantly cont

Test results provided by the CA for 2018 show that when comparing results of official sampling with FBO sampling,, the detection rate was approximately 15 times higher from official samples,of 3.48% (3 of 86 tests) versus 0.22% (1 of 453 tests). The CCA accredits the higher prevalence in official samples to the higher detection sensitivity of official sampling (additional faecal sample taken). The CCA had decided not to replace one faecal sample or one pair of boot swabs with a dust sample as allowed in point 2.2.2. of the Annex to Regulation (EC) No 517/2011; inclusion of dust in the official sampling would provide the CA with a more sound basis to establish if the difference in detection r

Test results for 2018, show a Salmonella positive detection rate approximately five times higher than official samples of 8.1% (4 of 36 tests) versus 1.6% (75 of 4 667 tests) from FBO samples. The CA has been aware of this difference in detection rates for several years but cannot identify a reason. To some extent this difference may be explained by the selection of broiler holdings with a high risk for Salmonella in official controls (holdings with recurrence of Salmonella).

label_heading: Conclusions on welfare of the animals arriving at the port
paragraph_text: Port inspectors are aware of the official controls they are required to do, but the absence of any records for these checks and for any subsequent action that might have been taken does not make it possible to verify whether they were in fact performed, their quality or 5 effectiveness.

label_heading: Conclusions on welfare of animals during sea transport
paragraph_text: The insufficient information and instructions for port inspectors together with the absence of suitably qualified staff for assessing technical requirements for livestock vessels translates into a poor evaluation of technical requirements (such as air changes per hour on each deck of a livestock vessel, and the equipment used for watering and drainage systems on board a livestock vessel) during the approval and inspection before 8 loading. Therefore, official controls do no contribute to minimise the animal welfare risk linked to facilities and equipment.

label_heading: Conclusions on welfare of animals during sea transport
paragraph_text: Procedures include the relevant legal requirements but do not provide instructions for CSVFSD official veterinarians and port inspectors on how to verify these requirements as part of a practical inspection of a livestock vessel. Inspections of livestock vessels are therefore dependant on the experience of the inspectors, but not all requirements are adequately verified, which could have major implications for animal welfare during sea journeys.

The documented procedure for the inspection of a livestock vessel prior to approval is substantially a checklist which is part of Order 16/2010. This checklist covers all points included under Section 1 of Chapter IV of Annex I to the Regulation, with the exception of drainage systems (Point 5).

The documented procedure for the inspection of a livestock vessel prior to loading animals is substantially in the form of another checklist: As already described in report 2015/7425, this checklist includes instructions to calculate and record the minimum required quantities of water and feed and available stocking density on board the vessel in order to verify compliance with these three requirements (see also paragraph 27). This checklist was last modified after July 2018 in response to the follow-up action by the Commission's auditing services on a vessel which was seen during the audit to Slovenia to evaluate animal welfare during transport to non-EU countries (report DG(SANTE)2018-6449
ANSVSA is drafting a checklist for the inspection of vehicles arriving at the port. This document has not been finalised yet. 5.2 TRANSPORT CONDITIONS ON ARRIVAL AT THE PORT

CSVFSD official veterinarians are responsible for inspecting and approving livestock vessels. Procedures require that the transporter applying for the approval of a vessel submits all "relevant documents": The official veterinarians were not sure what "relevant documents" they had to collect in order to verify compliance with each of the technical requirements of Section 1 of Chapter IV of Annex I to the Regulation. There is no guidance or pre- established list explaining what should be included in the "relevant documents". Only one of the application files reviewed by the audit team had supporting documents for all the technical requirements indicated in Section 1 of Chapter IV of Annex I t

Procedures for the approval of livestock vessels do not explain how to verify compliance with the specific technical requirements of the vessel, in particular ventilation, drainage and watering systems: All approval records indicated that the vessel had been checked for, and complied with, the minimum air changes per hour of forced ventilation systems in each deck, as required by Point 2 of Section 1 of Chapter IV of Annex I to the Regulation. There was however no documentation to support this decision. The official veterinarians could not explain how they calculated the ventilation capacity on each deck without this documentation. All approval records indicated that the vessel had been chec

All pre-loading checklists seen by the audit team indicated that the vessels inspected complied with the requirements of Section 1 of Chapter IV of Annex I to the Regulation, with the exception of the missing check for drainage systems (see also paragraph 1). The port inspectors were however unable to explain how they verify that certain systems and the relevant equipment (forced ventilation systems, drainage systems and pumps, alarms, back-up generators, etc.) are in good working order.

label_heading: Conclusions on welfare of the animals arriving at the port
paragraph_text: The fact that deficiencies that port inspectors declare they detect are not recorded in Traces, nor transmitted to the national contact point, results in systematic unreported non- compliances to the Member State of departure concerned which, consequently, cannot take the necessary action to correct these issues.
ANSVSA is drafting a checklist for the inspection of vehicles arriving at the port. This document has not been finalised yet. 5.2 TRANSPORT CONDITIONS ON ARRIVAL AT THE PORT

ANSVSA indicated that port inspectors check all livestock vehicles arriving at the ports but those checks are not being recorded. This is not in compliance with the requirements of Article 9(1) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

For vehicles which travel long road journeys before reaching the port, checks on journey logs include checks that a livestock vessel and a transporter for the sea journey have been identified. The port inspectors indicated that these are generally absent for those few journeys starting in Hungary (only 13 consignments in 2018). Although they are aware of these non-compliances, the port inspectors did not reported any non-compliance to their national contact point for informing the departing authority. Instead, they reported the results of the checks as 'satisfactory' in Traces.
