label_heading: Conclusions on organisation and implementation of official controls
paragraph_text: The VIS perform various controls regarding bovine identification, checks on the FCI and on hygiene requirements during slaughter, including AMI/PMI and record their findings in the CA's information systems. Regarding the AMI of bovine animals, the implementation of the central level instructions does not ensure the required (supervisory) presence of OV in the slaughterhouses at all times required by EU legislation. Similarly, the PMI of bovine animals is not performed at all times under the OV supervision in slaughterhouses slaughtering more than 1000 LVU per year.

In the second slaughterhouse reviewed, also slaughtering over 1000 LVU per year it was explained that it is possible that on certain days, the OV is not permanently present throughout the day. Therefore, it is possible that the OA can carry out the AMI of bovine animals which do not present any abnormalities and those animals to be slaughtered. This is not in line with Article 3 of Regulation (EU) 2019/624 which requires that this task must be carried out under the supervision of the OV (that is, with the OV present in the premises). Animals presenting abnormalities are detained by the OA and undergo a second-level AMI, performed by the OV. This issue regarding the absence of the OV during A

It was also explained by the CAs that in the specific case where an animal is obviously in distress when the OV is not present at the premises, the OA informs the OV as quickly as possible and directly makes an appropriate decision, which may be: the immediate slaughter of the animals fit for human consumption (for example, an animal which has just been injured either in the lairage or during transport and is obviously in distress), retaining the carcase and offal for inspection by the OV. This practice is not in line is with Article 3 of Regulation (EU) 2019/624; the emergency killing of the animals unfit for human consumption (for example, a sick animal in obvious distress).

The audit team was informed that at local level, the local organisation and the priorities defined by the departmental authority may explain why the AMI might be carried out by 19 an OA under the responsibility and not under the supervision of the OV as required by Article 3(1) of Regulation 2019/624.

Based on the information provided by the CCA for bovine slaughterhouses, the staff of the VIS is systematically present during slaughter. The OV is present for decisions linked to the PMI and systematically validates this decision by signing the slaughterhouse seizure certificates. If the OV needs to be absent, including in slaughterhouses slaughtering over 1000 LVU per year, carcasses suspected of presenting abnormalities during the PMI are detained by the OA to be inspected at a later stage by the OV (see paragraph 87).

One OV in charge of a slaughterhouse slaughtering over 1000 LVU per year stated that it is possible that the OV might not be present at all times during slaughter since he/she might be assigned to other tasks elsewhere, during this period the OV can be reached by phone if needed. This is not in line with the requirements of Article 7 of Regulation (EU) 2019/624 that requires that PMI must be carried out under the supervision of the OV in slaughterhouses slaughtering over 1000 LVU.

The OV can carry out the PMI of slaughtered animals or entrust part of this task to one or more OAs under his supervision. If it is not the OV who directly performs the PMI, the OA performs the PMI of the animals after slaughter (first level of PMI). The OA sorts the animals depending on whether or not they present abnormalities. Animals presenting abnormalities are retained. The abnormalities might be pathological lesions, abnormalities requiring further investigations or inspection (e.g. identification or FCI issues, known health risks etc.) by the OV either on the same day or early the next day. 21 Due to the lack of continued presence of the OV highlighted in the paragraph above this pro

label_heading: Conclusions on organisation and implementation of official controls
paragraph_text: There are procedures and guidelines in place for official staff for the relevant controls, which provide guidance on how to act in different scenarios regarding the handling of cull cows (i.e. emergency slaughter, identification of unfit animals for transport and/or slaughter). The controls system identifies relevant non-compliances, which are followed up satisfactorily. Yet, as already identified in a previous DG Health and Food Safety audit, bovine animals that have suffered an accident are transported to the slaughterhouses accompanied by a CVI, without all EU requirements being met.

The following are (non-exhaustive) examples of animals considered unfit for transport: serious open wound; animal suffering from a severe prolapse; animal unable to move by itself without suffering (example: dairy cow with spread legs); newborn whose navel has not healed; calves less than 10 days old, transported over 100 km; pregnant female ready to give birth (more than 90% gestation)/or having given birth less than a week before transport.

It was evident from the documentation reviewed by the audit team that bovine animals that had suffered an accident (including a non-open fracture) or had a non-serious prolapse were transported to the slaughterhouses accompanied by a CVI document signed by a private veterinarian, provided that they were able to move independently/unassisted. In the CVI the private veterinarian attested their capability of transfer, the fulfilment of the requirements of Council Regulation (EC) No 1/2005 and indicated which additional measures should be taken in order to ensure that no additional suffering is caused during transport. This practice is permissible under DGAL's relevant guidance document contrary

paragraph_text: The number of available official staff and the procedures in place for their deployment while on operation do not ensure in 880 poultry slaughterhouses (30 % of total national production) compliance with the requirements of Article 18(3) of Regulation (EU) 2019/627 regarding the presence of official staff, of Article 25(1) of Regulation (EU) 2019/627 regarding the practical arrangements of the PMI of poultry and the supervision requirements of Article 18(2) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 and of Articles 3(2) and 7(1)(a)(ii) of Regulation (EU) 2019/624. 5.5. Similarly to domestic ungulates, there are no provisions in place to carry out AMI for poultry at the holding of provenance, therefore the AMI must be carried out at the slaughterhouse by or under the supervision of the OV, in line with Article 18(2) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. The requirement that the OV is present during slaughter activities is implemented only in those poultry slaughterhouses slaughtering more than 15,000 tonnes per year (34 out of 914 slaughterhouses covering 70% of production).

In 17 slaughterhouses with an annual throughput between 10,000 and 15,000 tonnes the procedures in place require the permanent presence of at least one member of official staff (OV/OA) during slaughter activities with a daily supervisory visit by the OV in case not permanently present. In the remaining 78 slaughterhouses (with a capacity ranging from 300 to 10,000 tonnes per year), at least one member of official staff (OV/OA) is present for certain days each week. These arrangements in place do always ensure that the AMI/PMI is carried out under the supervision of the OV. In the low-capacity slaughterhouses, the VIS is not present throughout the slaughter activities and only visits the slaughterhouses with a minimum frequency of two visits per year while the slaughterhouse is in operation. Besides the AMI issue highlighted in paragraph 95 the current arrangements are not in line with Article 18(3)(c) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 which allows slaughterhouse staff to assist in the performance of official control tasks in poultry and lagomorphs slaughterhouses when the task is carried out in the presence of the OV or the OA and following their instructions.

When permanently present at the slaughterhouse or during visits/inspections, the OV or OA carries out a PMI, which includes an inspection of the viscera and body cavities of a representative sample of each flock and an inspection of the poultry declared unfit for consumption by the slaughterhouse staff. The latter is not in line with Article 25(1)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2019/627 according to which the OV/OA shall inspect the viscera and body cavities of a representative sample of each flock, on a daily basis. In France, the derogation of Article 25(2) of Regulation (EU) 2019/627 has not been applied to date.

paragraph_text: The SVFA issues instructions in the form of guidelines to OVs and other staff. Their official controls system has all the components required to operate along the whole food chain and to fulfil all the legal requirements. The Farm Animal Central Registry's database offers the required assurances in relation to identification and registration of bovine animals and provide

However, one of the sections of the instruction entitled "Guidelines for Veterinary Inspectors-Fresh Meat of Domestic Ungulates- Part 1, Ante-Mortem Inspection" describes the following: "Where the official veterinarian is not present at the slaughterhouse on receipt of an animal which has suffered an injury and suffers from pain or an animal which is excessively exhausted after transport and, therefore, delaying slaughter by carrying out ante-mortem inspection could cause further unnecessary suffering, the slaughterhouse operator may in exceptional cases slaughter/kill it without delay without ante mortem inspection, but must immediately inform the official veterinarian and submit to him the

This instruction is in contravention of Article 45(a) of Regulation (EU) 2019/627 and in contradiction with another SVFA guidance "Guidelines for Veterinary Inspectors-Fresh Meat of Domestic Ungulates- Part 3, Post-Mortem Inspection" which, in the section on decisions concerning meat, clearly states as the first reason for considering meat as unfit for human consumption when it `comes from animals which have not undergone ante- mortem inspection'.

label_heading: Conclusions on legislation and implementing measures
paragraph_text: National rules (Orders Nos 168/2014, 111/2008 and 34/2008) had provided national derogations for use of non-compliant raw cow milk, for direct sale of foodstuffs and for manufacture of traditional products. However, these have not been notified to the Commission and Member States, contrary to the provisions of Directive (EU) 2015/1535. 5.2 COMPETENT AUTHORITIES Legal requirements Articles 4 and 5 of, and Annex II to, Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Findings

The Order of NSVFSA No 111/2008 of 16 December 2008 lays down rules for the registration of food businesses engaged in direct sale to final consumers, and supply of foodstuffs of animal origin and non-animal origin to other retail establishments. This Order was not notified to the Commission and Member States, contrary to what is required by Directive (EU) 2015/1535 of the European Parliament and of the Council. It lays down some relevant requirements: a. Article 2 defines direct supply of "small quantities" of raw milk to final consumers or other retail operators as up to 300 l/day for raw cow milk and up to 100 l/day for raw milk originating from other species; b. Article 7 permits the sal

The Order of NSVFSA No 34 of 14 April 2008 lays down veterinary health and food safety rules for granting derogations to establishments producing foodstuffs with traditional characteristics. The order has not been notified through TRIS despite the fact that this notification is required under EU legislation. Derogations are possible for some requirements of Regulations (EC) No 852/2004 and (EC) No 853/2004 concerning floors, walls, ceilings, doors-windows-other openings, and measures and methods for cleaning and disinfecting rooms-equipment-tools. The County Sanitary Veterinary and Food Safety Directorates (CSVFSDs) are responsible for granting such derogations, having such businesses regist

The 2018-2020 MANCP is incomplete regarding official controls in the animal welfare area. The absence of animal welfare objectives together with the absence of information from regional authorities to the progress report make it impossible to 10 assess whether the authorities are directing their efforts effectively or efficiently.

Belgium's 2018-2020 Multi-annual national control plan (MANCP) describes the protocol signed between FASFC and the three regions on delegation of responsibilities on animal welfare, providing the general framework. The MANCP (Section 3.2.11.15.6) states that the competent regional authorities undertake to periodically provide a contribution to MANCP and to the MANCP annual progress report. The audit team noted that information on the planning regarding animal welfare checks was very general, and it did not include objectives for animal welfare for any of the three regions. The MANCP is available at: http://www.afsca.be/apropos/mancp/mancpbelge/default.asp.

The responsibilities for animal welfare at slaughter are clear, but Belgium has not ensured efficient and effective coordination between all authorities involved. This translates into suboptimal cooperation and insufficient sharing of information between the federal and regional competent authorities. The high dependence on the federal checks in the slaughterhouses is more relevant for the Walloon region, where the shortage of resources limits their activities. The checklists filled in by federal official veterinarians do not add much value to the official system. They systematically miss existing non-compliances and create administrative burden for regional authorities due to the way they a

The Flemish competent authority explained that, as FASFC is under the Federal competent authorities, it is difficult to cooperate without updating and improving the protocol signed with them. The Walloon competent authority agreed with that view and added that the non-optimal sharing of information with FASFC is mainly due to the institutional set up and they always try to achieve a good direct communication with the slaughterhouse official veterinarians.

The Flemish competent authority indicated that its Animal Welfare Unit has prepared new checklists and procedures. This is to prepare for the start of a new system where the Animal Welfare Unit would appoint directly private veterinarians to carry out inspections on animal welfare in slaughterhouses, in addition to the official veterinarians of the FASFC. This revision will take into account the non-compliances detected by veterinarians working in the slaughterhouse and prioritise the less compliant establishments for visits by the Animal Welfare Unit. The appointed private veterinarians will start at the end of October 2020. They will daily check animal welfare in every slaughterhouse for a

The Walloon competent authority indicated that the shortage of resources limits their activities and for the time being they depend on the FASFC checks in the slaughterhouses and informed the audit team that: Its new plan is that its Animal Welfare Unit will do three controls per year for large scale slaughterhouses and one for the others. They did not provide a starting date. It has recently produced a new checklist for their Animal Welfare Unit. In March 2020, based on the protocol signed with FASFC, it issued new instructions for the FASFC official veterinarians.

The absence of risk-based method for establishing the frequency for official controls does not allow the Flemish and Walloon competent authorities to set the frequency of their controls based on risk and to ensure the level of compliance expected in different situations. This decreases the efficiency of their official controls to target problematic establishments.

The measures that Brussels-Capital regional authority put in place in its red meat slaughterhouse paid off. They improved animal welfare, in particular during slaughter without stunning. The use of video surveillance by the operator and authorities proved useful to improve the welfare of animals and to enforce the legislation. The current arrangements where the officials can only review the video footage from the establishment is a lost opportunity for the authorities for e.g. keep their controls on the slaughterhouse during the Covid-19 restrictions.

In response to Recommendation 2 of audit report DG(SANTE) 2014-7057 - to take account of previous inspection results when establishing the risk basis for controls - the Belgian competent authorities provided in their action plan a summary of the system for controls in place after regionalisation, indicating that: Wallonia and Flanders analyse the reports of the FASFC official veterinarians to establish a benchmarking between slaughterhouses. That would allow the regions to prioritise certain slaughterhouses or specific items for their inspections.

The audit team noted that, for 2017, 2018 and 2019, there was no evidence that the analysis for benchmarking to prioritise between slaughterhouses had been carried out. The Flemish and Walloon authorities agreed that a systematic risk analysis had not been carried out in those years.

The slaughterhouse of Brussels-Capital region installed video cameras after the request from the regional competent authority following an animal welfare incident. The authority uses them (see paragraphs 26 to 28) to complement on-site inspections and to monitor critical points during slaughtering. The audit team noted that the regional competent authority officials have to review the recordings of the cameras on site. Due to the COVID-19 restrictions on on­site visits, they could not reach the frequency of video checks planned for the year. The animal welfare officer indicated that following the use of video footage, the staff performance, and the public image of the company have improved.

The Walloon competent authority has not yet fully addressed recommendation 1 of audit report DG(SANTE) 2014-7059, as it has not yet published the necessary legislation to approve the training programme, and it has therefore not fulfilled its responsibilities as designated competent authority.

Since 1 July 2014, the government delegated to its three regions the responsibility to organise and perform official controls and other official activities for the requirements on the welfare of animals. Since 1 January 2015, Flemish, Walloon and Brussels- Capital Regional governments fully took on this responsibility in their territories and were given competence to adopt their own legislation. Each Region has a separate inspection unit dedicated to animal welfare - the Animal Welfare Unit.

The audit team verified the actions taken to address Recommendation 1 of audit report DG(SANTE) 2014-7059 - on improving the system for providing certificates of competence, by publishing the necessary legislation, targeting the animal welfare officer and covering tasks in slaughterhouses which present particular risks for animal welfare such as slaughter without stunning. The respective competent authorities stated that: In Flanders, the legislation approving the training programme has been published. The competent authority also indicated that although there is an examination module on slaughter without stunning available for cattle and for sheep and goats, the module on slaughter without

Recommendation 6 of audit report DG(SANTE) 2014-7059 requested the competent authorities to put in place a system for monitoring in the slaughterhouse the welfare of broilers in the farm of origin, in line with the requirements from Annex III to Council Directive 2007/43/EC.

The competent authorities have not addressed recommendation 7 of audit report DG (SANTE) 2014-7059. The absence of procedures to check compliance in producers operating at the higher stocking densities, together with the absence of monitoring signs of welfare problems at slaughterhouse level, leaves unmonitored the welfare of broilers from the farms presenting the greatest risks.

The protocol signed with the certifying body has not been implemented which leaves the regional competent authorities unaware of any possible shortcomings and welfare problems at farms. This impedes them to take effective action to solve existing issues.

The regional competent authorities cannot confirm compliance in the farms operating at the higher stocking densities. This creates the potential risk that broilers are kept at stocking densities under which the housing and management conditions are not able to ensure their welfare. 6 OVERALL CONCLUSION There has been limited progress since the previous audit in November 2014. The regional authorities (Flanders, Wallonia and Brussels-Capital) have taken the legal responsibility for animal welfare from January 2015. The 2018-2020 MANCP does not contain objectives for animal welfare in the three regions. This, together with the absence of information from the regional competent authorities to t

Audit report DG(SANTE) 2014-7059 recommended (Recommendation 7) setting up a procedure to ensure that the checks by a certifying body confirm that producers operating at the higher stocking densities comply with Directive 2007/43/EC.

In response to the pre-audit questionnaire for this audit, the competent authorities of the regions with broilers' farms (Flanders and Wallonia) indicated that they had signed a protocol with the certifying body. This protocol includes that this certifying body has to notify the Animal Welfare Units if it notices severe animal welfare infringements. The Animal Welfare Units will then follow up and carry out an inspection of its own.

The audit team noticed that: The certifying body provided a document of August 2020 with the items that they inspect and the way they carry out the inspections. In this document, the certifying body has grouped together, from the previous checklist, the animal welfare requirements laid down in Directive 2007/43/EC, to provide better information to the regional competent authorities and farmers. The two regional competent authorities have not yet analysed this document. The two regional competent authorities indicated that they do not have access to the database of the checklists completed by the certifying body and commented that if they had received the complete checklist, it would have bee

label_heading: Conclusions on management of official controls
paragraph_text: The Competent Authorities' approach to the setting of objectives in the MANCP is mainly operational with no defined targets, indicators or measurement of progress and, as such, they are insufficient to bring about measureable change.

label_heading: Conclusions on management of official controls
paragraph_text: There is a good well-developed prioritisation of controls and allocation of resources even though these do not link to clear objectives or targets in the MANCP or annual inspection plans.

label_heading: Conclusions on management of official controls
paragraph_text: Planning of cross compliance and animal welfare controls are well formulated on a demonstrable risk profiling basis using a range of risk criteria that target official resources to inspecting the potentially worst offenders. However, the introduction of post-mortem indicators as a risk criterion to target broiler farm inspections has had no impact on improving animal welfare outcomes for footpad dermatitis over a three- year period.

The Czech Multi-Annual National Control Plan (MANCP) (2016-2018 - latest version), section 3.3, Strategic Objectives, includes a policy objective relevant for animal welfare: Objective two: "Ensure a high level of protection of human and consumer interests, animal health, animal welfare and plant health." There is no further description of what the SVA considers a high level of protection or how this should be measured.

The first operational objective of the MANCP related to on farm controls aims to ensure the keeping of farm animals in accordance with the minimal requirements - ensuring compliance with the requirements of the national and EU legislation.

The second operational objective of the MANCP focuses on raising awareness about the activities and powers of the competent authorities; responsibilities of breeders and general public involvement. A third aims for more effective procedures and enhanced cooperation between competent authorities: SVA, Regional Veterinary Authorities (RVAs) and Municipalities with extended powers (those that are legally entitled to enforce and sanction legislative requirements for farm welfare laws).

As the first MANCP operational objective on farm welfare solely reflects basic monitoring of compliance, there is no link between the planned prioritisation of controls and the allocation of resources to reflect strategic objective two of the MANCP described in paragraph 1 of this report or any of the operational objectives described in paragraphs 2 and 3 of this report. This is not in line with article 110 (2) (a) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 that requires the prioritisation of controls and allocation of resources to reflect the strategic objectives of the MANCP.

There are no baselines set to measure if outcomes for animal welfare meet strategic or operational objectives. For example, the SVA has been monitoring post-mortem indicators in broiler slaughterhouses from each production unit (flock and house) since 2011. From 2013 this data was used to target the poorest performing farms and from 2017 it started including also the incidence of footpad dermatitis (FPD). According to the SVA thresholds, the data indicate unsatisfactory scores for lesions of approximately 75% of flocks sent to slaughter in 2017, 2018 and 2019. The SVA had access to full data from the end of 2018. The use of the indicators to target inspections has had no impact on the outcom

There are no specific, measureable strategic or operational objectives or targets indicated in the MANCP on what the Czech Republic wants to achieve for animal welfare outcomes. Examples could include: reduce incidence of tail docking by x%; reduce FPD levels by x%; decrease lameness levels in cattle by x% through official controls and related actions. These could include targeted training for poorly performing sectors, 3 targeted enforcement campaigns on certain issues or; liaison with the relevant sector to set agreed targets for improvement, etc.

paragraph_text: The absence of procedures and templates hinders consistent and effective implementation and enforcement of controls to prevent routine tail docking of pigs and follow up enforcement of unsatisfactory results found during post-mortem inspections of broilers. 7 5.2 REPORTING OF CONTROLS Under EU requirements, and until end 2019, Member States had to submit three different types of reports addressing animal welfare: a report on the implementation of the MANCP; a report on inspections carried to verify compliance with Directive 2007/43/EC (the "Broiler Directive") and, as required by Commission Decision 2006/778/EC, a report of inspections at farm level. The last two reports have been replaced b

The assessment of non-compliances detected during cross-compliance controls gives a clearer picture of animal welfare problems as it gives conclusions on the severity, 10 extent, permanence and recurrence of the non-compliance. The planning of other animal welfare controls could benefit from the use of this methodology. 5.3 ANIMAL WELFARE INDICATORS A Commission funded project: "Welfare Quality", has developed principles and indicators for assessing the welfare of farm animals (4). The Welfare Quality Principles require housing, feeding, health and behaviour to be included in any on-farm assessment of animal welfare. The project concluded that animal-based indicators are better for measuring

There are no official control procedures for animal welfare controls on pig or broiler farms. There are no procedures for assessing documentation accompanying broiler flocks to slaughter. There is some specific guidance on measuring microclimate on broiler farms and a specific instruction on the assessment of FPD and a requirement to follow up on unsatisfactory scores. The SVA has made available information documents relating to tail docking of pigs but these are not procedures for official controls. The SVA considers that inspectors should base their assessment primarily on legislative requirements. Although the SVA has given training and held meetings with RVAs, it provided no further docu

The lack of procedures described in paragraph 13 is not in compliance with 1) Article 5 and 2) Article 12 (1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 which require that: 1) Competent authorities... shall: (a) have procedures and/or arrangements in place to ensure the effectiveness and appropriateness of official controls and other official activities; and (b) have procedures and/or arrangements in place to ensure the impartiality, quality and consistency of official controls and other official activities at all levels; and 2) Competent authorities shall perform official controls in accordance with documented procedures, and that those procedures shall cover the subject areas for control procedures set o

The Methodology does not provide mandatory compliance criteria. Although farmers are taking some actions, it is insufficient to comply with the legal requirements relating 5 to risks for tail biting. The lack of binding criteria and detailed procedures for inspectors does not enable them to reliably, and consistently, address the legal requirements relating to risks for tail biting and the effectiveness of improvement measures. As a result inspectors cannot effectively enforce Point 8 of Annex I, Chapter I to Council Directive 2008/120/EC as to whether the mutilation should have been carried out in the first place.

For example: the pig premises visited was part of a larger group structure and fattened tail docked pigs received from its breeding premises. Tail biting on the fattening farm was extremely low (0.08%). The company carried out a trial of rearing pigs with intact tails in one batch on one of the four breeding farm locations in the group. This resulted in poor production results and increased tail biting compared to the docked pigs on site. However, the company did not substantially alter farm conditions prior to the trial. They reduced the stocking density by 4.5% and added some basic additional enrichment (sisal ropes) and barley grain to the trial batch. The company veterinarian made an ass

The SVA issued new instructions for slaughterhouse OVs on the assessment and scoring of FPD lesions, and the setting, and monitoring of thresholds. However, the procedures do not indicate when to take enforcement action for unsatisfactory results. It requires that "unsatisfactory" FPD scores should be included in the "feedback report" sent to the official services in charge of supervising the farm of origin. This had not been necessary for any flock slaughtered in the slaughterhouse visited in the last 3 years. Nevertheless, national level data showed that broilers from farms within this region had been slaughtered in other regions and had frequently been assessed as "Unsatisfactory". Despit

The OV at the slaughterhouse visited did not specifically check the plausibility of cumulative daily mortality rates and accepted the value as declared in the food chain information document. The food chain information document accompanying the poultry to the slaughterhouse always included the cumulative daily mortality rates, in line with legal requirements. The OV at the slaughterhouse stated that although this is not indicated in any procedures for monitoring food chain information, the SVA and RVAs agreed in meetings that if cumulative daily mortality rates exceeded 3% this should be 6 notified by the slaughterhouse OVs to the official services responsible for supervising the farm or ori

The animal welfare fields in the SVA information system for animal welfare checks at the slaughterhouse can indicate "compliant", "not compliant" or "not checked". However, for a number of the parameters evaluated, such as "mortality" (birds dead on arrival), or "fitness and condition of the animal", or "unloading" there is no objective guidance or instruction on how compliance should be assessed. Individual OVs at each slaughterhouse are responsible for deciding what is "compliant" or "non-compliant" and for when they should take enforcement action.

RVAs used different formats for reporting animal welfare inspections on pig farms in the two regions visited. In the first region, inspectors used a template form with prepopulated areas for inspection findings printed on the form and expanded these with free text when they noted non-compliances. The other region used a free text style that had no standard reporting format, leaving the option to individual inspectors to complete the findings. The lack of standard report templates and procedures for carrying out and reporting on inspections does not ensure consistent implementation of controls, scope of inspections and reporting, and calls into question the consistency of the data reported fo

The Annual Report on implementation of the MANCP and the report on animal welfare required under Regulation (EU) 2019/723 provide a partial analysis of the results of official controls on animal welfare. The former does not address whether the activities are suitable to reach the strategic and operational objectives and ensure effective operation of the MANCP, even if it does include enforcement action and its results. The latter does not provide measureable, focussed actions to target recurrent non-compliances in specific areas.

The annual report on the MANCP gives statistics on compliance for each of the areas covered by Regulation (EU) 2019/723. However, although it does contain enforcement action and its results, it does not indicate the measures taken to ensure effective operation of the MANCP, as required under Article 113 (1) (d) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

The former does not address whether the activities are suitable to reach the strategic and operational objectives and ensure effective operation of the MANCP, even if it does include enforcement action and its results. The latter does not provide measureable, focussed actions to target recurrent non-compliances in specific areas.

The CA introduced a requirement in 2019 for the monitoring of docked/undocked pigs and tail injuries at slaughter that could feed into policy development and objective setting once data reliability (calibration of scoring) and analysis of the data is complete.

In an extract from the 2019 Annual Report on implementation of the MANCP, the report on farm controls for 2018 indicated: Free Barn Enriched Calves Pigs range cage 10,515 2,393 603 334 Holdings subject to inspection 20 36 53 549 275 2 Inspected holdings 10 52 2 Production sites without non- 10 50 compliance 8 These inspections resulted in the following enforcement action: Category of Non-Compliance* Free Barn Enriched Calves Pigs range cage Non-compliance A 0 0 0 0 0 Non-compliance B 0 0 1 16 7 Non-compliance C 0 0 6 67 74 * Annex III to Commission Decision 2006/778/EC defined administrative categories of non-compliance The SVA concluded that the major problematic areas for most livestock sp

However, the SVA did not analyse why inspections on pig or calf farms resulted in higher rates of non-compliance than equivalent inspections on holdings for laying hens (18% for pigs and 9% for calves compared to 2-4% for laying hens). There is no indication as to why there were much higher percentages of serious non-compliances in category C for pigs and calves and not in other categories, or what can and should be done to address them.

There is potentially useful data within this framework but the reporting is not always reliable. For example, the report indicated that there was 100% compliance for the category "mutilations" in pigs. This is not the case as: approximately 99% pigs are routinely tail docked; the incidence of tail biting reported on farm and at slaughter was very low (from the sample reviewed); and only rudimentary efforts are being made in terms of complying with minimum requirements; including risk assessment, improvement measures, and enforcement.

The SVA explained that the inspection plan prioritised pig farms with fattening pigs for inspection. It considers that farms receiving tail-docked piglets are compliant with tail docking provision. However, the requirements of Point 8 of Chapter I of Annex I to Directive 2008/120/EC on the prohibition of routine tail docking apply to all pigs on either breeding or fattening farms. Even fattening farms that receive piglets already tail docked must have evidence that: there was tail biting on the fattening farm; they have taken improvement measures which attempted to improve the situation and attempted rearing full tailed pigs on site not at another farm under different conditions. The Directi

Holdings selected for cross compliance inspections on animal welfare are identified using a number of risk criteria including animal-based indicators such as post-mortem lesions in ruminants and numbers of animals sent to rendering plants. Indications of severity, duration and frequency are used when assessing and reporting welfare non- compliances detected during cross compliance inspections, and the information is used to establish payment reductions as required by EU legislation.

One quality assurance (QA) scheme for pigs and cattle has recently started in the Czech Republic and includes mainly on-farm resource requirements. For example, in the case of pigs keepers must provide partially solid flooring or mats for pigs up until weaning no earlier than 28 days. The QA company audits the slaughterhouses who in turn audit the suppliers' compliance with the QA standard. There is no monitoring of animal-based indicators in the standard.

label_heading: Conclusions on management of official controls
paragraph_text: DAFM has not translated its objectives into operational objectives and there is no indication on how the prioritisation of official controls and allocation of resources reflect those objectives. With this, DAFM misses the opportunity to demonstrate the level of compliance with AW legislation ensured, whether they are meeting their objectives and achieving demonstrable animal welfare improvements at farm level.

In line with the requirements of Articles 109 (1) and 110 (1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625, the thesis for animal welfare is at the heart of the DAFM's strategy, the MANCP. The (2018-2022) MANCP, section 1.2, includes the National strategic objectives with two of these objectives being relevant for animal welfare: Objective 2: The enforcement of food and feed law, animal health and animal welfare rules and plant health rules. Objective 4: The co-ordination of official controls, to ensure effective and efficient implementation at national, regional and local level official controls are carried out regularly, on a risk basis and with appropriate frequency, impartiality, quality and consistency

The FPD Programme for broilers uses slaughter plant data since 2017 and is designed as follows: Each incidence over 50% FPD in a slaughter cohort triggers a welfare notification that is received centrally. Previously, the cut-off point was 70% but it was amended reflecting improvement of the recorded performance. This notification is collated in a database to generate a league table of flocks or houses, At RVO level, they choose the flocks or houses at the top of the league- i.e. the ones with more problems. The officials open a FPD "Case" for the flock/house identified. The Case is followed with a regulatory visit and either the farm takes effective measures to address the welfare deficits

With this, DAFM misses the opportunity to demonstrate the level of compliance with AW legislation ensured, whether they are meeting their objectives and achieving demonstrable animal welfare improvements at farm level.

DAFM has put in place a range of tools and developed methodologies in order to gather information and report the results of the official controls internally and to the stakeholders, including the EU Commission. Reporting does not fully support the development and use of indicators, which means that DAFM misses the opportunity to integrate the available data and tools in order to reflect the overall status of animal welfare at farms and improve it.

The inadequate enforcement of certain legal requirements (pig stocking densities, routine tail docking in pigs) and the lack of arrangements to ensure that actions are taken as a follow-up to monitoring at the slaughterhouse (broiler sector) reduce the effectiveness of the official controls. 9 5.3 ANIMAL WELFARE INDICATORS A Commission funded project: "Welfare Quality", has developed principles and indicators for assessing the welfare of farm animals4. The Welfare Quality Principles require housing, feeding, health and behaviour to be included in any on-farm assessment of animal welfare. The project concluded that animal-based indicators are better for measuring animal welfare but resource a

DAFM introduced a new checklist for broiler inspections that focusses on legal requirements related to footpad dermatitis (FPD). Whilst this is very comprehensive for FPD, it does not cover all the legal requirements of Council Directive 2007/43/EC e.g. mortality. This means that it cannot fully serve as the tool to ensure compliance by checking and identifying different animal welfare issues at broiler farms. In addition, there is currently no instruction/procedure in place for the performance of official controls on broiler welfare at the farms. The available material for inspectors is a training presentation dating back to 2012, which means that apart from this not being a procedure, seve

DAFM introduced a new checklist for pig farm inspections that focusses on legal requirements related to tail docking. This too does not cover all the legal requirements of Council Directive 2008/120/EC and therefore cannot serve as a tool to ensure compliance with animal welfare requirements. 4 8. The competent authority has put in place a methodology to base its controls on risk. The planning process differentiates between species and it prioritises based on risks deployed by the competent authority. label_heading: Conclusions on welfare of animals during sea transport
paragraph_text: Documented procedures do not provide the necessary instructions for port inspectors on how to verify all the relevant legal requirements as part of a practical official control of a livestock vessel. In particular, these instructions are generally inadequate to support the port inspectors in verifying compliance with the specific technical requirements of the Regulation during official controls for approval of livestock vessels.

label_heading: Conclusions on welfare of animals during sea transport
paragraph_text: The effectiveness of controls of livestock vessels is dependent on the experience of the port inspectors. For some of the requirements, the port inspectors go beyond what the procedures indicate. Nonetheless, official controls are not adequately verifying all the requirements, and this could have implications for animal welfare during sea journeys. Controls carried out on vessels loading in France and during the French approval procedure for livestock vessels are inadequate to minimise the animal welfare risks linked to most specific technical equipment on board.

For many of the specific technical requirements, included under Section 1 of Chapter IV of Annex I to the Regulation, to be checked when approving a vessel and which are not of a veterinary nature the Vade Mecum: in some instances (ventilation air exchanges and backup water pumping system) indicates that only "the classification society referred to in Chapter IV, Section 1, Point 1 of the Regulation, is competent to" test/verify/certify the requirements, thus implying that the competent authority officials working at the port of exit (hereafter "port inspectors") do not have the skills to verify these requirements; in other instances (fire-fighting and power supply systems, all monitoring an

In addition, for pre-loading controls, the Vade Mecum only indicates that the presence of the equipment listed in Section 1 of Chapter IV of Annex I to the Regulation must be checked but not that these are in good working order (water and drainage pumps and backup pumps, alarm systems, firefighting equipment and power generation devices). This is not in accordance with Article 20(1)(c) of the Regulation.

In the pre-loading checklists, port inspectors confirm that the equipment listed in Section 1 of Chapter IV of Annex I to the Regulation was present. There is no indication that they verify that this equipment is in good working order, although this is required by Article 20 of the Regulation (see also paragraph 4).

label_heading: Conclusions on welfare of animals during sea transport
paragraph_text: This, together with the absence of suitably qualified staff for assessing specific technical requirements for livestock vessels translates into a poor evaluation of these requirements (such as air changes per hour on each deck of a livestock vessel, and the equipment used for watering and drainage systems on board a livestock vessel) during the approval and pre-loading inspections.

Documents submitted with the application include classification society certificates, deck plans and a contingency plan: The application files reviewed by the audit team had these supporting documents. According to the Vade Mecum, when carrying out the physical inspection, the port inspectors must verify that these systems are laid out according to the plans. label_heading: Conclusions on traceability and trade restrictions
paragraph_text: The official control on the handling and storage of wild boar carcases in general and on the destruction of carcases resulted positive to ASF in particular has improved since the FVS became responsible for this control in 2019. However, its efficiency is limited until official controls are more representative.

Since February 2019, the FVS has been responsible for the control of wild boar carcases in processing rooms and storage facilities of hunting grounds (chillers, freezers or other equipment), where wild boar carcases are stored while ASF test results are awaited. To date, the FVS does not have an overview of the facilities available for each hunting ground. When the FVS started to carry out official controls on hunting grounds, they set, mainly due to staff constraints, an objective for 2019 of inspecting 10% of the hunting grounds (the same objective of 10% for 2020), and a minimum number of carcases based on a statistical approach. From March to December 2019, 190 hunting grounds were inspe

label_heading: Conclusions on traceability and trade restrictions
paragraph_text: The official controls at the point of hunting, including for biosecurity, which remain under the competence of the State Forest Service, are still a very weak point in the control of ASF in Latvia and they increase the potential risk of spread of ASF 9 infection not only within the country but also in other Member States. 5.2 MEASURES IN CASE OF SUSPICION/CONFIRMATION OF ASF IN DOMESTIC PIGS Legal requirements Articles 4-5 and 8-11 of Directive 2002/60/EC; Article 1of Commission Decision 2003/422/EC. Findings

The objective of the State Forest Service for the current hunting season is to inspect 1,200 hunting grounds (they had inspected around 1,000 so far this season). Inspections are unannounced and, contrary to a legal requirement in force a few years ago, hunters do not have to inform the State Forest Service offices in advance of when they plan to hunt. For this reason, and according to the information provided to the audit team, inspectors have not been able to perform their tasks in half of the visits, as no hunting activities were taking place. In addition, inspections do not target any specific species so only in approximately 300 out of the 1,000 inspections wild boar was being hunted.

According to the State Forest Service, when wild boar is being hunted, inspectors must focus on biosecurity aspects. These are, for example, checking the presence of disinfectant at the point of hunting, the burial of offal if wild boars are gutted on the spot or the transport of offal to a watertight container or that carcases do not get in contact. However, inspectors have not received any specific training on biosecurity and there are no instructions or guidelines available to them.

The State Forest Service has prepared a checklist for the inspections, but it does not contain any detail on the biosecurity aspects checked (only yes/no). There is an online application to report the inspection results, but it does not contain details on the species that were hunted during the inspection therefore there is no overview of the wild boar hunting grounds visited. The State Forest Service assumed that there was hunting of wild boar if biosecurity was reported.

According to the data contained in the online application, inspectors have never found any non-compliance on biosecurity. An inspector clarified that although not reported, in cases of shortcomings, they normally prefer to instruct hunters to improve their awareness regarding biosecurity. 8 5.1.4 Control of ABPs of domestic and feral pigs Legal requirements Articles 2, 7 and 10 of Decision 2014/709/EU. Findings

The recruitment of almost 3,000 authorised veterinarians extends the veterinary authorities' capacity to monitor non-commercial (backyard) establishments. However, the lack of enforceable biosecurity requirements or limits on keeping breeding animals on these establishments means that they continue to play an active role in the persistence and circulation of disease.

The veterinary authorities do not have the full support and commitment of hunters or the hunting authorities to apply rigorously the measures needed to control the wild boar population and to eliminate the disease from affected meta-populations. As a result, these animals act as an important reservoir of disease, which can spill over into inadequately protected pig establishments.

The supervision and audit arrangements in place provide the veterinary authorities with reliable and up-to-date information on the completion of planned controls and activities. However, they do not systematically use this information to identify and tackle the issues that are impeding progress in tackling the disease. 9 6 FINDINGS ON PREVENTIVE MEASURES The combination of an up-to-date pig database and veterinary personnel deployed at local level provides the means to raise animal health standards on non-commercial establishments. paragraph_text: Planning of residue monitoring is, with some exceptions (absence of testing of caprine animals and some species of farmed fish and no on-farm sampling of farmed fish), largely in line with EU requirements. 5.1.3. Implementation of the residue monitoring plan

Previous years' non-compliances found were not considered as a risk factor for the planning of the 2018 and 2019 residue monitoring plans which is not fully in line with EU requirements (7). However, to mitigate this, the competent authority increased the minimum number of samples to be taken by 10% for all commodities. Staff from the NFCSO informed the audit team that they will consider the previous years` non-compliances for the 2021 residue monitoring plan and increase the number of samples for Group B1 from porcine animals, due to the non-compliant results found in previous years.

The 2020 national residue monitoring plan does not include caprine animals, which are commercially slaughtered in Hungary. The latter is not in line with EU legal requirements (8). The 2019 and 2020 residue plans cover all of the substance groups required and meet the sampling levels and frequencies laid down in EU law (9).

The risk-based distribution of samples to the 19 counties is based on production volumes for the most commodities and animal species but not for all, which is not fully in line with EU requirements (11). In case of honey, all sampling under the 2018 and 2019 plans was allocated to nine counties representing 77% of national honey production, no samples were assigned for collection in the remaining 10 counties although honey is also produced in the most of them. NFCSO staff stated that they plan in future to fully allocate the sample number for equine and ovine animals and for honey according to the production volume of the respective counties. label_heading: Conclusions on minimum requirements for border control posts
paragraph_text: The Border Inspection Post has been re-designated following the introduction of the OCR. The facilities, equipment and arrangements in place concerning animals and goods of animal origin for which the BCP was designated are satisfactory.

label_heading: Conclusions on minimum requirements for border control posts
paragraph_text: However, there were shortcomings in the facilities and arrangements in place concerning products of non-animal origin for human, and non-human consumption, and in the abbreviations used to indicate the categories of goods for which the BCP had been designated. Although the volume of imports through the BCP is low, the shortcomings identified may have an adverse impact on the hygienic handling and storage of goods for which the BCP has been designated. 6 OVERALL CONCLUSIONS There is a comprehensive system of official controls for animals and goods entering the Union through the BCP in the Czech Republic. Those controls were performed by well- trained officials, supported by detailed guidance,

The facilities are shared for food and feed of non-animal origin. CAFIA and CISTA informed the audit team that arrangements are in place to prevent risks, which may result in cross-contamination, in particular, time separation is used between the handling of different goods and the inspection facilities are cleaned and disinfected between consignments in line with Article 3(9)(b)(ii) of Regulation (EU) 2019/1014.

The audit team noted that the facilities and equipment at the BCP did not meet the minimum requirements for performing official controls of food and feed of non-animal origin. There are no dedicated storage rooms for commodities to be kept frozen or at ambient temperature under control of CISTA, and the arrangements in place for the shared facilities do not guarantee that CISTA and CAFIA have dedicated storage available to detain food and feed of non-animal origin under their control, in line with Article 64 of the OCR and Article 3(1) of Regulation (EU) 2019/1014. CAFIA did not have information available on the location of the dedicated storage rooms.

However, there were weaknesses in the notification of import and the implementation of certain documentary checks and reduced frequency of physical checks. While these were not sufficient to affect the validity of the decision to allow importation, the document checks for feed of non-animal origin are not carried out at the BCP as required. 15 5.3 MINIMUM REQUIREMENTS FOR BORDER CONTROL POSTS

The SVA and CISTA perform the documentary checks at the BCP while CAFIA indicated that their documentary checks for consignments of food of non-animal origin subject to special import conditions, are carried out at their office in Prague and not at the BCP, which is not in line with Article 49(1) of the OCR.

label_heading: Conclusions on minimum requirements for border control posts
paragraph_text: Border Inspection Posts have been re-designated following the introduction of the OCR. However, there were shortcomings in the required risk assessment for the sharing of facilities and the facilities for storing at appropriate temperatures the different categories of goods for which the BCPs were designated. 15 67. Although the volume of imports through the BCPs concerned is low, the non- compliances identified may have an impact on the hygienic handling and storage of goods for which those BCP have been designated. The competent authorities have initiated corrective actions to ensure that those risks are minimised or eliminated. 6 OVERALL CONCLUSIONS There is a comprehensive system of offi

The audit team noted that the five BCPs evaluated have shared facilities for different categories of goods, but in all cases, the risk assessments required by Article 3(9) of Regulation (EU) 2019/1014 for the shared use of facilities had not been completed. It also noted that the storage facilities at the selected BCPs were not suitable for simultaneously storing at the appropriate temperatures chilled and frozen goods for which the BCPs were designated, as required by Article 3(1)(c) of the same Regulation.

A number of shortcomings were noted with respect to the implementation of official controls, in particular the late notification of arrival of consignments and the performance of documentary checks for food of non-animal origin, other than upon arrival of the consignment at a designated BCP, which undermine the effectiveness and appropriateness of official controls and their overall compliance with Union legislation. 14 6.2 MINIMUM REQUIREMENTS FOR BORDER CONTROL POSTS

The EHD stated that due to a lack of staff, documentary checks for consignments of food of non-animal origin or kitchenware are carried out at the central office of the EHD, and not at the BCP, which for goods referred to in Article 47(1)(d) and (e) of the OCR, is not in line with Article 49(1) of that Regulation.

However, the lack of documented procedures and necessary arrangements, updated as appropriate, and delays in finalising and implementing the monitoring plan, have an adverse impact on both the effectiveness of the organisation of official controls on imports of animals and goods, and its compliance with Union legislation. The lack of recent internal audits or verification checks of the official controls for such imports, represent possible missed opportunities to identify and address those issues.

The VRD informed the audit team that no guidelines or documented procedures had been issued at the time of the audit for performing import controls on feed of non- animal origin and hay and straw. Prior to the UK's withdrawal from the EU such goods were not imported. The VRD confirmed at the closing meeting (see section 8 below) that documented procedures for the control of feed of non-animal origin, hay and straw would be in place by 31 May 2021. As a result of that action, the VRD will have by that date, documented procedures in place that include the relevant subjects 7 specified in Chapter II of Annex II to the OCR, and which have been updated as appropriate, in line with Article 12(3)(b

However a number of shortcomings were noted in the application of the prior notification of arrival of consignments and the implementation of certain documentary and physical checks. The authorities have taken immediate action, or plan to take action, to address the majority of those, however the documentary checks of glazed foods carried out in-line with internal guidelines do not ensure consistency between the entry document and documents accompanying the consignment. 5.3 MINIMUM REQUIREMENTS FOR BORDER CONTROL POSTS

The audit team noted that the documentary checks had not identified certain minor errors in a small number of entry documents. The errors in the documents were not sufficient to affect the validity of the decision to allow importation of the animals or goods concerned. label_heading: Conclusions on the planning and implementation of official controls
paragraph_text: With the exception of food business operators supplying food and food by-products for feeding of farmed animals, both the DoA and Veterinary Services carry out their controls ­ inspections and sampling ­ regularly and along the entire feed chain, even though the controls on operators handling medicated feed are not risk-based. On the evidence of the records seen by the audit team and the situation on the spot in the establishments visited, the controls are capable of, and have, with the exception of operators' obligations to have procedures in place to verify the correct functioning of their HACCP systems, correctly identified non-compliances in operators' performances.

Notwithstanding the above, the audit team noted that none of the operators had established the procedures required by Article 6(2)(f) of Regulation (EC) No 183/2005 12 to verify that the measures on HACCP outlined in points (a) to (e) of the cited Article 6(2) were complete and working effectively. The operators and the authorities met explained that absence of such procedures resulted from their collective misinterpretation of this requirement. Thus, these had neither been put in place by operators nor requested by the authorities.

label_heading: Conclusion on the planning and implementation of inspections
paragraph_text: The inspection planning system is based on appropriate risk-related factors and thus ensures that the official controls are carried out on all operators regularly, on a risk basis and with appropriate frequency. However, the effectiveness of the system is weakened by providing unjustified prior notice of inspections to feed manufacturers, shortcomings in the assessment of operators' HACCP plans, and incomplete verification of the appropriateness of operators' retained samples. The audit team noted that, although in practice this does not have any immediate negative impact on enforcement as both CtrlAs are competent and empowered to apply effective enforcement measures, MoRA i

Estonia has made use of Article 28(2) of Regulation No. 834/2007 to exempt from controls retailers who sell directly to the final consumer, and has made this decision, together with the conditions needed for the exemption, publicly available on the VFB website. As described in section 1(2)(5) of Regulation 26 of the Ministry of Agriculture, retailers selling unpacked organic products must apply for registration to VFB. This means that in practice, retailers who sell pre-packed products can be exempted without fulfilling all the conditions of Article 28(2). As a consequence, retailers who prepare or store pre-packed products other than in connection with the point of sale or who import organi

The national provisions give detail on the designation of tasks and responsibilities and the organisation of controls. However, there is no single authority or body designated to ensure coordination and consistency of controls. This is not in line with article 4(2) (b) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. The audit team noted the planning, implementation and effectiveness of controls differ between EAB and VFB (see Chapter 5.2.3). Furthermore, there is no full coordination between EAB and VFB to cover operators whose activities fall under the control of both authorities (see paragraph 40).

In addition, the audit team noted a lack of coordination between EAB and VFB to plan controls at the 71 operators whose activities are under control of both CtrlAs. As stated by both CtrlAs, multiple activities should be regarded as a risk criterion, however in practice EAB has not introduced it as part of their risk assessment and VFB does not take it into account for the rating of the operator (see paragraph 37). Moreover, the results of controls of such operators are not systematically shared between EAB and VFB. Conclusions on planning and prioritisation of inspections

MoRA is also responsible for the allocation of sufficient budget for controls and for the supervision of the control and certification tasks conferred to EAB and VFB. Supervision must take place once every five years in accordance with national rules. It is carried out either by MoRA´s internal audit team or by outsourcing it to external companies. In the period 2015-2020 an internal audit was carried out by MoRA to EAB, however no audits of VFB were carried out. MoRA and VFB stated that although an audit of VFB was in 5 principle planned to take place during 2020, it was deemed not necessary as the DG Health and food safety audit was considered to have similar value for the purpose of super

The audit team found that the internal audit carried out of EAB by MoRA was well- structured and detailed and with good follow-up which allowed for the closing of most of the recommendations. However, its scope did not cover the most relevant aspects of the tasks conferred to this CtrlA. For example, the effectiveness of inspections, sampling and laboratory testing and the certification activities were not covered. It also did not include on-the-spot activities at operators to observe inspections performed by EAB. However, the audit team considered that documentary checks only would not allow MoRA to evaluate how controls are carried out, as the inspection reports, in particular EAB´s, lack

However, the reports issued by EAB inspectors lack detail on how verification takes place, with no objective evidence attached to the reports except in cases of non-compliance. The reports consist of a digital template where inspectors tick off the aspects verified with no further description of, or references made, to the documents or records checked.

For example, the audit team reviewed a report of an additional inspection carried out at an operator who runs conventional and organic units as described in paragraph 35 above. The inspector stated that she focused on the verification of proper cleaning of the harvesting machinery and equipment shared between the conventional and organic units. The inspector also stated that she followed the guidance in the handbook of procedures and monitored the purchase and use of inputs, as well as the balance between the organic products harvested against their sales, to confirm that only the products sold as organic were those produced in the organic unit. However, these statements were not supported b

The audit team noted that the manner in which inspections are announced to operators differ between EAB and VFB. VFB generally carries out all inspections unannounced while EAB allows for short prior warning of up to 48 hours being given to farmers, even for additional inspections that according to Article 65(4) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008 should be primarily unannounced. Although the audit team fully understood the reasons given by EAB that in some cases it is difficult to carry out an inspection at farmers without prior warning, this should be the exception (for duly justified cases) rather than the rule. 9 As a consequence of this shortcoming, Estonia is not in the position to fulfil t

Additional inspections are planned at the beginning of the year by EAB and VFB. The audit team noted that both CtrlAs generally achieve the number of inspections planned. However, the manner in which EAB and VFB select operators for additional inspections differ greatly. VFB follows the working document agreed by Member States and issued by the European Commission, which instructs how to classify operators in risk categories following risk assessment made of them all. VFB thus uses a number of criteria (e.g quantities produced or traded, past non-conformities, potential of exchange of products, e-commerce, sales or pre-packed or unpacked products, subcontracted operations).

Every operator is rated for each criterion and given a final score based on the aggregated scores. The operators are selected for additional inspections in descending order starting with the one with the highest score. There are also additional factors that can be taken into account but not rated with points (e.g. textual remarks from the inspector, operator under control of EAB and VFB).

EAB sets up the risk criteria annually, with some criteria being used each year (e.g. past irregularities, risk of mixing organic and non-organic products) while others are introduced based on a thematic approach for the year in question (e.g. small potato growers with land area between 10-50 hectares for which complaints were received). EAB 10 then groups the operators under each of the criteria. Operators may be selected for additional controls based on one criterion only, also taking into account input from inspectors. This not in line with Article 65(4) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008, as no individual assessment is made to determine the risk profile defined for each operator, taking into

Even if selecting the operators based on one criterion only can be useful to detect non- compliant operators, the inspections carried out on this basis should not be counted as part of the minimum, required by Article 92c(2)(b) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008, of 10% of operators that must be subject to additional inspections based on their risk profile.

At the time of the audit there were eight private and 18 public CBs approved by MiPAAF for the control and certification of PDO/PGI wines. In the case of private bodies, accreditation to ISO/IEC 17065 is a pre-requisite for approval. The approval procedure for public CBs includes the checking by MiPAAF of all relevant aspects necessary to confirm the CB's competence. However, at the time of the audit only two public CBs were accredited as it was not a pre-requisite for the approval of public CBs. This is not in line with Article 90(3) of Regulation (EU) No 1306/2013.

ToBRFV was first found in the Netherlands in a tomato fruit producing crop in October 2019. The production site was checked during the annual survey. Samples of symptomatic plants were tested positive with the ELISA method and were later confirmed by RT-PCR and next generation sequencing methods. Up to the time of the audit, the presence of the virus was identified in tomato fruit crops at 27 production sites.

A considerable part of the specified seed lots which were in storage prior to 15 August 2020 were not tested with the molecular method. Although many lots have been tested with ELISA method, the potential plant health risk is only partially addressed due to the lower sensitivity of those tests.

The supervision of the ToBRFV tests carried out by the seed companies by annual audits provides a level of guarantee. Currently there is no obligation for the seed companies to report to the CAs the number of samples and the methods used for the tests they carried out on seed lots and batches in stock. Consignments or seed lots of Capsicum spp., for which the AD on the PC certifies that the variety is resistant, are accepted for import. NVWA stated that there are uncertainties about which genes ensure the resistance. During their monitoring activity for ToBRFV the NVWA tested positive pepper seed lots, which had been declared to be ToBRFV resistant. Resistance of a variety could be linked to only one of the two parental lines. Hence, a contamination of the hybrid seed may only be related to the parents whereas the seed itself is still resistant.

The competent authority could not provide the evidence requested by the audit team to confirm that the NFCSO had carried out any recent assessment to identify specific risk factors regarding the introduction in, and the transmission within and between poultry holdings of HPAI. Representatives of the NFCSO indicated that they consider the entire country to be a high-risk area. However, the epidemiological evidence from the previous epizootic, indicates that there are risk factors associated with specific geographical locations that experienced HPAI outbreaks in Hungary in the past. Those factors include the areas with a high density of domestic waterfowl. Although the audit team found evidenc

The NFCSO did not update the risk profile of those areas taking into account the epidemiological evidence of an increasing threat posed by the detection of HPAI. They did 7 not update the profile after confirmation of the first outbreaks in Hungary in January, and despite the presence of HPAI infection in migratory wild birds in neighbouring Member States. This is not in line with requirements laid down in Article 3(3) of Decision (EU) 2018/1136. Nevertheless, the competent authorities took some actions to reinforce the application of generic risk mitigation and biosecurity measures in the whole country (see the next points).

After confirmation of the first outbreaks in January 2020, the NFCSO issued CVO Decision 1/2020, ordering the enclosed housing of poultry in the territory of the whole country. This is in line with requirements on risk mitigation of HPAI laid down in Article 4.4(b) of Decision (EU) 2018/1136. CVO Decision 03/2017 had already established that keepers of commercial poultry holdings throughout the country should apply certain biosecurity requirements, and that the county and district veterinary services should regularly check and enforce them. They have not carried out similar assessments since 2018, and the competent authority could not provide the evidence requested by the audit team to confirm that they had enforced CVO Decision 3/2017 during the first months of 2020. This is not in line with Article 10(1) of Decision (EU) 2018/1136.

The approach taken to carry out the epidemiological investigations was not standardised or consistent along the epizootic, and there was a persistent lack of quality and completeness of the data obtained. This, in many cases, did not allow the competent authorities to investigate all the elements contained in points (a) to (d) of Article 6(2) of Directive 2005/94/EC.

The shortcomings described in the previous points precluded the NDCC from taking fully into account the results of the epidemiological inquiries to take well-informed decisions to: a) apply and adapt additional disease control measures, as necessary for each outbreak or affected area, and b) grant derogations to the restrictions applied as a result of the outbreaks. paragraph_text: Each county is obliged to develop and keep updated its own contingency plan, based on the national model, but including information and guidance tailored to the specific needs of the county. paragraph_text: The competent authorities detected 24 outbreaks during pre-movement testing: 23 of them in movements granted for direct slaughter and one to force-feeding. label_heading: Conclusions on official controls on bivalve molluscs
paragraph_text: The fact that IPMA: i) does not close or reclassify the production area when certain regulatory limits for microbiological quality are exceeded; ii) reverts the classification downgrade without an evaluation of the results for the review period; iii) excludes unexpected results without conclusive investigation, may result in the placing on the market of bivalve molluscs that exceed the health standards.

label_heading: Conclusions on official controls on bivalve molluscs
paragraph_text: The current monitoring programme for biotoxins covers most of the requirements of EU legislation but the fact that the IPMA does not fully respect the sampling points and frequencies diminishes its value.

The classification of production, included in the IPMA procedure MB 01, foresees three types of classification: permanent, provisional and not classified, depending on the number of results available during the review period. The audit team noted that: For provisional classification, a reduced number of sampling results (between 12 and 23) in three years is sufficient for IPMA to classify provisionally a specific species in a production area with a better class than other species in the same area. The audit team considered that less than 24 results in three years does not ensure that results are representative of a production area, as required in Article 57 of Regulation (EU) 2019/627. Nonet

According to the procedure MB 02, laboratory reports have to include the Most Probable Result (MPR) of E. coli per 100 grams. However, the number of dilutions made during the analyses of samples from class B production areas is not enough to provide an exact number when results are > 18,000. Therefore, it is not possible to determine if these areas exceed the limit of 46,000 established in Article 54.3 of Regulation (EU) 2019/627 for class B production, and decisions for reclassification and/or closure of production areas cannot be adequately taken. b) For the presence of toxin-producing plankton in water

According to the procedure MB 03, and in line with Article 61.4 of Regulation (EU) 2019/627, the indicator species shall be sampled on a weekly basis (other species only when testing of indicator species result is over the limits for biotoxins). However, for different reasons (e g. indicator species not available, weather conditions, etc.) IPMA does not always respect this frequency. IPMA does not always take the samples at the points designated in the procedure according to Article 61.1 of Regulation (EU) 2019/627. Indicator species are sometimes sampled in other locations or other species are sampled instead and used as indicator.

The decisions following results over the limits are included in the procedure MB 01, but it has a number of deviations from the legislation: a) For microbiological quality of live bivalve molluscs The procedure does not foresee the closure or reclassification of production areas when health standards for live bivalve molluscs are not met (i.e. between 230 and 700 E. coli NMP/100 g for class A production areas, between 4,600 and 46,000 E. coli NMP/100 g for class B production areas), contrary to Article 62.1 of Regulation (EU) 2019/627. paragraph_text: The IPMA's intention to formalise the procedure for sampling of classified production areas by non-official staff is essential to ensure that samples taken in the context of official monitoring are reliable.

According to the procedure MB 02, monitoring samples have to be analysed using a method recognised by the National Reference Laboratory that should preferably be standardised. The audit team saw that the analyses of a certain number of samples from two production areas (they are remoter therefore more difficult to transport the samples on time) deviated from the method accredited and their analyses started more than 24 hours after collection. Accordingly, laboratory reports do not display the accreditation logo. However, IPMA used these results for classification and for decisions following monitoring. IPMA informed the audit team of an ongoing project to estimate the difference in results w

The head of the biotoxins laboratories presented the facilities and equipment of the laboratories. The facilities of the three laboratories are appropriate. The equipment of the ASP and PSP laboratories is also adequate. There was only one piece of equipment validated for lipophilic toxins. In case of breakdown or regular maintenance (which is regularly required for this type of equipment), samples were analysed using a screening test which does not comply with the requirements of Chapter III.B of Annex V to Regulation (EU) 2019/627. In addition, this test only detects two of the regulated compounds (OA and DTX) so the total toxicity of the lipophilic toxin group can be underestimated.
