paragraph_text: The flow of information regarding monitoring results and the prompt update of available information helps the system to avoid mistakes due to delays. The decisions taken by IPMA following results over the limits apply only from the moment when they are formalised (e.g. some days after the sample was taken). label_heading: Conclusions on organisation and implementation of official controls
paragraph_text: There are procedures and guidelines in place for official staff for the relevant controls, which include guidance on how to act in different scenarios with regard to the handling of animals unfit for transport. Yet, the non-existence of emergency slaughters at farm level, combined with the findings regarding the condition of some animals arriving at slaughterhouses, implies that bovine animals are transported to the slaughterhouse irrespective of their fitness for transport. Official controls at slaughterhouses identify animals unfit for transport, however, as those animals have already been certified by the local DVMs , no further investigation is carried out nor any enforcement implemented

Transporters are considered primarily accountable in the case of animals unfit for transport. However, due to limitations in the national legislation in relation to imposing and receiving payments of administrative fines, (the fines must be imposed and paid on- the-spot) no administrative sanctions have been imposed to date. The CCA is currently working on an amendment of this legislation. Conclusions on competent authorities

Movement declarations were also granted for animals that were unfit for transport (see paragraph 75); even though the existing procedures clearly indicate that such animals should not be transported (see paragraph 97). Once the local DVM's OVs have issued the 12 movement declaration, OVs at slaughterhouses accept the animals without questioning their fitness for transport.

None of the OVs in the 3 slaughterhouses mentioned identifying cases of bovine animals that were considered as unfit of transport and should have been slaughtered at farm. It should be noted that the movement declaration contains a specific clause that explicitly mentions that animals covered by the movement declaration are fit for transport, in line with Regulation (EC) No 1/2005.

Even though the local DVM's OVs responsible for issuing the movement declaration would indicate on the document that the animal(s) listed is/are destined for emergency slaughter (the reason of injury was not always indicated), the ante-mortem records rarely indicated any issues with the animals concerned. Similarly, there was no reference made to this in the accompanying FCI documents.

In several cases, although the cattle had been classified as emergency by the DVM's OV issuing the movement declaration, this was not indicated in the system nor was any further detail documented as to the reasons for the emergency, or the findings identified during the AMI (see paragraph 72). paragraph_text: Cross-checks carried out revealed significant under-reporting of events in the database, both for slaughters and deaths, which prevents reliable and timely reconciliation of the existing records; this, in turn, hinders the identification of possible non compliances.

With regard to updating the CBD, farmers have the possibility to directly enter the births of bovine animals of their holdings up to 27 days after birth (i.e. up to 20 days to ear tag new-borns and up to another 7 days to notify). If a farmer is not able to enter the information her/himself, (s)he can request the local DVM to do it. Any other changes are notified in the CBD by the local DVMs, after farmers have informed them of such. This 10 concerns movements and deaths, which need to be notified by the famers within 7 days of the actual event. Generally, as was explained by the CAs, since this is quite demanding it is possible that there can be delays by the DVMs in updating the database.

There is no integration of the database with the collection companies for dead animals. Each company may keep records of the ears tags that it collects but that information is not cross-checked with that of the CBD. This information is communicated to the RUs/DVMs.

With regard to slaughtered bovine animals, in 2019 the CCA performed cross-checks between the bovine database and a database used by slaughterhouse operators to report 11 the classification of the carcases (see paragraph 17) and identified that a number of slaughtered animals were not notified by the OVs in the CBD as having been slaughtered. Based on the information collected by the CCA, around 10% of the bovines slaughtered were not recorded in the bovine database.

The CCA attributed this to understaffing and the workload of the OVs, who, in addition to their other tasks, are also expected to enter the ear tag numbers of the animals slaughtered into the database. Based on the outcome of that cross-check, the CCA sent out a reminder letter to the RUs of their obligations to notify the CBD. A similar cross- check, to be carried out in 2020, did not materialise.

In relation to fallen bovine animals, cross-checks carried out by the audit team in one RU between CBD data and those held by the company appointed for the collection of fallen stock, revealed an underreporting of fallen animals in the CBD. 5.4.2 Official controls at establishment level (slaughterhouses) Legal requirements Article 18 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. label_heading: Conclusion on legislation and implementing measures
paragraph_text: The CAs have issued national legislation and guidelines necessary to ensure the implementation and/or enforcement of EU requirements applicable to the bovine meat sector. From a summary analysis, they are in line with EU legislation and mostly adequate, with the exception of those dealing with cases of bovine animals with traceability issues. 3 5.2 COMPETENT AUTHORITIES Legal requirements Articles 4, 5, 6, 138 and 139 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Article 13 of Regulation (EU) 2019/624. Findings 5.2.1 Structure and organisation

While the audit team did not carry out a comprehensive review of these guidelines, it was noted that they cover all of the food chain and controls related to the production of beef. However, the audit team noted that the "Instruction on procedures to be followed in slaughterhouses" does not provide sufficient information for the OVs on how to act appropriately in case of bovine animals with traceability issues (e.g. lost ear tags) detected at AMI. This has a negative impact on the official controls on bovine traceability. (See also paragraphs 79 and 81).

One of the OVs interviewed explained that where the traceability of a bovine animal is not established (e.g. lost ear tag(s)), it will be slaughtered and the carcass will be detained and tested for antibiotic residues. If the result of the analysis is negative, the meat is declared fit for human consumption. The audit team noted that these actions were the initiatives of the OV, as they are not included in the VS instruction. The audit team was provided with examples of such cases and noted that a 400 fine was imposed on the farmers in each case.

In addition, the audit team reviewed a case when a bovine animal arrived at the slaughterhouse with one ear tag. After verification of the identification of this animal in the CBD, the OV ascertained that this ear tag belonged to an animal which, according to the data in the CBD, had already been declared dead. Despite the fact that the traceability of this animal was clearly not established, its meat was released for human consumption by the OV. The CA imposed a 400 fine on the farmer. Cooperation and coordination arrangements between and within the CAs involved in the controls for the areas covered by this audit are in place. The mechanisms in place (such as documented procedures and training) give the CAs a reasonable level of assurance that controls are carried out uniformly and consistently. However, the contracted OVs are not included in the CAs' training system, which could have an impact on the sustained level of competence of contracted staff responsible for official controls of the bovine sector.

The prerequisites for private veterinarians to be contracted as OVs are previous experience and training. The audit team was informed by the VPHD that the last training sessions, provided by the VS for contracted staff, were in 2019. These included, among others, training on AMI, PMI and slaughterhouse inspection. However, the audit team also noted that the contracted OVs are not included in the CA`s training plan, therefore the VS do not provide them with regular training.

The cooperation and coordination arrangements between and within the CA(s) are satisfactory for the performance of official controls and enforcement, apart from the provision of feedback information to slaughterhouse OVs that report welfare-related 10 issues to the department dealing with farms and primary production, and which in one of the ACs was not in place.

The procedures of communication regarding animal welfare issues between the Health and Agriculture departments in one of the ACs were not satisfactory, resulting in a lack of feedback from Agriculture of the impact of the actions taken by the OVs working for the Health department at slaughterhouse level. This does not allow the OVs to understand how effective their work is or, potentially, to learn from mistakes. 5.2.2 Impartiality, freedom from conflict of interest,

Both CAs have procedures to train, support and control the OVs delivering official controls on a regular basis, but neither have a specific and structured procedure for those veterinarians that work for them occasionally.

Neither of the two CAs have a specific and structured training procedure for those veterinarians that work for them occasionally, covering absences of permanent OVs. The audit found evidence of some problems related to PMI in two out of six establishments, in both ACs, where the resident OV was not present and a locum one was in charge.

Equally, private veterinarians doing AMI on farm for ES are not included in these training activities. As mentioned in paragraph 15, one of the CAs has already taken steps to resolve this. 9 5.2.5 Supervision and audits
The two ACs have a system of internal audits and checks to monitor the performance of their OVs and ensure they deliver official controls adequately.

In one of the ACs, there are no arrangements to ensure that, following the approval process, a suitably short period of time for newly approved establishments other than slaughterhouses is established in which to carry out an FBO's audit or an operational inspection.

The system for review of approvals does not currently ensure, in one of the ACs, that the establishments maintain the approval for only those activities that are relevant or that the approval conditions for activities not carried out, continue to be met. 5.4 ORGANISATION AND IMPLEMENTATION OF OFFICIAL CONTROLS 5.4.1 Official controls on cattle identification and movements of animals Legal requirements Articles 3, 5, 6, 7, and 9a of Regulation (EC) No 1760/2000 of the European Parliament and of the Council. label_heading: Conclusions on organisation and implementation of official controls
paragraph_text: The implementation of the official controls does not ensure that PMI of all carcases and offal takes place in accordance with Article 19 of Regulation (EU) 2019/627.
According to the OVs' explanations and descriptions of the activities, in two of the six slaughterhouses audited (one in each AC), the PMI was not carried out in accordance with the legislation.

In one of them, the OV stated to have passed as fit for human consumption the carcase of an ES bovine without having inspected the lungs and green offal, as the FBO staff did not present them for inspection.

In the other slaughterhouse, where only one veterinarian is normally present, the OV explained that they would not be able to inspect the green offal (which would go directly to the gut room) of the carcases processed during the time they would spend in the lairage for AMI reasons as the slaughtering line would not stop. Nevertheless, those carcases would be health marked and passed as fit for human consumption. This is not in line with Article 19 of Regulation (EU) 2019/627.
In both cases, the OVs explained that, if any doubt, the slaughterhouse staff know what is fit and unfit for human consumption and would save for them any offal with signs of being unfit.

It has to be noted that, in the second AC and in order to address the fact that the PMI was not carried out in accordance with the EU requirements, management at central level took immediate action and arranged for a second and more experienced OV to be deployed to the slaughterhouse as a support mechanism.

Also in two of the six slaughterhouses, the FBO staff carried out the removal of the spinal cord, which is classed as a specified risk material, after the carcases had been inspected and health marked as fit for human consumption. This is not in line with Article 45 (q) to Regulation (EU) 2019/627. Procedures for poultry

Pending dispatch to the laboratory, samples can be stored in fridges or freezers, depending on the matrix and analyte concerned, under the control of the official sampler. Interviewed officials indicated that samples taken at slaughterhouses were sometimes be placed into the transportation boxes without preceding chilling/freezing.

Data requested by the audit team showed that, although most samples arrived at the laboratories on the day of sampling or one to two days afterwards, in some cases the time between sampling was much longer (up to 42 days). The AFB immediately responded to this new information, identified the main source of the delays and put in place corrective action.

The screening method for aminoglycosides in muscle was initially validated as a confirmatory method in line with pertinent EU requirements (26). However, due to consistently and unacceptably high reproducibility levels, the conclusion stated that the method would be used only as a semi-quantitative screening method. The audit team noted that no further elaboration/evidence was provided in a documented traceable manner to demonstrate that the method had a false compliant rate lower than or equal to 5 % ( error) (27).

The screening method for antibacterial agents in kidney was verified in line with applicable EU provisions (28). However, the documentation submitted for the screening method for antibacterial substances in milk suggested that only 12 samples (per concentration) were used for the verification, which did not correspond to the minimum number of 20 samples required to ensure that the method had a false compliant rate lower than or equal to 5 % ( error) (27).

The documentation submitted regarding the method for hormones in urine and serum demonstrated that the repeatability and reproducibility values were consistently identical which is not in line with EU requirements (29). These phenomena were not commented on or discussed in the validation report and the method was considered fit for purpose as a confirmatory method. The situation with non-commented identical repeatability and reproducibility values was seen for certain fortification levels in several other validation files scrutinised by the audit team, questioning the validity of the laboratory's conclusion that said methods were fit for their intended use.

The audit team noted numerous occasions where recovery or/and reproducibility values exceeded the ranges established in the EU legislation (30), e.g. for diclazuril and salinomycin in the coccidiostats confirmatory method. These occurrences were largely not evaluated/discussed in the validation files and consequently not taken into account for the decisions on methods' fitness for purpose.

The audit team noted that in all of the validation files scrutinised, stability was mentioned as a performance characteristic. However, the procedure for its assessment was substantially different from the protocol suggested in EU law (31) and essentially not adequate to provide sufficient knowledge on the stability of analytes, in particular in matrix. Combined with the absence of a temperature check on the incoming samples (see finding 51), this might influence the test results. The audit team scrutinised the implementation of internal quality controls for four samples (analysed in 2020-2021 by the largest national laboratory) where measurable quantities of veterinary medicinal products were found. In two of the four samples (diclofenac in bovine muscle and antibacterial substances in raw milk, both from 2020), the audit team observed that no matrix-based `positive control' samples were included in the analytical runs, which is not fully in line with EU requirements (33). The laboratory representative explained that this was due to absence of pertinent control samples and that this practice was discontinued since the beginning of 2021.

The audit team observed the control charts for the methods used for the four samples scrutinised and found that: a. in the control chart for penicillin V, the trueness based on results of more than 30 analytical runs was 184%, which substantially exceeds the range established in EU law (80-120%) (34). While the laboratory representative was aware about that breach, no action had been taken to address the situation. b. for the non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs method, very few points were available due to the low number of analytical series (since the relevant samples are collected during a narrow time window to ensure that the laboratory processes those in one go). For the screening method for antibacterial substances in milk, no sufficient evidence was submitted that quality control samples had been regularly used for the purpose of verifying ongoing method performance, which contradicts pertinent EU requirements (33).

For the same method, the audit team noted that once a suspect non-compliant result was identified, the same sample was run up to three times more before a decision was made to confirm the screened positive result with a chemical confirmatory method. This practice may lead to the situation where non-compliant results would not be identified due to false-compliant outcome of screening testing, is not in line with legal requirements (27), and contradicts the bioassay manual.

paragraph_text: The residue monitoring plan is generally implemented in accordance with legal requirements and planned arrangements. However, targeted sampling was not consistently ensured and the sampling strategies applied for several commodities were not adequate. In addition, the evident lack of supervision or other verification procedures, in relation to sampling officers not following the detailed instructions, contributes to the persistence of sampling errors and weakens the effectiveness of the residue monitoring. 5.1.4. For several samples taken at slaughterhouses, one sampling officer did not follow the existing procedures and guidelines regarding the selection of animals for sampling. E.g., samples for hormone testing were taken from male animals while only females should have been sampled according to the plan. For bovine sampling at slaughterhouse level, targeted sampling was not always implemented. The sampling inspector interviewed had no access to information on the outcome of official controls (e.g. previous non-compliant results) or background information about the producer and the farming system. The outcome of the ante mortem inspection (e.g. sex and age of the animal, secondary sexual characteristics, behavioural changes, signs of disease or chronic disorders, different health status of specific animals within a group) was also not considered in the choice of the animal to target for sampling and not in line with the applicable legal requirements (14). The system in place for collection, use and disposal of ABP and DP is largely adequate. For ABP derived from some species (fish, horses), the entire territory of Finland has been defined as a `remote area'. However, such designation is not justified since operational means of collection, disposal and use of ABP are available throughout the entire country. In practice, despite the absence of a risk assessment carried out by the competent authority, the impact of this shortcoming is probably limited and the quantities of ABP that might be disposed of by burial or landfilling are likely to be small, as most operators seem to make use of the existing collection arrangements. 5.3 OFFICIAL CONTROL

Domestic legislation defines the areas that have been categorised as `remote' under Article 19(1)(b) of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009. For ABP derived from some species, the entire territory of Finland is considered a remote area. In particular, ABP from slaughtering of horses and from aquatic animals can be disposed of by burial or landfilling throughout Finland, when authorised under environmental rules. However, according to the FFA, operators do not routinely avail of these possibilities.

This was confirmed during interviews held in a region where fish processing is an important economic activity. The audit team noted that, while this area was categorised as `remote' for ABP from aquatic animals, there were arrangements in place for collection and use of such ABP, in particular for feeding to fur animals or for other purposes outside the feed chain. Some of the inspection reports of food operators processing fish in other parts of Finland indicated similar collection arrangements for ABP.

The audit team noted that slaughtering of horses usually takes place in multi-species slaughterhouses, the majority of which are located in areas where ABP of the other species slaughtered are collected. ABP from horses can therefore be collected from such slaughterhouses. This was confirmed during the interview of an official veterinarian, who was substituting for other official veterinarians in several slaughterhouses, some of which were slaughtering horses.

Based on the above-mentioned, the audit team noted that there are viable collection and transport arrangements in areas that have been categorised as `remote' and consequently such areas do not meet the definition of a `remote area', as laid down in Article 3(23) of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009.

FFA representatives stated that for those species for which the entire territory of Finland is categorised as a `remote area', the risk assessments referred to in point (d) of Section 2 of Chapter III of Annex VI to Regulation (EU) No 142/2011 were not carried out. 5 Conclusion on the system in place for collection, use and disposal on ABP and DP

label_heading: Conclusion on registration, approval and listing
paragraph_text: Arrangements in place for registration, approval and listing provide assurance that the vast majority of operators active along the chain of ABP and DP are known, which facilitates the implementation of official controls. However, an incomplete and, currently, not reliable registration of fur farms concerned with intra-species recycling prevents the system from being fully in line with Union rules. 5.3.2 Planning of official controls

The FFA has implemented a system for registration of fur animal farms where the feeding of fur animals (foxes and racoon dogs) with proteins derived from animal of the same species can take place (such feeding is hereafter referred to as `intra-species recycling'). An accurate and complete registration of farm is important for the purpose of official controls, as operators must comply with specific requirements (Chapter I of Annex II to Regulation (EU) No 142/2011). Farms where intra-species recycling take place are registered in the animal keepers' register with an indication of the concerned species (for other farms there is a statement that intra-species recycling is not carried out). 6 2

The audit team noted that inspections of fur animal farms must verify that these are correctly registered for intra-species recycling, if applicable. However, some MVO interviewed stated that they usually rely on the farmers statement that they are registered (or not) rather than checking the register. This led to situations where, when comparing register information and the corresponding inspection reports, the audit team noted contradictory information.

The audit team also noted that the information contained in the register was not fully reliable. The FFA explained that the migration of data between the previous and current IT system supporting the animal keepers' register resulted in inconsistencies in the information recorded. The FFA stated that the data contained in the register would be corrected.

RVO carry out checks on animal welfare, including at fur farms, during which is it required that the information contained in the animal keepers' register is checked (in general and not only for intra-species recycling). Some RVO interviewed stated that during such checks, in case of incorrect registration, the farmer is asked to update the register and that this is usually done orally. As a consequence, the FFA could not provide evidence of such checks or that follow-up had taken place in case of incorrect registration (which, in any case, would prove difficult in the absence of official records).

Based on the above-mentioned gaps, the ability of the current system to ensure that the register of fur animal farms (where intra-species recycling occurs) is updated over time is rather limited and this register is likely to remain incomplete. This does not ensure that the requirements of point 3(a)(i) of Chapter I of Annex II to Regulation (EU) No 142/2011 are fulfilled. Conclusion on registration, approval and listing

This is, in part, further aggravated by the lack of updated documented procedures. 5.2 IMPLEMENTATION OF OFFICIAL CONTROLS ON IMPORTS/TRANSITS OF ANIMALS AND GOODS

The DGAL informed the audit team that BCP staff have access to guidance documents and instructions via its quality assurance intranet websites. The documents include three vade mecums respectively for import controls on animals, goods of animal origin and feed of non-animal origin. The DGAL staff also have access to the IMPADON database for further information to support documentary checks. With the exception of the vade mecum for live animals, the guidance documents and instructions have yet to be updated in order to take account of EU legislation which entered in force as of 14 December 2019.

The DGAL "guide d'inspection" contains general instructions for the performance of official controls at BCPs by its staff. It includes measures to be taken in the case of non- compliant consignments, in particular, destruction, redispatch and special treatment. This guide has also yet to be updated to take account of the measures provided for in Articles 65, 66 and 67 of the OCR.

The DGAL stated that the reasons for not having updated these instructions were due the prioritisation of staff resources in the preparations for the withdrawal of United Kingdom from the EU and the management of business continuity during the Covid-19 pandemic. The DGAL confirmed they would update the documented procedures in the period 2022-2023.

The competent authorities have documented procedures and guidance for the performance of official controls on consignments of animals and goods entering the EU, 8 in line with Article 12(1) of the OCR. However these have not been updated as appropriate, which is not in line with Article 12(3)(b) of that Regulation.

However, the lack of recent internal audits of the system of official controls on imports of animals and goods, including verification of compliance of the BCPs with minimum requirements, has had an adverse impact on the effectiveness of implementation of official import controls, and on the competent authorities' obligation to ensure the availability of suitable border control facilities (see section 5.3.), in particular for checks on goods of animal origin and feed of non-animal origin. This is, in part, further aggravated by the lack of updated documented procedures. 5.2 IMPLEMENTATION OF OFFICIAL CONTROLS ON IMPORTS/TRANSITS OF ANIMALS AND GOODS

However, a number of shortcomings were noted in the implementation of official controls. They concerned, for example, prior notification of arrival of consignments, documentary checks, transhipment and transit, and decisions on consignments and, in addition, the performance of documentary checks for food of non-animal origin other than upon arrival of the consignment at designated BCPs. These shortcomings collectively undermine the effectiveness and appropriateness of official controls to ensure that only compliant consignments of animals and goods enter the Union. 5.3 MINIMUM REQUIREMENTS FOR BORDER CONTROL POSTS

The audit team evaluated one CHED-P authorised for transhipment at a port BCP. For this consignment, there was a five-month delay in notification of the arrival. The CHED- P for this consignment was, following a documentary check only, finalised as a transhipment to a third country. In reality, this consignment was stored for at least five months at the terminal. The competent authority, although having a transhipment procedure in place, was not aware of this consignment until its notification in TRACES.

All consignments notified at an airport BCP were subjected to at least a documentary check and an identity check, even in cases where the transhipment period was not exceeded. However, for 19 of these consignments, no date of departure was indicated in part I of the CHED-P, thus not allowing calculation of the transhipment period. In 17 of 21 cases where a physical check was not done, it was stated that the reason for not performing the physical check was `reduced checks'. For three of the five consignments 14 on which physical checks were performed, the transhipment period had not been exceeded.

The DGAL technical instruction for transhipped consignments does not require any pre- notification or checks other than in cases where the transhipment period has been exceeded. In such cases, those consignments should be subject to a documentary check, and with an identity and physical check only in cases of suspicion of non-compliance.

The DGAL could not provide evidence that the BCPs of transhipment acted in line with their instruction. In addition, as noted in section 5.1.5, BCPs do not have systematic access to customs declarations or manifest data, and as a consequence, BCPs only rely on the operator's notification of transhipment.

The audit team noted that the procedure in place does not ensure that, in the event that a transhipment takes place, it is done in line with Articles 13 and 16 of Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2019/2124. 5.2.3 Transit and ship supply procedures

During the current audit cycle, five audits were planned in 2017, whereas six were carried out, and in 2018, three out of six planned audits were carried out. No audits took place between 2019 and 2021, with none planned for the remainder of 2021. The DGAL explained that during this period, audits could not be carried out for resource reasons, activities related to the preparedness for the withdrawal of United Kingdom from the EU and the COVID-19 pandemic.

The audits are concluded with individual audit reports, detailing the objectives, scope, findings and conclusions, and recommendations if applicable. Follow-up of previous audit recommendations is carried out by desk-based assessment or during the subsequent on-the-spot audit. As no audits have taken place since 2018 for above-mentioned reasons, follow-up on the 2018 audits is still outstanding.

The General Inspectorate of Services of the DGCCRF also carries out internal audits and verification checks. The prioritisation of these internal audits is based on an analysis of risk factors which leads to the establishment of a multi-year program for 2016-2020. The audit of official controls on imports of food of non-animal origin and food contact materials, which was scheduled for 2020, did not take place. The DGCCRF stated that this was due in part to the COVID-19 pandemic and the transfer of responsibilities to the DGDDI).

The DGCCRF stated that the multiannual audit programme is currently being revised, but that there are no plans to integrate import control audits in view of the transfer (see section 5.1.1). The DGDDI stated that it did not yet plan any audits for the same reason.

The audit team noted that the competent authorities have procedures in place to verify the effectiveness of their controls and carry out internal audits in line with Articles 5(1)(a), 6(1) and 12(2) of the OCR. However, there has been a shortfall in its implementation as no such internal audits have been carried since 2018, prior to the entry into force of the OCR. paragraph_text: Significant delays in obtaining laboratory test results for some biotoxins lower the effectiveness of weekly monitoring, delays area closures and can increase the risk of placing unsafe product on the market.

The monitoring programme indicates that biotoxins monitoring results that exceed the limits established in in Annex III, Section VII, Chapter V Point 2 to Regulation (EC) No 853/2004, trigger an immediate closure of production areas and, in one autonomous community, an increased sampling of water and bivalve molluscs in the adjacent production areas. Only one of the autonomous communities had a closure in the last two years due to exceedance of biotoxins. The audit team was informed that in Spain these controls are performed by food safety/public health authorities at auction halls, dispatch centres and processing 9 establishment. The controls are documental, on identity, and on results of sampling performed by operators. However, some autonomous communities do not take official samples to verify compliance with the health standards laid down in Chapter V of Section VII of Annex III to Regulation (EC) No 853/2004. 5.1.6 Movement of live bivalve molluscs and registration document accompanying batches

The absence of national reference laboratories for biotoxins and E.coli at primary production, with the consequent gap on their tasks and responsibilities, is an important shortcoming in a control system for which laboratory performance has high impact.

The competent authority has not designated National Reference Laboratories either for E. coli or for biotoxins testing of live bivalve molluscs sampled at primary production level for the monitoring of production areas, contrary to the requirements of Article 100(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

Due to the above currently there is no coordination of activities of the official laboratories involved in testing of live bivalve molluscs sampled at primary production level. Nor organisation of proficiency testing and respective follow up for those laboratories or of any of the other tasks under the responsibility of a national reference laboratory, contrary to the required by Article 101 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

The designation of official control laboratories does not yet include all relevant laboratories, and is lacking in details to ensure timely provision of results, and efficient and effective coordination and supervision. As a consequence laboratory underperformance or failures may be detected with delay, or go undetected, negatively impacting on the quality of official controls.

One of the laboratories for biotoxins could be evaluated and was determined to be providing reliable results for the ASP and lipophilic toxins testing it performs. The other laboratory could not be fully evaluated and the data received causes doubts on PSP method validation and accuracy, and on PSP proficiency testing. Therefore, quality and reliability of the testing it performs is doubtful. 6 OVERALL CONCLUSION The control systems in place in Spain generally meet the requirements of the relevant EU legislation and are correctly implemented. The competent authority has established the location and boundaries of "production zones", monitors them individually for microbiological quality and classifies them. They conform to the EU concept of production areas, but the use of the term "production zones" is misleading.

The current classification of production areas (or "production zones" in those production areas that are further divided) is not in line with the EU requirements. This poses certain doubts that the level of contamination of molluscs harvested corresponds to the value expected according to their classification. In addition, as the plan does not consider sampling other mollusc species available in the same geographical location, this generates a risk of misclassification of the corresponding areas.

The lack of sanitary surveys questions the validity of the designated sampling points for microbiological monitoring and their representativeness for production areas, which has direct implications in the adequate classification of production areas.

The fact that the competent authority: does not close or reclassify the production area when certain regulatory limits for microbiological quality are exceeded for the first time, has not established review periods, and reverts the downgrade of classification with a few good results, may result in the placing on the market of bivalve molluscs with amounts of E. coli higher than the permitted ones, therefore being a potential risk for consumers.

Although biotoxin episodes can be therefore overlooked or underestimated during monitoring, the risk of presence of biotoxins in Croatian molluscs does not seems high as data from previous years show very few episodes of biotoxins in Croatian waters.

Laboratories provide, in principle, reliable results but there is certain risk of underestimation of biotoxins as laboratories did not find conclusive explanations for unsatisfactory and questionable results in proficiency tests.

Regarding the ASP laboratory reviewed: The laboratory validated and accredited this method in 2009 and it has not renewed the validation since then (according to the information provided, it was due to the considerable amount of certified reference material that it implied and the corresponding costs, and because there was no ASP in Croatian waters). The laboratory carried out the validation in mussels, although some of the samples tested in this laboratory were from other molluscs' species. This may have an impact on the testing results due to the potential matrix effect. The laboratory carried out the testing according to a SOP, using reference material tissue as internal quality control.

Regarding the PSP laboratory visited: The laboratory recently revalidated this method in December 2020. The accreditation of this method did not have within its scope all the compounds that this laboratory tested. The laboratory carried out the testing according to a SOP, and used only certified reference material. There were internal quality controls established for the method, tested in each sequence of analysis. The laboratory tested all the relevant PSP compounds, however the SOP did not reflect it (i.e. GTX 6 and C3, 4). One of the laboratories recently started the revalidation of the method and the other laboratory scheduled a revalidation in 2021. In both cases, the revalidation was going to include other mollusc species, which is imperative in order to take into account the potential matrix effect in the testing results. The national legislation that incorporates the EU requirements is obsolete and does not correctly interpret some of these requirements, which is of particular relevance in relation to the decisions that the competent authority takes subsequent to the monitoring of production areas for microbiological quality. The MoA, which designs the monitoring plan that is the basis for the official control of production areas, has a reduced oversight of the sector. This is partly due to the currently significant lack of input from NRLs into the monitoring plan. All this has a negative impact in the effectiveness of the control of production areas.

The NRL for biotoxins is not entirely fulfilling all its responsibilities and tasks, which can affect negatively the harmonisation and improvement in the performance of testing methods by other official laboratories and the competence of staff when using these complex analytical methods. 6 OVERALL CONCLUSION The national legislation that incorporates the EU requirements does not provide an adequate framework for the official control of production areas as it is obsolete and does not correctly interpret some of these requirements, particularly relevant in relation to the decisions subsequent to microbiological monitoring of production areas. label_heading: Conclusions on oral vaccination of foxes
paragraph_text: The absence of oral vaccination campaigns in 2018 had negative impact on rabies eradication, and resulted in a decrease of the wildlife population immunity and a higher risk of spread of the disease. Similar negative effect on the rabies eradication is likely to happen in 2021 due to the absence of campaign during the spring.

label_heading: Conclusions on oral vaccination of foxes
paragraph_text: The official controls on vaccine quality, its storage conditions, and manual and aerial distribution provided timely verification that the vaccine quality met the contract specifications, and that vaccine distribution was in line with the approved vaccination plan. The late implementation of the spring campaigns increases the risk of reducing the vaccine efficacy after their distribution. The authority and contractor took some actions to mitigate this risk but they had not verified their effectiveness. 5.1 MONITORING, AWARENESS AND SURVEILLANCE Legal requirements 8 Articles 10 to 13, 15, 18, 24, 26, 27, 31(1), 32(1), 34, 46, 57, 72 to 75, 77 to 79, 81 and 257(1)(a)(ii) of Regulation (EU) 201

The central authority did not apply the programme in 2018, which had a negative effect on the progress of eradication. The national legislation on public procurement caused the authority to miss another spring vaccination campaign in 2021, with likely similar negative effect on the rabies eradication as in 2018 (See Table 1 in Annex 3). Therefore, it could not follow the recommendations of the 2015 EFSA report and the 2015 Commission guidelines advising vaccination continuation for at least two years after the last reported case of rabies. This is not line with Section 2 (point 1(a)) of Chapter 1 in Part 1 of Annex V to Regulation (EU) 2020/689.

The spring campaigns in 2019 and 2020 started at the end of May or beginning of June and finished in July, when the outside temperature was higher. The regular late start and finish of spring campaigns were not in line with the 2015 Commission guidelines. 4 7. The central authority and contractor took some preventive actions to mitigate risk associated to high temperatures (e.g. reduce efficacy of the vaccine), in particular by adapting the vaccination plan and the daily vaccine distribution schedules prioritising distribution early in the morning and trying to avoid days where temperatures rose over 30ºC. But the authority had not verified their effectiveness, e.g. they had not monitored th

paragraph_text: The inadequate implementation of monitoring of vaccination effectiveness in some areas of the country, combined with the sub-optimal surveillance for rabies, do not allow the authority to detect promptly the potential issues in the rabies eradication, in particular in oral vaccination of wild carnivores. This hinders the authority's capability to identify quickly the areas of the country at a higher risk of rabies spread where they need to focus additional prevention, surveillance and control efforts.

In 2019, the majority of counties sampled 4 or more animals /100 km2, therefore reaching their sampling targets. The percentage of the target reached varied between counties, ranging from 51.33% to 165.46 % (for the fluorescent antibody test (FAT) tests). Seven counties (out of 40) took less than 80 % of their targeted number of samples, with two counties presenting data well below their targets. Those counties sampled only two animals /100 km2 (just above 50% of their plans).

In 2020, the variation between the counties in the percentage of the target reached was similar to the one in the previous year, ranging from 48% to 153.09 % (for the FAT tests). 26 counties achieved their sampling targets. Nine counties reached less than 80 % of their planned number of samples, with four counties well below their targets (less than 60 %). One county, bordering Ukraine; i.e. with a high risk of rabies incursion from the adjacent infected area, was not able to reach 50 % of the planned sampling target (less than 2 animals /100 km2).

The audit team analysed data provided for 2019 and 2020 for some counties showing that there had been an uneven geographical distribution of the samples taken within their territories. Both aspects; i.e. some counties not analysing the necessary number of samples and the potentially biased sample taken only from some hunting grounds, can significantly reduce the representativeness and reliability of the results obtained from their analysis and the validity of the conclusions drawn up at county and national level on the levels of immunity reached.

The authority has access to estimates of the geographical distribution of the population of wild carnivores in Romania, including the yearly hunting quotas and the hunting bags obtained at the end of the season, broken down per species and for each hunting ground. The data (see Map 5 in Annex 3) show an increased density of the jackal population in the southern part of the country, even exceeding in some counties that of the fox population. However, the authority does not take into account the estimates of all population of wild carnivores to fine-tune the planning of the rabies monitoring activities; e.g. targeting the jackal population in the selected area to obtain a representative image

The authority designed the rabies monitoring activities in accordance with the approved rabies programme and with general obligations in that respect laid down in Articles 3(points 1(a)(iv) and (b)(ii)) and 4 (point 1(b)(i)) of Regulation (EU) 2020/689. However, they did not apply those activities as planned. This is not in line with the provisions of the rabies eradication programme, recommendations of the 2013 WHO report and of the 2015 Commission guidelines, and point 1(d), of Section 2 of Chapter 1 of Part I of Annex V to Regulation (EU) 2020/689.

Despite the activities mentioned above, the authorities still lack sufficient understanding of how different factors contribute to the weaknesses identified in some areas of the country, e.g. underperformance in monitoring vaccination effectiveness, low levels of 16 immunity in wildlife in certain counties and under-notification and investigation of suspect cases and indicator animals. They have not identified and shared good practices that resulted in the adequate application of those measures in some well performing counties.

label_heading: Conclusions on monitoring, awareness and surveillance
paragraph_text: Although there are well-tailored information campaigns to raise public awareness on the disease, there has been an obvious decrease in the reporting of suspect cases and indicator animals investigated to exclude the presence of rabies in the last two years. This prevents the authorities from having more accurate and up-to-date epidemiological information on the rabies incidence and its geographical distribution in wild carnivores in Romania. Consequently, they might not be able to apply the measures promptly and to adapt them to reduce the risk of spread of rabies.

label_heading: Conclusions on the organisational aspects of the plant health controls
paragraph_text: There is an established laboratory network for the implementation of official controls. However, the performance of the official testing for ToBRFV in official laboratories is not verified by the NRL, who does not organise ring tests for this purpose. The official laboratories do not participate either in ring tests, organised by other entities, to achieve the same verification. As a consequence, the CA has no information on how reliable these tests are in detecting the presence of the virus. Any 7 measure based on an unreliable laboratory result has negative influence on the controls. 5.2 SURVEYS ON THE PRESENCE OF TOBRFV Legal requirements Article 34(4) and (5) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

Up until the time of the audit, the NRL provided technical and scientific assistance on request. However, it has not organised inter-laboratory comparative testing or proficiency tests between the official laboratories, although this is appropriate and therefore required by Article 101(1)(c) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

Almost each RPS has their own official laboratory where initial tests and the vast majority of confirmatory tests are carried out. The regional laboratories have experienced staff for working with molecular methods, and have already performed analysis with at least one of the methods listed in the Annex to Regulation (EU) 2020/1191. The RPS laboratory is nominated as Regional Reference Laboratory in those regions where more than one laboratory carries out the tests of official samples. However, the proficiency of the official laboratories' ToBRFV analysis with the listed methods has never been assessed by ring tests.

paragraph_text: The National Contingency Plan was prepared and updated according to the provisions of the EU legislation and provides a general framework for the implementation of the necessary actions in the case of an outbreak. However, it does not contain specific provisions required by the EU legislation, which are within the competency of the 12 ACCAs. The absence of information on how these provisions are addressed by the regions calls into question the ability of ACs to control any future outbreaks.

The regional autonomy established in the Spanish Constitution means that the National Contingency Plan cannot specify the minimum resources for controls that each AC shall make available, including procedures for making additional resources available as necessary. Similarly, it cannot specify rules detailing how to identify the owners of plants subject to measures or how to notify the order of removal and powers to access private properties. These are specifically required by Article 3 of Regulation (EU) 2020/1201. These issues may be dealt at AC level and annexed to the national contingency plan. paragraph_text: The official controls and other official activities of the RPS regarding the application of the eradication and containment measures against A. chinensis, A. glabripennis and P. japonica are not sufficiently coordinated and there is a lack of procedures, which lead to inconsistent application of the control measures and decreases their effectiveness. 5.2 SPECIFIC SURVEYS AND NOTIFICATIONS Legal requirements Article 22 to 24 of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031. Article 5 of Decision (EU) 2012/138. Article 6 of Decision (EU) 2015/893. Article 32(1) of Regulation (EU) 2019/1715. Findings

There are general documented procedures in place, but there are none regarding the application of the eradication and containment measures to be taken following official controls against A. chinensis, A. glabripennis and P. japonica, contrary to Article 12 (1) of Regulation 2017/625. This has contributed to the different implementation of the eradication measures in the regions (see also sections 5.5 and 5.6).

The DGAV informed the audit team that according to the national Decree Law, professional operators carrying out the activities referred to in Article 65(1) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031, in Portugal, are obliged to be registered in a register kept by, or accessible by, the DGAV, and shared a summary list of registered operators to the audit team. Other operators, such as producers of citrus fruits (orchards) are registered under agricultural legislation, but the DGAV does not have direct access to those registers.

According to Article 65 referred to above, Member States may decide for further categories of operators to be registered if so justified by the pest risk presented by the plants that they grow. paragraph_text: The administrative delays in providing formulation details to the formulation laboratory during 2020 delayed the timely delivery of analytical results, and weakened the overall effectiveness of the control programme.

In 2020, the laboratory processed samples in an average of 34 days from receipt of the sample to reporting the results. The laboratory explained that analysis can take considerably longer (up to six months) in a small number (circa. 5%) of cases. This occurs in cases where the laboratory requests the formulation details from MARD and there are delays in receiving this information. This information is necessary for the laboratory to conduct the most appropriate analysis and to determine if the analytical result demonstrates compliance. In all cases, the report template was used. However, in two of the reports reviewed, there was no evidence that the inspectors had checked that the risk-based selection of operators for sampling was properly carried out by the CBs. For these operators an attestation of conversion was granted stating that the operator is engaged in organic production but it is not allowed to market products with an organic reference. In addition, the two CBs visited have risk analysis procedures in place to select operators for additional visits. The CBs have a mixed risk assessment based on quantitative and qualitative factors. However, one CB did not have the volume of production as a risk factor in its procedure, which is not in line with Article 65(4) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008 and the INAO Directive.

The two CBs also have procedures for sampling based on risk. The audit team noted that even if most of the operators selected for sampling are based on risk there is also an important number of operators that are randomly selected by the inspectors. Therefore, it 10 is very difficult for the CBs to have an overview to ensure that operators selected for sampling in the end are those posing the highest risk. In one CB, around 30 % and 40% operators classified as low risk were selected for sampling in 2019 and 2020 respectively. This is not in line with Article 65(2) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008.

At the beginning of the year, inspectors are given an indicative annual plan of inspections with the operators to inspect and, in the CB's database, inspectors have online access to all necessary information concerning previous controls of the operators, and any pending non-compliances. However, the two CBs could not provide evidence that inspectors have the information the operator must submit to the CB when engaged in organic production in line with Article 63 of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008 (a full description of the unit and of the precautionary measures).

The reports issued by the CB inspectors lack detail on how verification takes place, with no objective evidence attached to the reports. The reports consist of a template where inspectors tick off the aspects verified with little or no further description of, or references made, to the documents or records checked or any explanation to provide evidence that the item checked was in line with requirements.

For example, the audit team reviewed a report of an inspection carried out at an operator who has plant and livestock production. The inspector stated that the density of animals was in line with the requirements as were the records of veterinarian medicines and the 12 consumption of feed. The inspector also stated that the purchase and use of inputs and the quantity of feed produced and used was in line with requirements. However, these statements were not supported by evidence as the reports lack details on how the checks had been made. This constitutes significant misconduct on the part of the CB given there is an ongoing alert about Ethylene oxide contamination of sesame seeds and other products from India and there should be immediate exchange of information between the CBs and the CAs in order to enable the CAs to notify the Commission and other Member States through OFIS.

The epidemiological investigations of the most recent outbreaks were incomplete and/or incorrectly estimated the time during which ASF virus may have existed on the holding. This could negatively affect the ability to identify the possible sources of disease and to implement forward and backward tracing correctly.

The effectiveness of ASF surveillance varies across the island, but data demonstrates a decline in the presence of ASF in the wild boar population and of seropositive pigs in farms. There is an under-reporting to the Commission and member states on ASF outbreaks, as Italian authorities do not consider seropositive pigs on holdings as confirmed cases. The temporal and spatial clustering of passive surveillance creates a risk of new cases not being detected quickly, in particular outside the defined infected area.

So far, the impact of this initiative has been limited. Indeed, most on low or medium risk of the outbreaks on commercial establishments during 2021 establishments occurred on premised in the low or medium risk categories. Out of the commercial establishments keeping more than 65 pigs, around 60 % are assigned a medium risk, and 20% a low or high risk respectively.

The audit team was provided with a copy of the co-operation agreement with Customs and the SPSMoA, which outlines their responsibilities. Customs also have a dedicated plant health liaison o

The representative from Customs stated that it is the Customs official's responsibility to check for the presence of a phytosanitary certificate (PC) when carrying out checks on plants, plant products and other objects. Furthermore, it is the responsibility of the SPSMoA to carry out the checks on any items of plants for planting contained in passenger luggage and in postal and courier consignments. According to the documented procedures, any non-compliances found by the Customs services are rejected, returned to the country of origin/sender or destroyed. label_heading: Conclusions on the surveys on the presence of ToBRFV
paragraph_text: The annual surveys for ToBRFV concentrated on high-risk production sites, related to outbreaks and to the follow-up of contaminated seed lots. As the planned number of random surveys at tomato producers was not achieved, and pepper growers were not checked, the actual outbreak situation may not be entirely known, which could compromise the eradication efforts. 5.3 MEASURES RELATED TO THE CONFIRMED PRESENCE OF TOBRFV Legal requirements Articles 17, 29, 31 and 52 and Annex II Section 1 of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031. Article 4 of Regulation (EU) 2020/1191. Findings

In 2020 and 2021, the FASFC carried out annual surveys for the detection of ToBRFV, which were planned after a risk assessment, as required by Article 5(2) of Regulation (EU) 2020/1191. Only tomato fruit growers were targeted. Growers of Capsicum sp. were included in the 2020 and 2021 survey programmes, but sampling was not carried out, on the assumption that pepper producers generally cultivate resistant varieties. Concerning the surveys on the market the FASFC stated that growers comply with the marketing standards, i.e., sort out of symptomatic fruits. Therefore, it is difficult to find symptomatic fruits on the market.

The controls at the places of production of specified plants for planting are in line with EU requirements and aimed at reducing the risk of introduction of the virus to fruit production establishments. As the timing of the inspections is not appropriate for each lot at sites with various growth periods, there is a risk of not detecting some infections. 5.5 CONTROLS ON MOVEMENT OF SPECIFIED SEEDS WITHIN THE EU Legal requirements Article 7 of Regulation (EU) 2020/1191. Findings

The audit team noted that the inspection and sampling procedure of the production of specified plants for planting is in line with provisions of Article 6(1)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2020/1191. However, the inspections which are carried out once a year per production site cannot cover those specified plants for planting which are not present during the official visit. For sites with continuous production of multiple crops with various sowing times, a single inspection may not be considered as appropriate to obtain comprehensive information about the status of the production site. Conclusions on the controls of the movement of specified plants for planting within the EU

label_heading: Conclusions on the eradication measures against A. chinensis
paragraph_text: The presence of the pest in previously and regularly surveyed areas show that SI monitoring is incapable of detecting even heavy infestations of A. chinensis. This significantly undermines efforts to stop the further spread of the pest.

The audit team visited an area just next to the outbreak site of Jankolovica, in the DA established in 2019, where the SI informed the audit team that they had carried out one survey in June 2020, three surveys in 2021 (July/July/August), and one survey in the beginning of June 2022, all with negative results. HAPIH also conducted eight surveys in this DA in 2020, all of which had negative results. During the visit, the audit team quickly noted a large number of flying beetles, and at least 18 adult specimens of A. chinensis were caught in a 30-minute period during the visit. The ANSES-LSV is the National Reference Laboratory (NRL) for Xf. It coordinates and supervises the activities of the laboratories, which are designated for testing official plant and insect vector samples for Xf. label_heading: Conclusions on the eradication measures in the Region PACA
paragraph_text: Although there were notable improvements since the 2021 audit in the number of IZs with completed eradication activities, the removal of plants including the positive tested and the potentially infected ones was carried out with substantial delays in most of the IZs, facilitating the spread of the disease.

Consequently, the extent of the infection in the BZs cannot be comprehensively identified with the applied statistical methods, and the established IZs only partially reflect the current spread.

label_heading: Conclusions on the containment measures against A. glabripennis
paragraph_text: The intensive monitoring activity of the regional CAs within the DAs is suitable to detect the occurrence of any additional infested plants. Although the change to containment strategy was not in line with EU requirements, the measures implemented by the regional phytosanitary services are generally in line with the provisions of the EU legislation regarding containment. However, issues with the potential movement of green waste out of the DA in Centre-Val de Loire could decrease the effectiveness of the official measures.

Although the order of the prefect specifies that transport of plants and plant material of the specified plants from the DA is prohibited, compliance with this requirement is not ensured. The municipal green waste disposal site, where the public can bring pruned material or any green waste, is located outside the DA. The movement of such material is not controlled, which does not comply with Annex II section 3 (1)(d) of Decision (EU) 2012/138. 5.5.4 Tracing activity

label_heading: Conclusions on planning of official controls
paragraph_text: According to the data reviewed by the audit team, the ten regions that implemented the programme collected 13,551 bovine animals, 15,304 small ruminants and 3,551 pigs (9).

label_heading: Conclusions on planning of official controls
paragraph_text: The public awareness of the programme varies between the regions. In two of the four regions visited, the regional authorities had actively informed animal keepers about the programme, using leaflets, local media and local administrations. In the other two, the information action had a much smaller scale. Consequently, farmers' awareness of the programme varies and is best in those regions where the programme is already being implemented.

label_heading: Conclusions on planning of official controls
paragraph_text: Out of the nine regions currently implementing the programme, two have already achieved the foreseen target for collection of fallen bovine animals. In the remaining seven, the collection of fallen cattle ranges from almost half of the expected number of fallen animals (a region with a longer period of implementation) to zero (in a region where the programme has been implemented only since November 2021) (10). In those regions where the collection programme is not fully operational or has not started yet, farmers are burying fallen animals on their own lands (see finding 31).

paragraph_text: The programme covers the collection of ABP and fallen animals of the following species: bovine, porcine, ovine and caprine. For all of these species, DGVS has estimated the annual collection target (i.e. the mortality rate) at 4% of the total population. The programme does not cover collection of other farmed species, e.g. poultry or equidae; however, regions may include these upon their own decision. While one of the four regions visited included poultry in the programme, another one excluded pigs. The RVS representatives from the region where the programme did not cover pigs, stated that this situation will change because operators of smaller scale pig holdings and backyard farmers have re

label_heading: Conclusions on planning of official controls
paragraph_text: The collection of pigs, sheep and goats is by far less effective than that of cattle. For pigs, the percentage of fallen stock collected (by region) ranges from zero to 29.71% of the expected number of fallen stock (4% of the population). The VS representatives met informed the audit team that in some regions, including those visited during the audit, the outbreaks of African swine fever happening in the recent years resulted in the issuing of a decision allowing for on-site burial of pigs to prevent further spread of the disease. Moreover, large pig farms usually have their own arrangements for collection and disposal of fallen animals directly by ABP processors. However, there are no data

label_heading: Conclusions on planning of official controls
paragraph_text: For sheep and goats, the percentage of fallen animals collected (by region) remains far from the expected target (4% of the population) and ranges from 0.01 to 9.28% of the target. In the regions visited, the RVS officials met explained that sheep and goats spend more than half of the year free-grazing in mountainous areas with difficult access, where collection is practically not possible. This part of the year represents also the period with the highest proportion of deaths of small ruminants as losses usually happen around and shortly after the lambing season.

label_heading: Conclusions on implementation of official controls
paragraph_text: With the exception of controls on low capacity incinerators and, more significantly, official sampling, official controls are mostly implemented as planned and are largely suitable to check operator compliance with the applicable Union requirements on ABP and DP. However, and similar to what has been seen in the plant approval process, in some instances official controls have erroneously concluded on operator compliance when in fact this is not the case, thus weakening confidence in the reliability of said controls.

label_heading: Conclusions on registration, approval and listing
paragraph_text: The registration of establishments and regular updating of the lists of establishments is effective and facilitates the planning of official controls. The national rules for approval of establishments are in line with EU requirements, however, the implementation of the rules is deficient resulting in a situation where an ABP plant whose conditional approval has expired, can continue to operate. This undermines an otherwise well-functioning approval process with resulting risks to public and animal health. 5.2.2 Planning of official controls

paragraph_text: Official controls do not verify compliance with the requirements for milk-derived products used for feeding of farmed animals. This, combined with procedures for the authorisation of farms (using milk-derived products for feeding pigs) that do not include an assessment of the risks of feeding such ABP in the context of possible outbreak of epizootic diseases, could present a risk in case of an outbreak of such diseases, in particular foot-and-mouth disease. 10 49. label_heading: Conclusions on planning of official controls
paragraph_text: In the dairy sector, official controls covering food hygiene requirements include checks on the disposal of ABP from the processing of milk. However, such controls do not cover the use of milk-derived products for the feeding of farmed animals contrary to the requirements of Article 4.3 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009. In particular, the audit team noted that there were no controls on sweet whey (a by-product of the manufacture of semi- hard cheeses) dispatched to farms for the feeding of pigs. As a result, such whey, which originates from the clotting of pasteurised milk but whose pH is not necessarily below six, was sent to farms that were not authorised to receive it on the basis of the r

label_heading: Conclusions on planning of official controls
paragraph_text: The audit team noted that, while there is a process for the authorisation of such farms, it is incomplete as it does not require the abovementioned assessment. The process is based solely on a declaration by the farmer, which results in the registration of the farm. At the time of the audit, there were no farms registered for the use of milk-derived products for the feeding of animals (such as pigs) susceptible to foot and mouth disease.

The system in place for collection, treatment and disposal of ABP is largely capable of ensuring a safe management of ABP an DP. However, ABP from the treatment of hides are not disposed of in line with EU rules and some ABP from on-farm slaughter are disposed of by burial, while this is not authorised under EU rules for ABP.

Domestic legislation authorises, throughout the country, on-site burial of animal carcasses and Category 2 material, consisting of ABP from on-farm slaughter, provided that the amount does not exceed 40 kg a week. This is not in line with EU rules, in particular Article 13 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009, which do not provide for any exemption for routinely burying these types of ABP (outside of remote areas).

For bovine animals, an authorisation from DGAV (regional services) is required before on-farm slaughter takes place; animals must be younger than 12 months and the number of slaughters is limited to two per year. As part of the authorisation process, DGAV must verify that ABP from such slaughter is collected by an authorised ABP operator. In one of the regions visited, where more than 800 authorisations were granted between 2019 and 2022, the abovementioned rules were enforced. In the other region visited, where between 10 to 20 authorisations were given on an annual basis, the on-farm slaughter was in certain cases authorised without any prior check that ABP would be collected by an authori

In one of the regions visited, official controls identified that ABP from the treatment of hides by tanneries (before the tanning process) were incorrectly disposed of as municipal waste, contrary to Article 14 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009. DGAV informed the audit team that, to date, no solution had been found to process such material in Portugal. Category 3 (and Category 1) processing plants were not willing to accept these by- products from hides due to difficulties in processing them. Consequently, at the time of the audit, such ABP were not disposed of in line with ABP rules. Conclusions on the system in place for collection, use and disposal of ABP and DP

Domestic legislation defines the areas that have been categorised as `remote' under Article 19(1)(b) of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009. In mainland Portugal, five geographical areas are designated as `remote'. The reasons being that these areas have low density of animal population, include natural parks or mountains and, because of their geography, present collection difficulties and are distant from establishments for processing and disposal of ABP. In these areas, on-the-spot burial of bovine, ovine, caprine, and porcine animals is authorised. Based on discussions held with the ABP operator managing collection of fallen stock in the northern and central parts of Portugal, collection is possible in most areas, except those 5 where trucks have no physical access. In addition, the fact that ABP are collected from farms with intensive animal production located in remote areas implies that trucks have access to, at least, part of these areas. Therefore, since there are viable collection and transports arrangements in parts of the areas categorised as `remote', such areas do not meet the definition of a `remote area' in Article 3(23) of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009.
