label_heading: Conclusions on implementation of official controls
paragraph_text: Official controls on collection and disposal of ABP are in place at food business operators. However, they are not effective enough to verify compliance with all applicable requirements and can either overlook incorrect disposal of ABP or not ensure timely correction by the operators. There is also an insufficient level of attention paid to the operators' documented procedures for management of ABP. Finally, no regular controls have been implemented to verify burial conditions in areas designated as remote. All of this weakens the guarantees that ABP and DP generated by food business operators are collected and disposed of in line with EU rules.

However, the fact that some documented procedures and arrangements are not up-to-date and a training programme for staff assisting the official veterinarians in the conduct of their controls has not been fully established, and the absence of sufficient verification that the monitoring plan has been implemented, may undermine the overall effectiveness of official controls. 5.2 IMPLEMENTATION OF OFFICIAL CONTROLS ON ANIMALS AND GOODS ENTERING THE EU

The audit team noted however, that the competent authorities of one Land did not provide evidence that staff authorised to assist the official veterinarian in carrying out physical checks or to carry out physical checks had successfully completed a training programme that meets the requirements of Article 3 of Regulation (EU) 2019/1081. 5.1.4 Documented procedures and arrangements in place

Whilst official controls on animals and goods entering the EU are conducted by appropriately trained staff and underpinned by documented procedures and comprehensive information technology systems, verification of consistent application of controls and compliance of facilities is weak. This is compounded by an ineffective internal audit and control verification system which either did not identify shortcomings or, if they were identified, did not follow-up on the timely rectification of these shortcomings. 5.2 IMPLEMENTATION OF OFFICIAL CONTROLS ON ANIMALS AND GOODS ENTERING THE EU

Whilst consignments of animals and goods of animal origin entering the EU are presented for official controls, and said controls are carried out in line with documented arrangements, some are not performed in line with EU rules (e.g. documentary checks are not performed at the BCP of entry in all cases) and a long-standing shortcoming concerning controls on consignments of goods of animal origin in transit remains. Regarding goods of non-animal origin, systematic, and in some cases long-standing shortcomings in the implementation of those controls remain, notably concerning the performance of documentary checks, the locations at which those checks are performed and the frequencies at which i

The NVWA has issued documented procedures for performing official controls on consignments of animals and goods of animal and non-animal origin entering the EU through Dutch BCPs, which include an import inspection manual (Werkhandboek Importkeuring) and instructions on the use of the electronic national veterinary border control system of the NVWA (Veterinaire Grens Controle Systeem ­ VGC system). The audit team noted that procedures are incomplete or are not in line with relevant EU requirements regarding transit (see section 5.2.3), internal audits, control verification procedures (see section 5.1.6) and identity checks on consignments of bulk liquid oils and fats (see section 5.2.4.2), w

The audit team noted that the procedure for the performance of documentary checks on goods of non-animal origin (K-IK-INV-PR03) was not in line with the requirements of Article 2 of Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/2130. The procedure provides that, for products listed in Annex I to Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/1793, the documentary check (see also sections 5.1.5 and 5.2.4) is solely for the verification of the completeness of part I of the Common Health Entry Document (CHED-D); there is no cross-check to see if the information in the CHED-D corresponds with that provided in official certificates, official attestations or other documents accompanying the consignme

Furthermore, the Commission audit team noted that the findings in the ABB reports had been poorly communicated to the import control team and there was little evidence that the shortcomings identified had been followed-up by the import control team. The Commission audit team also observed that most of the non-compliances were repeatedly found in subsequent audit or verification control reports. Most of the NVWA staff interviewed stated that they were unaware of the reported non-compliances and had no access to the ABB reports recorded in the NVWA database.

The audit team found that the failure by the NVWA to take appropriate measures in the light of the results of its internal audits or corrective actions in all cases where its control verification procedures identified shortcomings was not in line with Article 6(1) and 12(3) of the OCR respectively.

The audit team identified that for three consignments of animal origin which were split during transit, the traceability of those consignments was not ensured: · For one non-conforming consignment of over 100 000 kg fish, the CHED issued on arrival at the BCP indicated that the consignment arrived in bulk by vessel. Before the consignment was transported to a free warehouse, a second CHED had been issued at the BCP indicating that the consignment had arrived at the BCP in one container with a fictitious container number and 12 seals. The NVWA clarified that the consignment was transported from the BCP to the free warehouse in 12 road trips. The original consignment in transit was therefore s

The audit team noted that the identity checks on consignments of bulk liquid oils arriving in vessels were performed either (a) on the basis of a seal check in the absence of an (14) https://ec.europa.eu/food/audits-analysis/audit-report/details/3853 13 official seal, which is not in line with Article 3(2) of Regulation (EU) 2019/2130, or (b) a full identity check. The NVWA stated that it does not verify the quantity of bulk liquid oils when performing identity checks. This is not in line with Article 3(1) of Regulation (EU) 2019/2130. The audit team also observed that in this respect, the NVWA's procedures do not require verification of the quantity of consignments of bulk liquids. 5.2.4.3

The NVWA stated that documentary checks on consignments of goods of non-animal origin, when not selected by the VGC system for identity and physical checks, are performed automatically by the VGC system based on the completeness of the information contained in part I of the CHED-D, and without taking into account the information contained in official certificates, attestations or other documents accompanying the consignment. This is not in line with Article 2(3) of Regulation (EU) 2019/2130.

The NVWA further confirmed that documentary checks on consignments of goods of non-animal origin which are selected for identity and physical checks are performed on scanned copies of official certificates, attestations or other documents accompanying the consignment rather than on the original documents. This is also not in line with Article 2 of Regulation (EU) 2019/2130.
Consequently, the previous recommendation made in audit report DG(SANTE) 2017- 6054 regarding the performance of documentary checks on consignments of goods of non-animal origin remains unaddressed.

The audit team found that two of the 14 inspection centres visited were compliant with the minimum requirements for BCPs. The other 12 inspection centres and the two control points visited were not compliant with the requirements laid down in Articles 64(3) and 53(1)(a) of the OCR respectively and Articles 3, 4, 5, 6 and 8 of Regulation (EU) 2019/1014. Many of the shortcomings identified by the audit team (and listed in findings 69 and 70) had not been identified by the ABB in its internal audit and control verification activities (see finding 31).

paragraph_text: The official control system is supported by updated national legislation and guidelines. Certain provisions in the guidance documents are contrary to the requirements of Regulations (EU) 2019/627 and (EC) No 2073/2005 which impacts the application of related EU requirements.

label_heading: Conclusions on organisation and implementation of official controls
paragraph_text: There is a system in place for meat inspection on bovine, ovine, porcine and poultry that covers most relevant aspects. However, the effectiveness of AMI and, to a larger extent, PMI is impacted by a number of systemic shortcomings. 5.4 RAPID ALERT SYSTEM FOR FOOD AND FEED (RASFF) Legal requirements Article 50 of Regulation (EC) No 178/2002 of the European Parliament and of the Council and Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/1715 (IMSOC Regulation). Findings

The CCA has adopted several legal acts and guidelines, relevant for the scope of this audit, in recent years. According to the CCA, the changes introduced by these are mainly updates to reflect changes made to EU legislation. The CAs and food business operators (FBOs) are implementing the updated legislation and guidance documents. However, · Guidance No 9504/2021 (on meat inspection), contains certain provisions for post- mortem inspection (PMI) in red meat slaughterhouses that are not in line with Regulation (EU) 2019/627 (see paragraphs 49 and 50). · Guideline No 9853/2017 (on microbiological criteria for foodstuffs) contains certain provisions that are not in line with Regulation (EC) No

There are cooperation and coordination mechanisms in place within DVFA's departments and a system of notification of other CAs when the non-compliances identified need follow-up by other CAs. The OVs at slaughterhouse level notify welfare and animal identification issues that may concern the transport or farm level. Nonetheless, the outcome of on the farm/database controls is not considered when making decisions on animal identification (see paragraphs 40 and 41). 4 5.2.2 Impartiality, freedom from conflict of interest

The CA considers that, the recommendation on enforcing provisions that animals are clean prior to slaughter, has been addressed. Nonetheless, the findings at the time of the current audit suggest that the recommendation was not adequately addressed. AMI in cattle did not include checking animal cleanliness (see paragraph 39). This was replaced by CA audits of FBOs' systems for dealing with dirty cattle. 5.2.6 Enforcement

In large slaughterhouses the OVs permanently present during slaughter perform AMI. In the small slaughterhouses, private veterinarians employed on a contract basis for AMI perform this task. AMI includes controls on most of the relevant aspects (e.g. health status, identification, food chain information and animal welfare). However, AMI does not include verification of FBOs compliance with their obligation to ensure that animals have a clean hide, skin or fleece, so as to avoid any unacceptable risk of contamination of the fresh meat during slaughter. This is not in line with Article 11(4) of Regulation (EU) 2019/627.

Animal health and animal welfare findings of AMI are reported to the relevant services 9 and on-farm investigations are conducted when considered necessary. However, the OVs allow slaughter for human consumption of unidentified or incorrectly identified bovine animals in the absence of an adequate investigation to ascertain the identity of the animal.

When a bovine is presented for slaughter with eartags of an animal that appears as belonging to the category of stolen/dead on large grazing areas (and not found) in the central bovine database or is without eartags, the owner is allowed to make a sworn declaration for a change of details in the central bovine database. The CA allows slaughter for human consumption if the breed, sex and age of the animal matches the (new details) notified by the farmer and accepted by the database. The CA does not receive the outcome of a(possible) investigation before making the decision on the animal. (2)

In the cases assessed, the OVs were aware that red meat animals need to be inspected less than 24 hours after arrival and less than 24 hours before slaughter and had agreed arrangements with the FBOs to ensure this happens, including when animals were delivered during the weekend. AMI of all animals is documented. Nonetheless, should the agreed arrangements for the FBOs (to call the OV for AMI when new animals are presented for slaughter) fail to deliver, there is no reconciliation carried out between the number of animals passing AMI with the number passing PMI, nor are the OVs required to do so.

The CA has put provisions in place for AMI to be carried out at the holding of provenance. This option is used for emergency slaughter of animals and for animals that are difficult to handle. Approximately 350 private veterinarians have been designated as OVs for AMI on farms. The designation was not precluded by training or a system of measures to safeguard potential conflict of interest. The CA organised an information session and plans for more such sessions to be delivered to reach all designated OVs. Ante-mortem inspection - poultry

In the cases assessed there were sufficient OVs/OAs to cover all inspection posts during production and for all carcases to receive PMI. There are arrangements in place for PMI including official controls for Trichinella in pigs, tuberculosis and cysticercosis in bovines and pigs. The "in principle" standard are Articles 18-24 of Regulation (EU) 2019/627, while in certain circumstances (e.g. for outdoor pigs) the inspection maintains the additional incisions and palpations as per previous Regulation (EC) No 854/2004. Nonetheless, certain provisions of Guidance 9504/2021 differ from the provisions of Regulation (EU) 2019/627 · The guidance allows carcases with certain pathology and contaminat

In addition, PMI does not check for the presence/safe removal of SRM, contrary to the requirements of Article 17(d)(ii) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Carcases with SRM are health-marked, contrary to the requirements of Article 45(q) of Regulation (EU) 2019/627. The OVs do not subsequently check if the FBO has removed SRM from all health-marked carcases either. The OVs check FBOs' procedures for SRM removal, during audits on related FBOs procedures, a few times a year.

The cows' udders were not inspected unless they went for human consumption and/or pet food in the case assessed. The OV explained this is in line with the clarification received from central level. However, this approach is contrary to the requirements of Article 19(1)(k) of Regulation (EU) 2019/627.

The audit team identified different additional gaps in PMI in the sheep and bovine slaughterhouses visited, contrary to the requirements of Articles 12(3), 17 and 45(r) of Regulation (EU) 2019/627: · In the large bovine slaughterhouse, the inadequate presentation of the spleen by the FBO (long highlighted by the OV, but not addressed) resulted in the spleen not being routinely inspected;. · In the small slaughterhouses, several gaps in PMI had been noted by the audit team, but not by the supervisor present that day [e.g. in the sheep slaughterhouse, the OV was not checking the lower part of the carcase (and therefore missing several carcases with contamination in the lower part), not palpati

The CA has arrangements in place for poultry PMI to be carried out by OVs and OAs as well as in some cases by authorised slaughterhouse staff under the supervision of the OV. The slaughterhouse staff is authorised to perform certain PMI tasks only after undergoing relevant training and passing an assessment by the CA. The arrangements for poultry PMI were found to be largely satisfactory in the case assessed, where slaughterhouse staff were performing PMI, apart from the absence of a system for the OV/OA to check viscera and body cavities on a representative sample for each flock, contrary to the requirements of Article 25 of Regulation (EU) 2019/627. 5.3.2 Official controls over food busine

The OVs check FBO procedures to ensure that only animals/batches of animals that are properly identified and traceable to origin are slaughtered and these checks have been satisfactory in the cases assessed, with FBOs bringing inadequately identified and unidentified animals to the attention of the OVs. Nonetheless, the action taken by the CA in these cases is not fully satisfactory (see paragraphs 40 and 41). General and specific hygiene requirements, including HACCP based procedures Legal requirements Articles 4 and 5 of Regulation (EC) No 852/2004, Article 3 of Regulation (EC) No 853/2004 and Article 46 of Regulation (EU) 2019/627. 13 Findings

Health-marking is applied either by the OV or by the FBO under the supervision of the OV. In the case assessed, the health mark was kept under official control outside of working hours. Controls on the application of identification marks are included in the audit plan and are carried out at least once a year. However, contrary to the requirements of Article 48(2)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2019/627, the health mark is also applied in certain cases when there are grounds for declaring the meat unfit for human consumption (see paragraphs 49-52).

However, given that the notification of national measures on delayed PMI, carried out in accordance with the procedure laid down in Directive (EU) 2015/1535, was incomplete, the Commission has not granted the (already implemented) derogation. 5.2 COMPETENT AUTHORITIES Legal requirements Articles 4, 5, 6, 138 and 139 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. In accordance with the same procedure, the CA notified the national derogation on increased (slaughterhouse capacity) thresholds for performing delayed PMI compared to those provided in point (a), (i) and (ii) of Article 13(1) of Regulation (EU) 2019/627. However, the notification concerns 11 slaughterhouses whilst, at the time of the audit, delayed PMI was performed in most of the small slaughterhouses in the scope of the audit. Contrary to the requirements of Article 13(2) of Regulation (EU) 2019/627, the CA did not take into consideration, in the above notification, the combined annual production of the establishments where delayed PMI is performed. Conclusions on legislation and implemen

The CA structure, organisation and resources, including support, are adequate, overall, to deliver effective controls in large slaughterhouses. However, this is not the case for small slaughterhouses, where the system relies heavily on a small number of staff to perform audits, act as supervisors, determine training needs and deliver the training of OVs. This system has proved inadequate in terms of detecting poor hygiene practices as well as poor staff performance/knowledge gaps and has resulted in ineffective controls.

The CA provides training to the official control staff, including OVs and official auxiliaries (OAs). In the absence of a national system to deliver OV training in line with Article 13 and Chapter I of Annex II to Regulation (EU) 2019/624, the supervisors assess the training needs upon recruitment of an OV and deliver the training considered needed. The CA highlighted that a centrally developed/harmonised training is in the process of being developed. The training needs for OVs already active are identified during routine supervision and then custom made for the respective OV, sometimes also delivered by the supervisor. When the supervisor is not able to adequately detect knowledge gaps and

The training topics for a new OV (developed by one of the four supervisors of OVs in small slaughterhouses) did not cover aspects on which the OV is required to perform controls such as animal welfare and animal identification. In addition, no control procedure is available for the latter. The OV performing AMI, PMI and some animal welfare controls in one of the small slaughterhouses visited did not have a satisfactory knowledge of PMI requirements (see paragraph 52) and of certain animal welfare 5 requirements (e.g. 0.7- 0.8A for 15 seconds was considered better than the 1A for effective electric stun).

The OVs benefit from the technical support of the supervisors. The supervisors for the teams in large slaughterhouse met by the audit team were knowledgeable in the areas under review. Nonetheless, the audit team identified gaps in the knowledge of the supervisor for small slaughterhouses, met during the audit (e.g. as regards prevention of cross-contamination and PMI ­ see paragraphs 52, 60-62, 64). The supervisor also had an incorrect understanding of certain animal welfare requirements (e.g. considering captive bolt a stun-to-kill method for which effectiveness of stunning did not need to be checked).

As the supervisor is the only CA member of staff performing controls on FBOs' hygiene requirements, as well as supervision of OVs contracted for AMI, PMI and some animal welfare controls, these knowledge gaps have impacted the effectiveness of the controls in the small establishments visited during the current audit (see paragraphs 60-62, 64, 66). The same supervisor was in charge of controls in 25 small slaughterhouses, assessing the training needs, training and supervising the contracted OVs in these establishments. This questions the effectiveness of the controls in the remaining small slaughterhouses.

The design and implementation of the official control system does not provide assurance that controls over EU requirements and their enforcement are carried out correctly and uniformly across the 15 large and 44 low-capacity slaughterhouses. The system does not ensure that controls in respect of general hygiene requirements and welfare during slaughter actually take place with an appropriate frequency, or at all.

There are shortcomings in the identification, rating, action taken and follow-up of enforcement of non-compliances by the establishment OVs and in the CA supervision of those OVs that weaken the effectiveness of the enforcement that takes place.

label_heading: Conclusions on organisation and implementation of official controls
paragraph_text: The time dedicated to official controls by OVs in low-capacity slaughterhouses, other than to carry out AMI and PMI, is very limited and affects the OVs' capacity to observe and assess the slaughterhouse hygiene practices and take necessary enforcement action where and when required.

Senior Meat Inspection Unit officers carry out approximately six `assessment and guidance' visits to slaughterhouses annually, where meat inspection arrangements and controls by OVs are checked and assessed. Normally, two of these visits take place in large establishments, the rest in low-capacity ones. The Animal Welfare and Identification Unit also carries out control visits to slaughterhouses. Regional managers' visits focus on staff support and HR-style aspects but also on mentoring and advising staff on meat inspection and official controls matters.

Taking into account the number of approved establishments and the frequency of visits, large slaughterhouses should receive an `assessment and guidance' visit every seven or eight years, and a low-capacity establishment once every ten or eleven years.(2)

The system to prioritise slaughterhouses to be visited by senior officers considers aspects like issues identified by OVs and enforcement taken. Establishments where OVs identify no or very few non-compliances are given low priority.

There are no regular checks at central level in order to establish if the OVs in approved slaughterhouses have a system in place to ensure that all the required controls are carried out within the agreed three-year cycle. In all establishments reviewed by the audit team, there were some controls that had not been completed at all during the last three years. Examples included `compliance with requirements of approval' or `vermin control'.

Although the CA provided some good examples of suitable and timely enforcement that had achieved positive outcomes, the audit team observed several examples where non- compliances were not identified or inadequate rating was given to those non- compliances that had actually been found. As lower rating non-compliance do not require the FBO to produce an action plan to resolve them or the OV to follow them up, an inadequately rated non-compliance has an impact on the likelihood of it being satisfactorily resolved.

Equally, there was also evidence of lack of follow up actions by OVs in some instances that the rating of a non-compliance required it, to ensure the FBO remedied the identified problems and/ or prevented the recurrence of the problem. paragraph_text: The delivery of official controls is adequate in preventing bovine animals unfit for (slaughter for) human consumption from entering the food chain. Nonetheless, the continued performance of AMI and PMI by OA without the presence of the OV in the slaughterhouse is contrary to EU requirements (except for PMI in low throughput slaughterhouses). The same applies to the absence of visual inspection of udders and its lymph nodes and the visual inspection of the gastro-intestinal tract and palpation of the gastric and mesenteric lymph nodes. Currently, green offal and udders are not inspected as part of PMI. This is not in line with the requirements of Article 19 of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/627. The audit team was informed that the CCA is in the process of drafting a guideline clarifying the regulatory requirements, but noted that the requirements in question were already contained in EU legislation well preceding the above Regulation (i.e. in repealed Regulation (EC) No 854/2004 of the European Parliament and of the Council). Red offal including kidneys are examined during PMI, as required.

According to national rules, AMI of poultry can be done at slaughterhouse by OVs or, when necessary, at the holding of origin by approved veterinarians. In this regard, there is a specific procedure under Order 23/G/2016 (see paragraph 3), which describes the steps to follow and, among other things, requires OAs to perform a simplified AMI under the responsibility of the OV. Initial validation data for screening of stilbenes and steroids were revised by the laboratory in response to the findings made in the 2020 audit report (see finding 32 of that report) to eliminate most of the obvious discrepancies. However, some data at the lowest calibration levels still showed that the performance characteristics (e.g., identical repeatability and reproducibility values for methylboldenone and 17- clostebol chlorandrostenedione) were not in line with legal requirements (8). These shortcomings in the method performance characteristics were neither spotted nor evaluated by the laboratory. In addition, the calculation of CC was not in line with legal provisions (9).

In the method validation file for confirmation of thyrostats, a number of recoveries were outside the acceptable range laid down in EU legislation (10). This was not noticed by the laboratory and thus no assessment of the possible influence of that phenomenon on the suitability of the method had been carried out. The linearity of the calibration curve for propylthiouracil was below the criteria set by the laboratory ­ however, this was not reflected and concluded on in the validation documentation. The laboratory representative informed the audit team that the revalidation of the method was planned for 2025.

In the validation documentation for the screening and confirmatory method for beta- agonists, there was inadequate assessment of several method performance characteristics (e.g., recoveries outside the established range (10), reproducibilities identical to repeatabilities (8)).

At the time of the audit, the screening and confirmatory method for chloramphenicol, thiamphenicol and florfenicol was under validation. Consequently, no properly validated method was available in the laboratory for monitoring residues of these analytes.

The validation of the screening method for antibacterial substances was stated to be finalised just prior to the audit. The available documentation included only data on specificity and results of measurements at one fortification level for each analyte/matrix combination. This level was assumed as the CC with no justification for that decision. This is not in line with legal requirements (11). Since the validation did not address all of the performance characteristics required for quantitative screening methods (12), the method could not be considered as properly validated.

The validation report for the coccidiostats confirmatory method dated from 2014 and contained implausibly identical values for repeatabilities and reproducibilities (8) and numerous recoveries outside the established range (10). These observations were not commented on in the validation documentation. Moreover, during the routine application of the method, the analyst met stated that "no CC were used due to erroneous values obtained during the validation". The system in place for the control of ASF in wild boar is effective. The constant reduction in wild boar density over the last three years should help the authorities to slow down the spread of the disease. The effective passive surveillance, the good testing and correct disposal of carcases helps preventing the spread of the disease from wild animals.

The authorities use unclear risk criteria to decide how many and which establishments the counties should target for their biosecurity inspections. Their control plan is poorly implemented and the authorities do not inspect the vast majority of small commercial establishments and non-commercial ones. Therefore, for these sectors, the authorities are not aware of level of compliance with basic 8 requirements, the degree of preparation to avoid the entry and spread of ASF and the awareness of operators regarding the disease. This is a major risk to prevent the disease entering such establishments and to detect the disease promptly if this happened.

The competent authority maintains that there are no "outdoor" pig establishments in Hungary as defined in the EU strategy for ASF, although they keep a list of "outdoor" pig establishments and there are establishments allowing pig access to outdoor pens. The absence of legal definition of "outdoor establishments" creates different interpretations between officials2. All this creates some uncertainty when evaluating the risk of introduction of ASF.

The contingency plans at county level are still incomplete, as they lack guidance for depopulation, information regarding availability of equipment and materials necessary for the effective control of the disease and provisions to dispose of the carcases safely and quickly. This compromises the readiness of Hungary to deal effectively with outbreaks in the event that ASF is confirmed in domestic pigs.

The competent authority is incorrectly certifying consignments of live pigs as compliant with the ASF Regulation, as they originate from establishments without approved biosecurity plans. Therefore, there is an unknown proportion of live pigs moving out of restricted zone II without complying with the requirements and their meat being placed on the intra-Union market. The risk of disease spread due to these shortcomings is partially mitigated by the systematic pre-movement testing.

The absence of verification activities over county authorities and approved veterinarians jeopardises the continuous improvement of the official control system and favours the persistence of non-compliances.

The low number of suspected ASF cases reported from establishments (i.e. pigs with clinical symptoms compatible with ASF) put in question the effectiveness of the awareness campaigns or the willingness of key stakeholders to notify. This might jeopardise early detection of ASF in domestic pigs.

There are records of the official controls, but the authorities do not record the outcome of the verification of these controls. This does not allow to confirm whether the controls are effective in achieving their intended purpose, whether verification checks detect any issues and whether the authorities take timely corrective actions to improve the effectiveness of official controls when needed.

The competent authorities use the wide range of effective and proportionate enforcement actions available when non-compliances are detected. They promptly suspend transporters, drivers and/or vehicle certificates if necessary to bring operators to take the desired corrective actions and comply with EU animal welfare requirements. There are records of the official controls, but the authorities do not record the outcome of the verification of these controls. This does not allow to confirm whether the controls are effective in achieving their intended purpose, whether verification checks detect any issues and whether the authorities take timely corrective actions to improve the effectiveness of official controls when needed.

The national programme established as the main risk factors for animal welfare, firstly the transport of unweaned (and cull animals), secondly the transport over long journeys (and by sea) and thirdly transport during adverse weather conditions. label_heading: Conclusion on the planning and implementation of inspections
paragraph_text: While the planning of inspections is largely based on appropriate risk-related factors and official controls are carried out on all operators on a risk basis and with an appropriate frequency, the effectiveness of controls is weakened by some shortcomings in inspectors' assessment of (i) feed business operators' hazard identifications within their hazard analyses and critical control point plans, and (ii) operators' traceability systems (in particular collection and storage of retained samples). 5.2.2 Sampling and analysis 5.2.2.1 Planning of official sampling

In all of the establishments visited, the audit team scrutinised the most recent inspection reports and interviewed the inspectors on their assessment of the operators' HACCP plans. The audit team noted that the inspectors' assessment of the hazard identification part of the HACCP plan was deficient in several establishments. In general, the hazard identification part of the operators' HACCP plans was generic (e.g., the same hazards were identified for all incoming feed materials and other ingredients with an identical risk score) without the level of detail necessary for a proper hazard identification (as required by Article 6(2)(a) of Regulation (EC) No 183/2005) and consequent risk assess

In one feed material producer, the operator used direct drying. In the hazard analysis of this processing step, the assessment of the possible occurrence of dioxins/polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs) had not been carried out and, consequently, there were no measures in place to monitor/control that relevant hazard. This omission was overlooked in the records of the previous official controls.

label_heading: Conclusions on implementation of official controls
paragraph_text: Official controls at ABP plants are largely effective to verify infrastructural and hygiene requirements. However, they are usually notified in advance and they do not pay sufficient attention to the implementation of HACCP-based procedures and the operators' own checks. Similarly, checks on the validation of processing plants remain limited or poorly documented. All of this limits the ability of the competent authorities to verify whether ABP and DP are handled and processed to the high safety standards provided for in EU legislation.

label_heading: Conclusions on planning of official controls
paragraph_text: All district veterinary inspectors met confirmed that inspections of ABP plants are carried out with prior notification and that unannounced inspections are the exception. In some cases, inspections are announced one or two days before the due date and, in other cases, up to a week in advance, when the inspectors prepare their weekly schedule of activities. Routine prior notification of inspections in not in line with Article 9(4) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

label_heading: Conclusions on implementation of official controls
paragraph_text: For operators under veterinary supervision (meat establishments), official controls on ABP generated in such food establishments are largely effective, except for controls on the marking of specified risk material.

label_heading: Conclusions on planning of official controls
paragraph_text: In one processing plant for Category 1 material visited, the audit team noted, in the raw material received from domestic slaughterhouses, the presence of heads of adult bovine animals (specified risk material) that were not stained with a dye or otherwise marked, contrary to the requirements of point 3 of Annex V to Regulation (EC) No 999/2001. According to the operator of the processing plant, there was an agreement with slaughterhouses not to mark specified risk material as this resulted in staining of the processing equipment. Officials from the province visited confirmed that specified risk material was usually not stained on removal.

label_heading: Conclusions on implementation of official controls
paragraph_text: In contrast, for food business operators under supervision of the food inspectorates (e.g. milk, eggs, fish and retail sectors) official controls are inadequate, mainly due to 13 insufficient knowledge of ABP requirements, to monitor the correct handling, use and disposal of such materials. This weakens the guarantees that ABP and DP generated by food business operators are collected and disposed of in line with EU rules.

label_heading: Conclusions on planning of official controls
paragraph_text: The food inspectors met stated that they had not received training on ABP and that in the absence of knowledge of the rules applicable to ABP, they were not able to critically assess the degree of compliance of the food operators in this area. They stated that their main point of attention was to verify that food and waste (this included ABP for the food inspectors) were adequately separated and that there was no contamination of food by waste.

label_heading: Conclusions on planning of official controls
paragraph_text: The audit team reviewed several records of inspections carried out by food inspectors at randomly chosen food operators. From these records, it was visible that some information was available on the type of ABP produced by the operators and the operators collecting them. However, the food inspectors met stated that such information was collected but not assessed. For instance, they did not check the presence of commercial documentation or if the operator collecting such ABP was approved for handling these types of ABP.

label_heading: Conclusions on planning of official controls
paragraph_text: The audit team reviewed some cases where non-conformities were identified in relation to ABP at some operators under the supervision of food inspectors. These cases were either identified by the inspectors or were investigated following complaints. From the discussion held with the audit team, it was clear that in the few cases where food inspectors had some knowledge of ABP or had investigated ABP-related complaints, they were able to adequately follow-up on such issues, in particular by liaising with the veterinary inspectors in charge of controls at ABP operators.

label_heading: Conclusions on planning of official controls
paragraph_text: The food inspectors met stated that, at retailers, they verified that meat and meat products not fit for human consumption (e.g., products with expired shelf life or spoiled meat) were kept separated from food. They also verified that unsold food of animal origin was not given to farmers for feeding their animals. They confirmed that no other checks were carried out to ascertain the destination of ABP as this was, in their opinion, the responsibility of the business operator to dispose of them in line with the applicable rules.

label_heading: Conclusions on planning of official controls
paragraph_text: Based on the above findings, the audit team noted that official controls carried by food inspectors at food business operators are not suitable to verify compliance with ABP rules, contrary to the requirements of Article 4(3) of Regulation No 1069/2009.

The competent authority has made significant improvements to increase the registration of non-commercial pig establishments in the national register system. It also made improvements in the system to facilitate the use of information to plan certain official controls for ASF. However, the fact that the system does not always keep records of the number of pigs present in certain establishments (i.e., one pig farms) prevents the accurate 5 and risk-based planning of official controls, both during peace time and during disease outbreaks.

The national plan to reduce the wild porcine population seems to have been effective in recent years. The strategy is based on reliable data. However, the population is still high and even increasing in certain areas of the country. The competent authority acknowledges the need to develop a national action plan to continuously manage the wild porcine animals' population to avoid the spread of ASF, in line with Annex IV of the Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2023/594 by 17 September 2023.

The competent authorities implement both passive and active surveillance of hunted and dead wild boar. There is no evidence that the authorities systematically verify the implementation of these official control and thus, confirm that all wild porcine meat intended for human consumption originates from carcases with negative results.
The laboratory network provides reliable and consistent support for the implementation of ASF control programme.
Home slaughter is not always reported to the authorities in order to supervise it, not allowing the competent authority to comply with their approved eradication programme.

The epidemiological enquiries do not always include the required information. This prevents the competent authority from taking informed decisions to implement adequate prevention and control measures to avoid the spreading and ensure the eradication of the disease.

There are unnecessary delays in confirming ASF in domestic pigs, resulting in the setting of restriction areas five days after the suspicion of the disease was reported. This creates an unnecessary time window during which the infection can be spread to both domestic pigs and wild porcine animals.

The system implemented by the competent authorities to verify that official controls are planned on a risk basis (e.g., identification and registration; biosecurity measures, surveillance), and are implemented with appropriate frequency to ensure that the objectives of the legislations are effectively achieve is weak.
The veterinary authorities have suitable contingency plans, equipment, and the capacity to deal with confirmed ASF outbreaks.

The last internal audit report issued in March 2023 included nine recommendations and a deadline of 10 working days for the creation of an action plan to address those recommendations. Up until the closing meeting of this audit (4 July), no action plan had been created and no reminder had been issued. The competent authority did not provide evidence that they have officially addressed those important shortcomings and weakens the prevention and control system for ASF in the country. 6 PREVENTIVE MEASURES The compliance with registration of pig establishments and data on the national database is generally good. label_heading: Conclusions on organisation and implementation of official controls
paragraph_text: The shortcomings identified in how the OVs deal with contamination on carcases, with lack of enforcement to ensure that FBOs monitor the hygiene of operations and take suitable and timely action before carcases are presented for PMI with visible contamination.
FBO staff regularly presented carcases with visible contamination for PMI, which created extra work for the vacataires, some of which were busy removing the contamination during PMI.

The audit team did not observe, in any of the two establishments, any FBO staff checking on carcase contamination and taking suitable corrective action (i.e. immediately removing all visible contamination, before presenting those carcases for PMI). The official staff had taken up the task of removing the contamination before declaring the carcases fit for human consumption. HACCP Legal requirements Article 5 of Regulation (EC) No 852/2004. Findings

The FBOs food safety management systems checked by the audit team included sufficient controls on animal identification, FCI and on the cleanliness and the state of health of the livestock. In relation to carcase monitoring for the presence of contamination, the FBOs had decided to set a frequency of two checks per week.

The CA accepted this frequency of controls over FBO monitoring of carcass contamination as sufficient. At the time of the visits, especially during cattle production, the OVs and vacataires were seen to be busy removing visible faecal contamination from 9 a significant number of carcases. No monitoring by the FBO on the carcases presented for PMI was observed, nor any action to avoid or to eliminate the contamination on those carcases. Microbiological criteria Legal requirements Articles 35 and 36 of Regulation (EU) 2019/627. Commission Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005. Findings
The lack of documented procedures or guidance affects the effectiveness of delivery of official controls and results in some controls not fully carried out or not carried out in a consistent manner.

There are several official checklists that the CCA have created and are used during the day-to-day activities at the establishments and also during yearly audits. The daily checklist includes pre-operational checks and animal welfare checks. There are no checklists, nor documented procedures in place for other official controls, including operational hygiene related activities. For those cases, the system relies on verbal instructions and guidance and support from central office staff.

Occasionally different officers gave very different deadlines to similar non-compliances. This was evident when comparing several yearly audit reports. As explained by the CA, this has improved as a result to recent changes in the official controls team, with the current team providing more realistic and suitable enforcement.

Despite these daily checks, in some instances, the OVs didn't manage to identify some problems concerning lack of cleanliness that were later identified during the yearly audit carried out by central office staff.
There are no dedicated checklists or written guidance to aid the OVs when monitoring the hygiene standards during the slaughter operation.
In relation to the operational hygiene requirements, the OV controls did not identify a number of generalised and recurrent unhygienic practices (see p.20) which were observed during the audit.

According to the records checked and discussions with CA staff, the establishment OVs had not identified any problems in relation to FBO's own sampling. However, the audit team found that the sampling programmes were not fully in line with legislation. Issues including the fact that FBOs do not take the samples randomly during production but tend to sample batches or the use of alternative sampling arrangements without demonstration of equivalence (i.e. chicken tested before chilling or beef tested during chilling).

paragraph_text: The post-mortem inspection arrangements in the slaughterhouse that makes use of the time of inspection derogation is not in line with EU law which requires correlation of carcases and offal irrespective of the delay in PMI. 6 OVERALL CONCLUSION The organisation and structure of the CA and its control system provide a largely adequate framework for the delivery of official controls, which are delivered at the established frequency and generally cover the relevant aspects. label_heading: Conclusions on legislation and implementing measures
paragraph_text: National legislation and guidelines, necessary to ensure implementation and/or enforcement of the EU requirements applicable to the meat sector, are in place and they are largely in line with EU legislation, with the exception of one guideline, which was not up-to-date and, as a result, certain provisions of its content are contrary to EU legislation.

However, the audit team noted that the guidance on ante-mortem inspection (AMI) of poultry at the holding of provenance (NSVFSA Service Note 25901/12.04.2019) allows that "designated veterinarians" perform AMI at the holding of origin (EU legislation requires that AMI should be carried out by an OV). In this regard, NSVFSA informed the audit team that this document had been in place before the new EU legislation was applicable and it has not been updated as yet. In addition, NSVFSA stated that they intend to amend the provisions contained in this document in order to bring them in line with EU requirements.

According to national rules, AMI of poultry is carried out at the holding of origin by "designated veterinarians". In this regard, there is a specific procedure under the Service Note 25901/12.04.2019 (see paragraph 3), which describes the steps to follow and, among other things, requires OVs or OAs (under the supervision of the OV) to perform a simplified AMI at the slaughterhouse.

label_heading: Conclusions on official controls on bivalve molluscs
paragraph_text: There is no system of official controls of bivalve molluscs and marine gastropods at primary production level in Bulgaria and the majority of the requirement of EU legislation are not met. Although there are certain official controls in place after primary production (carried out at establishments), they are insufficient to provide adequate food safety assurances if the primary production is not controlled. 5 5.3 LABORATORIES Legal requirements Articles 5(1), 18(2)(d)(iv), 34, 37 to 39, 100 and 101 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Article 60 and Annexes IV and V to Regulation (EU) 2019/627. Points 1.16, 1.17 and 1.25 Chapter 1 of Annex I to Commission Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005. Sections 3.1.1

Bulgaria has not fixed the location and boundaries of production areas, contrary to Article 52(1) of Regulation (EU) 2019/627. The BFSA stated that each mussel farm is considered as an individual production area, and that the BFSA's Directorate of Animal Health and Welfare has a register of mussels' aquaculture farms publicly available at the BFSA website, with the farm location and boundaries coordinates provided by the Black Sea Basin Directorate.

Bulgaria has not carried out the sanitary surveys required in Article 56 of the same Regulation. Consequently, it has not classified them, contrary to the requirements of Articles 52(2) and (3) of the same Regulation.

At the time of the audit, there was no monitoring of production areas (or aquaculture farms if they are individually considered, see paragraph 4) for microbiological, chemical contaminants, biotoxins or phytoplankton, contrary to the requirements of Articles 57 to 61 of Regulation (EU) 2019/627.

Consequently, there is neither management of production areas nor record and exchange of information to interested parties, which conditions are established respectively in Articles 61 and 62, and 66 of the same Regulation, with the exception of the BFSA's register of mussels' aquaculture farms (see paragraph 4), which could partially meet the recording of information required in Article 66(a) of that Regulation.

As required by Article 64 of Regulation (EU) 2019/627, the BFSA has in place a sampling programme of final products of bivalve molluscs' origin, either at establishments or at retail level. Official samples of mussels and wedge clams are tested for biotoxins at the NRL and for E. coli and salmonella at the regional official control laboratories. Non- compliant results trigger the recall and withdraw from the market of the batch of bivalve molluscs tested. 5.2.2 Official controls of certain bivalve molluscs harvested outside classified production areas

In the case of aquaculture mussels, wedge clams and rapana seasnail, the information contained in this document meets the relevant requirements of Chapter I (3) and (4) of Section VII of Annex III to Regulation (EC) 853/2004.
