In line with Article 12(1) of the OCR, the competent authority has made available a guide (vademecum) for the inspections of animal welfare in cattle farms. The vademecum contains instructions for the checks, legal references and how to apply them and occasionally refers to the Recommendation of the Council of Europe concerning cattle. The inspectors use the vademecum and report on a generic checklist template. The competent authority intends to make available to the inspectors in 2023 a detailed checklist, specific to animal welfare of cattle. The vademecum does not include, for example, how to evaluate the isolation of sick or injured animals in suitable accommodation and comfortable beddi

The use of c-section is generalised in farms with Belgian Blue cows. C-section protects cow and calf from suffering associated to calving difficulties caused by the selection of the breeding animals. However, official controls do not cover breeding procedures and Appendix B of the recommendation concerning cattle of the Convention requires that breeding should be carefully selected to reduce calving difficulties and c-section shall not be a routine measure.

The access of the involved authorities to information for the official controls is incomplete reducing the effectiveness and efficiency of the system: (i) The database containing the result of the planned animal welfare checks is kept by FASFC. Regions can access the checklist of individual inspections and receive regular automatic notification of identified non-compliances, but their access does not facilitate the data analysis (verification of compliance with established inspection frequencies, reports containing officials' comments, points marked as not applicable). (ii) FASFC cannot access enforcement data kept by the Regions and there is no alternative system for informing FASFC officia

Weaknesses in the registration of poultry establishments and the insufficient reliability of data prevent the authorities from having a properly updated information on the poultry establishments. The oversight of non-registered establishments raises concerns about the potential underreporting of suspicions in those flocks and their real role in the recent HPAI epidemics. This hinders the capacity of the competent authority to ensure the efficient application of the disease prevention, surveillance and control measures.

The authorities exempted from the registration requirement non-commercial (backyard) poultry establishments as they consider them compliant with criteria laid down in Article 3 of Regulation 2022/1345. The authority also considers the risk of those establishments insignificant, since in their view those establishments have limited, respectively no direct or indirect contacts with other poultry, insignificant epidemiological role in recent HPAI epidemics, and they were relatively rarely infected (4 % of all outbreaks).

The authorities assert that backyard flocks are unlikely to contribute significantly to the spread of the virus. However, this assertion lacks strong support from epidemiological enquiries due to inherent limitations (as detailed in finding 65) and an incomplete epidemiological analysis (see also finding 56). The authorities had not consistently performed census within protection or surveillance zones around the outbreaks, and they could not demonstrate that those establishments were included in the screening activities, except for one instance in May 2023. Furthermore, five out of twelve infected non- registered establishments kept more than 100 birds (up to 235), prompting doubts about whe

The TIR system does not contain information on the number of birds at each location. County authorities stated that many small-scale establishments registered in TIR had been inactive due to underreporting of a cessation of their activities. This is not in line with the provisions laid down in Articles 84, 93(a) and 101(1)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2016/429, and in Article 18 of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2019/2035.

The local authorities organise their activities mainly based on the information provided by bird keepers prior each repopulation/re-stocking of establishments and the information provided by private veterinarians. However, these arrangements resulted in unnecessary delays of some official actions e.g., more than one week delay in a census of establishments located in the surveillance zone.

The shortcomings above had an impact on the application of control measures laid down in Regulation (EU) 2016/429 (Article 65) and Delegated Regulation (EU) 2020/687 3 (Chapters I and II of Part II) requiring the availability of accurate and updated inventories of poultry establishments in the event of suspicion and confirmation of HPAI to establish restricted zones, apply and regularly adapt those measures, and grant derogations therefrom.

Risk assessment and identification of high-risk areas has allowed the competent authority to implement additional prevention, surveillance and control measures but this have not been sufficient to prevent the recurrence of epidemics waves. The inability of the authorities to reduce poultry density in areas proved problematic for epidemics will continue to challenge the veterinary service's capacity to deal timely with outbreaks.

The non-compliances on biosecurity, in particular in daily operational practices, contribute to an increased risk of the virus being introduced to poultry farms and would make it challenging to contain and control the spread of HPAI. The new compensation scheme for losses due to infection and wider engagement of poultry industry in biosecurity on commercial poultry establishments should contribute to improve compliance with biosecurity requirements.

A model to estimate the risk of virus introduction in different areas of the country was completed by 31 March 2023. However, at the time of the audit, the experts that developed this model have not obtained yet complete population data for wild birds, nor the location of resting sites and migration1. Therefore, they were predicting new cases using a model that takes into account only the poultry population data, data on type of land/coverage, meteorological data and the previous outbreaks of poultry and wild birds. In addition, the authority and experts have plans to work on risk assessment for spreading of the infection between establishments, but the work has not started yet. The data tha

The authorities named the main challenges they faced during recent epizootics: areas with high density of birds and poultry establishments, multiple birds movements (in particular waterfowl), airborne transmission of the virus, and inadequate biosecurity measures in establishments (e.g., inadequate disinfection of people and vehicles visiting establishments, sharing of staff and mechanisms). They have been trying to address some of those issues, (e.g., role of bird's catchers or vehicles from rendering plants, feed mills) 6 in spreading the disease by strengthening the measures applied to them. They also plan to introduce a wider monitoring of daily biosecurity operation on establishments by

The fact that operators of many infected establishments did not comply with biosecurity rules is not in line with requirements laid down in Articles 10(1)(a)(iii), (b) and (c), (4)(b) and 11(1)(b) of Regulation (EU) 2016/429, on their responsibilities regarding disease prevention and knowledge and application of biosecurity measures. Completeness and updates of the Contingency plan

Epidemiological investigations were generally done at the time of sampling or one or two days after. In the majority of instances, the local authority performed both the initial and final investigation. They used standardised form. In the initial inquiry they collected information on movements on and off suspected establishments during the incubation period (birds, vehicles, and personnel). However, in some cases, the official veterinarians did not include in the investigation report the likely origin of the infection or the full list of all contacts or had not followed these epidemiological links adequately due to lack of resources (e.g., links related to feed truck routes or establishments
The training and simulation exercises enhanced the knowledge of local authorities. But their limited scope prevented authorities to address some weaknesses identified in the recent HPAI epidemics.

The simulation drills held aimed only at certain aspects of dealing with outbreaks and did not cover other essential components of emergency response (e.g., collection of 7 epidemiological data during epidemics, including enquiries, census and visits to establishments in the restricted areas). The authority had not verified the local authorities' preparedness for these tasks, or the ability to launch a rapid response. They missed an opportunity to share the experience gained in these areas during the previous period2. This is not in line with Article 44 of Regulation (EU) 2016/429.

The fact that veterinarians are frequently dealing with HPAI epizootics might justify the lack of exercises but does not excuse the authorities of incorporating lessons learnt and measures to correct deficiencies which have been already identified during the previous two Commission audits. Currently, the authorities face the risk of continuing making the same mistakes in future epidemics unless they introduce the appropriate changes in their contingency plan, and unless they appropriate train the staff to follow the contingency plan. Early detection

Although there is no evidence that the significant delays in confirming the infection in wild birds had a negative effect on the early detection of poultry outbreaks, these delays undermine the investigation of transmission pathways in poultry during the epidemics. 10 53. The NRL provides reliable results. The reliability of the results provided by the other laboratory recently designated for avian influenza diagnostics, is currently weakened by existing gaps in its inter-laboratory proficiency testing4.

In 2021 and 2022 not all counties reached their targets for sampling of wild birds. A lower number of samples were noted also in two heavily affected counties in the South (which took less than 40% of their targets).

Since 2021 the authorities detected 73 outbreaks of HPAI in wild birds. However, 20 outbreaks were laboratory confirmed with more than one-week delay: in five instances with more than two weeks delay. At the time when the first few index outbreaks were detected in poultry, for which the authorities determined that introduction of the HPAI virus by wildlife was the most likely cause, the circulation of that HPAI virus had not yet been detected in wild birds in the affected areas. This undermines the effectiveness of the surveillance in wild birds and its role as early warning system and demonstrates inadequacy of the number and location of samples taken. That sub-optimal effectiveness of the

For certain information not included in these three documents and in the national coordinated plan for alerts on animal health, MAPA requires the authorities of the regions to elaborate any necessary instructions reflecting their regional information and needs in case of an emergency (i.e., regional communication protocols in case of crisis, human resources available and their deployment in case of a crisis, protocol for the slaughter of birds of establishments in the restricted zones, resolutions on burial, exceptional movements, restocking procedures and compensations). It also requires the national disease crisis centre to approve the regional contingency plans. Six Autonomous Communities

The audit team noticed some examples of missing information in the contingency plans at Autonomous Community level: a. Contact emergency telephone numbers for the general public and operators to notify any suspicion (including holidays and weekends). b. Framework of cooperative communications with veterinary services at regional level, designated bodies or natural persons, relevant stakeholders, and local designated laboratories. c. Human resources and specific roles of all animal health professionals who should be involved in the implementation of the control and eradication measures. d. Location of local disease crisis centres, list of facilities and equipment required in case of an emerge

Since 2019, the authorities conducted several simulation exercises concerning responses to epizootic outbreaks. No simulation exercises specifically relating to HPAI have been carried out. Some of the Autonomous Communities most affected by the last HPAI epidemic in 2022, did not have a written contingency plan with the regional information necessary for rapid response in case of emergency. The audit team did not see any evidence that this last epidemic led to any updates on their contingency plans' procedures. The competent authorities do not sufficiently ensure that simulation exercises concerning the contingency plans are carried out regularly or at appropriate intervals to verify their f

In the event of suspicion of HPAI in poultry, the competent authority set restrictions on the suspected establishments without delay. However, the initial veterinary investigation and sampling was delayed in several cases. Although in most cases, informal communications with the national disease crisis centre occurred immediately, there were delays in the regional authorities conducting the required investigation to confirm or rule out the presence of HPAI. This is not in line with Article 54 of Regulation (EU) 2016/429.

Epidemiological investigations were generally done at the time of sampling. They were regularly incomplete. In most cases, the official veterinarians did not include in the investigation report the likely time that the infection was already present in the establishment, the likely origin of the infection or the full list of direct and indirect contacts. This is not in line with Art 54(1)(g) and 57(1) Regulation (EU) 2016/429.

Identification of epidemiological contacts (tracings back and forth) were regularly delegated to the private sector. However, the audit team rarely saw any evidence that the authorities followed up on those tracings and applied control measures on possible contact establishments. This is not in line with Articles 57(1) and 62 of Regulation (EU) 2016/429 and Articles 17, 18 and 19 of the Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2020/687.

The standard procedure does not include, within the minimum information required during the preparation process, the need to plan such depopulation in such a way as to avoid any risk of spreading the relevant category A disease agent during and after killing. The audit team saw strong evidence that some of the secondary cases, could be due to airborne transmission of virus during depopulation of the nearby primary case. The dates on which the secondary case could have been infected, coincided with the dates when the depopulation of the primary case was carried out.5 This is not in line with Article 12(1)(a) and (b) of Delegated regulation (EU) 2020/687.

The authorities ordered the depopulation of suspect cases during the epidemic, sometimes without waiting for their confirmation. The competent authority had already identified that they had an important shortage of resources and personnel during the epidemic to timely implement the depopulation of cases. Nine of the 38 outbreaks (24%) did not need depopulations measures because all birds were already dead due to the disease by the time the depopulation could be implemented6 (Table C). This is not in line with Articles 13(1)(a) and 61(1)(b) of Regulation (EU) 2016/429. Table C Days from suspicion to depopulation (source- ADIS) Days Number of outbreaks (%) <5 12 (32) 5-7 9 (24) >7 8 (21) No de

The authorities identified logistics as the main difficulties for the disposal of dead birds and products, due to the concentration -in a short period of time- of outbreaks with a high number of birds. The authorities encountered lack of processing plant capacity, shortage of trucks for the transfer of manure and dead birds and big difficulties for establishing dedicated burial sites for mass disposal of birds (lack of machinery and sometimes rain). This is not in line with Articles 3(1)(a) and 61(1)(b) of Regulation (EU) 2016/429.

The audit team noted significant delays between depopulation or disposal of infected birds and products and the subsequent implementation of preliminary cleaning and disinfection measures. In 38% (14) of the outbreaks, the preliminary cleaning and disinfection was carried out 10 to 47 days after the disposal of dead birds. This is not in line with 62(1) and 65 of Regulation (EU) 2016/429 and Article 15 and points A and B of Annex IV of the Delegated regulation (EU) 2020/687 2020/687.

The EU reference laboratory provided the authorities with a phylogenetic analysis that helped understand from which areas in Europe the virus was introduced. The competent authority did not provide any evidence to the audit team of other epidemiological analysis that has been carried out on the 2022 epidemic to identify possible risk factors that contributed to the introduction and the spread of diseases and thus, to develop and implement better informed policies on prevention and early detection accordingly. The authorities have not identified and addressed their gaps in the response to the HPAI epidemic in 2022 and thus they have not used the lessons learnt during the epizootic, to improve

For the early detection in wild birds, the veterinary authorities also worked closely with the environmental departments and conservation agencies and stakeholders. The audit 7 team considered the number and location of samples taken, both for active and passive surveillance of wild birds adequate and in line with high-risk areas and high-risk periods of introduction of the infection. In 2021, the NRL in Spain processed 1,225 samples from wild birds, of which two were positive. In 2022, there were 3,040 such samples of which 144 were positives.

There were major delays in confirming the infection (Table A) for the positive samples taken either by active or passive surveillance of wild birds (172 from September 2020 to April 2023). Nearly 99% of all cases were confirmed more than three days after sampling, and 50% of them were confirmed two weeks after sampling. The timescales were due to the involvement of two laboratories in the diagnosis of the disease ­ the Autonomous Community laboratory where the generic Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) test is carried out and the national reference laboratory where the virus is subtyped and its pathogenicity determined. The authorities explained that in many of those cases, confirmation was not

The authorities took samples of dead and sick wild birds reported under passive surveillance in the same areas where the first cases of poultry were confirmed a few days after (January and February 2022). However, the fact that those wild birds' samples were processed and confirmed several days after the poultry cases were detected, prevented the competent authority from implementing the enhanced surveillance in poultry, that should have been triggered after confirmation of the infection in wild birds. This is not in line with Section 2, paragraph 2(a)of Annex II of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2021/689.

During passive and active surveillance, the NRL detected six positives to avian influenza virus other than H5 or H7 in 2020, 43 positives to other than H5 or H7 avian influenza virus in 2021 and, 67 non H5 and no H7 avian influenza virus in 2022. All these were detected in wild birds. Laboratory capacity- Diagnostics used for general early detection.

In the event of suspicion of HPAI in poultry, the competent authority set restrictions on the suspected establishments without delay. However, the initial veterinary investigation and sampling was delayed in several cases. Although in most cases, informal communications with the national disease crisis centre occurred immediately, there were delays in the regional authorities conducting the required investigation to confirm or rule out the presence of HPAI. This is not in line with Article 54 of Regulation (EU) 2016/429.

The competent authorities need to update the contingency plan, together with the epidemiological inquiry to be used for the investigation of aquatic diseases, taking into account the new provisions set by the AHL. This would allow the competent authorities to act, in line with the EU legislation, if a Category A disease is occurring in the country.

The competent authority have implemented effectively the new process of registration and approval of the aquaculture establishments, according to the AHL, with clear guidelines and instructions for the correct implementation from the VIU. However, in some cases the Team Aqua has assessed the risk of the approved establishments not taking into account all the criteria listed in Annex VI to Delegated Regulation (EU) 2020/689. This may increase the risk of not detecting the IHN during the regular health visits carried out by the Team Aqua.

The audit team visited one trout establishment approved and ranked as medium risk by the Team Aqua, since aquatic animals are sent to put and take lakes only. However, the competent authority didn't consider the high risk of infection due to the close proximity to an angling lake next to it, the recurrence of the IHN infection with two outbreaks occurred respectively in 2021 and 2022 and the high number of movements in and out the establishment. This is not in line with Chapter 2 a) and b), Part I of Annex VI to Regulation (EU) 2020/689, as regards the risk ranking to be applied in certain approved aquaculture establishments in this regard.

The audit team visited another trout establishment approved and ranked as medium risk, which has been infected with IHN in September 2022. Fish is kept for approximately three months, from 200 to 500 grams. The operator is consigning to more than 50 establishments, of which approximately 70 % are put and take lakes, and it is receiving from other 20 establishments. Nevertheless, the competent authority didn't consider the high risk of infection due to the high number of movements going in and out the establishment. This is not in line with Regulation (EU) 2020/689, as mentioned in the previous finding. The competent authority agreed with the audit team on the need to review the risk assessme

The official veterinarians of the Team Aqua are implementing, in particular, the risk-based health surveillance in all approved aquaculture establishments, as foreseen by Chapter 1, Part III, Annex VI of Regulation (EU) 2020/689. The frequency of the health visits and possible sampling depends on the risk of the approved aquaculture establishment, determined by the DVFA as high, medium or low. However, the DVFA ranked some of the establishments visited by the audit team, as explained in previous findings 36 and 37, with a risk ranking (i.e. "medium" instead of "high) which is resulting in a frequency of health visits too low.

The competent authorities implemented the certification for the trade of aquatic animals from Denmark to other Member States as required by EU legislation. However, the competent authority deemed transportation of aquatic animals, transiting through a water exchange point in Denmark without proper disinfection procedures, as the possible cause of the transmission of IHN to another Member State This is not in line with the EU legislation, that requires that the competent authorities must certify that animals are not transported under conditions that jeopardize their health status.

The competent authorities in Finland notified an IHN outbreak in June 2022, following a consignment of aquatic animals received from Denmark. The DVFA traced and tested, with negative results, the two establishments delivering respectively eggs and fishes to the confirmed outbreak in Finland, explaining to the audit team that a possible transmission of the disease was 24 due to the transit through one of the two water exchange points registered in Denmark. As a consequence, the DVFA established a specific procedure for the cleaning and disinfection of one of the two water exchange points, with all transporters requested to transit that specific water exchange point when delivering fish for i

The competent authorities have approved the procedures for the cleaning and disinfection of the transporters, one water exchange point, and for all the other documents foreseen by the EU legislation. However, they are not applying regular official controls on transporters and water exchange points, on a risk basis, to verify compliance with the approved procedures and the activities under the control of operators. This is not in line with the EU legislation, and it is not assuring the absence of risk of transmission of IHN or other aquatic diseases with the 25 movement of aquatic animals. 6. OVERALL CONCLUSIONS The competent authorities have established a system with effective coordination a

The VIUs are carrying out spot-checks of transporters according to Regulation (EU) 1/2005, for animal welfare. However, they are not carrying out the official controls of the transporters registered in the Country. This is not in line with the provisions of paragraph 1 of Articles 9, 10 and 20 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 (Official Controls Regulation - OCR), regarding the regular risk based official controls on all operators, including transporters, at any stage of production, processing and distribution of animals, products of animal origin and germinal products. Those official controls would need to address, as well, the activities under the control of operators, i.e., the general obligati

Official personnel at central and local levels are clearly designated. They have followed comprehensive training on aquaculture animal health and the EU requirements. However, in the Federal States visited, the Fish Health Services and private veterinarians and/or aquatic animal health professionals, perform certain tasks related to other official activities, such as the health visits and sampling that are part of the risk-based health surveillance that is designed and should be conducted by the competent authority. The competent authorities have not formally delegated those responsibilities, or audited or inspected the Fish Health Services and/or private professionals, to verify that they p

Those veterinarians and professionals are providing animal health services, but neither them nor the Fish Health Services can carry out the official controls required by Article 5 of Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2022/160 and Article 3 of Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2022/671. They count also on the support of private designated and accredited 6 laboratories to investigate situations where they are notified by operators and need to take samples for examination in accordance with Article 18(1)(c) of the AHL. The authorities of the Federal States visited have not delegated formally to the Fish Health Services (that are not part of their organisation) or to private veterinaria

However, failures in the proper implementation and disregard of exceeding result without reaching a robust conclusion could jeopardise this protection mechanism.

Since the CCA carried out the final classification of production areas, the revision of classification has been based on monitoring results obtained during the harvesting period (see section 4), which could be sufficient if harvesting is officially allowed exclusively during this part of the year. label_heading: Conclusions on official controls of live bivalve molluscs
paragraph_text: The current design of the monitoring programme for microbiological quality seems adequate for the harvesting period, but the programmes for the presence of biotoxins and phytoplankton are not fully aligned with EU requirements and are not fully implemented. This could compromise the ability of the competent authority to detect possible exceedances of biotoxins limits. The delays in obtaining laboratory test results lower the effectiveness of the monitoring.

According to the relevant procedures, competent authorities periodically monitor classified production areas in order to check the microbiological quality of LBM, and the presence of marine biotoxins and chemical contaminants in LBM and, since recently, for the presence of toxin-producing plankton in water, as required respectively in Article 59(b)(c) and (d) of Regulation (EU) 2019/627. The monitoring in one of the production areas was very limited, therefore not meeting these requirements. a) For microbiological quality of live bivalve molluscs

According to the relevant procedure, all points have to sampled once per month, which comply with the requirements of Article 61(1) of Regulation (EU) 2019/627; however, in practice, this frequency is only implemented during the harvesting period and the months immediately prior and subsequent to it (see section 4 and paragraph 9, regarding seasonal harvesting), which could be sufficient if harvesting was officially allowed exclusively during this part of the year, which was not the case at the time of the audit.

According to the relevant procedure, monitoring has to be carried out with a frequency that varies between once per week (during the harvesting season) to once per month (from October to April), which would be in line with Article 61(1) an (4) of Regulation (EU) 2019/627 if harvesting was officially allowed exclusively during part of the year. However, at the time of the audit, this frequency was not met. According to the information provided to the audit team, there were different factors that prevented the sampling plan to be fulfilled (e.g., availability of vessels and other logistic problems, rough weather conditions), or that undermined the usefulness of complying with these frequencies

According to the relevant procedure, monitoring has to be carried out with a frequency similar to the biotoxins; therefore, the same observations made above (paragraph 17) regarding required frequencies and the difficulties faced by counties CA are relevant here.

The competent authorities were considering the inclusion of a second sampling location per production area that would allow the early detection of changes in the composition of plankton containing toxins and the geographical distribution of this plankton that can suggest an accumulation of toxins in LBM flesh, as required in Article 61(3)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2019/627.

According to the relevant procedure, monitoring has to be carried out with a frequency similar to the biotoxins; therefore, the same observations made above (paragraph 17) regarding required frequencies and the difficulties faced by counties CA are relevant here.

According to the relevant procedure, the competent authority must temporary close production areas when monitoring results show E. coli most probable number exceeding 700 per 100 grammes of flesh and intravalvular liquid (it is important to note that all production areas in Romania are class A and at the time of the audit there were no purification centres in the country). This closure is in line with Article 62(1) of Regulation (EU) 2019/627. Based on the information provided to the audit team, this closure is only enforced when such situation occurs during the harvesting period. This approach would be acceptable if harvesting is officially allowed exclusively during this particular time of

According to the relevant procedure, the competent authority should conduct intensive sampling when monitoring results surpass the thresholds established at national level 7 (see paragraph 23). This aligns with Articles 61(3)(a) and 61(7) of Regulation (EU) 2019/627. However, the competent authority confirmed that they currently do not adhere to this procedure. They consider its effectiveness is limited value due to several reasons: the same sampling locations are used for water and LBM, there are no additional water sampling locations for early warning, the long turnarounds times for results established in national legislation, and delays from laboratories results for biotoxins and phytopla

label_heading: Conclusions on official controls of live bivalve molluscs
paragraph_text: In addition, the monitoring programme for biotoxins does not include marine gastropods, and there are no data that compare the rate of accumulation of biotoxins with the indicator species. This poses a risk that marine gastropods with biotoxins content above the regulated limits might be placed on the market.

Although NRLs for E. coli and biotoxins are designated, the fact that they do not always fulfil the conditions of EU legislation for this designation or that they do not carry out all the tasks and responsibilities prescribed can have an impact in the quality and consistency of the results delivered.

The designation of official control laboratories includes all relevant laboratories (except for phytoplankton). As these laboratories do not always fulfil all the conditions for their designation and the designation does not always include all the necessary details to ensure timely and quality provision of results, this can have a negative impact in the quality of official controls over LBM and affect their efficient and effective supervision.

The technical competence and capacity of the official control laboratories for E. coli and phytoplankton, their fitness for purpose and their generally adequate analytical methods, instils confidence in the reliability of their results. This supports the authorities in the monitoring of production areas, allowing them to make informed decisions to safeguard the safety of molluscs.

Despite the technical competence and capacity of the official control laboratory for biotoxins, the fact that the validation of ASP and PSP testing methods is not internationally recognised, makes the reliability and accuracy of the results produced questionable for these two biotoxins. In addition, the fact that the laboratory for lipophilic toxins cannot analyse a number of compounds of this group (although it uses the EU reference method, internally validated and accredited) raises concern about the risk of underestimation of this biotoxin.
The absence of participation of official control laboratories in proficiency testing prevent the authorities to demonstrate the reliability of their results.

The long turnarounds times established in national legislation, together with the laboratories delays in providing timely results, have a negative impact on the quality of 13 official controls. 6 OVERALL CONCLUSION Although the official system for controlling bivalve molluscs and marine gastropods was only established in 2019, the authorities at different levels show good understanding of legislative requirements, and willingness to solve the deficiencies and to improve the system. The control system in place generally aligns with EU provisions, but it is implemented in full only during the harvesting period. Therefore, it would be consistent with the EU requirements if harvesting is officia

The competent authority has designated NRLs for E. coli and for biotoxins in LBM, as required in Article 100(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. However, at the time of the audit, the NRL for biotoxins did not meet certain legislative requirements (i.e., Article 100(2) and (3)(c)(e)). 10 46. The audit team showed evidence of the implementation of part of the tasks established in Article 101(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 by the NRL for E. coli (e.g., participation in proficiency testing organised by the EURL, provision of training and support to official control laboratories); however, this laboratory has not been able to organise an inter-laboratory comparative testing or a proficiency test bet
At the time of the audit, the NRL for biotoxins was not in a position to comply with most of the responsibilities and tasks established in Article 101(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

The competent authorities have designated official control laboratories, as required in Article 37(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. In particular, they have designated three laboratories for E. coli (two testing LBM from production areas and one testing final products from dispatch centres) and one for biotoxins. However, designations do not include all the details required by Article 37(3) and, in the case of biotoxins laboratory, it does not require to use testing methods in line with EU requirements (see paragraph 57). At the time of the audit the laboratory testing for phytoplankton had not yet been designated as it did not comply with part of the national requirements for designation.

With regard to supervision of the designated laboratories, the CCA, in collaboration with the NRL for E. coli, carries out audits of these laboratories at county level, as required in Article 39(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625, although limited to the conditions described in the previous paragraph. However, the CCA informed the audit team that a similar type of supervision cannot be carried out over central level laboratories designated for official controls; therefore, audits required by Article 39(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 are not performed over the biotoxins laboratory. 5.3.1 Laboratories for microbiology
These laboratories regularly participate in proficiency testing but they have never participated in a proficiency testing with LBM sample matrix. 11 5.3.2 Laboratory for phytoplankton
There are two analysts qualified for the identification and quantification of plankton species. Both were internally trained and have plans to participate in external training in 2024.

The laboratory consistently conducts internal quality controls, with every sample being analysed by the two analysts by default to ensure the accuracy and consistency of phytoplankton results. The laboratory has never participated in a proficiency testing, but it intends to participate in one in 2024.

At the time of the audit, the long turnarounds times established in national legislation, together with the length of the analysis in this laboratory, limited the value of this monitoring for the competent authorities. 5.3.3 Laboratories for biotoxins

The official control laboratory for PSP and ASP uses testing methods which validation has not been internationally recognised, therefore they do not meet the requirements of Chapters I(A) and (B) and II(A) and (B) of Annex V to Regulation (EU) 2019/627, respectively.

The laboratory for lipophilic toxins uses the EU reference method established in Chapter III(A) of Annex V to Regulation (EU) 2019/627. It mostly follows the EU reference laboratory standard operational procedure with a few deviations (e.g., it does not include part of the certified reference materials, certain quality control criteria, recovery correction and matrix correction). It is accredited by the national accreditation body, as required in Article 37(5)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. The laboratory has carried out an internal validation for mussel matrix, as this is the species routinely analysed in this laboratory. However, the validation was not carried out for all the relevant tox

According to the information provided to the audit team, biotoxins results are normally issued in 4-5 days; however, it most of the laboratory reports assessed, the reporting time was one week. Despite the fact this is within the deadline established in national legislation, this provides limited value to the competent authorities to adequately manage production areas, therefore it cannot be considered as a timely delivery of test results as required in Article 37(4)(d) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Regarding the BCPs designated by AFSVSPP for food and feed of non-animal origin, the facilities were in general not compliant at the BCP Luka Koper port. At the BCP Ljubljana Brnik airport the facilities for controls on consignments of goods of animal origin were shared with controls of food and feed of non-animal origin. The audit team noted that the unloading and storage facilities for food and feed of non-animal origin at the BCP Luka Koper port did not have adequate drainage and most floors were constructed of tarmac which is not easy to clean and disinfect. This is not in line with Article 3(2) and (3) of Regulation (EU) 2019/1014.

The audit team noted that both BCPs designated by HIRS for controls on food contact materials and food supplements were not compliant with the minimum requirements for BCPs due to a lack of facilities and equipment. This is not in line with Article 64(3)(b) and (c) of the OCR and Articles 3 and 4 of Regulation (EU) 2019/1014. In the absence of BCP control facilities, the documentary controls are carried out in regional offices outside the port or airport. The identity and physical checks take place in the storage facilities within the BCP Luka Koper port which do not meet the minimum requirements (see finding 48) or at Ljubljana airport, which also did not have adequate drainage.

The control system ensures that consignments of animals and goods entering the EU are presented for official controls, and that those controls are carried out in line with documented procedures and, with few exceptions, EU requirements. 5.3 COMPLIANCE OF BORDER CONTROL POSTS AND CONTROL POINTS WITH MINIMUM REQUIREMENTS The audit team selected both designated BCPs Ljubljana Brnik airport and Luka Koper port and two control points from the lists published on the Commission webpages to verify their compliance with the applicable minimum requirements. This is not in line with Article 64(3)(b) and (c) of the OCR and Articles 3 and 4 of Regulation (EU) 2019/1014. In the absence of BCP control facilities, the documentary controls are carried out in regional offices outside the port or airport. The identity and physical checks take place in the storage facilities within the BCP Luka Koper port which do not meet the minimum requirements (see finding 48) or at Ljubljana airport, which also did not have adequate drainage.

The system in place ensures that consignments of animals and goods entering the EU are presented for official controls, and that those controls are, generally carried out in line with guidelines, documented procedures and Union legislation. A limited number of shortcomings were identified, the most significant of which related to the performance of physical checks on consignments of animals in transit, which are based on a visual check rather than a clinical examination as required.

The SFVS stated that consignments of bovine animals in transit are not partially or fully unloaded for identity and physical checks at the BCP of arrival, but that they conduct a visual check of the animals on the means of transport, using fixed platforms. The audit team noted that this does not allow an appropriate clinical examination of the selected 10 animals to be performed, which is not in line with Article 4(3) and Part II of Annex I to Regulation (EU) 2019/2130.

The information kept in the database makes possible full traceability of PDO and PGI wines. CAFIA verifies the origin and the quality of PDO wines and issues administrative decisions for the classification and marketing of PDO wines. Such controls are not required for wines intended to be marketed as PGI (see also paragraphs 33, 46 and 66 below). The eligibility for using PDO/PGI designations is also checked when the products are placed on the market, particularly in the retailers' chain.

Operators wishing to market their wine as PDO have to request the classification of every batch of wine produced by CAFIA. This is achieved at the expense of an administrative fee paid to CAFIA, which becomes income of the state budget. The classification procedure is based on the verification of grapes and on analytical and organoleptic testing. The wine classification carried out by CAFIA ensures the traceability of the origin and the quality of every batch of wine intended to be marketed as PDO (e.g. "quality wine" or "quality wine with an attribute"). However, such a system is not in place for PGI wines.

The authenticity of the marketed wines is verified through official analytical testing carried out in the laboratory of CAFIA. The sensory commission of CAFIA carries out organoleptic testing. Where the traceability of sampled wines cannot be otherwise verified, the laboratory is requested to carry out isotopic analysis of wine samples. However, the examination of the authenticity is not an option for PGI wines, as no classification involving at least sampling for analytical testing is carried out for wine batches intended to be marketed as PGI products. The CA carries out regular surveys in the demarcated areas for D. citri in parallel with the survey for C. Liberibacter. However, as a result of the buffer zone not being clearly defined (see paragraphs 23 and 24), these surveys were conducted all over Cyprus.

ADO staff have been instructed to focus the survey on citrus trees in places of production at the time of new flushing, in spring, mid-summer and late autumn. The ADO staff follow an "S-shape" course within the citrus orchards and focus on the recently developed flushes of young stems and leaves of trees. However, this is not always possible, in particular for the developing upper parts of the tree canopy and surveillance efforts are mostly limited to leaves growing within the lower interior central part of the trees.

paragraph_text: Emergency authorisations may each include multiple crops and/or targets or extend to a total period beyond 120 days. This is not in line with Article 53 of Regulation No (EC) 1107/2009. Furthermore, emergency authorisations generally involve approved active substances and PPPs authorised elsewhere. The dangers these authorisations are addressing could therefore, at least in the medium term, be contained by the regular authorisation procedures laid down in Articles 33, 40, or 51 of Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009. Using emergency authorisations repeatedly instead, waters down the integrity of the authorisation system. 5.2. ORGANISATION OF OFFICIAL CONTROLS ON THE MARKETING AND USE OF PLANT PROTE

Tukes has a rule of thumb that emergency authorisations should not be given for more than five years, but exceptions have been made and the audit team noted cases of repeated emergency authorisations for many years (e.g. in one case, 8 years, so far). The audit team considered that these applications would be more correctly accommodated within the conventional authorisation framework maintaining the system's integrity as referred to in Commission Staff Working Document on emergency situations according to Article 53 of Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009. In addition, there are cases of single emergency authorisations granted for multiple crops or targets, which is also not in line with the said Article.

The official controls for the use of PPPs are always announced in advance. The instructions stipulate that notice should be `as short as possible' The FFA stated that controls cannot be carried out without the presence of the farmer, as they also need to check the farmer's records on the use of PPPs. In addition, given the long distances between inspection sites, the advance notice helps to prevent wasted resources by ensuring the farmer is present at the agreed time. The audit team considered that such general use of prior notifications is not in line with Article 9(4) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. This issue was also noted in the 2014 audit.

Consequently, the CAs are unable to verify the absence of unacceptable co-formulants in PPPs, as outlined in Article 27 of Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009 and listed in its Annex IIII. They are also unable to determine whether certain impurities exceed the maximum content permitted in the approval of the relevant active substances, as referred to in Article 6(b) of the same Regulation. This is not in line with Article 24(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

The CA stated that the technical capabilities for detecting impurities, co-formulants and auxiliary substances do exist, since the laboratory is equipped with suitable analytical tools. Disease control measures on suspected cases were generally adequate. However, the lack of routine sampling and testing in suspected cases may have delayed outbreak confirmation, and potentially increased the viral load in the farm, or weakened the basis for ruling out suspected cases.

For confirmed cases, the authorities implemented appropriate control measures, except they fail to trace animal products dispatched from infected farms. Although the oversight is unknown, it could have led to the unintentional spread of sheep pox 4 https://food.ec.europa.eu/horizontal-topics/official-controls-and-enforcement/legislation-official-controls/better- training-safer-food_en. 4 to other farms and regions, presenting inconsistent risk-mitigation measures and hampering the assurance provided by the disease containment measures.

Temporary official veterinarians ("seasonal veterinarians") have been hired to implement ASF measures in four areas of higher risk. During their work they also detected a significant number of not registered non-commercial farms. Since 2023, the number of small pig farms has decreased significantly in Greece as many did not meet minimum biosecurity standards and a depopulation programme was put in place. Nevertheless, there are gaps as regards the registration of non-commercial farms. Incomplete entries and delays in updating the national pig database as well as the farm registers do not allow the competent authority to have a reliable overview of the pig population for animal health control

Despite a national plan for implementing official controls on biosecurity measures during hunting activities, the competent authority does not carry out such controls as planned; related activities have also not produced any impact so far. In addition, the national plan is not well established as regards scope, inspection records and addressing non-compliances. This means that the competent authority has limited control over the risk of the virus spreading by hunted wild boar.

Passive surveillance of the domestic pig population is implemented through testing of dead animals notified to authorities by farmers. The level of notifications is overall satisfactory for larger establishments, whereas absent or incomplete mortality records in smaller farms make verification of compliance in these operations difficult to estimate.

The number of reported wild boar found dead by hunters is very low compared to the hunting bag (total number of wild boars hunted per year). This is compounded by underreporting and thus a lack of testing of carcasses hunted in restricted areas and destined for private consumption. As a result, the competent authority misses important information on the epidemiological status of the disease. Although the hunting community has comprehensive knowledge of the wild boar population and its dynamics, it has failed to achieve the targets set by the competent authority for reducing the wild porcine animal population. 6 7. The control procedures, on the use of sulphites by operators of primary production fishing vessels, do not cover all the relevant EU rules, in particular with regard to the maximum admissible levels for such additives, and are therefore not adequately checked by the competent authorities.

label_heading: Conclusions on recommendation No 2 of the 2021 audit
paragraph_text: As regard the remuneration system of staff performing official tasks in slaughterhouses with automatic conveyor belt, the measures announced in the AP, and that will address the relevant part of the recommendation, have not been introduced. No deadline is foreseen for solving this long-standing situation. Furthermore, it is particularly worrying that the scale of this non-compliance appears to affect most of the slaughterhouses in the country. 5.3 RECOMMENDATION NO 3 OF THE 2021 AUDIT "To ensure the correct application of Article 79 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 in respect of the collection of fees or charges to cover the costs occasioned by official controls". Findings

The changes in the national legislation on the remuneration system of AVs supervising the slaughter of animals announced in the AP have been partially introduced: in slaughterhouses without automatic conveyor belt the AVs are paid per hour. (EU) 2017/625 as compromises the impartiality of staff performing official tasks. Concerning this latter system, the audit 4 team was informed that almost all the slaughterhouses in Poland use it. label_heading: Conclusions on recommendation No 5 of the 2021 audit
paragraph_text: Despite nearly all the actions from the AP being implemented and GVI's' efforts to strengthen enforcement measures for non-compliance with animal welfare rules, significant progress has not been made. Many cases are still being dismissed or rejected by enforcement authorities. According to the Polish legal system, the VI has no competence on this matter. 9 5.6 RECOMMENDATION NO 6 OF THE 2021 AUDIT "To ensure that approved establishments meet the relevant requirements of food law and that those requirements are kept under review when carrying out official controls in order to comply with Article 148(3) and (5) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Particular attention should be paid to the assessment

The CVO received feedback from the NPO in February 2024. The document indicated that from 2020 to October 2023, the prosecutor's offices handled 1 928 cases concerning the violation of the animal welfare law. All these cases were initiated by the VI, and following their verification were discontinued at their initial stage. The primary reason for not proceeding with the cases was that the acts in question did not constitute a criminal offense. The audit team noted that the document lacked detailed analyses or explanations to help the DVOs understand the reasons behind the dismissals and prevent similar situations from occurring in the future.

During the meetings the audit team had with the DVOs and RVOs they noted that it is difficult to monitor the prosecutors' duties, as they are independent from any other governmental body, and explain that they usually do not receive information about the follow up of the cases they transmitted to the NPO. One of the DVOs met provided figures of the number of cases transmitted to the enforcement authorities and number of cases 8 dismissed/rejected during the investigation phase (e.g. in 2023, 180 cases were notified, 80 cases dismissed/rejected and no information on 29 cases). The DVO lodged 19 complaints for the refusal to open an investigation or closure of the case at the pre-trial stage.

According to the DVO and RVO when they identify non-compliance related to animal welfare, they do not take into account whether the same operator has repeatedly committed these breaches, nor do they maintain any records. Consequently, they lack awareness of whether an FBO has a history of repeated offenses and are unable to include this information in their notifications to the NPO.

label_heading: Conclusions on recommendation No 8 of the 2021 audit
paragraph_text: Although the measures from the action plan were implemented and improvements have been observed since the 2021 audit, the actions are not effective or do not have the expected results. They often fail to identify the source of contamination or prevent its recurrence, suggesting that the measures taken by the FBOs to address this recommendation are not adequate and/or sufficient. 5.9 RECOMMENDATION NO 9 OF THE 2021 AUDIT "To ensure that in case of suspicion of non-compliance (e.g. reliability of Salmonella test results provided by some private laboratories), the competent authorities perform an inves- tigation to confirm or to eliminate the suspicion, as prescribed by Article 137(2) of Regula

In all the poultry slaughterhouses visited the implementation of the measures and corrective actions provided in the HACCP plans in case of Salmonella detection could not identify the source of the contamination and prevent recurrence. It was noted that the FBO's actions and investigations were repeatedly focused on primary production (e.g. visits to farms and verification of the biosecurity measures) and did not pay attention, for example, to possible cross contamination points or production shortcomings at establishment level.

label_heading: Conclusions on legislation and implementing measures.
paragraph_text: The official control system is supported by national legislation covering the relevant as- pects within the scope of the audit. However, the absence of guidance docu- ments/instructions for the official staff compromises the guarantees that official controls are effective and are carried out in a uniform and consistent way.

label_heading: Conclusions on organisation and implementation of official controls
paragraph_text: An official control plan, based on risk, is implemented by the CA. However, the limited 14 detection and/or recording of non-compliances at establishment level and, consequently, the lack of enforcement actions to correct the non-compliant situations compromise the effectiveness of the control system in place. In this regard, significant shortcomings in relation to the sanitary conditions and to the animal welfare conditions were noted that had not been previously identified or recorded in any level of official control.

label_heading: Conclusions on organisation and implementation of official controls
paragraph_text: Certain official controls at slaughterhouse level are not carried out in line with the EU requirements. In particular, the serious deviations from the legally required practical ar- rangements concerning PMI and the controls on HACCP-based procedures undermine the reliability of the OVs' decision on the fitness of meat for human consumption.

label_heading: Conclusions on organisation and implementation of official controls
paragraph_text: The AMI and the controls on FCI, animal identification and traceability are in general in line with the EU requirements. As a result, the audit team noted in the four domestic ungulates' large capacity slaughterhouses visited that FBOs took these samples within two to four hours after slaughter when the carcasses already underwent blast-chilling. The audit team also noted some inconsistencies regarding the deadlines given to rectify non-compliances which could have been eliminated by an immediate action, in order to comply with the requirements of Article 137(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. paragraph_text: Official controls at ABP plants cover HACCP-based procedures when required but they are not sufficient to reliably verify the operators' level of compliance with all of the key requirements of these procedures, resulting in incomplete identification of hazards by ABP operators.

paragraph_text: The petfood and processing plants visited maintained HACCP-based procedures as re- quired by Article 29 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009. There is a system of official controls in place for animals and goods of animal and non- animal origin entering the EU though BCPs in Romania, which is supported by information technology systems and cooperation and communication within and between the competent authorities. However, shortcomings related to the lack of up-to-date documented procedures and arrangements in place and a shortage of staff have an adverse impact on the effectiveness of implementation of official import controls. 5.2 IMPLEMENTATION OF OFFICIAL CONTROLS ON ANIMALS AND GOODS ENTERING THE EU The audit team evaluated the implementation of official controls on consignments of animals and goods entering the EU through BC

The audit team noted that the majority of the documented procedures had not been updated to reflect the requirements of the OCR and could not therefore ensure the effectiveness and appropriateness of official controls, which is not in line with Article 5(1)(a) and 12(3)(b)of the OCR. For example, the competent authorities do not have up- to-date documented procedures for prior notification, the performance of documentary, identity and physical checks, including the frequency rates, on consignments of animals and goods and official controls on consignments of goods of animal origin in transit (see section 5.2).

The audit team also noted that the arrangements in place for the implementation of the measures referred to in Articles 65, 66 and 67 of the OCR and contingency arrangements are incomplete, which is not in line with Article 64(3)(d) and(e) respectively of the OCR.

The system of official controls on animals and goods entering the Union though BCPs in Romania showed significant shortcomings in the frequencies at which identity and physical checks are performed on goods of animal origin and in the performance of official controls on consignments of goods of animal origin in transit. Other shortcomings were noted concerning the implementation of official controls on certain consignments of animals and goods of non-animal origin. Collectively, these shortcomings significantly undermine the overall effectiveness and appropriateness of official controls to ensure that only compliant consignments of animals and goods enter the EU. 5.3 COMPLIANCE OF BORDER CON

At one BCP of introduction visited, the BCP staff stated that in case of official controls on consignments of goods of animal origin in transit, the vehicles or transport containers in which such consignments leave the BCP were not sealed by the BCP staff, which is not in line with Article 19(d) of Regulation (EU) 2019/2124. This practice was further confirmed to the audit team during subsequent meetings with staff at other Romanian BCPs.

During the visit to a port BCP of exit, the BCP staff stated that they did not perform an identity check to ensure that consignment of goods leaving the EU through this BCP corresponded to the consignment referred to in the associated CHED. This is not in line with Article 33 of Regulation (EU) 2019/2124. The staff at this BCP of exit explained that part III of the CHEDs was completed solely based on receiving copies of CHEDs from the relevant customs agents. According to TRACES-NT, this port BCP accounted for 8 402 out of a total of 12 317 consignments exiting in transit through Romanian BCPs of which about 7 000 have part III completed. 10 35. Other shortcomings were noted concerning the implementation of official controls on certain consignments of animals and goods of non-animal origin. Collectively, these shortcomings significantly undermine the overall effectiveness and appropriateness of official controls to ensure that only compliant consignments of animals and goods enter the EU. 5.3 COMPLIANCE OF BORDER CON

The audit team noted that the frequency of physical checks performed on goods of animal origin was not in line with the baseline frequency rate set out in Articles 4(1) and 11 5(1) and Annex I to Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/2129. This finding predominantly relates to consignments of poultry meat from Ukraine entering the EU; approximately 3 000 consignments of poultry meat in 2023 were subjected to physical checks at a rate of 3% compared to the required minimum frequency of 30%. 5.2.4.3 Checks on consignments of goods of non-animal origin

However, identity and physical checks on consignments subject to measures set out in Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2020/1158 had not been carried out in line with the minimum frequency rate set out in Article 5(2) of that Regulation. Based on data provided by the competent authorities, approximately 1.7% (4 out of 240) of such consignments in 2023 were subjected to identity and physical checks compared to the required minimum frequency of 20%.

The evaluated BCPs, except for a suspended BCP for animals, had the minimum facilities and equipment in place for the categories of animals and goods of animal origin for which they had been designated, but the three BCPs visited were not well maintained. In addition, the Romanian authorities perform official controls on consignments of food contact materials entering the EU without having designated BCPs for this category of goods. The control point visited does not comply with the minimum requirements for BCPs for the categories of goods for which it has been designated. These shortcomings have the potential to reduce the overall effectiveness of the official control system. 5.4 FOLLOW ­ U

The audit team noted that no BCPs have been designated and listed for food contact materials, (i.e. category PNAO-NHC(other)), and that official controls on consignments of food contact materials entering the EU are instead performed at the importers' warehouses, which is not in line with Article 49(1) of the OCR.

The audit team found that facilities and equipment at the port BCPs Constana North and Constana South and the airport BCP Bucharest Henri Coand were generally compliant with the minimum requirements for BCPs for the categories of goods for which they had been designated. However, the loading and storage facilities for goods of animal and non-animal origin at these three BCPs, and the inspection facilities at the airport BCP Bucharest Henri Coand, were not maintained and thus not easy to clean and disinfect. This is not in line with Article 3(2) and (3) of Regulation (EU) 2019/1014 and 64(3) of the OCR.

The audit team visited one control point used for identity and physical checks on consignments of non-animal origin. The audit team found that the control point was not compliant with the minimum requirements for BCPs, which is not in line with Article 53(1)(a) of the OCR. There were no clearly dedicated unloading, inspection and storage areas, there was no drainage in these areas, and the floors of these areas were poorly maintained and thus not easy to clean and disinfect. In addition, the inspection area did not have a supply of hot and cold running water and hand washing facilities and it was equipped with a table that was not easy to clean and disinfect. The audit team noted that in some of those CHEDs, the goods have been described with the customs nomenclature (CN) code 9930 for goods delivered to vessels and aircraft rather than the relevant CN code for each of the commodities men- tioned in the accompanying official certificate according to the model referred to in Part I of the Annex to Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/2128.

The audit team further noted that, based on data in TRACES-NT for 2023 and 2024, the majority of CHEDs issued for non-conforming goods intended either for storage in ap- proved warehouses, ship supply vessels leaving the EU, or exit at BCPs for ship supply vessels located in a third country port relied on the use of the CN code 9930, which is not 10 in line with Article 40(1) and Part I of Annex II to Commission Implementing Regula- tion (EU) 2019/1715 and does not allow traceability of goods in transit.

Whilst the Ministry of Health stated that identity checks are full checks or limited to a checks on the seals on containers or means of transport, the audit team noted that, at the BCP with the highest throughput of consignments of goods of animal origin, identity checks are being carried out digitally based on information provided by the terminal op- erator on such consignments, which is not in line with Article 3(2) of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/2130. The Ministry of Health was not able to explain to the audit team how this digital control system operated. The audit team evaluated five CHEDs for consignment of goods of animal origin re- entering the EU, of which three consignments were authorised to re-enter in compliance with Articles 2 and 3 of Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2019/2074. paragraph_text: The control and surveillance plans for residues of pharmacologically active sub- stances, pesticides and contaminants are generally implemented in line with planned arrangements, EU legal requirements and are effective, underpinning assurances on the residues status of food of animal origin. The Romanian authorities made resolute efforts in recent years to increase among backyards' operators the levels of awareness about, and compliance with requirements on animal traceability. However, despite introducing new legislation and strengthening official controls on the matter, the inadequate powers available to officials to enforce those new provisions keep holding back progress in this area.

An undetermined, but still significant number of illegal movements in the backyards population, and the underreporting to the national database of other events from those establishments (e.g., on-site slaughter), have an uncertain impact on surveillance for ASF and keep impairing epidemiological investigations when the disease is suspected or confirmed.

When ASF outbreaks occur in backyards, authorities do not always take effective measures to mitigate the risk of local disease spread. Persistent shortcomings in animal traceability and biosecurity allow the virus to circulate between backyards, leading to clusters of outbreaks that last longer than expected, even when the number of primary cases is limited.

Implementation of surveillance for ASF in wild boar varies significantly between counties, but it confronts since the 2021/22 hunting season increasing challenges to find and test dead animals, which became a rare event in many of them4. Besides, the reluctance of the competent authorities to enforce requirements on ASF surveillance in hunting grounds, and delays in approving new legal provisions to introduce economic incentives to encourage searching for and testing of wild boars, keep impairing early detection and control of the disease.

The national action plan and legal framework to manage wild boar populations for ASF control, alongside the natural impact of the disease, led to a steady population decline until spring 2023. However, disagreements with part of the hunting community in some areas of the country, resulting in weak compliance with and enforcement of hunting quotas, exacerbated by recent climatic and environmental challenges, contributed to reverse that trend. While many hunting grounds apply biosecurity measures effectively, inconsistencies in population management and limited enforcement of ASF control policies create uncertainty about long-term disease control.

label_heading: Conclusion on the implementation of official controls
paragraph_text: While there is a clear designation of competent authorities and distribution of the tasks, and the sampling officials are adequately trained and equipped, the overall effectiveness of the residue control plans for pharmacologically active substances and contaminants is seriously undermined by incomplete implementation of the plans combined with uneven distribution of the sampling over the year. 5.5. Follow-up of non-compliant results and enforcement

In recent years, the implementation of residue control started only in the second half of the year, which is not in line with EU requirements (20) and did not allow the fulfilment of the plans and of the minimum sampling frequencies laid down in EU legislation (21), even if the competent authority always planned 0.5% more samples than required by EU legislation.

In 2024, the sampling plans were transmitted to the regional offices in September, and 4911 (74%) of the 6654 planned samples were taken, and 4631 samples were analysed, therefore only 70% of the samples planned were taken and analysed. In addition, 70% of all samples were taken in October and November, which is not in line with EU legislation (22) to ensure an even spread of sampling throughout the year.

A total of 280 taken samples in 2024 could not be analysed in the laboratory analysing most samples. For four of the 280 samples, transport-related matters were indicated as the reason, for 70 ­ sampling-related obstacles and for 206 ­ the laboratory highlighted breakdowns of the technical equipment and staff holidays and shortages. In June 2025, the competent authority cancelled the request of analysis for 44 samples taken in 2024, as the analyses had still not started.

For both years 2023 and 2024, the auditors observed that, in addition to the sampling carried out largely in the second half of those years, in several cases, multiple sampling was performed to fulfil the requested sample numbers, especially during the last weeks of the respective years. This multiple sampling was not always performed in line with EU legal requirements which set the conditions to be respected for double sampling. Notably, no specific identification of the operator could be found, nor any risk-based justification. This appeared to be done only to improve overall sample numbers at the end of the year. Official veterinarians use a standard template to carry out the epidemiological enquiries of outbreaks. The template follows the requirements of Article 57 of Regulation (EU) 2016/429. Most outbreak investigations concluded that wild birds were the source of infection. However, they did not consistently include detail on possible biosecurity breaches. For instance, in one case, minks that had got into the hen house had killed laying hens, but this was not further examined or linked to biosecurity breaches.

The DVFA did not document the tracing back and forward of all possible sources (people, vehicles or otherwise) that may have led to the introduction of the virus to the outbreak or to other possible epidemiological links of the outbreaks. The DVFA acknowledged the lack of records and expressed that there are plans to develop a system to record the steps and conclusions of the investigations of all possible epidemiological links to the cases. This was not in line with Article 57(2) and Article 62 of Regulation (EU) 2016/429. 13 68. In one outbreak, a private veterinarian, not delegated to take official samples, took swabs under the active surveillance program. These tested positive to H5N1. O

The DK-VET carried out epidemiological analysis for each outbreak and each epidemic year. They include findings from the epidemiological investigations and laboratory results, including whole genome sequencing. These reports include information gathered on the outbreaks from the DVFA officials and explore links between viruses detected in poultry and wild birds.

Private veterinarians take samples for active and sometimes also for passive surveillance. The DVFA has not delegated official activities, such as sampling within this active surveillance program, to private veterinarians (see also finding 66). This is not in line with Articles 28, 30 and 31 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

The DVFA consistently documented certain verification steps, such as movement derogation reviews and disinfection validations. At the time of the audit, the authorities did not have plans to establish regular biosecurity controls, enforce these proportionally, or delegate and supervise private veterinarians tasked with carrying out official activities. 16 4.2.2 Conclusions on control and eradication

Most operators have the necessary knowledge and motivation to ensure proper animal welfare at slaughter. Improvements in animal welfare at slaughter are driven by that, supported by effective official control activities with adequate follow-up actions from operators. However, administratively burdensome and lengthy sanctioning process reduce the dissuasive effect of enforcement when operators are reluctant to comply. Sanctioning procedures are not dissuasive, risking repeated or prolonged animal suffering.

French authorities carry out the controls at port effectively. French authorities have five staff trained on welfare issues who have also gathered some technical knowledge to ensure that vessels are constructed and equipped to transport animals without causing injury or undue suffering. There are still weaknesses as regards updating and completing the documentation of procedures and methodologies.

The system is non-compliant as regards the composition of the team of inspectors and the required on-board official controls during the first voyage following approval. The team of inspectors carrying out approval and pre-loading inspections does not systematically include the required official veterinarian and maritime expert. It only includes official veterinary auxiliaries who have acquired knowledge from maritime safety experts. In addition, there is no provision for an official veterinarian to carry out official controls on board the vessel during the first voyage.

Despite having approved ten vessels since 1 January 2024, French authorities have not implemented the requirement for an official veterinarian to carry out on-board official controls during the first voyage with animals after the approval (see finding 21). Moreover, the team of inspectors does not include a maritime expert, nor an official veterinarian (see finding 14). These two are contrary to Articles 9 and 10(1) of Regulation (EU) 2023/372.

DGAL district has approved ten livestock vessels since Regulation (EU) 2023/372 entered into force (6). The team of inspectors for these approval inspections included veterinary auxiliaries but not systematically a maritime expert nor an official veterinarian, contrary to Article 9 of Regulation (EU) 2023/372. The approval itself is signed by the official veterinarian heading the team but participation of the official veterinarian in actual inspections is sporadic due to their wider responsibilities (which also include the controls over fisheries, bivalves, export certifications and as border control post).

paragraph_text: The system of planning of inspections is based on appropriate risk-related factors and ensures that the official inspections are carried out regularly, on a risk-basis and with appropriate frequency. While feed inspectors regularly use checklists and guidance documents and official inspections are documented, the effectiveness of these inspections is weakened by several shortcomings in their execution. The feed inspector correctly assessed the plan. In the two other establishments the hazard identification section of the operators` HACCP plan was very generic. In all establishments visited FeBO`s HACCP systems contained instruction on sampling, cleaning and on other relevant procedures. However, most of these procedures were deficient or did not reflect the real procedures which were implemented by these operators. These are not in line with the requirements of Article 7(1b) of Regulation (EC) 183/2005 and these shortcomings were overlooked during previous official inspections.

The DAFP has also prepared guidance on the assessment of testing methods and test results of FeBOs' tests on homogeneity of mixing and cross-contamination. Although, these set of guidance contained several useful information, but some key elements (e.g. acceptance levels of homogeneity tests, criteria of adequate sampling techniques), which are necessary for a comprehensive assessment of these tests, were not described. Local feed inspectors need to carry out a comprehensive assessment of the FeBOs' tests on homogeneity of mixing and on cross contamination.

One establishment visited used a manual cleaning procedure to avoid potential cross- contamination. However, it was evident that the procedure is not effective to prevent cross-contamination.
