Although a training system is in place, covering topics pertinent to the sector audited, the observed gaps in the CA's knowledge of HACCP requirements and to the applicable microbiological criteria for Listeria monocytogenes in RTE meat products raise doubts about its effectiveness, thus jeopardizing the quality of the official controls.

Evidence was provided to the audit team of staff participation in training sessions that are particularly relevant for carrying out official controls on production of meat preparations and meat products in all the regions visited. However, in certain areas - mainly in relation to Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Point (HACCP) requirements and some of the requirements of Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005, which have an impact on the effectiveness of official controls over the production of ready-to-eat (RTE) food - the audit team found gaps in CA inspection staff knowledge (see also paragraphs 50 and 52).

The audit team noted that the non-compliances detected by the CA auditors were mainly related to the pre-requisite programmes of the establishments (e.g. to maintenance and hygiene issues). This was confirmed by the data provided by the SFVS on the summary of the non-compliances detected in establishments during the HACCP audits in 2024. However, significant non-compliances, not detected during HACCP audits, were observed in the establishments visited: · Concerning the physico-chemical characterisation of a RTE product, which is fundamental to deciding whether it supports or does not support the growth of Listeria monocytogenes. In some establishments, there were no specifications for physic

Listeria monocytogenes sampling and testing included both final products and environmental samples. However, in several establishments visited producing RTE meat products able to support the growth of Listeria monocytogenes, it was noted the following: · Samples from the processing area and equipment were taken mostly after cleaning and disinfection. The EURL Guidelines on sampling the food processing area and equipment for the detection of Listeria monocytogenes recommends that the sampling should be carried out during processing (in order to increase the probability of detecting a persistent strain). Sampling only after cleaning and disinfection makes the detection of the pathogen difficul

In addition, the audit team saw examples, when reviewing the CA's follow up actions 11 after RASFF notifications (i.e. when Listeria monocytogenes was detected in RTE meat products), that when another batch of the product concerned was tested for Listeria monocytogenes to prove the safety of the product, the FBO used enumeration with the 100 cfu/g criterion without the FBO's adequate demonstration (i.e. without a shelf-life study) to the satisfaction of the CA that the product will not exceed the limit 100 cfu/g throughout its shelf-life. This is not in line with point 1.2, (in particular the provisions laid down in footnote 5) of Chapter 1, Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005.

The FBOs visited by the audit team did not perform any shelf-life studies for Listeria monocytogenes. The CA highlighted that they only were aware that FBOs in Lithuania in the fish sector carried out shelf-life studies. When discussing the above reported issues with the CA staff and FBOs, the audit team found gaps in their knowledge regarding the requirements of Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005, in particular related to the studies (including the shelf-life studies) referred to in Annex II to the mentioned Regulation. The SFVS explained that in the SFVS strategic plan 2025-2027, it is foreseen to strengthen communication with FBOs and conduct training/seminars on important topics.

Concerning the frequency of own-check sampling of RTE meat products, the audit team noted large discrepancies: in a large capacity meat products establishment producing over 30 tonnes of meat products on a daily basis, including RTE meat products, the frequency of own-check testing for Listeria monocytogenes is one product from a product group on a quarterly basis while, in a smaller capacity establishment, this frequency was once a month. These frequencies had been accepted, or were not noted, by the CA without assessing how the FBOs made the sampling frequency decision in the context of their procedures based on HACCP principles and good hygiene practice, taking into account the instructio

It was also noted that the sampling frequency, for both product and environmental sampling, was not changed (i.e. was not increased by the FBO or the increase was not requested by the CA when the risk changed) even after a RASFF notification related to the detection of Listeria monocytogenes in 25g of one of the RTE meat products.
The audit team noted that during the last years in the establishments visited the own checks meat product and environmental laboratory tests did not identify any Listeria monocytogenes or Salmonella.

Although a system to deliver instructions, information and training material to CA staff is in place, covering topics relevant to the sector audited, it is not effective to routinely cater adequately for training needs on specific subjects, in particular official controls on the production of RTE meat products with high risk of microbiological contamination. This weakness impacts the effectiveness of the official controls.

label_heading: Conclusions on organisation and implementation of official controls
paragraph_text: Official controls are risk based, supported by instructions and checklists and there is evidence that, in general, they are effective in identifying relevant non-compliances, in particular those regarding maintenance and hygiene requirements. However, these controls are not sufficiently effective to identify and enforce correction of non- compliances in relation to high-risk RTE production areas and in relation to shortcomings in the FBOs' food safety management systems.

Despite the above procedures, and training arrangements, the audit team found gaps in the knowledge of a number of CA staff, especially in relation to Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005 and also on Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Points (HACCP) principles. This failure to keep the knowledge of staff conducting official controls up to date is not in line with article 5(4) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. The appreciation of the risk level of some hazards, in particular in high-risk RTE production areas, had an impact on the effectiveness of official controls in those areas. See also findings 50, 54 and 60. 5.2.2 Supervision of CA staff and audits

In three of the six establishments visited, the audit team found that, in areas where exposed RTE meat products were produced, handled and/ or stored, the OVs failed to identify some non-compliances, did not correctly assess the importance of non- compliances identified or did not take the necessary measures to ensure that the FBO tackled the root cause(s) of some issues which, as a result, recurred. For instance: In one establishment, producing high volume of sliced product able to support the growth of Listeria monocytogenes, the following points, observed in the high-risk production area, were classed as minor by the OV: · Some condensation over the area feeding final product to the slice

However, during the on-site visits, the audit team identified some non-compliances that had not been identified or reported by the CA in some of the establishments, mainly: · Product flow diagrams incomplete or not reflecting reality in one of the establishments. · Some hazards not considered or inadequately assessed. For instance, in one of the establishments Listeria monocytogenes and Staphylococcus aureus had not been identified as hazards in the packing/ slicing area. · In one establishment, the critical limit of the critical control point `temperature of fresh liver at reception' was set at 60 C, above the legal requirement of 40 C as specified in Annex III, Section II, Chapter V, point

In two establishments visited producing RTE meat products able to support the growth of Listeria monocytogenes, it was noted that the CA accepted that samples from the processing area and equipment were preponderantly taken after cleaning and disinfection. The European Union Reference Laboratory on Listeria monocytogenes (EURL Lm) Guidelines on sampling the food processing area and equipment for the detection of Listeria monocytogenes recommends that the sampling should be carried out during processing in order to increase the probability of detecting a persistent strain. Sampling only after cleaning and disinfection makes the detection of the pathogen difficult and can lead to a false sense

label_heading: Conclusions on organisation and implementation of official controls
paragraph_text: Some of the shelf-life studies carried out by FBOs producing RTE meat products to demonstrate compliance with food safety criteria, and accepted by the CA, were not carried out in accordance with Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005. As a result, their validity to demonstrate that Listeria monocytogenes will not exceed the limit of 100 cfu/g throughout the shelf-life of the product could be called into question.

label_heading: Conclusions on organisation and implementation of official controls
paragraph_text: The ability of some FBO's own-controls to detect Listeria monocytogenes in environmental samples is weakened by the FBOs choice of the timing of sampling. This timing, which is accepted by the CA, can impact the ability of the FBO to identify the sources of persistent strains of Listeria monocytogenes and provide a false sense of security.

In two establishments visited producing RTE meat products able to support the growth of Listeria monocytogenes, it was noted that the CA accepted that samples from the processing area and equipment were preponderantly taken after cleaning and disinfection. The European Union Reference Laboratory on Listeria monocytogenes (EURL Lm) Guidelines on sampling the food processing area and equipment for the detection of Listeria monocytogenes recommends that the sampling should be carried out during processing in order to increase the probability of detecting a persistent strain. Sampling only after cleaning and disinfection makes the detection of the pathogen difficult and can lead to a false sense

The audit team reviewed some of the shelf-life studies used to demonstrate the aforementioned point and found that the demonstrations for different products in one of the establishments visited were done on the basis of a single durability study per meat product. These products had pH and water activity characteristics that supported the growth of Listeria monocytogenes.

According to the EURL Lm technical guidance document on challenge tests and durability studies for assessing shelf-life of ready-to-eat foods related to Listeria monocytogenes, it is not recommended to implement durability studies to validate a shelf-life related to Listeria monocytogenes because of its low prevalence, its low contamination level and its heterogeneous distribution in the food. The guidance mentions in this regard that, in most cases, results will be obtained from samples not contaminated with Listeria monocytogenes making it impossible to conclude on its 12 evolution in the product.

It was also noted that the above shelf-life studies did not take into account the expected storage temperatures at final consumer level and had therefore not been carried out under reasonably foreseeable conditions of distribution, storage and use as required in Article 3.1(b) of Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005.

In cases where PPPs contain candidates for substitution, the CA does not perform comparative assessments, relying instead on evaluations conducted by the MS that authorised the reference PPP product. The audit team expressed concerns that relying on the other MS evaluation is not correct, as safer, equally suitable alternatives may be available in Cyprus, that were not available in the MS that conducted the evaluation. The fact that the CA does not consider performing the comparative assessments, even at the renewal phase, is not in line with article 50(4) of Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009.

Conclusions on authorisation of plant protection products

Re-packaging activities may involve PPPs imported from non-EU countries for re-export or PPPs from other EU MSs marketed in Cyprus under parallel-trade permits. The CA considers parallel trade a high-risk activity and requires distributors to obtain approval for each movement of PPPs. Additionally, distributors must notify the CA at least three days in advance of any intended re-packaging. The audit team considered this a good practice, as it provides insight into the volume of products entering the Cypriot market and the proportion subject to re-packaging. However, at the time of the audit, this information was not being used to plan controls for re-packaging operators. The absence of regul

The results from previous inspections and samples collected by LCS inspectors serve to identify the high-risk crops for the upcoming year's inspection planning. However, there is no specific criteria for selecting operators who grow these high-risk crops, leading to a random selection process. This approach does not fully comply with Articles 9(1) and 24(1) and (2) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Moreover, with the low number of inspections, it becomes more important to target operators who may pose the higher risk.

The results of the national pesticide residue programme mentioned in paragraph 27 are not taken into account for the planning of inspections. This is not in line with Article 24(2)(b) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. The audit team considered that the results that show exceedance of maximum residue levels for authorised PPPs would be relevant for follow-up during inspections, as growers might have either use an excessive amount of PPPs or applied them too close to harvest. Results showing unauthorised use of PPPs are taken into account for the sampling programme, see below.

The relatively high non-compliance rate of samples taken by the LCS (18 out of 79 in 2024) compared to favourable results from formulation analysis (see paragraph 51) suggests that there is a higher risk associated with the misuse of authorised products by growers or the use of illegally traded PPPs (see paragraph 26) than with the marketing of unauthorised PPPs. This is not adequately considered by the CAs when determining the number of inspections at growers, which is significantly less representative than the number carried out at market level.

label_heading: Conclusions on planning of official controls
paragraph_text: Official controls at market level are carried out unannounced. However, prior notice is given to growers in all cases, with no justified reason, and long time in advance. This undermines the effectiveness of the inspections.

label_heading: Conclusions on planning of official controls
paragraph_text: There is a certification system implemented to provide training to users, distributors and advisors that overall works well. However, there are no measures foreseen for the withdrawal of certificates as necessary. 5.2.3. Delegation of certain tasks Findings

The national legislation includes provisions for the potential withdrawal of certificates. However, at the time of the audit, no procedures were defined for the conditions under which certificates might be withdrawn, and no certificates had yet been withdrawn since the system's implementation. This lack of defined procedures is not in compliance with Article 5(2) of Directive 2009/128/EC, which mandates that certification include criteria and processes for granting, renewing, and withdrawing certificates. Planning of official controls on marketing and distribution of PPPs

However, at the time of the audit, the laboratory had not yet been accredited to ISO/IEC 17025, which according to article 37(1) and 37(4)(e) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 is a requirement for the designation of laboratories to carry out analysis of samples of goods taken during official controls.

Furthermore, the laboratory's analysis focuses solely on active substances, without considering unacceptable co-formulants and regulated impurities. This prevents the CA from fully complying with Article 24(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. The CA noted that currently, there are accredited methods for only a few impurities, and this poses a 14 common challenge across all Member States, suggesting that this issue requires discussion and resolution at EU level. Conclusions on laboratories used for formulation analysis of plant protection products as part of official controls

The audit team noted that the primary aim of inspections, both at market and user levels, is to verify basic compliance aspects without further thorough verification (see paragraphs 70, 73 and 90). These weaknesses had not been detected by the central CA, as there was no supervision of inspectors' work at the time of this audit. This oversight deficiency does not comply with Articles 5(1) (a) and (b) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. The CA indicated that a recent internal audit identified this issue and announced plans to initiate supervision activities shortly. Conclusions on the competent authorities

As described in paragraph 42, at the time of the audit, re-packers were not subject to regular inspections. As part of the audit, a visit was made to a re-packer of PPPs for demonstration purposes, allowing the CA to discuss with the audit team the key areas inspectors would focus on during their inspections. The audit team noted that the checklist designed for inspecting this activity generally provides sufficient guidance for ensuring compliance with relevant legislation. However, some aspects, such as the process inspectors should follow to verify the source and quantities of PPPs through invoices, or whether they need to take samples, may require further clarification.

The audit team noted that the checklist used for this inspection contained only one point related to the control of PPPs, specifically the verification of input/output flow. All other checklist items pertained to structural and storage conditions. Inspectors are not required to verify whether the purchased and stored PPPs were authorised or whether operators maintain records of these products for at least five years. The checklist also lacked items related to verifying stocks or ensuring that stored PPPs were labelled in accordance with their authorised conditions. This lack of comprehensive guidance for inspections is not in line with Article 12(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Additionally,

Formulation analysis of PPPs is planned for active substances but checks for other important components of the composition of PPPs, such as regulated impurities and unacceptable co-formulants, are not included in the regular planning. 5.2.3. Delegation of certain tasks Findings

However, the analyses do not cover unacceptable co-formulants and have only once included a regulated impurity, which is subject to a maximum threshold. The CA is currently exploring options to expand the scope of formulation analysis to include these elements. 9 Conclusions on planning of official controls

The Agricultural Institute of Slovenia (Kmetijski institut Slovenije) and Benaki Phytopathological Institute in Greece are the designated official laboratories to carry out formulation analysis of PPPs. The latter is the designated official laboratory for the same task in Greece. label_heading: Conclusions on planning of official controls
paragraph_text: Risk criteria are in place for planning controls, but they do not include data from the pesticide residue monitoring programme or the water monitoring programme, which reduces the targeting and efficiency of the controls. 5.2.3. Delegation of certain tasks Findings

Inspections of PPP end users are organised in a way that allows each one to be eligible for selection based on risk every three to four years. Risk criteria are defined annually in internal guidelines and include: · Previous PPP use violations · Lack of inspection in the past three years (e.g., new users) · Crop types (e.g., pollinator-attractive crops like oilseed rape, beans, peas) · Use of high-risk PPPs (e.g., first registration class products for fumigation) The audit team noted that data from the pesticide residue monitoring programme or the water monitoring programme are not taken into account in the prioritisation of controls, which is not in line with Article 24(2)(a) of Regulation

The SCA uses a list of first-tier suppliers derived from the companies listed in the SCA's product register. The SCA acknowledged that the list is not complete as regards first-tier suppliers as the operators that have registered themselves are not always the operators responsible in Sweden. Moreover, the information collected about the operators´ activities in the PPP register is very basic (only name and address of the headquarters of the company) and limits the planning of controls (see paragraph 64). In addition to the product register, the SCA may also consult the SCA's pesticide register which contains information on all PPPs that are authorised or have been authorised in Sweden.

Regarding marketing and agricultural users, each MUP is responsible for maintaining its own register/list. The audit team visited four MUPs and all stated that they are working with lists. All MUPs acknowledged that the list of operators is a work in progress. It is updated with the information they get from their activities, complaints gathered during 8 visits carried out in the framework of projects intended for other purposes, etc. They acknowledged that the lists may not include all operators relevant for the controls of PPPs. Training for acquiring PPP certificates

The CABs organise training programmes for operators and advisors. This training results in the issuance of certificates that qualify individuals for activities related to the distribution, sale, or use of PPPs. The SBA maintains a list of those who have successfully completed the training. Planning of official controls on marketing and distribution of PPPs

The inspection covered most aspects relevant for the official control of PPPs. The SCA checked the labelling of seven products, asked for the training certificate of staff and verified some of the records kept by the company. However, the warehouse and re-packer facilities, mentioned above, were not part of the inspection (see also paragraph 36). Controls at retailers/distributors of PPPs

The audit team noted good examples of collaborations between the SCA and Customs. Customs sent 11 inquiries to the SCA in 2023, and 3 illegal PPPs were detected as a result. In 2024, 46 inquiries were sent, and 39 illegal PPPs were detected. Conclusions on controls on the marketing of plant protection products

MUPs are responsible for controls at non-agricultural users. In one MUP visited, inspections are determined by an assessment following the guidance issued by the Environmental Agency and also on experience gained from previous controls. For example, golf courses are classified as low risk, with a frequency of one visit every 5 years. The MUP stated that due to limited resources, visits do not always cover all aspects relevant for the use of PPPs. Sometimes inspections are part of projects that focus on only one or a few specific aspects. For example, the previous inspection focused on whether the required distances between spots where PPPs were applied and ditches and water courses were resp

The audit team found that inspection of farmers has not been consistently conducted in recent years, according to information provided by the MUPs. The MUPs reported difficulties in meeting the inspection frequency recommended by the SCA and the SBA due to resource constraints. In one MUP visited, out of approximately 350 farmers, only three were inspected in 2023, and those inspections were solely for fertilizer controls. In 2024, only 11 farms were inspected, despite an annual target of around 55. Another MUP visited indicated that they do not maintain specific statistics on the controls of PPP users. 10 They can provide numbers for the total inspections conducted, but these may not align

The water framework directive results are taken into account for controls. However, the results of the national pesticide residue programme mentioned are not always taken into account for the planning of inspections. This is not in line with Article 24(2)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. The audit team considered that the results that show use of unauthorised PPPs, as well as those showing exceedance of maximum residue levels for authorised PPPs would be relevant for follow-up during inspections.

Inspections of users are announced, normally four weeks in advance. Inspections to follow up on problems found previously can be "unannounced" (although warning can be given 24 hours in advance). The CAs stated that the advance notice is necessary, as growers are often not present on farms. This is not in line with Article 9(4) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Moreover, advance notice could compromise inspection effectiveness by allowing operators ample time to alter conditions at their premises, such as removing unauthorised PPPs. Planning of sampling for formulation analyses of PPPs

label_heading: Conclusions on planning of official controls
paragraph_text: There is guidance for MUPs to determine inspection frequency based on risk criteria. However, the lack of a well-defined and comprehensive list of operators for control, the currently reduced frequency and limited scope of routine inspections may reduce the general effectiveness of these controls. In addition, the sampling procedure is not in line with the official control regulation.
The tasks related to the authorisation and control on the marketing and use of PPPs have not been delegated and are carried out by the CAs. Conclusions on delegation of certain tasks

MUPs are in charge of controls of operators marketing PPPs not covered by the SCA controls, i.e. retailers, wholesalers and distributors. The SCA, in collaboration with the SAB has prepared guidance for risk assessment and determining the frequency of the visits. The MUPs may use this guidance but are not obliged to follow it. In principle, inspections carried out by the MUPs of marketing of PPPs are unannounced. 9 43. The audit team visited four MUPs. Representatives from these MUPs indicated that they generally adhere to the inspection and risk assessment guidelines prepared by the SCA/SBA. However, the audit team noted that MUPs have different approaches to planning inspections. For insta

Agricultural users are selected for inspections based on risk criteria outlined in the guidance prepared by the SBA. One of the key criteria is farm size. For example, farms smaller than 50 ha must be inspected at least every five years and larger ones every three or four years. The MUPs also consider the results of previous controls, adjusting the frequency accordingly. These criteria mainly apply to arable crops, while different risk criteria apply for other type of users The MUP stated that for inspections of greenhouses, they follow the Swedish Environmental Code, focusing primarily on structural integrity and checking for potential leakages, rather than concentrating on PPP usage. This

The SCA develops an annual sampling plan based on risk criteria. These criteria follow the EU draft 2018 guidance document, version 1, and include: 50% of the products selected are those with high sales volumes, 25% are high-risk products with, for example, a history of non-compliance, and 25% are chosen randomly. Additionally, the focus is on whether products are intended for professional or private use, with a priority given to products for professional use. The PPPs analysed in 2023 were selected on the basis of the following criteria: all the products contained active substances included in the price list agreed with the laboratory, were approved for professional use in Sweden and were i

This approach does not comply with Articles 2(1), 14(h) 24(1) and 34(5) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625, as samples collected and sent by the operators cannot be considered as part of official controls. It is also not correct to allow for a counter sample without meeting all the conditions outlined in Article 35 of the same regulation.

The laboratory reports of the samples analysed in recent years revealed only a few non- compliant results. Apart from a reservation on the independence of the sampling, referred to above, it would provide reasonable assurance that PPPs marketed are those that have 11 been authorised. From 2018 to 2023, analyses were conducted on 19, 50, 20, 19, 24, and 29 products respectively, with only three cases of non-compliance detected during this period.

The laboratory carrying out the analysis for the quality control of PPPs is designated and accredited to ISO/IEC 17025. However, not including analyses for unacceptable co- formulants and regulated impurities in the sampling programme reduces the overall capability of the control system to ensure the safety of the PPPs placed on the market. 5.3. paragraph_text: The roles and responsibilities of the CAs are clearly defined, with cooperation between CAs.
The audit team observed three inspections conducted by two MUPs at two retailers/distributors selling PPPs for professional use and at a garden centre selling PPPs for non-professional use.

The inspectors carried out an exhaustive check of the conditions of the storage with the aim to ensure that storage of PPPs is safe and that operators have all measures in place to avoid contamination of the surroundings in case of accident.

The audit team interviewed the customs officials at the border control post and noted that the officials were well-versed in the procedures and authorised to sign import approvals. According to the procedure, Customs carries out controls at the import points of any consignment of PPPs or active substances declared by importers and identified by relevant tariff codes. The SCA presented good examples of collaboration with customs to detect the illegal trade of PPPs. The audit team visited the custom offices and the custom warehouse where a physical check was carried out. The customs officials conduct documentary checks for all imports of PPPs and active substances notified, ensuring all docume

The inspectors reviewed the application records to confirm that they contained the minimum information required by the checklist, but did not cross-check the accuracy and reliability of these records. They do not request invoices to verify whether PPPs recorded were purchased or if recorded quantities are realistic for use on the corresponding areas where PPPs were used. This lack of verification goes against Article 14(e) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 and Article 55 of Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009 and prevents a technical evaluation of PPP usage. 16 87. There are some IT programmes developed by the SBA that are very useful for the proper application of PPPs. The farmers visited used such programmes. Another positive aspect that the audit team noted during all their visits to farms, is that measures to limit or avoid the contamination of water courses or ground waters are always checked. Control of non-agricultural users

The audit team examined cases of non-compliances found during MUPs inspections and noted that the follow-up is satisfactory, and sanctions are imposed on the non-compliant operators, including the taking of corrective actions. Evidence of these was provided to the audit team. Conclusions on controls on the use of plant protection products

label_heading: Conclusions on the planning and implementation of official controls
paragraph_text: While inspections cover requirements for veterinary prescriptions, they overlooked that, although medicated feed was routinely prescribed for metaphylaxis, the veterinary prescriptions did not contain a statement to that effect. 5.2.3 Actions taken on non-compliances

At the time of the audit, there was no prescription template laid down in domestic legislation. The prescriptions seen by the audit team were often based on a former national template, adapted to cover the information required under Annex V to Regulation (EU) 2019/4. However, the audit team noted that none of these prescriptions had a dedicated section that could be filled in by veterinarians in case of use of antimicrobials in accordance with Article 107(4) (metaphylaxis) or Articles 112, 113 or 114 (cascade) of Regulation (EU) 2019/6.

The private veterinarians interviewed by the audit team routinely prescribed medicated feed for treatment of diseases in pigs. The audit team noted that in most cases, antimicrobials used in medicated feed, such as tylosin, were prescribed following a metaphylactic approach as groups of pigs (e.g. 700 to 1400 animals) containing both sick animals and animals in close contact which may already be subclinically infected, were treated with antimicrobials. The veterinarians interviewed did not specify on the prescriptions issued that these animals followed a metaphylactic treatment, contrary to the requirements of Article 16(6) and point 7 of Annex V to Regulation (EU) 2019/4. NÉBIH relies on the clause in the cooperation agreements that the companies `shall ensure the availability of personnel with the necessary qualifications and appropriate 5 experience'. It is not aware of and does not verify the qualifications and competence of the experts used by the companies for the evaluations.

An accredited company will only be involved in the evaluation of PPP authorisations if the applicant requests it in the application and specifies which of the two companies he has selected. If the competent authority accepts the request, the applicant will then enter into a contractual agreement with the company for the work and pay for it. Thus, it is not the competent authority that contracts the actual evaluation work or pays for it; in the cooperation agreement with NÉBIH, it is specifically stated that `the evaluation body shall carry out its evaluation activities in accordance with this cooperation agreement with NÉBIH without any financial compensation'. NÉBIH is not privy to the cont

The competent authority has the final say in the evaluations and remains the authority for the subsequent authorisation. Nevertheless, the audit team considered that the arrangement of a direct financial agreement between the applicant and the evaluating company is not transparent. Article 74(2) of Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009 requires that fees or charges are established in a transparent manner. Furthermore, the arrangement does not protect against potential influence on the outcome of the evaluation due to the payment made and to the lack of an effective mechanism against possible conflict of interest, even if there are examples in practice of the evaluating company making negative proposa

Emergency authorisations are overall granted in line with documented procedures. However, they are often granted for wide groups of crops and pests and for longer periods than 120 days, which is not in line with Article 53 of Regulation No (EC) 1107/2009.

The emergency authorisations often also involve approved active substances. The dangers which these authorisations are addressing could therefore, at least over time, be contained by obtaining PPP authorisations as per Articles 33, 40, or 51 of Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009. Using emergency authorisations repeatedly instead, waters down the integrity of the authorisation system.

Most emergency authorisations are not communicated immediately to the Commission and other Member States, and many are notified incorrectly or incompletely. In view of the risk of creating antimicrobial resistance, the audit team had some concerns about the repeated authorisations of kasugamycin. 5.2. Furthermore, while each notification to the EU database indicated no more than the maximum of 120 days

For several active substances, PPP emergency authorisations have been issued repeatedly for 6, 7 or 8 years. The audit team noted that at least some of these applications, where the active substances are approved in the EU, would be more correctly accommodated, at least over time, within the conventional authorisation framework maintaining the system's integrity as referred to in `Commission Staff Working Document on emergency situations according to Article 53 of Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009'. Penoxulam (a herbicide) is the approved active substance with the most repeated PPP emergency authorisations (8 years in a row). The authorisations have included use in sorghum and rice. NÉBIH stated that a risk assessment for antimicrobial resistance had been carried out. Nevertheless, the audit team had concerns about these authorisations from a one-health policy point of view. For planning the controls, the results of the programmes for the monitoring of water status are not taken into account, which is not in line with Article 24(2)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. But the results of the pesticide monitoring programme, which is implemented by NÉBIH itself, is taken into account in the way that non-compliances found regarding maximum residue levels or unauthorised PPPs are followed up by inspections. label_heading: Conclusions on implementation of controls on the marketing of PPPs
paragraph_text: Official controls at production and marketing level are comprehensive and overall carried out well. However, for manufacturers and packers, it is not verified that PPPs destined for other Member States are authorised there.

label_heading: Conclusions on implementation of controls on the marketing of PPPs
paragraph_text: Import controls of PPPs intended for use in Hungary and other Member States are in place and largely carried out satisfactorily. However, for imports destined for other Member States, it is not verified that the PPPs are authorised there.

Although the inspections observed were overall effective and carried out competently, some flaws were noted by the audit team: · At the retailer, packets with a PPP containing acetamiprid had an outdated label. Next to them on the shelf was a pile of papers with the updated label text, so that for each 15 sale, the customer would be given a copy of the updated text together with the wrongly labelled PPP. This was considered acceptable in the inspection, even if the authorisation for the product stipulates that an additional, self-adhesive label must be placed on the package. · For PPPs destined for other Member States at the manufacturer and the packer, Customs controls do provide some guara

Customs identify consignments of PPPs from the tariff codes and refer them to the plant health inspectors, who then carry out documentary and physical checks. This is done for 100% of the PPP consignments. The checks include verification that the active substance is approved in the EU. PPP or active substance imports do not require prior notification from the importer or pre-approval from the CA. Nevertheless, the integrity of each import is checked by verifying the batch numbers with the authorisation holder. paragraph_text: The NAP addresses all necessary aspects of the SUD and sets quantitative objectives, targets, measures and timetables to reduce risks and impacts of PPP use, with the exception of active substances of particular concern. Interim review reports of the NAP allow for a comprehensive assessment of its implementation at the end of each five- year cycle. For the period 2018-2022, the review concluded that 90% of the measures were fully or partially implemented.

For arable crops, the CAs have converted the general principles of IPM into practical and measurable criteria. However, these criteria are not verified during on-farm inspections. Only agricultural practices that relate to specific obligations under certain SMRs and GAECs are verified by inspection. Fruit and vine growers may voluntarily participate in IPM accreditation schemes. Consequently, the enforcement of the general 17 principles of IPM is limited. 5.9 RISK INDICATORS Legal Requirements Article 15 and Annex IV to Directive 2009/128/EC Findings

In 2014, CISTA made an initial attempt to assess the implementation of each of the general principles of IPM for field crops by introducing a point-based system. Under this system, failure to reach a minimum required score resulted in penalties. However, the initiative was eventually abandoned due to its administrative burden and the difficulty with enforcing strict rules against the general principles in the SUD. In addition, CISTA also stated that the usefulness of the results produced following this process is questionable.

Building on this experience, the monitoring of the implementation of IPM general principles in Czechia is now carried out through an annual survey of a representative sample of 104 arable crop producers. Since a large proportion of fruit and vine growers voluntarily participate in the integrated crop production system, they are not included in the IPM survey carried out by CISTA. This approach is not in line with Article 14(4) of the SUD stipulating that the MS should ensure that the general principles of the IPM set out in Annex III of the SUD are implemented by all professional users. In addition, this approach does not provide for the penalties required by Article 17 of the SUD (and Artic

The questionnaire used in the annual survey provides a detailed breakdown of the components of the general principles of IPM. The data collected offers insights into soil and fertilisation practices, cultivation strategies, and plant protection methods. Completing the questionnaire is mandatory. Responses indicating non-compliance with the IPM principles do not result in penalisation of the farmers. This approach ensures that the data collected is unbiased. Based on the survey results, it has been estimated that farmers with arable crops implement on average 54% of the detailed breakdown of the IPM general principles. The Research Institute for Forest Management is responsible for implementing IPM in forestry. IPM implementation for non-agricultural uses does not fall under the competence of CISTA and is therefore not included in the survey or in any specific scheme, such as those for vineyards and orchards. Risk mitigation measures for protecting water bodies are specified as conditions for use in all PPP authorisations. These are specified on the PPP labels and are generally enforced during official controls. However, enforcement of required buffer zones to protect water bodies is limited to the general minimum measure of 3m. This enforcement is inadequate when larger buffer zones are necessary, which does not ensure the overall level of water protection.

The audit team noted that the afore-mentioned risk mitigation measures and restrictions are priority areas for attention in the 2025 official controls programme (see paragraph 8) and this is reflected in the revised general guidance and checklist provided to inspectors. Risk-mitigation measures and restrictions in relation to water were generally verified during the official controls observed. However, with regard to buffer zones to protect surface water, inspectors generally only verify/measure compliance with the 3 m buffer zone. label_heading: Conclusions on handling and storage of pesticides
paragraph_text: Clear instructions for safe storing and disposal are given on the label of all PPPs and on the Tukes website. The collection of PPP packaging and remnants is well organised and verified by the municipalities. Nonetheless, during official controls, certain aspects like the safe preparation of PPPs and the cleaning of PAE after use are generally not checked. This reduces the ability of the CA to ensure the necessary protection of the health of professional users of PPPs and the environment. 5.8. BACKGROUND 4.1. LEGAL CONTEXT AND ACTIONS TAKEN BY THE EUROPEAN COMMISSION The 2006 Thematic Strategy on the sustainable use of pesticides led to a new legislative framework for the approval and use of pesticides. This includes a strict framework for the approval of active substances by the European Commission and the authorisation of PPPs by MS, introduced by Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009, adopted on 21 October 2009. This 2 Regulation requires that active substances may be approved, and PPPs be authorised, only if they have no identified harmful effects on human and animal health, and no unacceptable effects on the environment. It also requires that PPPs be applied according to their authori

Compared with CAP conditionality controls, the PPP/SUD specific official controls also include the verification of compliance with the use of PPPs as laid down by Article 55 of Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009, and with the general principles of IPM, set out by Annex III to the SUD. Given the scope and objectives of the audit, the audit team paid more attention to these official controls. On an annual basis, the FFA defines a risk- based theme and allocates the number of controls to each ELY centre. Overall, between 80 to 100 of professional users of PPPs are subject to these controls annually. Each ELY centre selects the various operators to inspect taking into account the annual theme and the

During the inspections at professional users, the audit team noted that the storage conditions are generally verified. However, operations such as the preparation of PPPs 17 before use and cleaning of PAE after use are generally not verified, or are only superficially checked, and are not included in the inspection checklist. This does not allow the CA to ensure that these operations are carried out without endangering human health and the environment, as laid down by Article 13(1) of the SUD.
